docs.title: 15.8 Nano and Micro Unmanned Air Systems
15.8.1 Scale Classification
docs.text:
• Micro Air Vehicle (MAV): 100 g – 1 kg; rotor diameter or wingspan \(<\)30 cm. Example: AeroVironment Wasp AE (430 g, 72.4 cm wingspan, 45 min, EO/IR).

  • Nano UAV: \(<\)100 g; fits in palm. Example: FLIR Black Hornet 3 (32 g total, 16 g vehicle).

  • Pico / chip-scale: \(<\)1 g; experimental; DARPA SHRIMP (SHort-Range Independent Microrobotic Platforms) — piezoelectric insect-scale crawlers and fliers.

docs.title: 15.8.2 Black Hornet 3 PRS — Technical Detail
docs.text:
The FLIR (now Teledyne FLIR) Black Hornet 3 Personal Reconnaissance System is the most operationally deployed nano UAV, in service with USSOF, UK, Australian, Norwegian, German forces and others.

  • Vehicle mass: 16 g (aircraft only); full PRS kit 190 g

  • Dimensions: 168 mm length; 120 mm rotor diameter (coaxial contra-rotating)

  • Endurance: 25 min per charge (Li-poly battery, \(\sim\)0.8 Wh)

  • Range: 2 km encrypted HD video link (2.4/5.8 GHz FHSS)

  • Payload: EO (720p colour) + uncooled LWIR microbolometer (160\(\times\)120, 9 \(\mu\)m)

  • Navigation: GPS-aided; optical flow for indoor/GPS-denied; \(\pm\)2 m hover accuracy

  • Wind resistance: 10 kt; gust tolerance 15 kt

docs.title: 15.8.3 Low-Reynolds-Number Aerodynamics
docs.text:
At nano UAV chord scales of 10–50 mm and speeds of 2–8 m/s:

\[Re = \frac{\rho V c}{\mu} \approx \frac{1.225 \times 5 \times 0.025}{1.81\times10^{-5}} \approx 8,500\tag{15.40}\]

At \(Re < 10^4\), viscous effects dominate over inertial; conventional cambered sections fail due to large laminar separation bubbles that dramatically increase effective camber and reduce \(L/D\). Bio-inspired flapping-wing approaches offer significant advantages through unsteady aerodynamic mechanisms:

Clap-and-Fling Mechanism.

At the end of each half-stroke, the wings clap together (extinguishing bound circulation) and subsequently fling apart, generating a strong leading-edge vortex (LEV) on each wing. Time-averaged \(C_L > 2.5\) is achievable at \(Re \sim 10^4\), far exceeding quasi-steady attached-flow limits.

The Strouhal number governs propulsive efficiency of flapping flight:

\[St = \frac{f \cdot A_{stroke}}{U_\infty}\tag{15.41}\]

where \(f\) is flapping frequency, \(A_{stroke}\) is peak-to-peak wingtip stroke amplitude, and \(U_\infty\) is forward speed. Biological flyers and efficient engineered FMAVs operate at \(St = 0.2\)–0.4.

Quasi-steady flapping-wing lift model (Ellington 1984 extended):

\[F_{lift}(t) = \frac{1}{2}\rho C_L(\alpha(t)) \hat{c} \int_0^b (r \dot{\phi}(t))^2 \, dr = \frac{1}{2}\rho C_L \hat{c} \,r_2^2(S) \dot{\phi}^2(t)\tag{15.42}\]

where \(\hat{c}\) is mean chord, \(r_2(S)\) is the non-dimensional second moment of area of the wing, and \(\dot\phi\) is instantaneous angular velocity about the stroke-plane normal.

docs.title: 15.8.4 Power and Energy Budget at Nano Scale
docs.text:
Hover power scales with weight and disc area:

\[P_{hover} = \frac{W^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2\rho A_{disk}}} \cdot \frac{1}{\eta_{FM}}\tag{15.43}\]

For Black Hornet 3 vehicle (16 g, \(A_{disk} \approx 2\times\pi(0.06)^2 = 0.0226\) m\(^2\) coaxial), \(\eta_{FM} = 0.60\):

\[P_{hover} = \frac{(0.016 \times 9.81)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2 \times 1.225 \times 0.0226} \times 0.60} = \frac{0.00618}{0.163} \approx 0.38\ \text{W}\]

Practical system power (motors + avionics + comms): \(\approx\) 0.8 W. Battery energy: \(\approx\) 0.8 Wh; therefore endurance \(\approx\) 0.8/0.8 = 60 min theoretical; \(\sim\)25 min actual accounting for inefficiencies and forward flight.

docs.title: 15.9.1 Last-Mile Delivery Architecture and Economics
docs.text:
Last-mile delivery drones target the final-segment cost problem: the last leg of a delivery chain is typically 30–50% of total logistics cost yet often covers only a few kilometres. The drone delivery value proposition:

  • No traffic congestion — point-to-point air route

  • No driver labour cost (autonomous)

  • Zero-emission (electric)

Cost-of-delivery metric:

\[CoD = \frac{C_{capex} / N_{life} + C_{opex}}{N_{parcels/flight}}\tag{15.45}\]

Competitive threshold: \(\approx\) USD 3–5/delivery vs. van delivery last-mile. Analysis by McKinsey (2022) projects drone delivery CoD reaching USD 1–2.50 at scale by 2030. Key operators:

  • Wing (Alphabet): Fixed-wing VTOL hybrid; 1.5 kg payload; FAA Part 135 Air Carrier Certificate (first granted 2019); operations in Christiansburg VA, Logan City QLD Australia; 350,000+ deliveries as of 2024.

  • Amazon Prime Air MK30: Tiltrotor; 2.27 kg payload; operations College Station TX and Lockeford CA (2024); on-board detect-and-avoid radar.

  • Zipline P2 Zip (Platform 2): Fixed-wing electric; 3 kg payload; docking cradle on vehicle for in-air exchange; 60 km range; operates in USA (Home Depot partnership), Ghana, Rwanda, Kenya, Nigeria.

docs.title: 15.9.2 Medical Logistics — Zipline Rwanda Programme
docs.text:
Zipline’s Rwanda operation (launched 2016, now expanded to seven distribution centres) is the most extensive drone logistics network in the world. Blood products (packed red cells, platelets, plasma) are delivered to over 2,500 health facilities:

  • Average flight time to served facility: 27 min (vs. 3 hr by road in rainy season)

  • Package drop accuracy: within 10 m of target using parachute deployment triggered by GPS waypoint

  • Blood wastage at served hospitals: reduced from \(\geq\)14% to \(<\)1%

  • Emergency order fulfilment time: \(<\)3 min from order to wheels-up

docs.title: 15.9.4 Pipeline and Infrastructure Inspection
docs.text:
Autonomous inspection of linear infrastructure (pipelines, power lines, bridges) combines drone-based sensing with AI-driven anomaly detection. The detection probability for a surface defect of size \(d\) at ground-sample distance GSD:

\[P_D = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{A_{defect}}{GSD^2} \cdot SNR_{contrast}\right)\tag{15.46}\]

Sensor integration: RGB photogrammetry (3D point cloud, crack width \(>\)0.5 mm); thermal FLIR (leak detection, electrical faults); LiDAR (geometry, clearance measurement); LaserMethane (TDLAS, path-integrated CH\(_4\) concentration, threshold \(\sim\)1 ppm·m). Lateral guidance to maintain alignment with the pipeline heading uses a proportional-integral controller on cross-track error \(e_{CT}\):

\[\delta_{lat}(t) = K_P e_{CT}(t) + K_I \int_0^t e_{CT}(\tau)\, d\tau\tag{15.47}\]

docs.title: 15.10.1 Aerial Application System Design
docs.text:
Agricultural spray drones are the largest commercial drone segment in Asia by revenue. The critical agronomic and engineering parameters:

Droplet Size.

Characterised by Volume Median Diameter (VMD, \(D_{V0.5}\)) — the droplet diameter at which 50% of total spray volume is in smaller droplets. ASABE S572.3 categories:

  • Very Fine (VF): \(D_{V0.5} < 136\ \mu\)m — excellent coverage; unacceptable drift in field conditions

  • Fine (F): 136–177 \(\mu\)m — good coverage; high drift risk

  • Medium (M): 177–218 \(\mu\)m — balanced performance; most applications

  • Coarse (C): 218–349 \(\mu\)m — low drift; reduced surface coverage

Hollow-cone pressure nozzles at 2–4 bar pressure produce Medium to Coarse at 0.5–2 L/min per nozzle. Rotary atomisers (spinning disk) allow precise \(D_{V0.5}\) control by adjusting disk RPM:

\[D_{V0.5} = \frac{K_{atomiser} \cdot \sigma^{1/3}}{(\rho_L \cdot n_{disk}^2 \cdot r_{disk})^{1/3}}\tag{15.48}\]

Effective Field Capacity.

The area covered per unit time:

\[FC_e = v_{ground} \cdot W_{boom} \cdot E_f \cdot 3600 \times 10^{-4} \quad [\text{ha/hr}]\tag{15.49}\]

where \(v_{ground}\) is ground speed (m/s), \(W_{boom}\) is effective boom width (m), and \(E_f\) is field efficiency (0.65–0.80). For DJI Agras T50 at 8 m/s, 9 m boom, \(E_f = 0.75\):

\[FC_e = 8 \times 9 \times 0.75 \times 3600 \times 10^{-4} = 19.4\ \text{ha/hr}\]

Application rate (L/ha) at system flow rate \(\dot{Q}\) (L/min):

\[AR = \frac{60 \, \dot{Q}}{v_{ground} \times W_{boom} \times 10^{-4}} \quad [\text{L/ha}]\tag{15.51}\]

docs.title: 15.10.2 Remote Sensing and Precision Agriculture
docs.text:
The Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is computed from reflectances \(\rho_{NIR}\) (750–900 nm) and \(\rho_{Red}\) (630–680 nm):

\[NDVI = \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{Red}}{\rho_{NIR} + \rho_{Red}} \in [-1,+1]\tag{15.52}\]

Healthy dense canopy: NDVI \(\geq\) 0.6. Stressed or sparse: 0.2–0.5. Bare soil: 0.1–0.2. Water: \(<\) 0.

The Normalised Difference Red Edge index (NDRE) is more sensitive to chlorophyll content at high biomass:

\[NDRE = \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{RedEdge}}{\rho_{NIR} + \rho_{RedEdge}}\tag{15.53}\]

where Red Edge is 700–730 nm. Ground sampling distance at altitude \(H\) with sensor pixel size \(p\) and focal length \(f\):

\[GSD = \frac{H \cdot p}{f}\tag{15.54}\]

At \(H\) = 30 m, \(p\) = 3.75 \(\mu\)m, \(f\) = 5.5 mm: GSD = 30 \(\times\) 3.75\(\times\)10\(^{-6}\) / 5.5\(\times\)10\(^{-3}\) = 0.020 m (2 cm/pixel).

docs.title: 15.10.3 DJI Agras T50 Specifications
docs.text:
The DJI Agras T50 (released 2023) is the current flagship agricultural spray drone:

  • Max takeoff weight: 103 kg; empty weight: 47.5 kg

  • Liquid tank: 40 L; solid spreader: 50 kg hopper capacity

  • Pump flow rate: 16 L/min (8-nozzle spray bar)

  • Effective spray width: 9 m (default); extendable to 11 m with boom extension

  • Claimed field capacity: up to 43 ha/hr (speed dependent)

  • Obstacle avoidance: 360° phased-array radar + binocular vision

  • Positioning: RTK GNSS, \(\pm\)1.5 cm horizontal accuracy

  • Operating temperature: \(-10^\circ\)C to \(+45^\circ\)C

  • Flight time per tank at full load: \(\sim\)8–12 min

docs.title: 15.11.1 Electronic Warfare Taxonomy
docs.text:
Electronic Warfare is subdivided per DOD JP 3-13.1:

  • Electronic Attack (EA): Offensive employment of EM energy — active jamming, decoy emission, directed-energy weapons, anti-radiation missiles.

  • Electronic Protection (EP): Defensive measures — frequency hopping, spread spectrum, notch filters, shielding, ECCM.

  • Electronic Support (ES): Passive collection — ESM, ELINT, COMINT, signal intelligence for targeting and situational awareness.

Drones extend each of these functions by placing EW payloads forward in contested airspace, improving geometry, and accepting attrition risk.

docs.title: 15.11.2 Standoff and Escort Jamming
docs.text:
An EW drone jams an enemy receiver by transmitting high-power noise or deceptive signals on its operating frequency. The Jamming-to-Signal ratio (J/S) at the victim receiver:

\[\frac{J}{S} = \frac{P_J G_J}{P_S G_S} \cdot \left(\frac{R_S}{R_J}\right)^2\tag{15.55}\]

where \(P_J, G_J\) are jammer power and antenna gain; \(P_S, G_S\) are signal-source (radar) power and gain; \(R_J, R_S\) are jammer-to-victim and source-to-victim ranges. For the escort jammer co-located with the strike package, \(R_J = R_S\) and \(J/S = P_J G_J / P_S G_S\).

Effective Radiated Power of the jamming system:

\[ERP_J = P_J \cdot G_J \quad [\text{W or dBW}]\tag{15.56}\]

Burn-through range.

The range at which the radar signal regains adequate SNR despite jamming:

\[R_{BT} = \left(\frac{P_T G_T^2 \lambda^2 \sigma_{target}}{(4\pi)^3 (J/S)_{min} P_J G_J}\right)^{1/4}\tag{15.57}\]

Reducing \(R_J\) (closer escort) is more effective than increasing \(P_J\) because of the \(R^{-4}\) radar detection dependence vs. \(R^{-2}\) jammer loss.

docs.title: 15.11.3 SEAD and Anti-Radiation Missions
docs.text:
Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) removes the adversary’s ability to effectively employ Surface-to-Air Missiles. SEAD drones may carry anti-radiation missiles (ARM) or execute kinetic strikes. The ARM seeker tracks the radar emission and homes on the transmitter. Angular tracking accuracy:

\[\sigma_\theta = \frac{\theta_{3dB}}{SNR^{1/2} \sqrt{2}}\tag{15.58}\]

Even without a kill, forcing the radar to stop transmitting achieves the SEAD objective. A typical SEAD campaign generates a “keep-off-air” window correlated to ARM time-of-flight (30–120 s), creating windows for strike packages to transit defended airspace.

docs.title: 15.11.4 Decoy Drones — ADM-160 MALD
docs.text:
The Miniature Air-Launched Decoy (MALD) ADM-160B is a powered decoy designed to replicate the radar cross-section, flight profile, and electronic emissions of strike aircraft:

  • Mass: 136 kg; length 2.82 m; wingspan 1.74 m (folding)

  • Propulsion: Williams International F121-WR-100 turbojet; 58 N thrust

  • Range: \(>\)900 km; speed: \(\leq\)0.9 Ma; altitude 15–15,000 m

  • RCS augmentation: active DRFM transponder transmits pre-recorded waveforms to mimic specific aircraft EM signatures

  • MALD-J variant: 72 kg jamming payload added for active EA role

The DRFM (Digital Radio Frequency Memory) technology captures an incoming radar pulse, digitises it at high fidelity (14-bit, 4+ GHz bandwidth), modifies it to create desired false target, and retransmits. Deception J/S at the victim radar:

\[J/S_{DRFM} = \frac{P_{retransmit} G_{DRFM}}{P_{radar} G_{radar} \sigma_{target} / (4\pi R_{MALD}^2)}\tag{15.59}\]

docs.title: 15.11.5 SIGINT Collection Drone Architecture
docs.text:
A tactical SIGINT drone carries a broadband Electronic Support Measures (ESM) suite. Typical receiver chain:

  1. Wideband ESM antenna: Spiral or log-periodic array covering 0.5–18 GHz; mounted on wing trailing edge or fuselage blister for 360\(^\circ\) coverage.

  2. Instantaneous Frequency Measurement (IFM) receiver: Measures pulse carrier frequency to \(<\)1 MHz accuracy; \(<\)100 ns response time.

  3. Digital receiver bank: Software-defined radio with 1–4 GHz instantaneous bandwidth; 14-bit ADC at 4 GSPS; FFT-based spectrum analysis.

  4. Direction-Finding (DF): Interferometric phase comparison between antennas separated by baseline \(d\):

\[\theta_{AoA} = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{\lambda \Delta\phi}{2\pi d}\right)\tag{15.60}\]

where \(\Delta\phi\) is the measured phase difference. Accuracy \(\sigma_\theta \approx 1\)–\(2^\circ\) RMS with baseline \(d = \lambda/2\) to \(3\lambda\). Geolocation via Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) between two drones at positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\):

\[\Delta t_{12} = \frac{\|\mathbf{r}_{emitter} - \mathbf{r}_1\| - \|\mathbf{r}_{emitter} - \mathbf{r}_2\|}{c}\tag{15.61}\]

docs.title: 15.11.6 GPS Spoofing and Cyber EW
docs.text:
A GPS spoofing drone transmits counterfeit GPS L1 C/A signals to deceive adversary UAS or precision-guided munitions into navigating to a false position. Signal level at ground from GPS SV: \(-130\) dBm. Required spoofer transmit power at 50 m range:

\[P_{spoof} = P_{GPS,SL} + FSPL(50\ \text{m}, 1575.42\ \text{MHz})\tag{15.62}\] \[FSPL = 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi \times 50 \times 1.575\times10^9}{3\times10^8}\right) \approx 70.4\ \text{dB}\]

Required \(P_{spoof} = -130 + 70.4 \approx -60\) dBm = 1 nW: trivially achievable. Commercial-off-the-shelf SDR (\(<\)USD 200) can provide this. Anti-spoofing countermeasures include multi-constellation GNSS, receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM), and IMU/DVL aiding (position jump detection).

docs.title: 15.12 Cross-Category Design Considerations and Technology Trends
15.12.1 Energy as the Universal Constraint
docs.text:
Across all special drone categories, energy density is the dominant design driver. The Breguet endurance equation adapted for electric-propulsion systems:

\[t_{endurance} = \frac{\eta_{prop} \cdot \eta_{motor}}{g} \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot \frac{e_{bat} \cdot m_{bat}}{W_{total}}\tag{15.64}\]

where \(e_{bat}\) is battery specific energy (Wh/kg) and \(m_{bat}/W_{total}\) is the battery mass fraction. Every doubling of battery energy density directly doubles endurance—hence the transformative impact expected from solid-state and lithium-metal batteries on the 2028–2035 timeframe.

docs.title: 15.12.2 Common Autonomy Architecture
docs.text:
Despite environmental diversity, the autonomy stack is functionally identical across categories: sense \(\rightarrow\) perceive \(\rightarrow\) plan \(\rightarrow\) act. The Model Predictive Control (MPC) formulation is applied universally, from UUV path planning to eVTOL urban obstacle avoidance to UCAV target engagement:

\[\min_{\mathbf{u}_{0:N-1}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \!\left[\mathbf{x}_k^T \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{u}_k^T \mathbf{R} \mathbf{u}_k\right] + \mathbf{x}_N^T \mathbf{P}_f \mathbf{x}_N\tag{15.65}\]

subject to dynamics \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k)\), control limits \(\mathbf{u}_{min} \leq \mathbf{u}_k \leq \mathbf{u}_{max}\), and state constraints \(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}_k) \leq \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has presented technically rigorous treatments of thirteen special unmanned-system categories. Several themes emerge:

  1. Physics determines architecture. The 837\(\times\) water-to-air density ratio forces UUVs to low speeds and acoustic communications. The \(\sim\)13\(\times\) Reynolds number drop at 20 km altitude forces HALE wings to high aspect ratio and low-Re airfoils. Urban noise requirements force eVTOL to low-tip-speed distributed rotors.

  2. Energy density is the universal limiter. From 16 g nano UAVs to 15 t XLUUVs, the ratio of energy store to vehicle weight dictates endurance. Advances in lithium-metal, silicon-anode, and solid-state batteries will unlock step-changes across every category on the 2028–2035 horizon.

  3. Autonomy architectures converge. INS/Kalman/SLAM/MPC/reinforcement learning chains are deployed across UUVs, USVs, HALE, UCAV, and logistics drones with only the sensor inputs and actuator outputs differing.

  4. Regulatory maturity lags technology. COLREGS compliance for USVs, FAA powered-lift certification for eVTOL, and spectrum allocation for HAPS are all active regulatory frontiers that will shape the commercial trajectory of these platforms as much as engineering innovation.

  5. EW is integral, not an add-on. Every military special-category drone must address EW both offensively (UCAV, dedicated EW drone) and defensively (HALE SIGINT awareness, UCAV self-protection, UUV acoustic counter-detection). The boundary between ISR, communications, and EW drone categories is increasingly dissolved.

Subsequent chapters develop the sub-systems introduced here—propulsion (Chapter 17–19), guidance and navigation (Chapter 20–21), payloads (Chapter 9 and 22), and regulatory frameworks (Chapter 28)—in the context of the specific design constraints identified for each category.

docs.title: 16.1.1 What is a Missile?
docs.text:
The word missile derives from the Latin mittere (to throw or send). In the modern engineering and military context, a guided missile is a self-propelled, aerodynamically or ballistically controlled projectile that carries a warhead to a designated target under the direction of an on-board or off-board guidance system. This definition distinguishes guided missiles from several related categories that are frequently confused in popular usage.

Missile vs. Rocket.

A rocket is an unguided, self-propelled projectile. A missile is guided. All missiles use rocket (or air-breathing) propulsion, but not all rockets are missiles. Artillery unguided rockets (e.g., BM-21 Grad, MLRS M26 unguided) are rockets; their GMLRS guided variants become missiles once they are equipped with a GPS/INS seeker and steering fins.

Missile vs. Guided Bomb.

A guided bomb (also called a Precision-Guided Munition, PGM, or glide weapon) is not self-propelled; it falls under gravity from an aircraft, steered by movable fins or wings. Examples include the GBU-31 JDAM and Paveway series. A missile is self-propelled by an on-board engine throughout all or part of its flight. The distinction blurs with powered glide weapons (AGM-154 JSOW, KEPD 350 Taurus), which carry a turbojet sustainer.

Missile vs. Torpedo.

A torpedo is a self-propelled, underwater-running weapon. By the strict modern definition, a torpedo is an underwater missile; US Navy doctrine classifies them separately, though the physics of guidance and propulsion are equivalent. The term “missile” in this text refers primarily to air, surface, or ground-launched weapons operating in the atmosphere.

Missile vs. Loitering Munition.

A loitering munition (also called a “kamikaze drone” or “suicide drone”) operates like an unmanned aircraft for an extended period while searching for a target, then dives into it. The distinction from a missile is gradual: loitering munitions (IAI Harop, Switchblade 600, Lancet-3) have longer on-station times and greater man-in-the-loop capability; true missiles typically have shorter time of flight and more limited guidance adjustment. Chapter 15 (section on EW drones) and Chapter 17 address loitering munitions in detail.

docs.title: 16.1.2 Weapon System vs. Missile System
docs.text: A missile is the physical object. A missile system encompasses the complete set of hardware and software required to detect, identify, track, and destroy a target: launcher, fire control radar/electro-optical sensor, command and control (C2) hardware, logistics and maintenance equipment, training, and the missile itself. The weapon system includes the missile system integrated with the platform (ship, aircraft, ground vehicle, submarine) and the operational C2 chain. This distinction is critical in programme management: the missile itself typically represents only 30–50% of the total system cost.

docs.title: 16.1.3 Historical Context
docs.text: The history of guided missiles is addressed comprehensively in Chapter 1. For context here: the German V-2 (Aggregat 4, 1944) was the first operational ballistic missile; the first guided anti-aircraft missile in combat service was the German Wasserfall (never deployed operationally but flight-tested); the first operational AAM was the AIM-4 Falcon (1956). The cold war drove explosive proliferation of all missile types. The transition from vacuum-tube analogue guidance to solid-state digital guidance (1970s–80s), GPS-aided navigation (1990s), and networked seekers with AI-enabled discrimination (2010s–present) defines the technology arc of the field.

docs.title: 16.2.1 Major Sections
docs.text:
A guided missile is conventionally divided into four to six major sections from nose to tail. The exact division varies by missile type (see Chapter 17 for type-specific anatomy), but the canonical arrangement for a radar-homing surface-attack missile is:

  1. Seeker/Sensor Section (Nose): Contains the terminal guidance sensor—radar antenna (active or passive), IR detector array, or laser receiver. Includes radome or nose fairing (RF-transparent or IR-transparent material), gimballed sensor head with \(\pm\)45\(^\circ\) to \(\pm\)90\(^\circ\) field of regard, and seeker electronics.

  2. Guidance and Control Section: On-board computer (mission processor, DSP); inertial measurement unit (IMU); GPS/GNSS receiver; data links; autopilot avionics. On older missiles this section is combined with the seeker; on modern missiles it is a modular Line-Replaceable Unit (LRU).

  3. Warhead Section: The lethal payload. May be high-explosive blast-fragmentation, shaped-charge HEAT, thermobaric, kinetic penetrator, or sub-munitions dispenser. The warhead section includes the safe-arm-fire (SAF) device.

  4. Fuze Section: Contact (point-detonating), proximity (radar, laser, or acoustic), or time fuze. Often integrated into the forward face of the warhead. On some missiles, the fuze is distributed (a fore-fuze and an aft-fuze flank the warhead).

  5. Propulsion Section: Solid rocket motor (SRM), liquid rocket engine (LRE), ramjet, scramjet, or turbojet. Includes propellant grain, igniter, case, and possibly a boost-sustain grain configuration.

  6. Aft Section / Nozzle and Fins: Nozzle(s) for thrust vectoring or fixed exhaustion; aerodynamic control surfaces (canards at the nose, mid-body strakes, tail fins); actuators (electromechanical, hydraulic, or pneumatic).

docs.title: 16.2.2 Missile Cross-Section Diagram
docs.text: Figure 16.1. Generic missile cross-section and major sections. Colours indicate: seeker (blue), guidance & control (green), warhead/fuze (red), propulsion (orange), aft/nozzle (grey).

docs.title: 16.2.3 Mass Breakdown and Centre of Gravity
docs.text:
The mass budget of a typical medium-range air-to-ground missile:

Table 16.1. Typical Mass Fractions for a Medium-Range Missile (\(m_{total} = 500\) kg) Subsystem Mass (kg) Fraction (%) Notes Propellant (SRM grain) 200 40.0 Primary driver of range Warhead (incl. explosive fill) 100 20.0 Blast-fragmentation Airframe and structure 80 16.0 CFRP/Al7075 Guidance and control section 55 11.0 Seeker, IMU, CPU, power Propulsion hardware (case, nozzle) 40 8.0 SRM case, igniter, TVC Fuze and SAF device 10 2.0 Safety device + fuze Miscellaneous (wiring, sealant) 15 3.0 Integration items Total 500 100

For stable flight, the Centre of Pressure (CP) — the point through which the net aerodynamic force acts — must lie aft of the Centre of Gravity (CG). The static stability margin:

\[SM = \frac{x_{CP} - x_{CG}}{d_{ref}} \quad [\text{calibres}]\tag{16.1}\]

Positive \(SM\) indicates static stability. Typical missiles are designed for \(SM = 1\)–3 calibres. Excessively large \(SM\) increases the control power required to manoeuvre; too small \(SM\) risks divergence from small disturbances.

docs.title: 16.3 Flight Mechanics — Six-Degree-of-Freedom Equations of Motion
16.3.1 Reference Frames
docs.text:
The missile dynamics are conventionally described in two reference frames:

  • Body frame \(\{B\}\): origin at CG; \(x_B\) along nose, \(y_B\) to starboard, \(z_B\) downward (right-hand system).

  • Earth-centred Inertial frame \(\{I\}\) (or local tangent NED frame for short flights).

The rotation from \(\{I\}\) to \(\{B\}\) is parameterised by the Euler angles \(\{\phi, \theta, \psi\}\) (roll, pitch, yaw) via the Direction Cosine Matrix \(C_{BI}\).

docs.title: 16.3.2 Translational Equations of Motion
docs.text:
Applying Newton’s second law in the body frame to a missile of instantaneous mass \(m(t)\) (decreasing due to propellant burn), with forces resolved along body axes:

\[m\dot{u} = F_{Ax} + F_{Tx} - mg\sin\theta + m(rv - qw)\tag{16.2}\] \[m\dot{v} = F_{Ay} + F_{Ty} + mg\cos\theta\sin\phi + m(pw - ru)\tag{16.3}\] \[m\dot{w} = F_{Az} + F_{Tz} + mg\cos\theta\cos\phi + m(qu - pv)\tag{16.4}\]

where \((u, v, w)\) are body-axis velocity components; \((p, q, r)\) are body-axis angular rates (roll, pitch, yaw); \(F_{Ax}, F_{Ay}, F_{Az}\) are aerodynamic force components; \(F_{Tx}, F_{Ty}, F_{Tz}\) are thrust force components; and \(g\) is gravitational acceleration.

In the more compact vector form:

\[m\dot{\mathbf{V}} = \mathbf{F}_{aero} + \mathbf{F}_{thrust} + \mathbf{F}_{gravity} - \dot{m}\mathbf{V}_{exhaust} - m\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{V}\tag{16.5}\]

The term \(-\dot{m}\mathbf{V}_{exhaust}\) accounts for the apparent force from mass ejection (rocket thrust by momentum exchange).

docs.title: 16.3.3 Rotational Equations of Motion
docs.text:
The Euler moment equations in the body frame, accounting for the asymmetric inertia of a slender body of revolution where \(I_{xy} = I_{xz} = 0\) but \(I_{xx} \neq I_{yy} = I_{zz}\):

\[I_{xx}\dot{p} = L_a + L_T + (I_{yy} - I_{zz})qr\tag{16.6}\] \[I_{yy}\dot{q} = M_a + M_T + (I_{zz} - I_{xx})pr\tag{16.7}\] \[I_{zz}\dot{r} = N_a + N_T + (I_{xx} - I_{yy})pq\tag{16.8}\]

where \(L_a, M_a, N_a\) are aerodynamic moments; \(L_T, M_T, N_T\) are thrust moments (non-zero when thrust is vectored or CG offset from motor axis); and the cross-product terms are gyroscopic. For a typical air-to-air missile: \(I_{xx} \approx 0.04\) kg\(\cdot\)m\(^2\), \(I_{yy} = I_{zz} \approx 4.2\) kg\(\cdot\)m\(^2\).

docs.title: 16.3.4 Kinematic Equations
docs.text:
The Euler angle rates relate to body-axis angular rates:

\[\begin{pmatrix} \dot{\phi} \\ \dot{\theta} \\ \dot{\psi} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \sin\phi\tan\theta & \cos\phi\tan\theta \\ 0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\ 0 & \sin\phi/\cos\theta & \cos\phi/\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} p \\ q \\ r \end{pmatrix}\tag{16.9}\]

This formulation has a singularity at \(\theta = \pm90^\circ\) (vertical flight). Quaternion representation avoids singularity:

\[\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\mathbf{q}\tag{16.10}\]

where \(\mathbf{q} = [q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3]^T\) is the unit quaternion and \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is the skew-symmetric matrix of angular rates. Quaternion formulation is standard in all modern missile autopilot simulations.

docs.title: 16.3.5 Aerodynamic Angles
docs.text:
Angle of attack \(\alpha\) and sideslip \(\beta\):

\[\alpha = \arctan\!\left(\frac{w}{u}\right), \qquad \beta = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{v}{V}\right)\tag{16.11}\]

where \(V = \sqrt{u^2 + v^2 + w^2}\) is the total velocity. For a slender body of revolution, the normal-force coefficient \(C_N\) is approximately:

\[C_N \approx C_{N\alpha} \alpha + C_{N\alpha^3} \alpha^3\tag{16.12}\]

where \(C_{N\alpha} \approx 2\) per radian (slender body theory, Munk 1924), and the cubic term accounts for nonlinearity at \(\alpha > 15^\circ\).

docs.title: 16.3.6 Guidance Frame and Homing Dynamics
docs.text:
In the line-of-sight (LOS) coordinate frame, the interception geometry is described by the LOS angle \(\lambda\) and its rate \(\dot\lambda\). For proportional navigation guidance:

\[a_c = N' V_c \dot{\lambda}\tag{16.13}\]

where \(N'\) is the navigation ratio (typically 3–5), \(V_c\) is closing velocity (positive when decreasing range), and \(\dot{\lambda}\) is the LOS rate. The manoeuvre required to achieve zero miss distance is the commanded lateral acceleration \(a_c\).

docs.title: 16.3.7 Guidance Frame Transformations: Roll-Stabilised vs. Skid-to-Turn
docs.text:
Roll-Stabilised.

The missile roll rate is controlled to keep a reference axis (e.g., fin plane) aligned with the LOS vertical. Pitch and yaw channels are decoupled. Used in many radar-homing missiles (AIM-7, RIM-66 SM-2).

Bank-to-Turn (BTT).

Like a conventional aircraft, the missile rolls to place the high-lift plane in the direction of the commanded manoeuvre, then pulls. Used in cruise missiles (Tomahawk, KEPD 350) for efficient long-range cruise.

Skid-to-Turn (STT).

Equal manoeuvre capability in pitch and yaw. The missile does not roll; it generates lateral force by combining fin deflections. Used in most short-range AAMs (AIM-9, ASRAAM, IRIS-T). The penalty is higher aerodynamic drag due to off-axis angles of attack.

Spin-Stabilised.

Unguided rockets and older guided missiles used high spin rates (\(p = 100\)–300 rad/s) for gyroscopic stability. Gyroscopic effects couple pitch and yaw, requiring careful guidance law design.

docs.title: 16.4.1 Range
docs.text:
The achievable range of a missile is governed by the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation applied to the propellant mass fraction, modified by aerodynamic drag losses:

\[\Delta V_{ideal} = I_{sp} \cdot g_0 \cdot \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\tag{16.14}\]

where \(I_{sp}\) is specific impulse (s), \(g_0 = 9.80665\) m/s\(^2\), \(m_0\) is initial mass, and \(m_f\) is final (burnout) mass. The velocity increment achieved is reduced by gravitational losses during ascent and by aerodynamic drag (drag velocity loss):

\[\Delta V_{actual} = \Delta V_{ideal} - \Delta V_{gravity} - \Delta V_{drag}\tag{16.15}\]

For an SRM-propelled missile at moderate altitude, \(\Delta V_{drag}\) is typically 100–500 m/s depending on body drag and burn duration. The range for a ballistic projectile after burnout (vacuum, flat Earth approximation):

\[R_{max} = \frac{V_{BO}^2 \sin(2\gamma_{BO})}{g_0}\tag{16.16}\]

maximised at \(\gamma_{BO} = 45^\circ\). Aerodynamic missiles maintain powered/gliding flight and achieve range determined by the sustained lift-to-drag ratio:

\[R_{cruise} = I_{sp} \cdot g_0 \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\tag{16.17}\]

docs.title: 16.4.2 Accuracy — Circular Error Probable (CEP)
docs.text:
Circular Error Probable (CEP) is the radius of a circle centred on the aim point within which 50% of rounds from an identical firing fall. For a bivariate normal distribution with equal standard deviations \(\sigma_x = \sigma_y = \sigma\):

\[CEP \approx 1.1774 \, \sigma\tag{16.18}\]

The probability that a hit falls within radius \(r\) from the aim point:

\[P(r) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-0.5 \left(\frac{r}{CEP/1.1774}\right)^2\right)\tag{16.19}\]

Operational CEP values: GPS-guided Tomahawk \(\approx\) 5–10 m; JDAM \(\approx\) 10–30 m; unguided bomb (dumb bomb) \(\approx\) 90–150 m; MIRV ICBM (Minuteman III, GPS-aided) \(\approx\) 120 m; Russian SS-18 Mod 6 \(\approx\) 200 m.

docs.title: 16.4.3 Lethality Metrics
docs.text:
Single-Shot Kill Probability.

The probability that a single missile destroys the target:

\[P_k = P_d \cdot P_i \cdot P_{kill|hit}\tag{16.20}\]

where \(P_d\) is the probability of detecting the target, \(P_i\) is the probability of intercepting (guidance success), and \(P_{kill|hit}\) is the conditional kill probability given the missile reaches lethal range.

Lethal Radius.

The effective lethal radius \(R_L\) of a blast-fragmentation warhead is defined as the range at which the probability of kill of an average area target is \(P_{kill|range} = 0.5\):

\[R_L = K_L \cdot W_{HE}^{1/3}\tag{16.21}\]

where \(W_{HE}\) is TNT-equivalent explosive mass (kg) and \(K_L\) is a target vulnerability constant (typically 1.5–4 for unarmoured vehicles; 0.5–1.0 for armoured targets).

Salvo Doctrine.

To achieve a required total kill probability \(P_{req}\) against a target with \(P_k\) per missile:

\[n_{missiles} = \frac{\ln(1 - P_{req})}{\ln(1 - P_k)}\tag{16.22}\]

Example: \(P_{req} = 0.95\), \(P_k = 0.70\): \(n = \ln(0.05)/\ln(0.30) = 2.48 \Rightarrow 3\) missiles.

docs.title: 16.4.4 Speed Classification
docs.text: Table 16.2. Missile Speed Regime Classification Regime Mach Range Speed (km/h) Aerodynamic Regime Representative Systems Subsonic \(<0.8\) Ma \(<\)980 Incompressible, low drag Tomahawk, Taurus KEPD 350 Transonic 0.8–1.2 Ma 980–1,480 Shock wave formation, buffet Many early SAMs Supersonic 1.2–5 Ma 1,480–6,120 Oblique/normal shocks SM-6, MBDA Meteor, Brahmos Hypersonic \(>5\) Ma \(>\)6,120 Aero-thermal heating; plasma DF-17 HGV, Kinzhal, AGM-183

docs.title: 16.4.5 Manoeuvrability
docs.text:
Lateral acceleration capability in units of \(g\) (9.81 m/s\(^2\)) is the primary manoeuvrability metric:

\[n_{lat} = \frac{F_{lateral}}{W} = \frac{q \, S \, C_N(\alpha,Ma,\delta)}{m g}\tag{16.23}\]

Modern short-range AAMs achieve instantaneous lateral accelerations of 50–80 \(g\) during terminal engagement. The maximum sustained lateral acceleration is limited by structural strength (usually expressed as the limit-load factor, typically \(n_{lat,limit} = 30\)–40 \(g\) for maintained manoeuvre).

The kinematic envelope defines the set of all target positions/velocities from which the missile can achieve an intercept. It is bounded by maximum lateral acceleration on one side and minimum seeker tracking rate / launch dead zone on the other, and is a strong function of target closing velocity.

docs.title: 16.4.6 Time of Flight and Reaction Time
docs.text:
Time of flight \(t_{TOF}\) from launch to intercept is critical for:

  • Target reaction time — a supersonic missile at 3 Ma leaves an aircraft with \(\sim\)15 s to respond from 15 km; a hypersonic missile at 10 Ma leaves \(<\)5 s.

  • Battery life of guidance system (power available for seeker and computer).

  • Maximum range achievable before motor burnout and kinetic energy exhaustion.

Average TOF for common missile types: short-range AAM (2 km): 3–8 s; medium-range AAM (50 km): 30–90 s; surface-to-surface ballistic (300 km): 5–8 min; ICBM (10,000 km): 25–30 min.

docs.title: 16.5 Propulsion Overview
docs.text:
Propulsion is treated in depth in Chapters 19–20. This section provides a comparative overview sufficient for system-level trade analysis.

Table 16.3. Missile Propulsion Technology Comparison Type Fuel/Oxidiser \(I_{sp}\) (s) Thrust Level Speed Range Applications Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) HTPB/AP/Al 240–300 100 N – 4 MN 0–5 Ma AAM, SAM, ATGM, ICBM Liquid Rocket Engine (LRE) LOX/RP-1, UDMH/N\(_2\)O\(_4\) 290–450 1 kN – 1 MN 0–5 Ma Ballistic, SCUD, V-2 Turbojet / Turbofan Kerosene (JP-10) 2,000–4,000 1–50 kN 0.5–1 Ma Cruise missiles Ramjet (liquid fuel) JP-10 + ram air 800–1,200 1–300 kN 2–5 Ma BrahMos, Meteor Scramjet H\(_2\) or JP-7 + ram air 1,000–2,000 1–100 kN 5–15 Ma X-51A, experimental Dual-Pulse SRM HTPB/AP, two grains 270–290 Variable 0–4 Ma AMRAAM, MBDA Aster Boost-Glide Rocket Solid + glide 280–310 (boost) Boost only 5–20 Ma DF-17, AGM-183 ARRW

The boost-sustain propulsion profile is common in many air-to-air and surface-to-air missiles: a high-thrust boost grain accelerates the missile to supersonic speed within 0.5–2 s; a lower-thrust sustainer grain maintains speed for the flight phase. An unpowered coast phase follows burnout; the missile decelerates due to drag. Terminal manoeuvre depletes remaining kinetic energy:

\[V_{terminal} = V_{BO} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{C_D A \rho}{2m} \int_0^{R_{coast}} dR\right)\tag{16.24}\]

The velocity at intercept must exceed the minimum manoeuvre speed:

\[V_{min,manoeuvre} = \sqrt{\frac{n_{lat,req} \cdot m \cdot g}{q_{min} \cdot S \cdot C_{N\alpha}}}\tag{16.25}\]

docs.title: 16.6 Guidance Overview
docs.text: Guidance is treated in depth in Chapters 20–21.

docs.title: 16.6.1 Guidance Law Classification
docs.text:
• Command Guidance: A ground or airborne radar tracks both the missile and the target. A ground computer calculates correction commands and uplinks them to the missile via radar beam or radio. SA-2/SA-6 SAMs use command guidance with terminal semi-active homing. Accuracy dependent on ground-radar resolution.

  • Beam Riding: The missile navigates to stay in the centre of a radar or laser beam pointed at the target. Simple, jam-resistant (if laser). Used in SACLOS ATGMs (Kornet, Milan), shoulder-fired SAMs (Starstreak). Accuracy degrades with range as beam width increases.

  • Active Homing: On-board radar transmits and receives — fully autonomous after launch (“fire and forget”). Used by AIM-120 AMRAAM, SM-6, Aster 30. Range limited by seeker radar power (typically illuminates to 25–50 km).

  • Semi-Active Homing: Ground or aircraft radar illuminates the target; the missile homes on the reflected energy. Requires continuous illuminator pointing at the target. AIM-7 Sparrow, SM-2 Block II. Disadvantage: the illuminating platform is committed until impact.

  • Passive (IR) Homing: Seeker homes on IR emission from target engine or skin heating. AIM-9X, ASRAAM, IRIS-T, Mistral. All-aspect capability on modern uncooled/cooled FPA seekers; jam-resistant (flare rejection algorithms).

  • INS/GPS + Terminal Seeker: Mid-course via INS/GPS; terminal via active radar (JASSM-ER), IIR (JSOW-C), or SAL (Brimstone). Combines long standoff range with precision terminal guidance.

docs.title: 16.6.2 Proportional Navigation Guidance Law
docs.text:
Proportional Navigation (PN) is the most widely deployed guidance law for homing missiles:

\[a_c = N' \, V_c \, \dot{\lambda}\tag{16.26}\]

True PN (TPN) generates acceleration normal to the line of sight:

\[a_{TPN} = N' \, V_c \, \dot{\lambda}\]

Augmented PN (APN) adds target acceleration term to improve engagement against manoeuvring targets:

\[a_{APN} = N' V_c \dot{\lambda} + \frac{N'}{2} a_T\tag{16.28}\]

Optimal PN (OPN) / Optimal Guidance Law (OGL) minimises a cost function of miss distance and control effort:

\[a_{OPN} = \frac{N'(t_{go})}{t_{go}^2} \left[ R_{LOS} + \dot{R}_{LOS} t_{go} - \frac{1}{2} (a_T - a_M) t_{go}^2 \right]\tag{16.29}\]

where \(t_{go}\) is estimated time-to-go. OPN requires target acceleration estimation (via target tracker).

docs.title: 16.7 Warhead and Effects Overview
docs.text: Warheads are treated in depth in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 16.7.1 Warhead Type Classification
docs.text:
• HE Blast-Fragmentation: Cylindrical steel or tungsten alloy fragmentation sleeve surrounds a cylindrical HE charge. Detonation creates a radially expanding fragment cloud (initial velocity 1,200–2,500 m/s) plus a blast wave. Effective lethal radius for soft targets: 10–30 m. Used in AAMs, SAMs, air-to-ground.

  • Shaped Charge (HEAT): A metal-lined cavity (copper or tantalum) is collapsed by HE detonation, forming a high-velocity jet (\(>\)8 km/s) capable of penetrating 600–1,200 mm RHA. Used in ATGMs (Kornet, TOW, Javelin), anti-ship missiles (Exocet). Defeated by reactive armour (ERA).

  • Thermobaric (FAE): Aerosol of hydrocarbon fuel dispersed then ignited; overpressure wave penetrates into enclosed spaces (caves, bunkers, vehicles). Blast pressure duration is 5–8\(\times\) longer than HE of equal mass. Used in TOS-1A, RPG-7TBG, and some cruise missile warheads.

  • Kinetic Energy (KE) Penetrator: High-density rod (depleted uranium or tungsten, \(L/D \approx 10\)–30) at \(>\)1 km/s. Penetrates armour by plastic deformation and shear. Effective against modern MBTs. Used in long-rod penetrators for APFSDS tank rounds; adapted to anti-ship kinetic impactors (Conventional Prompt Global Strike concept).

  • EMP/HPM Warhead: High-power microwave or E-bomb warhead generates electromagnetic pulse to disable electronics without kinetic effect. Flux-compression generator (FCG) can produce GW-level pulses.

  • Sub-Munition Dispenser (Cluster): A carrier payload opens at altitude and disperses bomblets over an area. Banned under the Convention on Cluster Munitions (CCM) for signatory states; still used by non-signatories.

The blast overpressure at range \(R\) from an HE detonation of TNT-equivalent mass \(W_{TNT}\):

\[P_{SO}(R) = \frac{K_1 W_{TNT}^{1/3}}{R} + \frac{K_2 W_{TNT}^{2/3}}{R^2} + \frac{K_3 W_{TNT}}{R^3}\tag{16.30}\]

where the Hopkinson-Cranz (cube-root) scaling law gives overpressure as a function of scaled range \(Z = R/W_{TNT}^{1/3}\). Structural damage thresholds: light structures destroyed at \(P_{SO} > 35\) kPa; reinforced concrete at \(> 350\) kPa.

docs.title: 16.8.1 Speed vs. Range Trade
docs.text:
Higher flight speed increases drag and therefore propellant consumption for a given range. For a constant-altitude cruise missile of drag area \(C_D A_{ref}\), the specific range (km/kg of fuel):

\[\frac{dR}{dm_f} = -\frac{I_{sp} g_0 V}{D} = -\frac{I_{sp} g_0}{C_D A_{ref} \rho V/2 \cdot (1/m)}\tag{16.31}\]

Drag scales as \(V^2\); thrust (for air-breathing engines) scales roughly as \(V\); fuel flow scales as \(V^2\) — so range decreases with increasing cruise speed for air-breathing propulsion. For rocket propulsion, Mach number does not directly affect \(I_{sp}\) (unlike ramjets), but higher speed still increases drag loss. The optimal cruise speed minimising propellant consumption for a given propulsion type:

\[V_{opt} = \left(\frac{2 T_{available}}{\rho C_D A_{ref}}\right)^{1/2}\tag{16.32}\]

docs.title: 16.8.2 Altitude Trade
docs.text:
• Low-altitude sea-skimmer (3–10 m): Exploits radar horizon masking; requires altimeter and terrain-following avionics; increases probability of radar non-detection; high risk from sea clutter; used by Harpoon, Exocet, BrahMos in sea-skimming mode.

  • High-altitude cruise (8,000–12,000 m): Reduced drag at low density; extended sensor/seeker range; visible to long-range radar; exploited by standoff cruise missiles (Kalibr, Storm Shadow/SCALP).

  • Lofted ballistic (IRBM/MRBM): High apogee (\(>\)300 km) for extended range; re-entry speed creates plasma blackout period; near-vertical terminal approach difficult to intercept.

docs.title: 16.8.3 Size and Weight Constraints from Launch Platform
docs.text:
The launch platform defines maximum missile dimensions and mass. Key examples:

  • Mk 41 Vertical Launch System (VLS): Cell dimensions: \(0.635\) m \(\times\) \(0.635\) m \(\times\) 6.10 m (Mk 41 Strike Length). Maximum missile mass \(\approx\) 1,500 kg. Accommodates SM-6, Tomahawk, ESSM (quad-packed in single cell), ASROC.

  • Aircraft pylon hardpoint: Maximum store mass per station: 1,000–2,300 kg for heavy aircraft (F-15E, Su-34); 500–1,000 kg for tactical fighters. Length limited by fuselage clearance. Width limited to \(\approx\)0.5 m for triple-ejector racks.

  • Internal weapons bay: F-22 main bay: \(4.9\) m \(\times\) \(0.6\) m; F-35A bay: \(3.2\) m \(\times\) \(0.57\) m. Limits weapon length, span, and mass.

  • Man-portable (MANPADS): Total system mass \(<\)20 kg; round mass \(<\)12 kg; tube diameter 72–90 mm. SA-18/SA-24, Stinger, Mistral Mini.

docs.title: 16.8.4 Cost vs. Performance Trade
docs.text:
The unit recurring cost breakdown for a representative medium-range missile (unit production cost \(\approx\) USD 500,000–2M):

  • Propulsion system: 25–35% of missile unit cost. SRM case, propellant, igniter, nozzle/TVC.

  • Guidance, Navigation, and Control: 30–40%. Seeker, IMU, GPS/INS processor, autopilot electronics, actuators. This fraction is growing as active seekers and AI processing capability increase.

  • Warhead and Fuze: 15–20%. Explosive fill, casing, SAF device, fuze electronics.

  • Airframe and Structure: 10–15%. Mostly CFRP/aluminium; relatively low cost for high volume.

  • Systems integration and testing: 5–10%. Acceptance test, environmental qualification.

The affordability tension is acute for attritable designs — expendable cruise missiles used in saturation attacks (Russian Kalibr in Ukraine 2022–present) must be cheap enough to expend in large salvos, while maintaining effectiveness. The unit cost target for the US affordable mass-effect JASSM-ER (AGM-158B): \(\sim\)USD 1.5M per round.

docs.title: 16.9.1 Requirements Definition
docs.text:
The missile design process begins with a rigorous system requirements document (SRD) driven by:

  1. Threat characterisation: Target type (aircraft, ship, ground vehicle, bunker), speed, altitude, RCS, countermeasures, probability distribution of encounter geometry.

  2. Platform constraints: Launch vehicle envelope, hardpoint load, electrical power available, datalink compatibility.

  3. Rules of Engagement (ROE): Man-in-the-loop requirements; IFF (Identification Friend-or-Foe) requirements; minimum safe range.

  4. Performance requirements: Range, CEP, \(P_k\), speed, manoeuvre capability, ECCM resistance.

  5. Operational constraints: Shelf life (\(\geq\)20 yr for strategic weapons), temperature range (\(-40^\circ\)C to \(+65^\circ\)C storage), vibration (launch/carriage spectra per MIL-STD-810H), EMI (MIL-STD-461G), nuclear hardening (if applicable).

docs.title: 16.9.2 Preliminary Design — Mass and Performance Estimation
docs.text:
The initial (point design) estimate of missile mass and geometry uses parametric methods. A useful mass estimating relationship (MER):

\[m_{missile} = K_{MER} \cdot W_{warhead}^{a_1} \cdot R^{a_2} \cdot V_{cruise}^{a_3}\tag{16.33}\]

Derived from regression across existing weapon datasets (Jane’s Weapons, public domain). Constants depend on missile class. Alternatively, the structural mass fraction method:

\[m_0 = \frac{m_{warhead} + m_{GCS} + m_{structure}}{1 - \mu_{prop}}\tag{16.34}\]

where \(\mu_{prop} = m_{propellant}/m_0\) is the propellant mass fraction, estimated from the Tsiolkovsky equation and required \(\Delta V\).

Aerodynamic shaping follows from the diameter-to-length ratio \(L/d\) (fineness ratio). For minimum wave drag at supersonic speeds, the Sears-Haack body gives:

\[C_{D,wave} = \frac{9\pi}{2} \left(\frac{A_{max}}{L^2}\right)^2\tag{16.35}\]

A fineness ratio of \(L/d = 10\)–15 is typical for supersonic tactical missiles, balancing wave drag against volume packaging.

docs.title: 16.9.3 Detailed Design
docs.text:
The detailed design phase resolves all subsystem interfaces. The Interface Control Document (ICD) specifies:

  • Mechanical: mating surfaces, harness routing, CG envelope as propellant burns

  • Electrical: power bus voltages, connector types (MIL-DTL-38999), harness routing, EMI shielding

  • Software: real-time operating system (VxWorks, LynxOS, INTEGRITY), message bus (MIL-STD-1553B or ARINC 825 CAN)

  • Thermal: heat sink requirements for electronics; ablative insulation for warhead near motor

docs.title: 16.9.4 Qualification and Test
docs.text:
The missile qualification programme follows a progressive test pyramid:

Table 16.4. Missile Qualification Test Programme Structure Phase Test Type Standard Objective Component Environmental stress screening MIL-STD-2164 Screen early failures Subsystem Vibration, shock, thermal cycling MIL-STD-810H Verify environmental tolerance Subsystem EMI/EMC MIL-STD-461G Verify electromagnetic compatibility System Captive carry (on aircraft) MIL-HDBK-1763 Airworthiness, carriage loads System Separation test (instrumented) NAWCWD TR-8678 Safe separation from platform System Guided flight test (range telemetry) DODI 5000.XX Verify guidance and propulsion System Live fire (warhead detonation) AOP-7 (NATO) Warhead lethality confirmation Production Lot acceptance test (motor) MIL-STD-1901 Motor-to-motor consistency Production Periodic reliability confirmation MIL-HDBK-189C Reliability growth validation

Reliability growth follows a Crow-AMSAA model:

\[\lambda(t) = \lambda_0 t^{\beta - 1} \quad [\text{failures per test hour}]\tag{16.36}\]

where \(\beta < 1\) indicates improving (decreasing failure rate) reliability. The cumulative number of failures:

\[E[N(t)] = \lambda_0 t^\beta\tag{16.37}\]

docs.title: 16.9.5 Production and Acceptance
docs.text: Lot acceptance testing (LAT) verifies that production rounds meet specification. Typical LAT for SRMs includes propellant burn-rate sample testing, motor static fire, and dimensional inspection. Statistical acceptance schemes follow MIL-STD-1916 (preferred over MIL-STD-105 for attribute sampling in modern DoD contracts).

docs.title: 16.10.1 Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR)
docs.text:
The MTCR (established 1987, 35 member states as of 2025) is an informal political arrangement — not a legally binding treaty — limiting exports of rockets and unmanned delivery systems capable of delivering WMD. The MTCR defines two categories:

  • Category I (most controlled): Systems with \(R > 300\) km and payload \(> 500\) kg; or systems "inherently capable of" such delivery. Includes complete ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, space launch vehicles. There is a strong presumption to deny all exports.

  • Category II (controlled): Less capable systems; propulsion components; guidance equipment; structural composites usable in Cat I systems. Case-by-case export decisions.

The threshold equation used to define Category I:

\[\text{Cat I if:}\quad R \geq 300\ \text{km} \quad \text{AND} \quad m_{payload} \geq 500\ \text{kg}\tag{16.38}\]

Note: the MTCR is self-policing — violating states (e.g., North Korea, Pakistan missile transfers) face unilateral US sanctions under the Arms Export Control Act but no multilateral enforcement mechanism.

docs.title: 16.10.2 INF Treaty (Now Defunct)
docs.text: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (INF, signed 1987 US-USSR) prohibited ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges 500–5,500 km. It eliminated entire weapon categories including the SS-20 Saber, Pershing II, and BGM-109G GLCM. The United States withdrew in August 2019, citing Russian development of the 9M729 (SSC-8) cruise missile exceeding 500 km in violation of INF. Russia suspended its participation simultaneously. The treaty is defunct; both sides are now developing new IRBM-class ground-launched systems.

docs.title: 16.10.3 New START and Strategic Arms Limitation
docs.text: New START (Treaty Between the United States of America and the Russian Federation on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms, 2010) limited each side to 700 deployed ICBMs, SLBMs, and heavy bombers, and 1,550 deployed warheads. Russia suspended its New START participation in February 2023, citing Western military support for Ukraine. As of 2026, no replacement strategic arms control treaty is in force, creating the first period of unconstrained strategic nuclear competition since the early 1970s.

docs.title: 16.10.4 Chemical and Biological Weapons Conventions
docs.text:
• Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC, 1993): Prohibits development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons; bans delivery systems specifically designed to deliver CW agents. Missiles modified for CW delivery are illegal under CWC for all 193 signatory states.

  • Biological Weapons Convention (BWC, 1972): Prohibits development and stockpiling of biological and toxin weapons, including their delivery systems.

docs.title: 16.10.5 Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) and LAWS
docs.text:
The CCW (Geneva, 1980) Protocol II governs mines, booby traps, and IEDs; Protocol III governs incendiary weapons; Protocol V addresses explosive remnants of war. The debate most relevant to this volume is the ongoing Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) discussion on Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems (LAWS).

LAWS are systems that, once activated, can select and engage targets without further human intervention. Loitering munitions (Harpy, Harop, Switchblade 600, Lancet) occupy a grey zone: some have autonomous terminal homing but require human approval for activation. Three positions dominate CCW discussions:

  1. Prohibition (ICRC / ICRC-aligned states): Meaningful human control is a requirement; a ban on LAWS should be negotiated.

  2. Regulation (US, UK, Russia, Israel, Australia): Existing IHL (International Humanitarian Law) applies; LAWS must comply with distinction, proportionality, and precautions principles; no new treaty needed.

  3. Non-position (China): Calls for prohibition of use but not development.

As of 2026, no binding legal instrument on LAWS has been adopted. The operational employment of AI-guided loitering munitions and UCAV weapon systems in active conflicts (Nagorno-Karabakh 2020, Ukraine 2022–present, Gaza 2023–present) is accumulating precedent-setting practice that will shape any eventual legal framework.

Table 16.5. Summary of International Missile-Related Treaty Regime Treaty/Regime Year Status (2026) Range Scope Primary Constraint MTCR 1987 Active (35 members) \(>\)300 km, \(>\)500 kg Export controls INF Treaty 1987 Defunct (2019) 500–5,500 km GLBM/GLCM All ground-launched New START 2010 Suspended (Russia 2023) ICBM/SLBM/\(>\)5,500 km 1,550 warheads cap CWC 1993 193 states parties All ranges CW-armed missiles banned BWC 1972 183 states parties All ranges BW delivery banned CCW GGE on LAWS 2014 Ongoing discussions All ranges No binding text yet Outer Space Treaty 1967 In force ICBM/orbital Bans WMD in orbit

docs.title: 16.11 Missile System Architecture — Systems Engineering Perspective
16.11.1 Functional Architecture
docs.text:
A missile system performs the following sequential functions:

\[\underbrace{\text{Detect}}_{\text{sensor}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Track}}_{\text{fire control}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Assign}}_{\text{C\textsuperscript{2}}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Launch}}_{\text{launcher}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Guide}}_{\text{autopilot}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Arm}}_{\text{fuze}} \rightarrow \underbrace{\text{Detonate}}_{\text{warhead}}\]

Each function maps to one or more physical subsystems. The Systems Engineering V-model maps requirements through design decomposition to integration and verification. At the top level:

  • System-level requirements: \(P_k\), range, CEP, launch-to-impact time, platform compatibility.

  • Segment-level requirements: Fire control segment, launcher segment, missile segment, C2 segment.

  • Subsystem requirements: Seeker, autopilot, propulsion, warhead, fuze.

  • Component requirements: Motor grain burn rate, nozzle throat erosion rate, seeker detector \(D^*\), IMU noise PSD.

docs.title: 16.11.2 System Error Budget
docs.text:
Total system CEP is a root-sum-square of independent error contributors:

\[CEP_{total} = 1.1774 \sqrt{\sigma_{INS}^2 + \sigma_{GPS}^2 + \sigma_{seeker}^2 + \sigma_{wind}^2 + \sigma_{fuze}^2}\tag{16.40}\]

For a GPS-aided strike missile: \(\sigma_{INS} = 5\) m, \(\sigma_{GPS} = 3\) m (SA-off, clear view), \(\sigma_{seeker} = 1\) m (IIR lock-on), \(\sigma_{wind} = 2\) m (average crosswind error), \(\sigma_{fuze} = 0.5\) m:

\[CEP = 1.1774\sqrt{25 + 9 + 1 + 4 + 0.25} = 1.1774\sqrt{39.25} \approx 7.4\ \text{m}\]

docs.title: 16.11.3 Reliability and Maintainability
docs.text:
The reliability of a missile in storage-then-fire mission is characterised by storage reliability \(R_s(t)\) and in-flight reliability \(R_f\):

\[P_{mission,success} = R_s(t_{storage}) \cdot R_f\tag{16.42}\]

Storage reliability follows an Arrhenius-accelerated life model for electrolytic components:

\[t_{life}(T) = A \exp\!\left(\frac{E_a}{k_B T}\right)\tag{16.43}\]

where \(E_a \approx 0.7\)–1.0 eV is the activation energy for electrolytic corrosion, \(k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}\) eV/K, and \(T\) is storage temperature (K). Requirements typically specify 20-year storage life at \(+25^\circ\)C with \(R_s > 0.90\).

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
This chapter has established the foundation for the detailed technical treatment of missiles in subsequent chapters. The key principles introduced are:

  1. Precise definition matters: Missiles, rockets, guided bombs, loitering munitions, and torpedoes are distinct engineering categories with different design drivers. Conflation leads to incorrect requirements and design choices.

  2. The 6-DOF equations of motion (Equations (16.2)–(16.9)) define the complete missile flight mechanics. Simplifications (2-DOF, linear aerodynamics) enable rapid trade studies; the full 6-DOF simulation is required for autopilot design and warhead fuzing.

  3. Performance is multi-dimensional: Range, CEP, \(P_k\), speed, and manoeuvrability are all functions of the same underlying parameters (propellant mass fraction, aerodynamics, guidance law, seeker performance). They cannot be optimised independently — every design is a trade.

  4. Propulsion type determines the mission envelope: SRMs are the workhorses of tactical missiles (simple, reliable, high thrust, any altitude); turbojets enable long-range cruise; ramjets and scramjets extend the high-speed frontier; LREs power strategic ballistic missiles.

  5. Treaties constrain technology: MTCR limits diffusion of long-range capability; INF is defunct, reopening the IRBM design space; CWC and BWC prohibit specific warhead types. Engineers must understand the legal regime in which their work operates.

  6. Cost is as binding a constraint as physics: A missile that cannot be produced in sufficient quantity to matter is tactically irrelevant. The unit cost breakdown and the affordability trade must be driven by the systems engineer from the first day of concept design.

The chapters that follow develop each of these topics in depth: missile types and operational categories (Chapter 17), aerodynamics of high-speed bodies (Chapter 18), propulsion systems (Chapter 19), guidance navigation and control (Chapter 20–21), warheads and effects (Chapter 22), and advanced topics including hypersonic vehicles (Chapter 25), UCAV integration (Chapter 26), and counter-missile defence (Chapter 27).

docs.title: 17.1 Introduction to Missile Classification
docs.text:
Missiles are self-propelled, guided munitions that deliver a payload—typically a warhead—to a designated target by means of aerodynamic, ballistic, or combined flight. Their taxonomy spans an extraordinary range of capability: from man-portable infantry weapons that weigh less than 2 kg and engage targets at 500 m, to intercontinental ballistic missiles whose 10,000 km range and 800 kg thermonuclear re-entry vehicles represent the apex of strategic deterrence. Rational classification relies on several overlapping schemes: trajectory type (ballistic vs. aerodynamic-lift sustained); launch platform (surface, air, subsurface); target type (air, surface, sub-surface, satellite); and speed regime (subsonic, supersonic, hypersonic).

A complete missile system is composed of five fundamental subsystems:

  1. Propulsion — solid-propellant rocket motor (SRM), liquid-propellant rocket engine (LRE), air-breathing engine (turbojet, turbofan, ramjet, scramjet), or combined-cycle.

  2. Airframe and Structures — body, fins, nose cone, control surfaces, thermal-protection system (TPS).

  3. Guidance, Navigation and Control (GNC) — seekers, inertial measurement unit (IMU), datalinks, autopilot, and flight-termination system.

  4. Warhead and Fuzing — energetic payload; proximity (radar, laser, optical), contact, or command detonation.

  5. Power — thermal battery, turbogenerator, silver–zinc battery for electronics and electromechanical actuators.

The NATO four-letter code (launch platform \(\to\) target type; e.g. SAM = Surface-to-Air Missile, AAM = Air-to-Air Missile) remains the lingua franca for categorisation and is used throughout this chapter.

docs.title: 17.2.1 Trajectory Mechanics and Phases
docs.text: A ballistic missile follows a free-fall Keplerian arc during the majority of its flight. Three canonical phases define the trajectory:

docs.title: Boost Phase
docs.text:
Thrust from one or more propulsion stages accelerates the missile from rest to burnout velocity \(V_{bo}\). Burnout typically occurs at altitudes of 100–400 km depending on range class and trajectory shaping. The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation gives the ideal velocity increment imparted by a single stage:

\[\Delta V = I_{sp}\,g_0 \ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\tag{17.1}\]

where \(I_{sp}\) is specific impulse (s), \(g_0 = 9.80665\) m/s\(^2\) is standard gravitational acceleration, \(m_0\) is initial (wet) mass, and \(m_f\) is final (dry) mass after propellant expenditure. For a multi-stage missile the total velocity increment is the sum over all stages \(i = 1, …, N\):

\[\Delta V_{total} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_{sp,i}\,g_0 \ln\!\left(\frac{m_{0,i}}{m_{f,i}}\right)\tag{17.2}\]

For an ICBM required to achieve \(V_{bo} \approx 7{,}200\) m/s (depressed trajectory) to \(7{,}900\) m/s (minimum-energy trajectory against a 10,000 km target), with realistic staging mass fractions \(\lambda_i = m_{f,i}/m_{0,i} \approx 0.10\)–\(0.15\) per stage and \(I_{sp} \approx 280\)–\(295\) s (composite solid propellant), three propulsion stages are required. Gravity and drag losses during boost reduce the achievable \(\Delta V\) by 150–400 m/s depending on trajectory profile.

docs.title: Mid-Course Phase
docs.text:
Post-burnout, the re-entry vehicle (RV) travels on a purely ballistic arc. In the exo-atmospheric environment (above \(\approx\)80 km) aerodynamic forces are negligible; the RV follows an elliptical orbit with the Earth’s centre at one focus. The apogee altitude \(h_{apo}\) for a minimum-energy ICBM trajectory to surface range \(R\) on a spherical Earth (radius \(R_E = 6{,}371\) km) is:

\[h_{apo} = R_E\!\left[\sec\!\left(\frac{\psi}{2}\right) - 1\right]\tag{17.3}\]

where \(\psi = R/R_E\) is the Earth-central angle. For \(R = 10{,}000\) km: \(\psi = 1.570\) rad, \(h_{apo} \approx 1{,}200\) km.

Modern ICBMs carry post-boost vehicles (PBVs) — manoeuvring buses with storable liquid-propellant engines — that release multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles (MIRVs) on precisely computed vectors to separate aimpoints within a lethal footprint spanning hundreds of kilometres. Bus propellant mass fractions of 0.05–0.10 of total launch mass are typical.

docs.title: Terminal (Re-entry) Phase
docs.text:
Re-entry commences at approximately 100 km altitude at velocities of 6–7 km/s. The ballistic coefficient governs both deceleration rate and aerodynamic heating:

\[\beta = \frac{m}{C_D\,A}\tag{17.4}\]

where \(m\) is RV mass, \(C_D\) is drag coefficient, and \(A\) is reference cross-sectional area. High-\(\beta\) RVs (heavy, compact) penetrate more deeply before appreciable deceleration; a Mk-21 RV has \(\beta \approx 10{,}000\) kg/m\(^2\). The deceleration–altitude equation of motion:

\[\frac{dV}{dt} = -\frac{\rho(h)\,V^2}{2\beta} + g\sin\gamma\tag{17.5}\]

where \(\gamma\) is flight-path angle (negative for descent) and \(\rho(h)\) follows an exponential atmosphere model \(\rho = \rho_0 e^{-h/H_s}\) with scale height \(H_s \approx 7{,}400\) m.

Terminal Mach number at detonation altitude (\(\sim\)500 m) ranges from Mach 5 (high-drag re-entry body) to Mach 25 (high-\(\beta\), low-drag slender RV entering at steep angle). The stagnation-point heat flux on a spherical-nose RV (Sutton–Graves relation):

\[\dot{q}_s = C_{SG}\sqrt{\frac{\rho_\infty}{R_N}}\,V_\infty^3\tag{17.6}\]

where \(C_{SG} = 1.83 \times 10^{-4}\) kg\(^{0.5}\)m\(^{-1}\)s\(^{-0.5}\) is the Sutton–Graves constant, \(R_N\) is nose radius (m), and \(\rho_\infty\), \(V_\infty\) are free-stream density (kg/m\(^3\)) and velocity (m/s). Integrated heat load for an ICBM RV reaches \(\mathcal{O}(10^9)\) J/m\(^2\); carbon–carbon composites with ablative phenolic back-fill plus a low-density silicone-based outer layer are required.

docs.title: 17.2.2 Range Categories

docs.title: 17.2.3 Re-Entry Vehicle Types
docs.text:
Single Re-entry Vehicle (SRV/MRV).

Early ballistic missiles carried a single RV. Multiple Re-entry Vehicles (MRV) spread warheads in a fixed, non-independently-targetable pattern (e.g. early Polaris A-3).

MIRV — Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicle.

The PBV releases each RV with a precisely computed velocity vector aimed at a separate aimpoint. Targeting flexibility is maximised: a single Trident II D5 can deliver up to 8\(\times\)Mk-5 RVs to aimpoints spread across a \(>\)1,000 km footprint. MIRV capability demands highly accurate IMU (drift \(<\)0.01 nmi/hr) and digital terrain maps for bus navigation.

MaRV — Manoeuvring Re-entry Vehicle.

The RV uses aerodynamic surfaces or small thrusters during terminal descent to manoeuvre, improving accuracy against moving targets and complicating intercept geometry. Manoeuvrability generates sustained lateral accelerations of 5–15\(g\). The DF-21D ASBM incorporates MaRV capability for carrier-strike missions; cross-range manoeuvre capability reportedly \(\pm\)50–100 km.

HGV — Hypersonic Glide Vehicle.

Released at burnout from a ballistic boost stage, the HGV glides at Mach 5–20 at altitudes of 30–80 km, providing continuous lateral manoeuvre capability with unpredictable flight path. Lift-to-drag ratio \(L/D \approx 2\)–\(4\) (blunt lifting body) extends range 30–50% vs. a purely ballistic RV. Examples: DF-17 (equipped with DF-ZF HGV), Avangard (reported Mach 20+, \(>\)2,000 km cross-range capability). The glide range addition over a ballistic baseline:

\[\Delta R_{glide} = \frac{L}{D} \cdot h_{entry}\tag{17.7}\]

where \(h_{entry}\) is entry altitude. For \(L/D = 3\), \(h_{entry} = 50\) km: \(\Delta R \approx 150\) km per glide segment; multiple skip-glide cycles compound this.

docs.title: 17.2.5 Submarine-Launched Ballistic Missiles (SLBM)
docs.text:
SLBMs introduce unique engineering constraints absent from silo-based systems. The Trident II D5 (UGM-133A) is ejected from Ohio-class SSBNs cruising at depths of 30–50 m. Cold launch (gas-generator ejection) accelerates the 59,090 kg missile from the 2.11 m-diameter tube at \(V_{exit} \approx 20\) m/s; the first-stage motor ignites approximately 5 m above the water surface. A solid rubber shroud protects the aerosurfaces during water-column transit.

Key trajectory milestones:

  1. High-pressure gas fills launch tube; missile ejected upward through water column (\(\Delta t \approx 2\) s).

  2. Rubber shroud ablates/burns away at first-stage ignition.

  3. Guidance computer receives GPS update within 30 s of emergence.

  4. Post-boost vehicle deploys MIRVs over \(\approx\)5 min bus-manoeuvre sequence.

Specifications: length 13.41 m; diameter 2.11 m; launch mass 59,090 kg; stage 1 \(I_{sp}\) = 283 s (HTPB composite); range \(>\)11,300 km; accuracy (CEP) 90 m with GPS-aided stellar-inertial navigation. The SWC-13A stellar-inertial navigation unit achieves positional accuracy of \(<\)30 m after star-fix update during mid-course.

docs.title: 17.2.6 Anti-Ship Ballistic Missiles (ASBM)
docs.text:
The DF-21D (CSS-5 Mod-4) pioneered the anti-carrier ASBM concept. Key parameters: range \(\approx 1{,}500\) km; warhead \(\approx 600\) kg conventional penetrator; terminal velocity Mach 10–12. The DF-26 intermediate-range ASBM extends the anti-ship engagement envelope to \(\approx 4{,}000\) km, covering the second island chain.

The terminal guidance challenge is formidable: the RV must detect and home on a manoeuvring carrier while decelerating from \(V \approx 3{,}000\) m/s to impact. The RV carries an active radar seeker (synthetic aperture or ISAR mode) combined with an inertial reference for mid-course. Cross-range manoeuvre capability \(\pm 50\)–\(100\) km requires aerodynamic control surfaces generating lift forces against a deceleration of \(\mathcal{O}(10^4)\) m/s\(^2\).

TPS heat load estimate using the Fay–Riddell correlation at the stagnation point:

\[\dot{q}_{FR} = 0.763\,\Pr^{-0.6}\!\left(\frac{\rho_w \mu_w}{\rho_e \mu_e}\right)^{0.1}\!\sqrt{\rho_e \mu_e \frac{du_e}{dx}}\,(h_{aw} - h_w)\tag{17.8}\]

Peak \(\dot{q}\) at Mach 12 re-entry is \(\approx 5\)–\(20\) MW/m\(^2\) depending on nose radius; C-SiC or AVCOAT ablative TPS is required.

docs.title: 17.3.1 Flight Profile and Operating Principles
docs.text:
Cruise missiles sustain aerodynamic lift throughout their flight, relying on air-breathing propulsion. This permits terrain-following flight at \(<\)50 m altitude and sea-skimming at 2–5 m, yielding extremely low radar-detection ranges. The Breguet range equation governs cruise-missile range:

\[R = \frac{V\,\eta_p}{c_T} \cdot \frac{L}{D} \cdot \ln\!\left(\frac{W_0}{W_1}\right)\tag{17.9}\]

where \(V\) is cruise speed (m/s), \(\eta_p\) is propulsive efficiency, \(c_T\) is thrust-specific fuel consumption (TSFC, kg N\(^{-1}\)h\(^{-1}\)), \(L/D\) is lift-to-drag ratio, \(W_0\) is take-off gross weight, and \(W_1\) is final weight.

Worked example (Tomahawk Block IV): \(V = 240\) m/s; \(\eta_p = 0.65\); \(c_T = 0.052\) kg N\(^{-1}\)h\(^{-1}\); \(L/D = 4.8\); \(W_0/W_1 = 1.38\):

\[R = \frac{240 \times 0.65}{0.052/3600} \times 4.8 \times \ln(1.38) \approx 1{,}590\text{ km}\tag{17.10}\]

This is consistent with the published \(>\)1,600 km range.

docs.title: 17.3.2 Propulsion Systems
docs.text:
Small turbofan (subsonic cruise).

The Williams International F107-WR-402 turbofan powers the BGM-109C/D Tomahawk: thrust 3.1 kN; TSFC 0.052 kg N\(^{-1}\)h\(^{-1}\); bypass ratio 1.0; mass flow 9.0 kg/s; overall pressure ratio 8:1; turbine inlet temperature 1,300 K; length 0.74 m; mass 60 kg.

Ramjet sustainer (supersonic/hypersonic cruise).

BrahMos employs a combined-cycle: solid-rocket booster (acceleration to Mach 2) followed by a liquid-fuel ramjet sustainer producing \(\approx\)20 kN at Mach 3, \(I_{sp,ram} \approx 1{,}400\)–\(1{,}600\) s. The specific thrust in a ramjet:

\[F_{ram}/\dot{m} = (1 + f)(V_e - V_0) + (p_e - p_0)A_e/\dot{m}\tag{17.11}\]

where \(f\) is fuel-to-air ratio, \(V_e\) is nozzle-exit velocity, \(V_0\) is free-stream velocity, and \(p_e\), \(p_0\) are nozzle-exit and ambient pressures.

docs.title: 17.3.3 Integrated Navigation Architecture
docs.text:
Modern cruise missiles combine multiple complementary navigation modes via a federated Kalman filter:

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k\bigl(\mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}_k\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}\bigr)\tag{17.12}\]

  1. Inertial Navigation System (INS): Ring-laser gyroscope (RLG) triaxial IMU provides autonomous dead-reckoning position; error growth \(\approx 0.8\) nmi/hr (LN-100G).

  2. TERCOM (Terrain Contour Matching): Radar altimeter measures ground-clearance profile; cross-correlated with stored digital terrain elevation data (DTED); fix accuracy 30–100 m; update rate \(\sim\)1 Hz. Ineffective over featureless terrain (desert, ocean).

  3. DSMAC (Digital Scene Matching Area Correlator): Terminal EO/IR image correlated with stored scene reference; CEP 3–10 m; sensitive to seasonal change, weather, and low-contrast scenes.

  4. GPS/GNSS: Anti-jam military M-code GPS; CEP \(<\)5 m in benign environment; vulnerable to jamming and spoofing in contested airspace.

Combined (Block IV Tomahawk): CEP \(<\)10 m vs. GPS coordinates; CEP \(<\)3 m with DSMAC terminal update.

docs.title: 17.3.4 Subsonic Cruise Missiles
docs.text:
BGM-109 Tomahawk (TLAM).

Length 6.25 m (with booster); diameter 0.52 m; wingspan 2.67 m (deployed); launch weight 1,590 kg; warhead 450 kg PBXN-107 blast-frag (TLAM-C) or WDU-36 1,000-lb penetrator (TLAM-D); cruise speed Mach 0.72 (880 km/h); range \(>\)1,600 km; CEP \(<\)10 m. Block V adds two-way data-link for in-flight retargeting and battle-damage imagery transmission.

AGM-86C/D ALCM.

Carried internally by B-52H (rotary launcher, 8 rounds; external, 12 rounds); Williams F107 turbofan; range 1,250 km; speed Mach 0.73; warhead W80-1 variable-yield nuclear (5–150 kT) or 900 kg conventional blast/penetrator; terrain-following flight at 50–100 m.

Storm Shadow / SCALP-EG.

Anglo-French; length 5.10 m; wingspan 3.0 m; mass 1,300 kg; Microturbo TRI60-30 turbofan; range 560 km; BROACH 450 kg penetrator warhead (initial hard-target penetrator followed by main charge); dual-mode IIR terminal seeker; CEP \(<\)3 m; very-low RCS due to faceted underside and S-duct intake.

docs.title: 17.3.5 Supersonic Cruise Missiles
docs.text:
BrahMos.

India–Russia joint development. Range 500 km (Block III extended); cruise Mach 2.8–3.0 at 14 km altitude; terminal sea-skim at Mach 3.5; length 8.4 m (ground-launched); mass 3,000 kg; warhead 200–300 kg general-purpose or penetrator; active radar seeker with sea-state bias; terminal altitude \(<\)5 m in final 15 km. Mach 3 provides warning time of \(\approx\)25 s from radar horizon (22 km) to impact.

3M22 Zircon (Tsirkon, SS-N-33).

Russia; Mach 8–9 at 30–40 km cruise altitude; range \(\approx\)1,000 km; propulsion: dual-mode pulse-detonation or scramjet-assisted ramjet; warhead \(\approx\)300 kg; plasma sheath during terminal phase theoretically defeats active radar intercept; ship-launched from Gorshkov-class frigates and Yasen-class SSGNs.

Kh-22 (AS-4 Kitchen).

Air-launched anti-ship/land-attack; Mach 4.6; length 11.67 m; mass 5,780 kg; warhead 1,000 kg conventional or nuclear; 22 km cruise altitude followed by steep terminal dive at Mach 4.6; R201-300 turbojet.

docs.title: 17.3.6 Stealth Cruise Missiles
docs.text:
AGM-158 JASSM / JASSM-ER.

JASSM: length 4.27 m; wingspan 2.40 m; weight 1,045 kg; WDU-42/B 450 kg penetrator warhead; range \(>\)370 km. JASSM-ER (AGM-158B): range \(>\)925 km (enlarged fuel tank); F107-WR-105 turbofan. Stealth features: composite structure; S-duct chin intake; RCS \(<\)0.01 m\(^2\) (X-band); no external wing tanks; IIR terminal seeker; CEP \(<\)3 m.

LRASM (AGM-158C).

JASSM-ER derivative for anti-ship role; adds autonomous multi-target discrimination algorithm; sea-state radar altimeter; passive RF/EO target detection; LRASM can coordinate between multiple missiles via RF datalink to deconflict aimpoints; Mach 0.9; range \(>\)900 km; 450 kg warhead.
