For each candidate position offset \((\delta x, \delta y)\) in a search grid, compute the Mean Absolute Difference (MAD) between measured profile \(h_m(i)\) and map profile \(h_s(i, \delta x, \delta y)\):

\[\mathrm{MAD}(\delta x,\delta y) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N |h_m(i) - h_s(i, \delta x, \delta y)|\tag{20.38}\]

The position fix is the \((\delta x^*, \delta y^*)\) minimising MAD. Accuracy depends on terrain roughness (standard deviation of terrain heights \(\sigma_T\)):

\[\sigma_{\text{TERCOM}} \approx \frac{\sigma_n}{\sigma_T}\,\Delta x\tag{20.39}\]

where \(\sigma_n\) is altimeter noise and \(\Delta x\) is pixel spacing. Flat terrain (low \(\sigma_T\)) gives poor TERCOM fixes — over oceans or deserts the system must coast on INS.

docs.title: 20.8.2 DSMAC (Digital Scene Matching Area Correlator)
docs.text:
DSMAC provides terminal guidance using electro-optical (EO) camera:

  1. Pre-programmed target image (DTED/SPOT imagery) stored in memory

  2. Terminal EO camera captures scene

  3. 2-D cross-correlation locates target centroid

  4. INS is updated; guidance corrects trajectory

Cross-correlation score:

\[C(\delta x, \delta y) = \frac{\sum_{i,j} I_{\mathrm{ref}}(i,j)\,I_{\mathrm{live}}(i+\delta x,j+\delta y)} {\sqrt{\sum I_{\mathrm{ref}}^2 \cdot \sum I_{\mathrm{live}}^2}}\tag{20.40}\]

DSMAC accuracy: \(<\!3\,\text{m}\) CEP. Limitation: requires pre-planned target image; vulnerable to camouflage, weather, and scene changes.

docs.title: 20.8.3 Tomahawk Block IV Guidance Suite
docs.text:
The Tomahawk (BGM-109) integrates four navigation modes:

  1. INS — continuous; degrades at \(\sim\!1.5\,\text{km h r}\) (navigation-grade)

  2. GPS — fixes INS every \(\sim\!1\,\text{min}\); maintains \(<\!15\,\text{m}\)

  3. TERCOM — terrain fixes at designated waypoints over suitable terrain

  4. DSMAC — terminal phase; improves to \(<\!5\,\text{m}\) CEP

Composite CEP: \(5\)–\(10\,\text{m}\) for fixed hard targets.

docs.title: 20.9.1 Seeker Angle Measurement
docs.text:
The seeker measures the angle from the missile body axis to the target. The total LOS angle in the inertial frame is:

\[\lambda = q + \theta_M\tag{20.41}\]

where \(q\) is the gimbal angle (seeker bore-sight to body axis) and \(\theta_M\) is the missile pitch angle. The LOS rate:

\[\dot{\lambda} = \dot{q} + \dot{\theta}_M\tag{20.42}\]

A rate gyro on the seeker gimbal measures \(\dot{q}\) directly; for a strapdown seeker, IMU rate must be subtracted.

docs.title: 20.9.2 Seeker Transfer Function and Noise
docs.text:
The seeker angle tracking loop has a first-order lag:

\[\frac{\dot{q}_{\mathrm{out}}(s)}{\dot{\lambda}(s)} = \frac{1}{1 + \tau_s s}\tag{20.43}\]

where \(\tau_s\) is the seeker time constant (typically \(0.1\,\text{s}\)–\(0.5\,\text{s}\)). Seeker noise \(\sigma_{q}\) appears at the seeker output; it is amplified by the navigation gain to produce acceleration noise:

\[\sigma_{a_c} = N\,V_c\,\sigma_{\dot{q}}\tag{20.44}\]

Seeker noise spectral density: \(\sigma_{\dot{\lambda}} \approx 10⁻³\,\text{r a d s}\) (typical IR seeker).

docs.title: 20.9.3 Parasitic Loop and Body Bending
docs.text:
The seeker measures \(\dot{q}\) which includes a contribution from missile body rotation \(\dot{\theta}_M\). The parasitic loop is the feedback path from acceleration command \(\to\) body motion \(\to\) gimbal rate \(\to\) guidance command (see Figure 20.2). The parasitic loop gain:

\[K_p = \frac{1}{V_M}\,T_M(\text{short-period pole})\tag{20.45}\]

Instability occurs when \(K_p\) exceeds the stability margin. Design requirement: seeker bandwidth must be low enough that body rates are attenuated.

Figure 20.2. Parasitic seeker-body coupling loop. \(G_G\) guidance, \(G_{AP}\) autopilot, \(G_B\) body dynamics, \(G_{sk}\) seeker.

docs.title: 20.9.4 Kalman Filter for Target State Estimation
docs.text:
For manoeuvring targets, a Kalman filter estimates target acceleration:

State: \(\mathbf{x} = [y_T, \dot{y}_T, \ddot{y}_T]^\top\) (cross-range position, velocity, acceleration).

Process model: Singer model for target acceleration:

\[\dot{a}_T = -\frac{1}{\tau_T}\,a_T + w_T, \quad w_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{a_T}^2/\tau_T)\tag{20.46}\]

Measurement: LOS angle \(\lambda = \arctan(y_T/x_T) + v_\lambda\), \(v_\lambda \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R_\lambda)\).

The standard EKF equations update the state and covariance:

\[\begin{align*} \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} &= \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k\bigl(z_k - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1})\bigr) \\ \mathbf{P}_{k|k} &= (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 20.10.1 Acceleration Autopilot Architecture
docs.text:
The autopilot converts the guidance law’s demanded lateral acceleration \(a_c\) into an aerosurface deflection command \(\delta_c\). The missile aerodynamic transfer function (short-period approximation) from fin deflection \(\delta\) to lateral acceleration \(a\) at CG is:

\[\frac{a(s)}{\delta(s)} = \frac{K_\delta\,(s + 1/T_2)}{s^2 + 2\zeta_\alpha\omega_\alpha s + \omega_\alpha^2}\tag{20.49}\]

where \(\omega_\alpha\) is the airframe short-period frequency, \(\zeta_\alpha\) damping ratio, \(K_\delta\) gain, \(T_2\) zero location (related to centre-of-pressure vs centre-of-gravity offset).

Three-loop autopilot.

The most common architecture has three nested loops:

  1. Inner loop — fin rate feedback (rate gyro); stabilises fin position

  2. Middle loop — pitch rate feedback \(q\) (rate gyro); improves damping

  3. Outer loop — accelerometer feedback \(a\); ensures \(a \to a_c\)

The closed-loop transfer function from \(a_c\) to \(a\):

\[\frac{a(s)}{a_c(s)} \approx \frac{\omega_{cl}^2}{s^2 + 2\zeta_{cl}\omega_{cl}s + \omega_{cl}^2}\tag{20.50}\]

Target: \(\omega_{cl} \approx 20\,\text{r a d s}\), \(\zeta_{cl} = 0.7\).

docs.title: 20.10.2 Gain Scheduling
docs.text:
Aerodynamic derivatives depend strongly on dynamic pressure and Mach number:

\[q_\infty = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2, \qquad M = V/a_{\text{sound}}\tag{20.51}\]

The normal force coefficient \(C_N\) and moment coefficient \(C_M\) vary with \(M\) and angle-of-attack \(\alpha\). Autopilot gains must be scheduled against \(q_\infty\) and \(M\) to maintain consistent closed-loop bandwidth across the flight envelope. A typical schedule uses a 2-D look-up table: \(K = f(q_\infty, M)\).

docs.title: 20.10.3 Roll Autopilot for Cruciform Missiles
docs.text: Cruciform missiles (4 fins in \(\times\) or \(+\) configuration) must maintain roll angle to decouple pitch and yaw. Roll rate command \(p_c = K_\phi(\phi_c - \phi)\); the roll loop bandwidth must be high enough (\(> 10\,\text{Hz}\)) to decouple from the pitch/yaw loops.

docs.title: 20.10.4 Thrust Vector Control Autopilot
docs.text:
At low dynamic pressure (immediately after launch), aerodynamic surfaces are ineffective. TVC (jet vanes, gimballed nozzle, or secondary injection) provides control forces proportional to thrust \(F_T\):

\[M_{\mathrm{TVC}} = F_T \cdot d_T \cdot \sin(\delta_T)\tag{20.52}\]

where \(d_T\) is the moment arm and \(\delta_T\) the nozzle deflection. The autopilot blends aerodynamic and TVC control according to dynamic pressure:

\[\delta_{\text{total}} = W_{aero}(q_\infty)\,\delta_{aero} + W_{TVC}(q_\infty)\,\delta_{TVC}\tag{20.53}\]

with \(W_{aero} + W_{TVC} = 1\) and weights varying linearly from \(W_{TVC}=1\) at launch to \(W_{TVC}=0\) at maximum speed.

docs.title: 20.11.1 Coordinate Frames
docs.text:
Four frames are required in a full 6-DOF simulation:

Inertial (I) Earth-Centred Inertial (ECI) or local NED; origin at launch point; non-rotating (or slowly rotating for long-range). Body (B) Origin at CG; \(x_B\) forward, \(y_B\) starboard, \(z_B\) down. Wind (W) \(x_W\) along velocity vector; \(z_W\) in plane of symmetry. Seeker Origin at seeker gimbal pivot; aligned with seeker LOS.

The Direction Cosine Matrix \(\mathbf{C}_B^I\) transforms vectors from body to inertial:

\[\mathbf{v}^I = \mathbf{C}_B^I\,\mathbf{v}^B\tag{20.54}\]

\(\mathbf{C}_B^I\) is a \(3\times3\) orthogonal matrix parameterised by Euler angles \((\phi, \theta, \psi)\):

\[\mathbf{C}_B^I = R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\phi)\tag{20.55}\]

docs.title: 20.11.2 Quaternion Attitude Representation
docs.text:
Euler angles suffer from gimbal lock (\(\theta \to \pm 90°\)). Quaternions avoid this:

\[\mathbf{q} = [q_0,\; q_1,\; q_2,\; q_3]^\top, \quad q_0^2 + q_1^2 + q_2^2 + q_3^2 = 1\tag{20.56}\]

The kinematic differential equation:

\[\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\Xi}(\mathbf{q})\,\boldsymbol{\omega}\tag{20.57}\]

where:

\[\boldsymbol{\Xi}(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix} -q_1 & -q_2 & -q_3 \\ q_0 & -q_3 & q_2 \\ q_3 & q_0 & -q_1 \\ -q_2 & q_1 & q_0 \end{bmatrix}\tag{20.58}\]

and \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = [p, q, r]^\top\) is the body angular rate vector. The quaternion must be renormalised at each integration step to prevent drift.

docs.title: 20.11.3 Equations of Motion
docs.text:
The full 6-DOF rigid body equations in the body frame:

Force equations:

\[\begin{align*} m(\dot{u} + qw - rv) &= F_x \\ m(\dot{v} + ru - pw) &= F_y \\ m(\dot{w} + pv - qu) &= F_z \end{align*}\]

Moment equations (Euler’s equations):

\[\begin{align*} I_{xx}\dot{p} - (I_{yy}-I_{zz})qr &= L \\ I_{yy}\dot{q} - (I_{zz}-I_{xx})pr &= M \\ I_{zz}\dot{r} - (I_{xx}-I_{yy})pq &= N \end{align*}\]

where \((u,v,w)\) are body-frame velocity components, \((p,q,r)\) angular rates, \((F_x,F_y,F_z)\) total body forces, \((L,M,N)\) total body moments, and \(I_{xx},I_{yy},I_{zz}\) principal moments of inertia.

docs.title: 20.11.4 Aerodynamic Coefficient Tables
docs.text:
Aerodynamic forces and moments are represented as tabulated functions of:

  • Mach number \(M\): typically \(0.3\)–\(5.0\) in 20–30 increments

  • Angle of attack \(\alpha\): \(-20°\) to \(+20°\) for small \(\alpha\); \(0°\)–\(180°\) for ballistic re-entry

  • Sideslip angle \(\beta\): \(-20°\) to \(+20°\)

  • Control deflection \(\delta\): \(-20°\) to \(+20°\)

Forces:

\[\begin{align*} L &= q_\infty S\,C_L(\alpha, M) \\ D &= q_\infty S\,C_D(\alpha, M) \\ Y &= q_\infty S\,C_Y(\beta, M) \end{align*}\]

Bilinear interpolation between table entries:

\[C_L(\alpha, M) \approx C_L(\alpha_1, M_1) + \frac{\partial C_L}{\partial \alpha}\Delta\alpha + \frac{\partial C_L}{\partial M}\Delta M\tag{20.68}\]

docs.title: 20.11.5 Actuator Model
docs.text:
The actuator is modelled as a first-order system with rate and position limits:

\[\frac{\delta(s)}{\delta_c(s)} = \frac{\omega_A}{s + \omega_A}\tag{20.69}\]

with limits:

\[\begin{align*} |\delta| &\leq \delta_{\max} \quad\text{(position limit, e.g. }{\pm 20°}) \\ |\dot{\delta}| &\leq \dot{\delta}_{\max} \quad\text{(rate limit, e.g. }150°/\text{s)} \end{align*}\]

Rate limiting is the dominant nonlinearity at high-frequency inputs and can destabilise the autopilot (pilot-induced oscillation analogue).

docs.title: 20.11.6 Monte Carlo Analysis
docs.text:
Deterministic 6-DOF simulation gives the nominal trajectory. Practical performance is assessed by Monte Carlo (MC) simulation:

  1. Define dispersions: sensor errors, IMU biases, aerodynamic coefficient uncertainty, target manoeuvre model, launch condition errors.

  2. Run \(N_{\mathrm{MC}} = 1000\)–\(10\,000\) trials, each with independently sampled dispersions.

  3. Compute miss distance CDF. CEP = median of \(|\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{miss}}|\).

  4. Compute Pk (probability of kill) using warhead lethal radius \(R_L\): \(P_k = 1 - \exp(-R_L^2 / (2\sigma_m^2))\) (Gaussian assumption).

Table 20.6. Typical 6-DOF simulation dispersion sources Parameter Symbol Typical \(1\sigma\) Value Gyro drift \(\varepsilon\) \(0.1\)–\(1.0\;\text{° h}\) Accel. bias \(b_a\) \(100\)–\(300\;\text{g}\) Seeker angle noise \(\sigma_q\) \(0.5\)–\(2\;\text{m r a d}\) \(C_N\) uncertainty \(\Delta C_N/C_N\) \(5\)–\(10\%\) Wind (cross) \(\sigma_w\) \(2\)–\(5\;\text{m s}\) Target position \(\sigma_{T}\) \(5\)–\(50\;\text{m}\) Target manoeuvre \(\sigma_{a_T}\) \(3\)–\(9g\)

docs.title: 20.11.7 Target Models in Simulation
docs.text: Constant velocity (CV) \(\ddot{\mathbf{r}}_T = 0\). Simplest; used for initial design. Constant acceleration (CA) \(\dddot{\mathbf{r}}_T = 0\). Accounts for steady manoeuvre. Singer model Target acceleration is first-order Markov with manoeuvre time constant \(\tau_T = 1\,\text{s}\)–\(5\,\text{s}\) and manoeuvre magnitude \(\sigma_{a_T} = 3g\)–\(9g\). Evasive weave Sinusoidal lateral acceleration at \(f = 0.1\)–\(0.5\,\text{Hz}\); adversarial case. Jink Random step accelerations; statistically specified.

docs.title: 20.12.1 Integrated Guidance and Control (IGC)
docs.text:
Traditional designs separate the guidance (outer) and autopilot (inner) loops with a clear time-scale separation. Integrated Guidance and Control merges the two, directly commanding control surface deflections from the target state:

\[\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{IGC}} = -\mathbf{B}^{-1}\bigl[\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{e}\bigr]\tag{20.72}\]

where \(\mathbf{e}\) is the full state error and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the control effectiveness matrix. IGC is particularly beneficial at high angles of attack and when fin authority is limited (agile AAMs).

docs.title: 20.12.2 Sliding Mode Guidance
docs.text:
The sliding surface \(s = \dot{\lambda} + c\lambda = 0\) defines the desired zero-miss manifold. The sliding mode guidance law:

\[a_c = N V_c \dot{\lambda} + k\,\mathrm{sign}(s)\tag{20.73}\]

provides robustness against target manoeuvre and model uncertainty at the cost of chattering (finite switching frequency). Higher-order SMC (HOSMC) reduces chattering.

docs.title: 20.12.3 Model Predictive Guidance (MPG)
docs.text:
At each time step, a finite-horizon optimisation is solved:

\[\min_{u_0,…,u_{N-1}} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\!\bigl[\ell(\mathbf{x}_k,u_k)\bigr] + V_f(\mathbf{x}_N)\tag{20.74}\]

subject to: \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_k, u_k)\), \(|u_k| \leq u_{\max}\), \(\mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f\).

MPG can handle mixed objectives (miss distance + arrival time + impact angle) and explicit control constraints. Real-time implementation requires warm-starting and quadratic programming (QP) solvers (\(<\!1\,\text{ms}\) with current FPGA implementations).

docs.title: 20.12.4 Machine Learning in GNC
docs.text:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated guidance laws competitive with optimal guidance in simulation:

  • Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) trained against evasive manoeuvring targets; achieves near-optimal miss distance

  • Neural network autopilots for non-linear flight regimes (post-stall)

  • Sensor fusion using deep convolutional networks for passive infrared homing (IIR terminal guidance)

Challenges: certification; training data coverage; adversarial robustness. No fielded system (as of 2025) relies on RL for the primary guidance law.

docs.title: 20.12.5 Multi-Hypothesis Target Tracking
docs.text:
When a target is obscured or when multiple objects are detected, the Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) filter maintains multiple hypotheses:

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \sum_{j=0}^M \beta_j^k\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k}^{(j)}\tag{20.75}\]

where \(\beta_j^k\) are posterior probabilities of association with measurement \(j\). The Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) estimator handles target mode changes (non-manoeuvring \(\to\) manoeuvring):

\[p_i^k = \frac{\Lambda_i^k \sum_j \mu_j^{k-1} p_{ji}} {\sum_i \Lambda_i^k \sum_j \mu_j^{k-1} p_{ji}}\tag{20.76}\]

where \(\Lambda_i^k\) is the likelihood of measurement under model \(i\) and \(p_{ji}\) is the transition probability.

docs.title: 20.13 Summary
docs.text:
Table 20.7 summarises the guidance systems discussed in this chapter with their performance characteristics.

Table 20.7. Guidance system performance summary Guidance Type Sensor Required Typical CEP Representative System PNG (IR seeker) Passive IR 3–10 m AIM-9X Sidewinder PNG (active radar) Active radar seeker 1–5 m AIM-120 AMRAAM CLOS/SACLOS Tracker + wire/radio 0.5–2 m Milan ATGM TVM Seeker + ground radar 5–20 m Patriot PAC-2 INS + GPS GPS + IMU 5–30 m JDAM INS + TERCOM + DSMAC Radar alt + EO + IMU 5–10 m Tomahawk Block IV INS + GPS + IIR GPS + IMU + IR FPA 1–3 m SDB II

The chapter has shown that guidance law design is fundamentally an optimal control problem, navigation is a stochastic state estimation problem, and autopilot design is a classical control synthesis problem — the three disciplines converging in the closed-loop GNC system. Future trends include integrated guidance-and-control, real-time MPC, AI/ML guidance laws, and multi-missile cooperative engagement.

docs.title: 21.1 Seeker Systems
docs.text:
Seeker systems constitute the perceptual front-end of a guided weapon. They measure the angular relationship between the missile body axis and the optical, electromagnetic, or acoustic line-of-sight (LOS) to the target, and they generate the angular rate signal that feeds the proportional navigation (PN) guidance law. Modern seekers combine precision stabilised gimbals, sophisticated detector arrays, and embedded signal processors into packages that must survive launch shock, sustain tracking through violent manoeuvring, and resist deliberate countermeasures—all within severe constraints on mass, volume, and cost.

This chapter treats each seeker modality in systematic engineering depth: infrared (IR), imaging infrared (IIR), semi-active and active radar, laser and electro-optical, and multi-mode architectures. Signal processing, gimbal design, hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL) testing, and future technologies complete the treatment.

docs.title: 21.2.1 Purpose and Information Flow
docs.text:
The primary function of a seeker is to measure the angular error between the missile longitudinal axis and the target LOS, and to differentiate that angle to produce the LOS rate vector \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} = [\dot{\lambda}_{az},\,\dot{\lambda}_{el}]^\top\). This two-component signal is the essential input to the proportional navigation (PN) guidance law:

\[\mathbf{a}_{c} = N' V_{c}\, \dot{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\tag{21.1}\]

where \(N'\) is the effective navigation ratio (typically 3–5), \(V_c\) is the closing velocity, and \(\mathbf{a}_c\) is the commanded lateral acceleration perpendicular to the current LOS. Any error or noise in \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\) propagates directly into miss distance; therefore seeker noise is the dominant performance driver in the terminal phase of flight.

docs.title: 21.2.2 Geometric Relationships
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{r}\) be the missile-to-target relative position vector. The LOS angle in the inertial frame is:

\[\lambda = \arctan\!\left(\frac{r_y}{r_x}\right)\tag{21.2}\]

and the LOS rate is:

\[\dot{\lambda} = \frac{r_x \dot{r}_y - r_y \dot{r}_x}{r_x^2 + r_y^2} = \frac{\dot{r}_\perp}{r}\tag{21.3}\]

where \(\dot{r}_\perp\) is the component of relative velocity perpendicular to the LOS and \(r = |\boldsymbol{r}|\). For an unguided (constant-velocity) collision course \(\dot{\lambda} = 0\); any deviation indicates the geometry is not collision and guidance is required.

docs.title: 21.2.3 Gimbal Stabilisation
docs.text:
In the inertial frame the seeker must hold its optical axis on the target regardless of missile body motion. This is achieved through a gyroscopically stabilised gimbal. An inner-loop rate gyro (mounted on the gimbal itself) measures gimbal inertial angular rate \(\dot{\theta}_{gimbal}\) and drives a torque motor to null the residual error. The closed-loop transfer function of the stabilisation loop is:

\[\frac{\dot{\theta}_{gimbal}(s)}{\dot{\theta}_{body}(s)} = \frac{K_s}{s + K_s}\tag{21.4}\]

where \(K_s\) is the stabilisation loop gain (typically 200–500 rad/s). The residual coupling from body motion to apparent LOS rate is:

\[\dot{\lambda}_{parasite} = \dot{\theta}_{body}\cdot\frac{s}{s+K_s}\tag{21.5}\]

For \(K_s = 300\) rad/s, the body coupling at 3 Hz (typical airframe bending mode) is attenuated by 20 dB.

docs.title: 21.2.4 Tracking Bandwidth and Noise
docs.text:
The seeker tracker must follow target angular motion, which may reach angular rates of 30–40 rad/s in a high-closing-speed engagement. The tracking bandwidth \(\omega_T\) (inner angle-tracking loop) must satisfy:

\[\omega_T \geq 2\,\dot{\lambda}_{max} / \varepsilon_{max}\tag{21.6}\]

where \(\varepsilon_{max}\) is the maximum allowable track lag. Typical values are \(\omega_T = 10\)–50 rad/s.

Seeker noise is characterised by the noise equivalent angle (NEA), \(\sigma_\lambda\), and the resulting LOS-rate noise density \(S_{\dot{\lambda}}(\omega)\). Via adjoint analysis, the contribution to miss distance variance is:

\[\sigma_{miss}^2 = \int_0^\infty S_{\dot{\lambda}}(\omega)\, \left|H_{miss}(j\omega)\right|^2 d\omega\tag{21.7}\]

where \(H_{miss}\) is the adjoint transfer function from LOS-rate noise to miss distance. A rule of thumb for PN guidance with \(N'=4\) is:

\[\sigma_{miss} \approx \frac{V_c\,t_{go}^2}{6}\,\sigma_{\dot{\lambda}}\tag{21.8}\]

where \(t_{go}\) is the time-to-go and \(\sigma_{\dot{\lambda}}\) is the RMS LOS-rate noise. This highlights why seeker noise is so consequential in the last few seconds of flight.

docs.title: 21.2.5 Signal-to-Noise Ratio Requirement
docs.text:
Reliable track-lock requires a minimum SNR at the detector or receiver:

\[\mathrm{SNR}_{min} = 10\;\text{dB} \quad\text{(track maintenance)}\tag{21.9}\]

Below this threshold, the tracking loop loses coherence and track is broken. Acquisition typically requires SNR \(\geq\) 15 dB to ensure unambiguous lock-on. The seeker designer must verify that SNR exceeds these thresholds across the entire engagement envelope: maximum range, minimum target signature, and worst-case atmospheric conditions.

Table 21.1. Key seeker performance parameters and typical values Parameter Symbol Typical Range LOS rate output range \(\dot{\lambda}\) \(\pm\)30–60 rad/s Tracking bandwidth \(\omega_T\) 10–50 rad/s Stabilisation bandwidth \(K_s\) 200–500 rad/s Noise equivalent angle NEA 0.05–0.5 mrad (IR); 0.1–1 mrad (radar) Boresight error BER \(<\)0.5 mrad Gimbal angle range — \(\pm\)35–60\(^\circ\) Acquisition FOV — \(\pm\)5–30\(^\circ\) Track SNR requirement SNR \(>\)10 dB Acquisition SNR SNR \(>\)15 dB

docs.title: 21.3.1 Overview and Detector Bands
docs.text:
Infrared seekers detect the thermal emission and reflected IR radiation from the target. The atmosphere has two primary transmission windows exploited by IR seekers:

  • MWIR (mid-wave IR): 3–5 \(\mu\)m — dominated by hot exhaust gas (CO\(_2\), H\(_2\)O emission bands near 4.3 \(\mu\)m) and hot metal surfaces. Detectors: InSb cooled to 77 K; HgCdTe (MCT).

  • LWIR (long-wave IR): 8–12 \(\mu\)m — aerodynamic heating and body skin emission; ambient background objects; uncooled bolometers are feasible. Detectors: uncooled VOx microbolometer; cooled MCT.

  • SWIR (short-wave IR): 1–2.5 \(\mu\)m — reflected solar illumination; laser spot (1064 nm, 1550 nm); InGaAs photodiode arrays; no cooling required.

Table 21.2. IR seeker detector materials and operating characteristics Material Band (\(\mu\)m) \(T_{op}\) (K) D\(^*\) (Jones) Cooling Application InSb 3–5 77 \(>10^{11}\) Stirling MWIR seeker HgCdTe (MCT) 3–5 / 8–12 77–120 \(>10^{11}\) Stirling Dual-band, LWIR VOx microbolometer 8–14 300 \(\sim10^9\) None Uncooled LWIR InGaAs 0.9–1.7 300 \(\sim10^{10}\) TEC (271 K) SWIR, laser PbS 1–3 243 \(\sim10^{10}\) TEC Older MWIR QWIP 8–9 70 \(\sim10^{10}\) Stirling LWIR FPA

D\(^*\) is the specific detectivity in cm\(\cdot\)Hz\(^{1/2}\)/W (Jones).

docs.title: 21.3.2 Reticle-Based Point-Source Seekers
docs.text:
Early and low-cost IR seekers use a reticle (chopper disc) to modulate the incoming target spot and derive angle-error information.

SpinScan (Amplitude Modulation).

A spinning reticle with alternating transparent and opaque sectors amplitude-modulates the target spot at frequency \(f_r = \Omega/2\pi\). When the target is centred on the optical axis the modulation depth is zero; off-axis, the signal amplitude is proportional to the angular error \(\varepsilon\) and the phase of the modulation relative to a reference encoder gives the error direction:

\[V_{signal}(t) = A\,\varepsilon\,\cos(\Omega t - \phi_{dir})\tag{21.10}\]

where \(\phi_{dir}\) is the azimuth direction of the target offset. SpinScan is susceptible to background bias: a uniform hot cloud can produce a false signal.

ConScan (Conical Scan).

The optical axis is nutated (precessed) around the seeker axis at rate \(\Omega\). When on-target the signal strength is constant; an off-axis target modulates signal amplitude at \(\Omega\). The error signal is:

\[\varepsilon_{AZ} = K_{cs}\,A_{ac}\cos\phi; \qquad \varepsilon_{EL} = K_{cs}\,A_{ac}\sin\phi\tag{21.11}\]

where \(A_{ac}\) is the AC amplitude and \(K_{cs}\) is a scale factor. ConScan is less susceptible to uniform background but vulnerable to amplitude-modulated jamming at frequency \(\Omega\).

Rosette Scan.

The spot traces a rosette pattern covering the FOV. Acquisition capability is superior to SpinScan; used in Stinger (POST variant). The scan pattern is generated by superposing two circular motions:

\[x(t) = A\cos(\omega_1 t) + B\cos(\omega_2 t); \quad y(t) = A\sin(\omega_1 t) + B\sin(\omega_2 t)\tag{21.12}\]

where \(\omega_1,\,\omega_2\) are incommensurate to ensure dense coverage.

docs.title: 21.3.3 Imaging IR (IIR) Seekers
docs.text:
IIR seekers replace the single-element detector and reticle with a focal plane array (FPA), producing a full 2D thermal image of the scene at each frame. This transforms the seeker into an imaging sensor and enables:

  • Target shape recognition and discrimination

  • Aimpoint selection at a specific vulnerable zone

  • Robust IRCCM via image-based tracking algorithms

  • Lock-on at longer ranges due to larger detector area

FPA Specifications.

Current military FPAs are typically \(320\times256\) or \(640\times512\) elements, with pixel pitch 15–30 \(\mu\)m and readout integrated circuits (ROICs) providing integration time control, non-uniformity correction (NUC), and serial digital output. The NETD (noise equivalent temperature difference) for cooled MCT arrays is 20–50 mK; for uncooled bolometers it is 30–80 mK.

The number of target pixels at range \(R\) is:

\[N_{pix} = \frac{A_{target}}{R^2} \cdot \frac{f^2}{p^2}\tag{21.13}\]

where \(f\) is focal length and \(p\) is pixel pitch. Reliable tracking requires \(N_{pix} \geq 4\); ATR requires \(N_{pix} \geq 25\)–64.

docs.title: 21.3.4 Stirling Cryocooler
docs.text:
Cooled detectors (InSb, MCT) require operation at 77 K. Linear Stirling cryocoolers are the standard solution:

  • Input power: 1.5–5 W electrical

  • Cool-down time: 3–10 minutes (typically reduced to \(<\)90 s for tactical seekers via pre-cooled dewar strategies)

  • MTBF: 5000–8000 h (military-grade)

  • Mass: 80–300 g depending on cooling capacity

  • Vibration export: \(<\)0.5 g at compressor frequency; requires dual-piston or active cancellation

The thermodynamic COP (coefficient of performance) of the Stirling cycle:

\[\mathrm{COP} = \frac{Q_{cold}}{W_{input}} = \eta_{Stirling}\,\frac{T_{cold}}{T_{hot}-T_{cold}}\tag{21.14}\]

where \(\eta_{Stirling} \approx 0.3\)–0.5 for practical devices.

docs.title: 21.3.5 Seeker Dome Materials
docs.text:
The forward dome must be transparent in the seeker’s spectral band, withstand aerodynamic heating, and survive rain erosion at high speed.

Table 21.3. Seeker dome material properties Material Band \(n\) \(T_{max}\) (\(^\circ\)C) \(k_T\) (W/mK) MOR (MPa) Germanium 2–15 \(\mu\)m 4.0 400 59 100 Zinc Sulphide 0.4–12 \(\mu\)m 2.2 650 18 103 Zinc Selenide 0.6–16 \(\mu\)m 2.4 300 18 55 Sapphire (\(c\)-cut) 0.2–5 \(\mu\)m 1.6 1600 30 400 ALON (AlON) 0.2–5 \(\mu\)m 1.78 1200 12 300 Silicon 1.2–7 \(\mu\)m 3.4 700 150 130 Spinel (MgAlO) 0.2–5 \(\mu\)m 1.73 1200 15 195

\(n\) = refractive index at band centre; \(k_T\) = thermal conductivity; MOR = modulus of rupture. Germanium is the most common LWIR dome; sapphire and ALON are preferred for high-speed (\(>\)Mach 2) applications where kinetic heating is severe.

docs.title: 21.3.6 Lock-On Range
docs.text:
The IR seeker lock-on range is derived from the radiometric link equation. Irradiance at the detector from a target of intensity \(I_{target}\) (W/sr) at range \(R\) after atmospheric transmission \(\tau_{atm}\):

\[E_{det} = \frac{I_{target}\,\tau_{atm}\,A_{opt}}{R^2}\tag{21.15}\]

Setting \(E_{det} \cdot A_{det} = \mathrm{SNR}_{req}\cdot \mathrm{NEP}\) and solving for \(R\):

\[R_{lock} = \sqrt{\frac{I_{target}\,\tau_{atm}\,A_{opt}\,A_{det}} {\mathrm{SNR}_{req}\cdot\mathrm{NEP}}}\tag{21.16}\]

Equivalently, in terms of the detector specific detectivity \(D^*\):

\[R_{lock} = D^*\,\sqrt{\frac{I_{target}\,\tau_{atm}\,A_{opt}} {\mathrm{SNR}_{req}\cdot\sqrt{A_{det}\,\Delta f}}}\tag{21.17}\]

where \(\Delta f\) is the noise bandwidth of the pre-detection filter.

docs.title: 21.3.7 IRCCM Techniques
docs.text:
Infrared countercountermeasures (IRCCM) protect the seeker against flares, laser jammers, and directed IR jamming. Major techniques:

Dual-band discrimination: Compare MWIR and LWIR signatures. Targets have characteristic spectral ratios; flares typically emit differently (flares peak in MWIR; plume peak in LWIR varies). A discrimination threshold \(R_{band} = I_{MWIR}/I_{LWIR}\) is compared against the expected target ratio. Kinematic rejection: Flares decelerate rapidly after ejection. The seeker tracks the rate of change of angular velocity; a genuine target maintains consistent kinematics, while a flare diverges rapidly. Spectral discrimination: High-resolution spectral analysis identifies CO\(_2\) and H\(_2\)O emission features unique to jet exhaust. Flares (magnesium-based) have different spectra. Image processing / shape tracking (IIR):

With FPA-based seekers, the target shape (fuselage, wing planform, exhaust nozzle) is tracked via template matching. Flares are compact point sources with different morphology. Normalised cross-correlation:

\[\mathrm{NCC}(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{\sum_{x,y} [I(x,y)-\bar{I}][T(x-u_x,y-u_y)-\bar{T}]} {\sqrt{\sum_{x,y}[I-\bar{I}]^2\sum_{x,y}[T-\bar{T}]^2}}\tag{21.18}\] Jam-to-signal ratio monitoring: The seeker processor monitors sudden signal-level jumps indicative of DIRCM (directed IR countermeasure) illumination and triggers IRCCM logic.

docs.title: 21.4.1 Semi-Active Radar Homing (SARH)
docs.text:
In SARH, the launch platform maintains a CW or pulsed-CW radar illumination on the target. The missile receiver tracks the reflected signal. The radar equation for the bistatic SARH link is:

\[P_r = \frac{P_t\,G_t\,G_r\,\sigma\,\lambda^2} {(4\pi)^3\,R_t^2\,R_m^2\,L}\tag{21.19}\]

where \(R_t\) is the illuminator-to-target range, \(R_m\) is the missile-to-target range, \(\sigma\) is the target radar cross-section, and \(L\) is the total system loss.

Doppler Processing.

The closing rate between missile and target is measured from the Doppler shift:

\[f_d = \frac{2\,f_0\,V_c}{c} = \frac{2\,V_c}{\lambda}\tag{21.20}\]

where \(V_c = -\dot{r}\) is the closing velocity and \(f_0\) is the carrier frequency. For \(f_0 = 10\) GHz and \(V_c = 500\) m/s, \(f_d = 33.3\) kHz. The Doppler filter centred on the expected \(f_d\) improves clutter rejection.

Monopulse Angle Tracking.

Angle measurement in SARH uses monopulse processing. A four-horn or five-horn cluster forms sum (\(\Sigma\)) and difference (\(\Delta_{AZ}\), \(\Delta_{EL}\)) beams. The angle error in azimuth is:

\[\varepsilon_{AZ} = k_{mon}\,\frac{\mathrm{Re}(\Delta_{AZ}/\Sigma)} {|\Sigma|^2/|\Sigma|^2} = k_{mon}\,\frac{\Delta_{AZ}}{\Sigma}\tag{21.21}\]

where \(k_{mon}\) is the monopulse slope (rad\(^{-1}\)). The monopulse technique is instantaneous (single pulse) and is immune to amplitude-modulated jamming that defeats sequential lobing.

docs.title: 21.4.2 Active Radar Homing (ARH)
docs.text:
Active seekers carry their own transmitter, making the weapon fire-and-forget after launch. The monostatic radar equation is:

\[P_r = \frac{P_t\,G^2\,\sigma\,\lambda^2} {(4\pi)^3\,R^4\,L}\tag{21.22}\]

where all quantities now refer to the seeker alone. The required minimum \(P_t\) to achieve lock at range \(R_{lock}\) with \(\mathrm{SNR}_{req}\) is:

\[P_t = \frac{(4\pi)^3\,R_{lock}^4\,k\,T_s\,B_n\,F\,\mathrm{SNR}_{req}\,L} {G^2\,\sigma\,\lambda^2}\tag{21.23}\]

and the SNR-limited lock-on range:

\[R_{lock} = \left[\frac{P_t\,G^2\,\sigma\,\lambda^2\,\tau\,B_n} {(4\pi)^3\,k\,T\,F\,\mathrm{SNR}_{req}\,L}\right]^{1/4}\tag{21.24}\]

Waveform Design.

Modern ARH seekers use Linear Frequency Modulated (LFM) pulse compression. A pulse of bandwidth \(B\) yields range resolution:

\[\delta R = \frac{c}{2B}\tag{21.25}\]

For \(B = 500\) MHz, \(\delta R = 0.3\) m. The time-bandwidth product (pulse compression ratio) is \(TB\); typical values are 100–1000. Velocity resolution from coherent integration of \(N\) pulses over integration time \(T_c\):

\[\delta v = \frac{\lambda}{2\,T_c}\tag{21.26}\]

AESA Seeker.

Active electronically scanned array (AESA) seekers replace the mechanically gimballed antenna with a phased array. A planar array of \(M\times N\) transmit/receive (T/R) modules provides:

  • Electronic beam steering at \(\pm\)60\(^\circ\) without mechanical motion

  • Simultaneous multiple beams for guidance + ESM functions

  • Bandwidth 1–5 GHz enabling pulse compression

  • Low probability of intercept (LPI) waveforms

  • Monopulse angle accuracy: \(\sigma_\theta \approx \theta_{3dB}/(2\sqrt{2\,SNR})\)

The beam steering phase shift for element \((m,n)\) to steer to angle \((\theta,\phi)\):

\[\psi_{mn} = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(m\,d_x\sin\theta\cos\phi + n\,d_y\sin\theta\sin\phi)\tag{21.27}\]

Constant False Alarm Rate (CFAR) Detection.

CFAR processing adapts the detection threshold to the local clutter level. In cell-averaging CFAR (CA-CFAR) with \(N\) reference cells:

\[T_{CFAR} = \alpha\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\tag{21.28}\]

where \(\alpha\) is the threshold multiplier chosen to achieve the desired false alarm rate \(P_{fa}\):

\[\alpha = N\left(P_{fa}^{-1/N} - 1\right)\tag{21.29}\]

docs.title: 21.4.3 Anti-Radiation Seeker (Passive)
docs.text:
Anti-radiation missiles (ARMs) home on the target’s own electromagnetic emissions, requiring no illumination from the launch platform.

Wide-Band ESM Receiver.

Coverage: 0.5–18 GHz (extendable to 40 GHz); instantaneous bandwidth typically 500 MHz with channelised or digital receiver scanning.

Interferometric Direction Finding.

Phase-difference interferometry using two antennas separated by baseline \(d\):

\[\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi\,d\,\sin\theta}{\lambda}\tag{21.30}\]

Solving for target bearing:

\[\theta = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{\lambda\,\Delta\phi}{2\pi\,d}\right)\tag{21.31}\]

Angle accuracy: \(\sigma_\theta = \lambda/(2\pi\,d\,\sqrt{\mathrm{SNR}})\). For \(d = 0.5\) m, \(f = 10\) GHz, SNR \(=20\) dB, \(\sigma_\theta \approx 0.1\) mrad.

Memory Mode.

When the target radar is switched off, the ARM’s inertial navigation system maintains the last-known LOS direction and the seeker continues guiding toward the estimated target location. Updated bearing estimates from brief radar re-emissions are fused with the INS propagated position.

docs.title: 21.4.4 ECCM in Active Radar Seekers
docs.text:
• Frequency agility: Pulse-to-pulse frequency hopping over \(>100\) MHz defeats narrowband noise jammers.

  • PRF agility: Randomised pulse repetition intervals defeat range-gate pull-off (RGPO) jamming.

  • LPI waveforms: Low peak power, wide bandwidth, random modulation reduces probability of intercept by target ESM receivers.

  • Adaptive CFAR: Detects jamming-induced threshold elevation; uses alternative reference cells.

  • Home-on-jam (HOJ): If a jammer is sufficiently powerful, the seeker switches from radar tracking to passive tracking of the jammer beam.

docs.title: 21.5.1 Semi-Active Laser (SAL) Homing
docs.text:
SAL seekers require a laser designator (airborne, ground-based, or SOF-carried) to illuminate the target. The designator pulses at a coded pulse repetition frequency (PRF) and the seeker’s quadrant photodetector measures the centroid of the returned laser spot.

Wavelengths and Atmospheric Windows.

  • \(\lambda = 1064\) nm: Nd:YAG; most common; good Si detector response; atmospheric transmission excellent in clear air.

  • \(\lambda = 1550\) nm: Er:glass fibre laser; eye-safe at Class 1 power levels at range; requires InGaAs detector.

  • \(\lambda = 532\) nm: frequency-doubled Nd:YAG; visible; limited tactical use.

Quadrant Detector Angle Sensing.

The quadrant (four-element) detector produces four signals \(Q_A\)–\(Q_D\). Angle error signals:

\[\varepsilon_{AZ} = K_Q\,\frac{(Q_A + Q_D) - (Q_B + Q_C)} {Q_A + Q_B + Q_C + Q_D}\tag{21.32}\] \[\varepsilon_{EL} = K_Q\,\frac{(Q_A + Q_B) - (Q_C + Q_D)} {Q_A + Q_B + Q_C + Q_D}\tag{21.33}\]

The normalisation by total signal makes the angle measurement independent of absolute signal level. \(K_Q\) is the quadrant detector scale factor (rad/\(\Delta\)signal).

Radiometric Link Equation.

The received power at the detector from a Lambertian target (reflectivity \(\rho\), area \(A_{spot}\), cosine factor \(\cos\theta\)):

\[P_r = \frac{E_L\,\rho\,A_{det}\,\tau_{atm}^2\,\cos\theta} {\pi\,R^2\,\Omega_{spot}}\tag{21.34}\]

where \(E_L\) is the designator pulse energy (J), \(\Omega_{spot}\) is the solid angle of the laser spot, and \(\tau_{atm}^2\) accounts for two-way atmospheric attenuation.

Atmospheric Attenuation.

Beer–Lambert law for laser propagation:

\[I(R) = I_0\,\exp(-\beta R)\tag{21.35}\]

where the attenuation coefficient \(\beta\) (m\(^{-1}\)) combines molecular absorption \(\beta_{mol}\) and aerosol scattering \(\beta_{aer}\):

\[\beta = \beta_{mol} + \beta_{aer}\tag{21.36}\]

For \(\lambda = 1064\) nm in clear air, \(\beta \approx 0.1\)–0.3 km\(^{-1}\); in moderate haze, \(\beta \approx 0.5\)–1 km\(^{-1}\); in thick smoke, \(\beta\) can exceed 5 km\(^{-1}\).

PRF Coding.

The designator transmits coded pulse trains (typically 4–8 pulse sequences) to prevent fratricide. The seeker performs temporal pattern matching:

\[\hat{c} = \arg\max_{c}\sum_{k} y(t_k)\cdot p_c(t_k)\tag{21.37}\]

where \(y(t_k)\) are the received pulse timestamps and \(p_c\) is the expected pattern for code \(c\).

Accuracy.

SAL seekers achieve CEP \(<\) 1–3 m in clear conditions. Accuracy degrades in turbulence (beam wander \(\sigma_{BW} \propto C_n^2 R^{11/6}\)) and smoke obscuration.

docs.title: 21.5.2 Active Laser (LADAR) Terminal Seeker
docs.text:
Missile-borne pulsed LADAR provides 3D point-cloud imagery of the target in the terminal phase. Range measurement:

\[R = \frac{c\,\Delta t}{2}\tag{21.38}\]

with timing accuracy \(\sigma_{\Delta t} \approx 0.1\) ns giving \(\sigma_R \approx 15\) mm. Flash LADAR illuminates the entire scene in one pulse, producing a \(128\times128\) range/intensity image per shot. Applications include:

  • Aimpoint selection on 3D target model (e.g., engine intake vs. cockpit vs. fuel tank)

  • Decoy discrimination by 3D shape comparison

  • Terminal navigation update: compare measured point-cloud to stored 3D target model; CEP \(<\) 0.1 m achievable

docs.title: 21.6.1 TV (Visible Band) Seekers
docs.text:
Television seekers use silicon CCD or CMOS arrays in the visible band (0.4–0.9 \(\mu\)m). Key characteristics:

  • Resolution: 640\(\times\)480 to 1920\(\times\)1080 pixels

  • Frame rate: 30–120 Hz

  • Tracking: centroid or correlation algorithm

  • Limitation: passive daylight only; cannot operate at night or in smoke/cloud

Centroid Tracker.

The target centroid in the image plane is computed as the intensity-weighted mean of the target-segmented pixels:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}} i\,I(i,j)} {\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}} I(i,j)}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}} j\,I(i,j)} {\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}} I(i,j)}\tag{21.39}\]

The angular error signals are then \(\varepsilon_{AZ} = (\bar{x} - x_c) \cdot \delta_{pix}\) and similarly for elevation, where \(\delta_{pix}\) is the pixel angular subtense (IFOV).

docs.title: 21.6.2 DSMAC: Digital Scene Matching Area Correlator
docs.text:
The Tomahawk cruise missile employs DSMAC as a terminal navigation update (TNI). A stored reference image of the target area (from satellite reconnaissance) is correlated with the live seeker image:

\[C(\mathbf{u}) = \sum_{x,y} I(x,y)\cdot T(x-u_x,\, y-u_y)\tag{21.40}\]

The peak of \(C(\mathbf{u})\) gives the displacement of the missile from the planned aimpoint. This correction is fed to the guidance computer to correct accumulated INS drift. DSMAC achieves CEP \(<\) 3–10 m even after long-range cruise.

docs.title: 21.6.3 Automatic Target Recognition (ATR)
docs.text:
Modern IIR and TV seekers incorporate CNN-based ATR. A neural network (typically MobileNetV3 or a bespoke lightweight architecture) is trained offline on thermal signature databases. Onboard inference:

\[\hat{c} = \arg\max_{c}\, P(class_c \mid \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta})\tag{21.41}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the image patch and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are the network weights stored in flash memory. ATR enables:

  • Classification of tank, APC, truck, helicopter, ship

  • Automatic selection of the high-value target in a scene containing multiple objects

  • Aimpoint offset selection (e.g., turret ring vs. engine deck)

  • Rejection of decoys whose thermal signature doesn’t match the target class

The ATR probability of correct identification (PID) must exceed 0.95 for autonomous operation; below this threshold, human-in-the-loop confirmation is required (man-on-the-loop ethics requirement).

docs.title: 21.7.1 Rationale and Architecture
docs.text:
No single seeker modality excels in all engagement conditions:

  • IR fails in cloud/smoke/flares

  • Radar is susceptible to ECM and has limited aimpoint precision

  • Laser requires target illumination and degrades in obscurants

  • EO is daylight-only

Multi-mode seekers combine two or more modalities on a shared gimbal to overcome individual limitations. Common pairings:

  • SAL + IIR (e.g., GBU-54 LJDAM concept, Dual Seeker variant): laser provides GPS-denied precision; IIR provides all-weather fallback.

  • ARH + IIR: active radar for acquisition at long range; IIR for precision terminal aimpointing.

  • ARH + SAL: fire-and-forget plus optional designator override; Brimstone dual-mode.

  • MMW + IIR: millimetre-wave radar penetrates smoke and cloud; IIR provides high-resolution aimpoint. Brimstone 2 uses this combination.

docs.title: 21.7.2 Fusion Algorithms
docs.text:
Weighted Combination.

The fused LOS rate estimate is a reliability-weighted sum:

\[\dot{\lambda}_{fused} = \frac{w_{IR}\,\dot{\lambda}_{IR} + w_{RF}\,\dot{\lambda}_{RF}} {w_{IR} + w_{RF}}\tag{21.42}\]

where \(w_k = 1/\sigma_{\dot{\lambda},k}^2\) are the inverse variance weights.

Interacting Multiple Model (IMM).

The IMM estimator maintains \(M\) parallel Kalman filters, each modelling a different target motion (constant velocity, constant acceleration, coordinated turn). The fused state estimate:

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_{k=1}^{M} \mu_k^{post}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k\tag{21.43}\]

where the model probabilities \(\mu_k^{post}\) are updated via Bayes’ rule on the likelihood of each model given the measurements. IMM provides smooth transitions between target motion modes and robustness against countermeasures.

Track-Before-Detect (TBD).

At low SNR (below the single-scan detection threshold), TBD integrates target energy across multiple scans before declaring detection. The optimal TBD test statistic is:

\[\Lambda = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log\frac{p(z_k | target)}{p(z_k | noise)}\tag{21.44}\]

compared against a threshold \(h\). TBD extends acquisition range by 20–40% compared to single-scan detection.

Table 21.4. Representative multi-mode seeker systems Missile Modes Freq/Band CEP Role AIM-9X Block II IIR MWIR 3–5 \(\mu\)m \(<\)1 m A-A AIM-120D ARH X-band AESA \(<\)5 m A-A Brimstone 2 MMW + SAL 94 GHz + 1064 nm \(<\)1 m A-G Javelin Dual-band IIR MWIR + LWIR \(<\)0.5 m A-T AGM-65H Maverick IIR MWIR \(<\)1 m A-G AGM-88E AARGM ARH + GPS X/Ku-band \(<\)3 m SEAD Spike-ER2 EO/IIR Vis + MWIR \(<\)0.5 m A-T

docs.title: 21.8.1 Gimbal Configurations
docs.text:
Two-Axis Gimbal (Pitch/Yaw).

The most common configuration for tactical missiles. The inner ring carries the detector/antenna and a rate gyro; the outer ring provides a second degree of freedom. The LOS is stabilised in two angular coordinates. Cross-coupling exists between axes; for small angles the coupling torque is:

\[\tau_{couple} = I_z\,(\omega_{body} \times \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{gyro})\tag{21.45}\]

Three-Axis Gimbal.

Full decoupled stabilisation; required for bank-to-turn (BTT) missiles where the body rolls. Adds mass and complexity; slip rings must carry signals through three axes. Total angular momentum of inner assembly must be minimised to reduce torque export from gimbal to airframe.

Strapdown Seeker.

Some modern designs (particularly IIR with very wide FPA) use a strapdown (fixed) detector and electronically stabilise the LOS by digitally de-rotating the image using IMU data. The angular compensation applied to pixel \((u,v)\):

\[\begin{pmatrix}u'\\v'\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{R}_{stab}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{body}) \begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}\tag{21.46}\]

Strapdown eliminates mechanical gimbal but requires very fast (>1000 Hz) IMU and image processing.

docs.title: 21.8.2 Stabilisation Loop Design
docs.text:
The inner stabilisation loop architecture uses a rate gyro on the gimbal to measure inertial angular rate \(\dot{\theta}_{gim}\) and drives a torque motor to null this rate:

\[G_{stab}(s) = \frac{K_p(1 + s/\omega_z)}{s(1 + s/\omega_p)}\tag{21.47}\]

where \(\omega_z\) is the lead compensator zero and \(\omega_p\) is the pole. Stability margins: gain margin \(>\)6 dB, phase margin \(>\)45\(^\circ\). The friction in gimbal bearings is a primary disturbance; flexure bearings (no contact friction) are used in precision seekers but limit angular range to \(\pm\)5–10\(^\circ\) and require an outer coarse gimbal.

docs.title: 21.8.3 Gimbal Angle Limits and Vignetting
docs.text:
The practical angular range of a gimballed seeker is \(\pm\)35–60\(^\circ\) from the missile boresight. Beyond this limit, vignetting (partial obscuration of the aperture by the dome rim or gimbal structure) reduces sensitivity. The vignetting transmission factor:

\[\tau_{vig}(\theta) = \cos(\theta/\theta_{max})\qquad \theta \leq \theta_{max}\tag{21.48}\]

This imposes a practical constraint on launch geometry: the missile must be pointed within \(\pm\)35\(^\circ\) of the target at launch for reliable acquisition.

docs.title: 21.8.4 Lock-Before-Launch vs Lock-After-Launch
docs.text: Lock-Before-Launch (LBL): The seeker is slaved (via databus) to the parent aircraft’s radar or IRST track. Before release, the seeker acquires the target and confirms lock (crosshair on track, SNR adequate). Only then does the pilot consent to release. Standard for short-range IR missiles (AIM-9, ASRAAM). Lock-After-Launch (LAL): The missile is released on a predicted bearing; after motor ignition the missile manoeuvres its seeker toward the target, acquires, and locks. Required when the target is beyond launch seeker acquisition range (long-range BVR engagements) or when rapid launch (spray-and-pray) tactics are used. The launch aircraft continues to provide target track updates via datalink until the seeker acquires.

docs.title: 21.9.1 Angle Tracking Filters
docs.text:
The seeker angle tracker maintains an estimate of target angular position and rate in the seeker frame. The Kalman filter state vector is:

\[\mathbf{x}_k = [\lambda_{AZ},\,\dot{\lambda}_{AZ},\,\lambda_{EL}, \,\dot{\lambda}_{EL}]^\top\tag{21.49}\]

with process model \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{w}_k\) where:

\[\mathbf{F} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & T & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & T\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\tag{21.50}\]

\(T\) is the sample interval (typ. 10–50 ms). Measurement noise covariance \(R = \sigma_{NEA}^2 \mathbf{I}\). Process noise covariance \(Q = q\,\mathrm{diag}(T^3/3,\, T,\, T^3/3,\, T)\) where \(q\) is the manoeuvre noise intensity.

docs.title: 21.9.2 Glint and Extended Target Effects
docs.text:
For an extended target (a ship, aircraft, or large vehicle), the radar or IR return originates from distributed scattering centres. The apparent centre of radiation wanders randomly—this is called glint. The glint noise spectral density is approximately:

\[S_{glint}(f) \approx \frac{\sigma_{glint}^2\,\tau_{glint}} {1 + (2\pi f \tau_{glint})^2}\tag{21.51}\]

where \(\sigma_{glint}\) is the RMS glint displacement (typically 0.1–0.5 of target extent) and \(\tau_{glint}\) is the correlation time (0.01–1 s). Glint is white noise at frequencies below \(1/(2\pi\tau_{glint})\) and is a significant terminal miss distance contributor for radar seekers engaging large targets.

docs.title: 21.9.3 MTI and Doppler Filtering
docs.text:
Moving Target Indication (MTI) processing rejects stationary clutter. A two-pulse MTI canceller output:

\[y_k = x_k - x_{k-1}\tag{21.52}\]

The MTI improvement factor for \(N\)-pulse canceller with target Doppler \(f_d\) and clutter spectral width \(\sigma_v\):

\[I_{MTI} = \frac{\mathrm{SNR}_{out}}{\mathrm{SNR}_{in}} = \frac{N}{\pi^2\,(2\sigma_v/\lambda)^2\,T_{PRI}^2}\tag{21.53}\]

For a pulse Doppler (PD) seeker the target return is isolated in the Doppler domain; the Doppler filter bank covers PRF/2 to PRF/2 with \(N_{FFT}\) bins, each of width \(\Delta f_d = PRF/N_{FFT}\).

docs.title: 21.10.1 Boresight Calibration
docs.text:
Boresight error (BSE) is the angular offset between the seeker null (zero-error output direction) and the missile mechanical axis. BSE must be \(<\)0.5 mrad (\(\sim\)0.03\(^\circ\)) to avoid systematic offset at target impact. Calibration procedure:

  1. Mount missile on precision boresight stand aligned to theodolite

  2. Command seeker to null (zero error output)

  3. Measure optical axis direction using retro-reflection collimator

  4. Compute BSE and apply electrical correction bias

  5. Verify residual BSE \(<\)0.5 mrad across temperature range \(-\)40 to \(+\)71\(^\circ\)C

docs.title: 21.10.2 Seeker Characterisation
docs.text: Table 21.5. Seeker characterisation tests and acceptance criteria Test Method Acceptance Criterion Boresight error Collimator alignment \(<\)0.5 mrad Noise equivalent angle Statistical noise floor per spec (typ. 0.1–0.5 mrad) Tracking bandwidth Swept frequency input \(-\)3 dB at \(\omega_T\) Acquisition range Range tower \(>R_{spec}\) at \(P_{acq} > 0.95\) IRCCM rejection Flare rack trials Track maintained \(>90\%\) Vibration survival Sine + random per MIL-810 Function after; no loose parts Shock survival Half-sine pulse 40 g/11 ms Function after Temperature \(-54\) to \(+71^\circ\)C ops Full spec across range EMI susceptibility MIL-STD-461 No degradation above \(E\)-field limits

docs.title: 21.10.3 Hardware-in-the-Loop (HWIL) Testing
docs.text:
HWIL seeker testing places the physical seeker hardware on a multi-axis flight motion simulator (FMS) table with the seeker looking at a simulated target scene:

  • IR scene projector: Resistive array (128\(\times\)128 to 512\(\times\)512 elements) heated to simulate thermal scenes; dynamic update rate 200–1000 Hz.

  • RF scene generator: Signal injection into seeker receiver; simulates target return, clutter, and ECM at correct power levels.

  • Laser spot simulator: Pulsed laser diode with beam steering mirror; coded PRF sequence; dithered position for noise.

  • 6-DOF FMS table: Reproduces missile body angular rates from simulated 6-DOF trajectory; bandwidth 50–200 Hz; angular rate \(\pm\)500 deg/s.

The HWIL simulation loop processes:

\[\text{Seeker output } \dot{\lambda} \longrightarrow \text{Guidance computer} \longrightarrow \mathbf{a}_c \longrightarrow \text{6-DOF sim} \longrightarrow \dot{\theta}_{body} \longrightarrow \text{FMS table} \longrightarrow \text{Scene projector update}\tag{21.54}\]

This closed-loop HWIL evaluates the complete sensor-to-guidance signal chain under realistic dynamic conditions.

docs.title: 21.10.4 Environmental Testing
docs.text:
All seekers must pass MIL-STD-810H environmental qualification:

  • Temperature-Altitude: Method 520; simulates high-altitude storage and operation; reduced convective cooling.

  • Vibration: Method 514.8; random vibration 0.04 g²/Hz across 20–2000 Hz; swept sine for resonance searches.

  • Shock: Method 516.8; functional shock 40 g, 11 ms; crash hazard 75 g, 11 ms.

  • Sand and Dust: Method 510.7; particulate ingestion.

  • Humidity: Method 507.6; 95% RH at 40\(^\circ\)C cycling.

  • Salt Fog: Method 509.7; maritime environments.

EMI/EMC compliance is verified to MIL-STD-461G: radiated emissions RE102 (10 kHz–18 GHz); radiated susceptibility RS103 (up to 200 V/m); conducted susceptibility CS114 (bulk current injection).

docs.title: 21.11.1 Wide-Band AESA Radar Seeker with SAR Imaging
docs.text:
Next-generation AESA seekers will achieve sufficiently wide instantaneous bandwidth to generate synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery of the target area. SAR cross-range resolution:

\[\delta_{cr} = \frac{\lambda R}{2\,L_{syn}} = \frac{D_{antenna}}{2}\tag{21.55}\]

This resolution is independent of range and depends only on the physical aperture size \(D_{antenna}\). For a 150 mm AESA seeker at \(Ka\)-band (\(\lambda = 8\) mm), \(\delta_{cr} = 75\) mm—sufficient to identify vehicle class from aimpoint selection. Inverse SAR (ISAR) uses target motion rather than missile motion to generate the synthetic aperture.

docs.title: 21.11.2 Quantum Dot IR Detectors
docs.text:
Conventional cooled IR detectors require cryogenic cooling to reduce dark current. Quantum dot (QD) nanocrystal detectors (e.g., PbS, PbSe, InAs QDs in colloidal suspension or epitaxially grown) exploit quantum confinement to tune the absorption cutoff wavelength by varying dot size:

\[E_{gap}(r) = E_{gap,bulk} + \frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2r^2} \left(\frac{1}{m_e^*} + \frac{1}{m_h^*}\right)\tag{21.56}\]

where \(r\) is the dot radius and \(m_e^*\), \(m_h^*\) are effective masses. MWIR QD detectors operating at room temperature have demonstrated \(D^* > 10^{10}\) Jones, approaching cooled InSb at 77 K. Elimination of the Stirling cryocooler would reduce seeker mass by 0.1–0.3 kg and remove the 90-second cool-down time constraint.

docs.title: 21.11.3 RF/IR Dual-Mode on Single Gimbal
docs.text:
Integrating a millimetre-wave (MMW) patch array antenna with an IIR detector on the same gimbal stabilisation platform reduces mass and cost compared to separate RF and IR gimbals. The shared gimbal must be transparent (or at least compatible) to both RF and IR; challenges include:

  • Dome material must transmit both 94 GHz MMW and 3–5 \(\mu\)m IR (no single natural material does this; solutions use a composite dome with a FSS element or a window aperture for each band)

  • Electromagnetic compatibility: high-power RF T/R modules must not saturate the sensitive IR detector

  • Gimbal cross-axis torque from the larger MMW antenna must not degrade IR stabilisation

docs.title: 21.11.4 Cognitive and AI-Enabled Seekers
docs.text:
The cognitive seeker paradigm applies machine learning throughout the signal chain:

  • Scene understanding: CNN detects and classifies all objects in the scene simultaneously, assigns lethality priorities.

  • Countermeasure recognition: Trained on jammer signatures; classifies jammer type and automatically selects the optimal IRCCM or ECCM response.

  • Adaptive waveform: Reinforcement learning agent selects radar waveform (frequency, PRF, bandwidth, power) to maximise SNR given real-time clutter and jamming environment.

  • Aimpoint selection: Identifies the most lethal aimpoint on the target structure (engine, fuel, crew).

The inference engine runs on a radiation-hardened AI accelerator (e.g., a radiation-tolerant version of a systolic-array chip) consuming \(<\)5 W, delivering \(>\)1 TOPS inference throughput.

docs.title: 21.11.5 Hyperspectral Seeker
docs.text:
A hyperspectral seeker acquires a full spectral cube (\(x\)-spatial, \(y\)-spatial, \(\lambda\)-wavelength) at each frame. Typical specification:

  • Spectral range: 1–5 \(\mu\)m or 8–12 \(\mu\)m

  • Spectral channels: 64–256

  • Spatial pixels: 128\(\times\)128 per frame

  • Frame rate: 10–30 Hz

Target discrimination uses the full spectral signature: paint type, metal alloy, exhaust composition, and fuel type leave unique spectral fingerprints. The detection statistic is the spectral matched filter:

\[d_{SMF} = \frac{(\mathbf{s} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1}(\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\mu})} {\sqrt{(\mathbf{s}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \mathbf{C}^{-1}(\mathbf{s}-\boldsymbol{\mu})}}\tag{21.57}\]

where \(\mathbf{t}\) is the measured pixel spectrum, \(\mathbf{s}\) is the target spectral signature, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is the background mean, and \(\mathbf{C}\) is the background covariance matrix. The hyperspectral seeker provides the ultimate IRCCM capability: flares, decoys, and jammers cannot replicate the full spectral signature of a real target.

docs.title: 21.11.6 Flash LiDAR Terminal Seeker
docs.text:
Flash LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) illuminates the scene with a single pulse and captures a 2D range image simultaneously on an InGaAs Geiger-mode APD array. Each pixel records the photon time-of-arrival:

\[R_{ij} = \frac{c\,(t_{ij} - t_{tx})}{2}\tag{21.58}\]

yielding a 3D point cloud. At terminal engagement distances (100–500 m), aimpoint precision is:

\[\sigma_{aimpoint} = \frac{R\cdot p_{det}}{f} \approx \text{1--10 cm}\tag{21.59}\]

This exceeds the precision of any RF or single-band IR seeker. Flash LiDAR enables selective aimpointing on specific structural elements (jet intake, cockpit, missile rail) that would maximise damage or kill probability.

docs.title: 21.12 Summary of Seeker Selection Trade Space
docs.text:
Seeker selection is ultimately a systems engineering trade driven by threat type, engagement geometry, operational environment, and cost constraints. The key trade factors are summarised in Table 21.6.

Table 21.6. Comparative assessment of seeker modalities across key attributes Attribute SpinScan IR IIR SARH ARH SAL TV/EO MMW All-weather capability Low Med High High Low Very Low Very High Fire-and-forget No Yes No Yes No Partial Yes Precision (CEP) 3–10 m \(<\)2 m 3–10 m 3–10 m \(<\)2 m \(<\)2 m 3–10 m IRCCM/ECCM robustness Low High Med High Med Med High Range capability Med Med High High Med Low Med Cost Low Med High Very High Low Med High Mass Low Med High High Low Low Med Collateral risk High Low Med Med Low Low Med Maturity High High High High High High Med

The trend across all programmes is toward multi-mode seekers combining at minimum two modalities, with embedded AI for scene understanding, target classification, and countermeasure adaptation. The cost of seeker hardware continues to fall as detector arrays, digital processing, and AESA components mature along semiconductor scaling curves. The seeker represents the highest-density engineering challenge in the guided weapon: it must achieve sensor, electromechanical, signal processing, and software functions in a volume often smaller than a 200 mm diameter sphere, surviving launch environments that impose \(>\)30 g vibration and \(>\)100 g shock, in temperatures from \(-54^\circ\)C to \(+71^\circ\)C, while resisting active countermeasures designed specifically to defeat it.

Key equations summary: PN guidance ((21.1)); LOS rate ((21.3)); IR lock-on range ((21.16)); SARH equation ((21.19)); ARH lock-on range ((21.24)); SAL radiometric link ((21.34)); Beer-Lambert ((21.35)); monopulse angle ((31.43)); interferometer DF ((21.30)); CFAR threshold ((21.28)); Kalman tracker model ((21.50)); AESA phase shift ((21.27)); quantum dot bandgap ((21.56)); flash LiDAR ((21.58)).

docs.title: 22.1 Warheads and Effects
docs.text:
The warhead is the lethal element of a guided weapon—the subsystem that converts stored chemical (or nuclear) energy into a physical mechanism that damages or destroys the target. Warhead engineering is a discipline that spans detonation physics, terminal ballistics, material science, structural mechanics, and probabilistic lethality analysis. Unlike propulsion, which drives the weapon toward the target, the warhead determines whether the kill actually occurs; a perfectly guided missile that delivers an ineffective warhead achieves nothing.

This chapter treats all major warhead types in systematic engineering depth: high-explosive (HE) blast and fragmentation; shaped charge (HEAT); explosively formed penetrators (EFP); thermobaric and fuel-air explosives; kinetic energy penetrators; EMP warheads; submunitions; and a public-domain overview of nuclear warheads. Lethality assessment methodology completes the chapter.

docs.title: 22.2.1 Function and Energy Conversion
docs.text:
A warhead performs energy conversion in three stages:

  1. Initiation: A fuze (Chapter 23) provides the initiation stimulus (electrical pulse, shock) at the correct moment and geometry.

  2. Detonation: Explosive decomposes exothermally in microseconds, producing a detonation wave at velocity \(D\) (velocity of detonation, VOD) and Chapman–Jouguet pressure \(P_{CJ}\):

    \[P_{CJ} = \frac{\rho_0\,D^2}{\gamma_{CJ}+1}\tag{22.1}\]

    where \(\rho_0\) is the unreacted explosive density and \(\gamma_{CJ} \approx 3\) for most high explosives. For TNT (\(\rho_0 = 1.64\) g/cm\(^3\), \(D = 6950\) m/s): \(P_{CJ} \approx 19\) GPa.

  3. Terminal effect: Blast wave propagation, fragment projection, jet formation, or fireball, depending on warhead type.

docs.title: 22.2.2 Lethality Probability
docs.text:
The probability of kill \(P_k\) against a target depends on the lethal area of the warhead \(A_{lethal}\) and the target vulnerable area \(A_{vuln}\):

\[P_k = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{A_{lethal}}{A_{target}}\right)\tag{22.2}\]

For a weapon with circular lethal radius \(R_L\) and a target of effective diameter \(d_t\), assuming a bivariate normal CEP distribution with CEP \(= \sigma\sqrt{2\ln 2}\):

\[P_k = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{(R_L + d_t/2)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\tag{22.3}\]

This shows the trade between warhead lethal radius and delivery accuracy. For a given \(P_k\) requirement, a 2\(\times\) improvement in accuracy (\(\sigma/2\)) allows a \(4\times\) reduction in lethal area (smaller warhead), or achieves higher \(P_k\) with the same warhead.

docs.title: 22.2.3 Warhead Mass Fraction
docs.text:
The warhead mass \(M_w\) as a fraction of the all-up missile mass \(M_{total}\) typically falls in the range:

\[f_w = \frac{M_w}{M_{total}} = 0.20\text{--}0.35\tag{22.4}\]

Higher mass fractions (heavy warheads) reduce the propellant available and shorten range; lower fractions reduce lethality. The trade is resolved by the intended target set: anti-personnel missiles carry small (2–5 kg) warheads (\(f_w < 0.10\)); heavy anti-ship missiles may carry warheads of 150–500 kg (\(f_w \approx 0.35\)).

Table 22.1. Target types and corresponding warhead requirements Target Mechanism Typical \(W\) (kg) CEP req. Example Personnel (unprotected) Frag/blast 1–5 \(<\)10 m Hellfire M (2 kg WH) Light armoured vehicle HEAT/frag 5–15 \(<\)3 m AGM-114K Main battle tank HEAT/KE 5–10 \(<\)1 m Javelin, NLAW Hardened bunker Penetrating HE 50–500 \(<\)3 m GBU-28, BLU-109 Ship (medium) SAP/blast 100–500 \(<\)5 m Exocet AM39 Aircraft (in flight) Frag/continuous rod 10–50 N/A (proximity) AIM-7 Bridge Blast/penetrating 100–1000 \(<\)3 m GBU-24 Runway / airfield Penetrating/cratering 50–500 \(<\)10 m JP233 Electronics / C2 EMP/HPM 0–explosive N/A CHAMP

docs.title: 22.3 High Explosive Blast and Fragmentation Warheads
22.3.1 Explosive Fills
docs.text:
The performance of a blast/fragmentation warhead depends critically on the explosive fill. Key parameters are the velocity of detonation (VOD), the detonation pressure \(P_{CJ}\), and the relative effectiveness (RE factor) referenced to TNT.

Table 22.2. Properties of common military explosive fills Explosive \(\rho_0\) (g/cm\(^3\)) VOD (m/s) \(P_{CJ}\) (GPa) RE Factor Notes TNT 1.64 6950 19.0 1.00 Reference explosive RDX (Cyclonite) 1.82 8750 33.8 1.60 Insensitive at density HMX (Octogen) 1.91 9110 39.3 1.70 Highest perf. CHNO PETN 1.77 8400 31.0 1.27 Detonator trains Comp B (60%RDX/40%TNT) 1.72 7980 29.5 1.35 Common fill Comp C-4 1.60 8050 26.3 1.37 Plastic explosive PBXN-109 1.68 7920 27.0 1.22 Insensitive munition TATB 1.90 7760 29.0 1.00 Extremely insensitive PBXN-110 1.75 7900 28.0 1.15 Very insensitive; W80

The TNT equivalence for blast purposes:

\[W_{TNT} = W_{HE}\cdot RE_{blast}\tag{22.5}\]

Note that blast RE factors differ from fragmentation or brisance RE factors; a single RE number is a simplification.

docs.title: 22.3.2 Blast Wave Physics: Friedlander Waveform
docs.text:
A detonation in free air generates a spherical blast wave. At range \(R\), the overpressure follows the Friedlander profile:

\[P(t) = P_s\left(1 - \frac{t - t_a}{t^+}\right) \exp\!\left(-b\,\frac{t-t_a}{t^+}\right), \quad t_a \leq t \leq t_a + t^+\tag{22.6}\]

where \(P_s\) is the peak overpressure, \(t_a\) is the arrival time, \(t^+\) is the positive phase duration, and \(b\) is the waveform parameter. The positive impulse per unit area:

\[i^+ = \int_{t_a}^{t_a+t^+} P(t)\,dt = \frac{P_s\,t^+}{b^2}\left[b - 1 + e^{-b}\right]\tag{22.7}\]

docs.title: 22.3.3 Hopkinson–Cranz Scaling
docs.text:
All blast parameters scale with the scaled distance:

\[Z = \frac{R}{W^{1/3}}\tag{22.8}\]

where \(R\) is the range in metres and \(W\) is the TNT equivalent charge mass in kilograms. The peak overpressure (Kingery-Bulmash):

\[P_s(Z) = \frac{0.84}{Z} + \frac{2.7}{Z^2} + \frac{0.43}{Z^3} \quad [\text{MPa, for }Z > 0.5\;\text{m/kg}^{1/3}]\tag{22.9}\]

This empirical expression is widely used in preliminary design. Key damage thresholds versus peak overpressure are given in Table 22.3.

Table 22.3. Blast damage thresholds for key targets Effect \(P_s\) (kPa) Notes Eardrum rupture (50% probability) 35 Personnel casualty Lung haemorrhage threshold 70 Below this: survivable Lung rupture (50% lethality) 100 LD\(_{50}\) for blast lung Window glass failure 3–7 Building damage indicator Residential wall failure 35–50 Unreinforced masonry Wood frame residential: severe 50–100 Partial collapse Reinforced concrete: cracking 300 Heavy structural damage Hardened bunker: damage 1000+ Requires direct hit

docs.title: 22.3.4 Natural Fragmentation
docs.text:
When a cylindrical HE-filled warhead detonates, the case is accelerated outward and fractures into fragments. The fragment mass distribution follows the Mott distribution:

\[\frac{dN}{dm} = \frac{N_0}{2\mu}\,\exp\!\left(-\sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu}}\right)\tag{22.10}\]

equivalently, the number of fragments with mass \(>m\) is:

\[N(>m) = N_0\,\exp\!\left(-\sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu}}\right)\tag{22.11}\]

where \(N_0\) is the total number of fragments and \(\mu\) is a characteristic fragment mass:

\[\mu = B\,t^{5/6}\,d^{1/3}\left(1 + t/d\right)\tag{22.12}\]

where \(t\) is the case wall thickness, \(d\) is the warhead diameter, and \(B\) is the Mott constant (depends on case material; for mild steel, \(B \approx 0.1\) g\(^{2/3}\)cm\(^{-5/2}\)).

docs.title: 22.3.5 Gurney Fragment Velocity
docs.text:
The initial fragment velocity is predicted by the Gurney equation. For a cylindrical warhead (charge mass \(C\), case mass \(M\)):

\[V_f = \sqrt{2\,E_G}\,\sqrt{\frac{C/M}{1 + C/(2M)}}\tag{22.13}\]

where \(\sqrt{2\,E_G}\) is the Gurney velocity (specific to the explosive):

Table 22.4. Gurney velocities for common explosive fills Explosive \(\sqrt{2E_G}\) (m/s) Notes TNT 2440 Reference Comp B 2700 Standard fill RDX 2930 Higher performance HMX 2970 Highest CHNO C-4 2840 Plastic PBXN-109 2590 IM formulation

For \(C/M = 1\) and Comp B: \(V_f = 2700\sqrt{1/1.5} = 2205\) m/s.

docs.title: 22.3.6 Fragment Pattern and Spray Angle
docs.text:
In flight, fragments are projected in a static pattern (determined by warhead geometry) but the dynamic spray angle is Doppler-shifted by the missile velocity \(V_m\):

\[\sin\theta_{dyn} = \frac{V_f\,\sin\theta_{stat}} {\sqrt{V_f^2 + V_m^2 + 2\,V_f\,V_m\cos\theta_{stat}}}\tag{22.14}\]

For high-speed missiles (\(V_m > 500\) m/s) the forward fragment pattern is strongly compressed toward the nose. Warhead design adjusts charge shape (conical forward face, hemispherical aft) to compensate and maintain the desired spray angle at the target.

docs.title: 22.3.7 Continuous Rod Warhead
docs.text:
Used against air targets, the continuous rod warhead contains a bundle of rods (typically 12 mm \(\times\) 100 mm, steel, welded alternately at ends) wrapped around the HE charge. On detonation the rods form an expanding hoop:

\[R_{rod}(t) = R_0 + V_{rod}\,t\tag{22.15}\]

where \(V_{rod} \approx 600\)–900 m/s. The continuous hoop remains coherent for 15–25 ms (expanding to 10–20 m diameter) and cuts through the structure of an aircraft target. The lethal condition is that the rod hoop intersects the target; lethal radius:

\[R_L = \frac{n_{rods}\,l_{rod}\,w_{rod}}{2\pi\,R_{hoop}}\tag{22.16}\]

docs.title: 22.4.1 Monroe/Munroe Effect and Jet Formation
docs.text:
The shaped charge exploits the Munroe effect: a conical metal liner (typically copper) backed by HE detonates from the apex rearward. The detonation wave collapses the liner progressively from tip to base. Each element of the liner is accelerated to velocity \(v\) by the detonation pressure and directed along the liner axis. The Birkhoff (PER) theory for jet tip velocity:

\[V_{tip} = V_{det}\,\frac{1 + \cos\beta}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sin(\beta/2)}\tag{22.17}\]

where \(\beta\) is the cone half-angle and \(V_{det}\) is the detonation front velocity in the liner. Practical tip velocities are 7000–10000 m/s. The jet tail velocity is 1000–2000 m/s; this velocity gradient stretches the jet over time, increasing its length.

docs.title: 22.4.2 Penetration Mechanics
docs.text:
Shaped charge jet penetration depth \(P\) in the hydrodynamic regime (tip velocity \(\gg\) plastic wave speed in target):

\[P = L_{jet}\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{jet}}{\rho_{target}}}\tag{22.18}\]

where \(L_{jet}\) is the effective jet length and \(\rho_{jet}\), \(\rho_{target}\) are jet and target material densities. For a copper jet (\(\rho_j = 8.9\) g/cm\(^3\)) into rolled homogeneous armour (RHA, \(\rho_t = 7.85\) g/cm\(^3\)):

\[\frac{P}{L_{jet}} = \sqrt{\frac{8.9}{7.85}} = 1.065\tag{22.19}\]

A 200 mm effective jet length penetrates approximately 213 mm RHA before the hydrodynamic limit applies. With jet break-up and particulation, effective penetration is 50–80% of the theoretical limit: \(P \approx 5\)–7 calibres for a standard design, \(P \approx 8\)–10 calibres for optimised design.

docs.title: 22.4.3 Stand-off Distance
docs.text:
The jet stretches and develops maximum coherent length at an optimal stand-off distance \(S_{opt}\):

\[S_{opt} = (4\text{--}8)\,D_{calibre}\tag{22.20}\]

where \(D_{calibre}\) is the warhead diameter. At shorter stand-off the jet has not fully developed; at longer stand-off, particulation and lateral dispersion reduce penetration. For the RPG-7 PG-7VM warhead (\(D = 70\) mm): \(S_{opt} = 280\)–560 mm. The piezoelectric fuze nose probe is sized to maintain this stand-off.

docs.title: 22.4.4 Liner Materials
docs.text:
• OFHC copper (70:30 Cu:Zn brass): Standard; grain size \(<\)50 \(\mu\)m; Vickers hardness 60–80 HV; excellent ductility sustains long coherent jet.

  • Tantalum: Density 16.6 g/cm\(^3\) (highest of practical liner materials); superior penetration over copper for the same \(L_{jet}/D\) ratio; cost-prohibitive for most applications.

  • Molybdenum: Intermediate density 10.2 g/cm\(^3\); harder; used in EFP liners.

  • Mild steel: Lower performance; used for low-cost applications (RPG warheads).

docs.title: 22.4.5 Explosive Reactive Armour (ERA) Defeat and Tandem Charges
docs.text:
ERA (e.g., Kontakt-5, Relikt) consists of explosive-filled tiles on the tank hull. When the shaped charge jet strikes the tile, the explosive detonates and drives flyer plates into the jet path, disrupting jet coherence and reducing penetration by 50–80%.

Tandem warhead design defeats ERA with two sequential charges:

  1. Precursor (forward) charge: Small shaped charge (50–70 mm diameter) mounted ahead of the main warhead. Detonates on contact with the ERA tile, consuming the ERA before the main charge arrives.

  2. Main charge: Standard or EFP warhead, following 1–5 ms behind; the ERA tile is now expended and cannot protect the base armour.

The precursor jet must arrive at the ERA with sufficient velocity (\(>\)3000 m/s) to initiate the tile explosive, but the precursor must not destroy the main warhead’s path of approach. Stand-off between precursor and main charge \(\Delta S \approx 200\)–400 mm.

\[P_{tandem} \approx P_{main} - \Delta P_{ERA} + P_{precursor_{ERA}} \approx P_{main}\tag{22.21}\]

docs.title: 22.5.1 Principle and Formation
docs.text:
The EFP warhead uses a shallow dish-shaped (concave) metal liner (typically molybdenum or copper) backed by the explosive charge. On detonation, the liner inverts and accelerates without forming a fine jet—instead it forms a coherent, dense, bullet-like projectile:

  • Projectile diameter: 50–85% of liner diameter

  • Projectile length-to-diameter: 1.5–5 (compact penetrator)

  • Projectile velocity: 1500–3000 m/s

  • Formation time: 50–100 \(\mu\)s

The EFP formation is governed by liner curvature \(R_c\), liner thickness \(t_L\), and explosive type. The axial velocity of the EFP:

\[V_{EFP} = \frac{2\,P_{CJ}}{\rho_L}\,\frac{t_L}{R_c}\,\eta_{EFP}\tag{22.22}\]

where \(\eta_{EFP} \approx 0.6\)–0.8 is an efficiency factor.

docs.title: 22.5.2 Stand-off and Penetration
docs.text:
Unlike the HEAT jet, the EFP does not particulate; it remains coherent from 20 to 50 calibres stand-off (versus 4–8 calibres for HEAT):

\[\text{EFP effective stand-off range: } S_{EFP} = (20\text{--}50)\,D\tag{22.23}\]

Penetration depth of an EFP in RHA using the modified Tate–Alekseevskii model:

\[P_{EFP} = L_0\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_t}} \left(1 - \frac{Y_t}{k\,\rho_t\,V_{EFP}^2}\right)\tag{22.24}\]

where \(L_0\) is initial projectile length, \(Y_t\) is target yield strength, and \(k \approx 1.5\). For molybdenum EFP at 2000 m/s into RHA: \(P_{EFP} \approx 0.8\)–\(1.5\,D_{liner}\). This is lower absolute penetration than a HEAT jet, but the large coherent projectile diameter creates a much larger behind-armour damage volume.

docs.title: 22.5.3 Selectable Warhead and IED Application
docs.text:
Selectable warheads switch between HEAT and EFP mode via a fuze logic signal:

  • Soft target detected \(\rightarrow\) EFP mode (long stand-off, large fragmentation effect)

  • Hard armour target detected \(\rightarrow\) HEAT mode (maximum penetration)

EFP technology was notoriously exploited in IED (improvised explosive device) construction by Mahdi Army forces in Iraq (2004–2011). Copper-dish EFPs buried in road surfaces were command-detonated to attack vehicle undersides. These side-attack EFPs from Claymore-type mines or top-attack systems (e.g., Intelligent Munitions System) demonstrate the dual-use nature of EFP physics.

docs.title: 22.6.1 Fuel-Air Explosive (FAE) Mechanism
docs.text:
The fuel-air explosive (FAE) warhead creates a dispersed fuel cloud that is subsequently ignited, producing a near-field detonation or strong deflagration. The two-stage process:

  1. Dispersal: A small bursting charge (central dissemination charge) ruptures the fuel container and atomises the fuel into a 5–30 \(\mu\)m aerosol cloud. Cloud radius:

    \[R_{cloud} = C_d\,\left(\frac{M_{fuel}}{\rho_{air}}\right)^{1/3}\tag{22.25}\]

    where \(C_d \approx 4\)–6 is an empirical coefficient.

  2. Ignition: After a timed delay (50–200 ms for cloud development), one or more igniter charges trigger combustion throughout the cloud volume. If stoichiometric mixing is achieved, a near-detonation (deflagration-to-detonation transition, DDT) occurs with VOD approaching 1500–2500 m/s.

docs.title: 22.6.2 Blast Characteristics
docs.text:
FAE produces a fundamentally different pressure-time profile than HE:

  • Extended positive phase: Duration 3–5\(\times\) longer than equivalent HE blast; impulse is very high.

  • Negative phase: Strong sub-ambient negative phase (partial vacuum) follows; particularly damaging to lungs and hollow organs.

  • Oxygen depletion: Consumption of atmospheric oxygen in confined spaces creates asphyxiation hazard.

The positive impulse of an FAE compared to TNT at the same mass:

\[\frac{i^+_{FAE}}{i^+_{TNT}} \approx 2\text{--}3 \quad \text{(at ranges } Z > 3 \text{ m/kg}^{1/3}\text{)}\tag{22.26}\]

The overpressure advantage is less at close range (FAE peak \(P_s\) is lower than HE for equivalent mass); FAE superiority lies in its impulse at medium range.

docs.title: 22.6.3 Thermobaric Explosives
docs.text:
Pure thermobaric warheads (as distinct from FAE) incorporate solid metal fuels—typically aluminium powder (1–20 \(\mu\)m)—into an explosive matrix. The aluminium reacts with detonation products (H\(_2\)O, CO\(_2\)) in an exothermic after-burn:

\[2\,\text{Al} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\,\text{H}_2 \quad \Delta H = -837\;\text{kJ/mol}\tag{22.27}\] \[4\,\text{Al} + 3\,\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\,\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 \quad \Delta H = -1676\;\text{kJ/mol}\tag{22.28}\]

The total heat release per kilogram of thermobaric explosive is 5000–9000 kJ/kg, compared to \(\sim\)4600 kJ/kg for TNT. The sustained high pressure in enclosed spaces (bunkers, tunnels, building interiors) is devastating; walls prevent pressure relief and extend the positive phase further.

docs.title: 22.6.4 Operational Systems
docs.text:
• BLU-73/B FAE: Ethylene oxide fuel; 45 kg; dispersed by M130 dispenser; 15 m lethal radius in open; BLU-72 uses propylene oxide.

  • TOS-1A Buratino (Russia): 220 mm thermobaric rocket; Al-powder thermobaric fill; 24-round launcher; maximum range 6 km; area denial in urban warfare.

  • RPG-7TBG-7 round: Single-shot shoulder-fired thermobaric; effective against bunkers, light armour; lethal radius 10 m in open, 40 m in enclosed space.

  • BLU-118/B: 2000-lb penetrating thermobaric bomb; used against Tora Bora cave complexes (2001); penetrates earth before detonating thermobaric fill.

docs.title: 22.7.1 Long-Rod Penetrator Theory
docs.text:
Kinetic energy (KE) penetrators attack armour by overwhelming its strength with the kinetic energy of a dense, fast rod. Above the ballistic limit, penetration occurs in the hydrodynamic regime where both rod and target behave as fluids. The basic hydrodynamic penetration depth (Tate-Alekseevskii):

\[P = L\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_t}}\tag{22.29}\]

where \(L\) is the rod length and \(\rho_p\), \(\rho_t\) are penetrator and target densities. For a tungsten rod (\(\rho_p = 17.6\) g/cm\(^3\)) into RHA (\(\rho_t = 7.85\) g/cm\(^3\)): \(P = L \times 1.497\). A 600 mm rod penetrates \(\sim\)900 mm RHA in pure hydrodynamic theory; accounting for strength effects the modified Tate model gives:

\[P = L\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_t}}\,\left(1 - \frac{R_t - Y_p} {\frac{1}{2}\rho_p V^2}\right)\tag{22.30}\]

where \(R_t\) is the dynamic target resistance (\(\sim\)5\(Y_t\)) and \(Y_p\) is the penetrator yield strength. At \(V = 1700\) m/s and \(Y_p = 1600\) MPa for tungsten alloy, the strength correction is approximately \(15\text{--}20\%\).

docs.title: 22.7.2 Materials: Tungsten vs DU
