docs.text: Tungsten Heavy Alloy (93W, WHA): Composition 93% W, 4.9% Ni, 2.1% Fe; density 17.6 g/cm\(^3\); \(Y_p \approx 1500\) MPa; elongation 8–12%. Adiabatic shear bands form at impact, but the rod tends to mushroom rather than self-sharpen. Depleted Uranium (DU, U-238): Density 18.5 g/cm\(^3\); \(Y_p \approx 1200\) MPa; key advantage is adiabatic shear plugging (self-sharpening): the nose continuously fractures away, maintaining a sharp tip and increasing effective penetration by 10–15% over WHA at the same geometry. Also pyrophoric: fragments ignite inside the tank on penetration (incendiary effect). Disadvantages: mild radioactivity (\(\alpha\)-emitter), environmental contamination, logistic and political restrictions.

docs.title: 22.7.3 Tank APFSDS Round
docs.text:
Armour-Piercing, Fin-Stabilised, Discarding Sabot (APFSDS):

  • Calibre: 120 mm gun (L55 or M256 smoothbore)

  • Muzzle velocity: 1680–1760 m/s

  • Penetrator L/D: 25–30

  • Penetrator dimensions: 22 mm \(\times\) 700 mm (typical)

  • Penetration at 2 km (0\(^\circ\) obliquity): 600–800 mm RHA

\[P_{APFSDS} \approx 0.6\,L\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_t}}\cdot\eta_{obliquity}(\theta)\tag{22.31}\]

where \(\eta_{obliquity}\) decreases with impact obliquity angle \(\theta\) (60\(^\circ\) obliquity reduces penetration by \(\sim\)40%).

docs.title: 22.7.4 Kinetic Energy Missile (KEM)
docs.text:
A missile-delivered KE weapon uses the closing velocity of the missile to impart kinetic energy. No warhead explosive is needed; the missile body itself is the penetrator. The impact KE:

\[E_k = \frac{1}{2}\,M_{missile}\,V_c^2\tag{22.32}\]

At \(V_c = 1500\) m/s and \(M_{missile} = 15\) kg: \(E_k = 16.9\) MJ \(\approx\) 4 kg TNT equivalent. However, the penetrator L/D is typically much lower than a tank APFSDS, so penetration per unit cross-section is less efficient. Used in anti-satellite (ASAT) and ballistic missile defence (hit-to-kill) applications where the closing velocity is 5–10 km/s and no explosive is needed.

docs.title: 22.8.1 Nuclear EMP (NEMP)
docs.text:
A nuclear burst generates an electromagnetic pulse through the Compton electron mechanism:

  1. Prompt gamma rays (0–100 ns) ionise air molecules, ejecting Compton electrons.

  2. The asymmetric earth/air boundary creates a net downward current surge.

  3. The rapidly varying current generates a broad-spectrum electromagnetic field pulse.

The three components of NEMP have distinct characteristics:

\(E_1\) (fast): Rise time \(<\)5 ns; peak 10–50 kV/m at ground level for a high-altitude (HEMP) burst. Destroys semiconductor junctions by dielectric breakdown. \(E_2\) (intermediate): 1 \(\mu\)s to 1 s; similar to natural lightning; most existing lightning protection handles this component. \(E_3\) (slow): 1–1000 s; geomagnetic storm from the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) interaction of the fireball; induces quasi-DC currents in long conductors (power lines, pipelines); transformer core saturation and burnout.

The peak \(E_1\) electric field for a HEMP detonation at altitude \(H\):

\[E_{1,max} = E_0\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{R_{slant} - H}{H_{scale}}\right)\tag{22.33}\]

where \(E_0 \approx 50\) kV/m is the peak field (from Compton electron theory) and \(H_{scale} \approx 7.5\) km is the atmospheric scale height. The \(E_1\) pulse can illuminate a continent-wide area from a single 300 km altitude burst.

docs.title: 22.8.2 Non-Nuclear EMP (NNEMP)
docs.text:
Flux Compression Generator (FCG).

The FCG converts explosive energy to electrical energy with very high efficiency (\(\eta \approx 30\text{--}50\%\)):

  1. A solenoid carrying initial current \(I_0\) (from a seed capacitor bank) surrounds an explosive-filled tube.

  2. Detonation compresses the magnetic flux within the tube, driving current to peak levels:

    \[I_{peak} = I_0\,\sqrt{\frac{L_0}{L_{min}}}\tag{22.34}\]

    where \(L_0\) is the initial inductance and \(L_{min}\) is the minimum inductance at full compression. Compression ratios \(L_0/L_{min} = 100\)–1000; \(I_{peak}\) reaches 10–100 MA in tens of microseconds.

  3. The output drives an antenna or HPM source.

High Power Microwave (HPM).

HPM warheads generate focused microwave energy to defeat electronics at range without direct contact:

  • Frequency: 1–35 GHz (typically 9–10 GHz for penetration through apertures); 95 GHz for Active Denial System

  • Peak power: 10 MW–1 GW; pulse width 10 ns–1 \(\mu\)s

  • Power density at target: \(S = P_{rad}\,G/(4\pi R^2)\); must exceed HPM threshold \(S_{HPM}\) to cause effect

  • Effect mechanism: couple energy through cable apertures, antenna ports, or seams; induce \(>\)1 V at sensitive nodes

  • Boeing CHAMP (Counter-electronics High Power Microwave Advanced Missile Project): AGM-86 airframe; 10 GHz HPM; demonstrated 7 target passes in single flight (2012)

\[S_{target} = \frac{P_{HPM}\,G_{ant}}{4\pi R^2}\,\tau_{atm}\tag{22.35}\]

docs.title: 22.8.3 EMP Hardening
docs.text:
Electronics protection against EMP:

  • Faraday cage: Continuous metallic enclosure; attenuation \(A = 20\log_{10}(1/|S_{21}|)~\text{dB}\); sealed seams required.

  • Transient voltage suppressors (TVS): Bi-directional Zener/avalanche diodes at all interface cable entries; clamp voltage \(<\)5 V; response time \(<\)1 ps.

  • Surge arrestors and gas tubes: First-stage protection for power lines; 10 kA discharge capability.

  • Fibre optic interconnects: Replace copper signal cables; immune to common-mode EMP coupling.

  • MIL-STD-461 / MIL-STD-464: Hardening requirements; \(E_1\) threat environment 50 kV/m; test to RS105 (radiated susceptibility, transient).

docs.title: 22.9.1 Dispenser Systems
docs.text:
Cluster munitions dispense multiple submunitions over a large area from a single delivery vehicle. The CBU-87 Combined Effects Munition (CEM):

  • Dispenser: SUU-65/B; 370 BLU-97/B submunitions

  • Area coverage: 100 m \(\times\) 400 m pattern

  • BLU-97/B: HEAT (12 mm penetration); fragmentation; incendiary zirconium disc; total mass 1.5 kg

  • Ribbon parachute on each submunition slows descent and orients HEAT cone downward

The fragment density at range \(r\) from the dispenser centreline:

\[\phi(r) = \frac{N_{sub}\,N_{frag}}{\pi\,r_{lethal}^2}\tag{22.36}\]

where \(N_{sub}\) is the number of submunitions and \(N_{frag}\) is the number of lethal fragments per submunition.

docs.title: 22.9.2 Sensor-Fuzed Weapon (SFW)
docs.text:
The Textron BLU-108 SFW (used in CBU-97 and CBU-105 WCMD) is the most sophisticated conventional submunition. Operation:

  1. Dispenser opens at \(\sim\)500 m altitude; 10 BLU-108 SFW sensors descend on parachutes.

  2. Each BLU-108 spins up (spin-arm) using aerodynamic vanes.

  3. At 30 m altitude: rocket motor fires; 4 Skeet EFP submunitions are ejected tangentially.

  4. Each Skeet contains an IR sensor (scanning arc below).

  5. IR sensor detects vehicle thermal signature; EFP fires downward into top armour (50 mm penetration).

  6. If no target detected after full rotation: self-destruct at ground impact (99% reliability to MIL-DTL-23659 IM standard).

\[P_{kill,SFW} = 1 - \prod_{k=1}^{4}(1 - P_{k,Skeet})\tag{22.37}\]

For \(P_{k,Skeet} = 0.35\) per Skeet: \(P_{kill,SFW} = 1 - 0.65^4 = 0.821\).

docs.title: 22.9.3 M85 DPICM and Insensitive Munitions
docs.text:
The M85 DPICM (Dual Purpose Improved Conventional Munition) combines shaped charge anti-armour and fragmentation anti-personnel effects. The IM (insensitive munitions) requirement (MIL-DTL-23659) mandates:

  • Bullet impact: 12.7 mm AP at 850 m/s; no detonation

  • Fragment impact: No detonation

  • Shaped charge attack: No detonation or sympathetic detonation

  • Fast cook-off: Fuel fire; controlled burn, no detonation

  • Slow cook-off: Slow heating; deflagration permitted; no detonation

IM explosive formulations (PBXN-109, PBXN-110, PAX-29) substitute less sensitive binders (HTPB, BDNPA-F) and use less brisant primary explosives. The trade-off is typically 5–15% reduction in \(P_{CJ}\) and Gurney velocity compared to standard fills.

docs.title: 22.9.4 Convention on Cluster Munitions (CCM)
docs.text:
The 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions (Oslo Treaty) prohibits the use, production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions. As of 2025:

  • Signatories: \(>\)110 states parties

  • Non-signatories include: USA, Russia, China, Israel, India, Pakistan (the primary users and producers)

  • Key exemption criteria (Art. 2): Self-destructing and self-deactivating submunitions with dud rate \(<\)1% are exempted from the CCM definition in some interpretations

docs.title: 22.10 Nuclear Warheads: Public Domain Overview
docs.text: The following section addresses nuclear warhead physics at the level of publicly available, declassified information. No classified design details are presented.

docs.title: 22.10.1 Fission Devices
docs.text:
Nuclear weapons derive their energy from nuclear fission of heavy nuclides (U-235 or Pu-239). A critical mass of fissile material is assembled rapidly to initiate and sustain a supercritical chain reaction.

Gun-Type Assembly.

Two sub-critical pieces of U-235 are brought together by a gun mechanism. The Little Boy bomb (Hiroshima, 1945): 64 kg U-235; gun barrel; total mass 4400 kg; yield \(\sim\)15 kt. The gun type is inefficient and cannot use Pu-239 (due to Pu-240 contamination causing pre-detonation).

Implosion Assembly.

A sub-critical sphere of Pu-239 (or U-235) is surrounded by shaped explosive lenses that produce a precisely simultaneous spherical detonation wave, compressing the core to \(2.5\text{--}3\times\) normal density, ensuring supercriticality. The Fat Man bomb (Nagasaki, 1945): 6.2 kg Pu-239; 32-point implosion lens design; total mass 4500 kg; yield \(\sim\)21 kt.

The critical mass for an uncompressed Pu-239 sphere:

\[M_c \approx \frac{4\pi}{3}\,\rho_{Pu}\,r_c^3;\quad r_c = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}\,\frac{M_c}{\rho_{Pu}}} \approx 6.2\;\text{cm (bare sphere)}\tag{22.38}\]

Reflectors (natural U, Be) reduce \(M_c\) to 5.6 kg; compression to 3\(\rho_0\) reduces effective \(M_c\) by \(9\times\).

docs.title: 22.10.2 Thermonuclear Devices
docs.text:
Two-stage thermonuclear (Teller–Ulam) devices use a fission primary to implode and ignite a fusion secondary (lithium deuteride, \(^6\)LiD):

  1. Primary fission weapon detonates; X-rays and soft radiation compress and heat the secondary.

  2. Li-6 + neutron \(\rightarrow\) T + He-4; T + D \(\rightarrow\) He-4 + n + 17.6 MeV (fusion).

  3. Fusion neutrons fission a U-238 tamper (sparkplug), adding yield (fission-fusion-fission).

Fusion reaction energy release:

\[\text{D} + \text{T} \rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n + 17.6\;\text{MeV}\tag{22.39}\]

Yields of 100 kt to 50 Mt are achievable. Modern strategic warheads (W88: 475 kt, W87: 300 kt) are compact and hardened for re-entry vehicle delivery.

docs.title: 22.10.3 Re-entry Vehicle and Fuzing
docs.text:
Strategic nuclear warheads are delivered in hardened re-entry vehicles (RVs) that must survive:

  • Re-entry heating: 8–12 km/s; peak stagnation temperature \(>\)6000 K; ablative heat shield (carbon phenolic).

  • Blast: hardened RV survives 200–500 psi overpressure for silo-killing missions.

  • EMP: nuclear-hardened electronics; radiation-hardened semiconductors.

Fuzing for air burst (\(\sim\)2 km altitude) uses radar altimetry and barometric sensing to optimise blast radius against area targets. Ground penetration fuze (e.g., B61-11 earth-penetrating bomb) delays detonation until the weapon has penetrated 1–3 m of soil, coupling more energy into the ground shock for hardened-target defeat.

docs.title: 22.11.1 Vulnerable Area Method
docs.text:
The standard lethality assessment methodology uses the target vulnerable area \(A_v\)—the presented area of components whose damage is sufficient to achieve the defined kill criterion (K-kill, M-kill, F-kill):

\[P_k = 1 - \exp\!\left(-A_v\,\cdot\phi\right)\tag{22.40}\]

where \(\phi\) is the fragment (or other effect) density (fragments/m\(^2\)) at the target.

For a fragmentation warhead, \(\phi\) at range \(r\) and warhead design angle \(\Omega_{spray}\):

\[\phi(r) = \frac{N_{frags}\,p_{let}(r)}{4\pi r^2\,\Omega_{spray}/(4\pi)} = \frac{N_{frags}\,p_{let}(r)}{\Omega_{spray}\,r^2}\tag{22.41}\]

where \(p_{let}(r)\) is the probability that a single fragment penetrates the target skin to reach the vulnerable component.

docs.title: 22.11.2 Pk Chain: System-Level Kill Probability
docs.text:
The overall kill probability from launch to kill is the product of conditional probabilities at each stage:

\[P_{k,system} = P_{detect}\cdot P_{acquire}\cdot P_{track}\cdot P_{launch}\cdot P_{intercept}\cdot P_{fuze}\cdot P_{k|hit}\tag{22.42}\]

where:

  • \(P_{detect}\): probability target is detected by sensor

  • \(P_{acquire}\): probability seeker locks on given detection

  • \(P_{track}\): probability track is maintained to intercept

  • \(P_{launch}\): probability launch is within envelope (safety, arming)

  • \(P_{intercept}\): probability missile reaches kill box (miss distance \(<\) warhead radius)

  • \(P_{fuze}\): probability fuze functions correctly

  • \(P_{k|hit}\): probability of kill given functioning detonation

docs.title: 22.11.3 Salvo Theory
docs.text:
When a single missile \(P_k\) is insufficient for the required mission \(P_{k,req}\), multiple missiles are fired in a salvo. The kill probability of \(N\) independent missiles each with \(P_k\):

\[P_{k,salvo} = 1 - (1 - P_k)^N\tag{22.43}\]

Solving for \(N\):

\[N = \frac{\ln(1 - P_{k,req})}{\ln(1 - P_k)}\tag{22.44}\]

For \(P_k = 0.5\) per missile and \(P_{k,req} = 0.95\): \(N = \ln(0.05)/\ln(0.5) = 4.3\), so 5 missiles are required.

docs.title: 22.11.4 JMEM and Target Hardness
docs.text:
The Joint Munitions Effectiveness Manual (JMEM) is the US DoD classified database of weapon-target pair effectiveness. The methodology defines:

  • Target hardness: Expressed in psi overpressure required for kill; ranges from \(<\)1 psi (personnel in open) to \(>\)1000 psi (hardened bunker).

  • P\(_k\)(R) curves: Kill probability as a function of burst range for each weapon-target pair; accounts for fragment density, blast pressure, and fuzing.

  • Lethal radius: The range at which \(P_k = 0.5\); used for quick salvo calculations.

docs.title: 22.11.5 Fragment Lethality Against Personnel
docs.text:
The Wound Ballistics criterion for fragment lethality (casualty production) uses minimum specific kinetic energy:

\[E_{sp,min} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}m_f\,v_f^2}{A_{frag}} \geq E_{sp,crit} \approx 80\;\text{J/cm}^2\tag{22.45}\]

where \(m_f\) is fragment mass, \(v_f\) its velocity, and \(A_{frag}\) its presented area. The lethal fragment velocity at range \(r\) accounting for drag deceleration:

\[v_f(r) = V_0\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{C_D\,\rho_{air}\,A_f}{2\,m_f}\,r\right)\tag{22.46}\]

where the exponential decay constant: \(\lambda_f = C_D\rho_{air}A_f/(2m_f)\). The lethal radius against unprotected personnel:

\[R_{let,pers} = \frac{1}{\lambda_f}\ln\!\left(\frac{V_0}{v_{let}}\right)\tag{22.47}\]

where \(v_{let}\) is the minimum lethal velocity (\(\sim\)120 m/s for standard 1–2 g steel fragments).

docs.title: 22.11.6 Fuze-Warhead Optimisation
docs.text:
The fuze functions at a specific burst point relative to the target. For a fragmentation warhead, the optimal burst range \(r_{opt}\) maximises the fragment density on the target:

\[r_{opt} = r_L\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda_f\,r_L}}\tag{22.48}\]

(approximate, from calculus of variations on \(\phi(r)\cdot p_{let}(r)\)). For proximity-fuzed warheads, the RF or laser fuze must trigger at this range with miss distance uncertainty \(\sigma_{MD}\) such that:

\[P_{fuze} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{r_{fuze,max} - r_{det}}{\sigma_{r}}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\frac{r_{fuze,min} - r_{det}}{\sigma_{r}}\right)\tag{22.49}\]

where \(\Phi\) is the normal CDF and \(r_{det}\) is the detection range of the fuze sensor.

docs.title: 22.12 Warhead Type Comparison and Selection Matrix
docs.text:
Table 22.5 provides a consolidated engineering comparison of all major warhead types across the key performance, cost, and operational attributes that drive selection for a given mission.

Table 22.5. Warhead type comparison across key engineering and operational attributes Attribute HE Frag HEAT EFP Thermobaric KE Rod EMP/HPM Anti-armour (MBT) Low Very High High None Very High None Anti-personnel Very High Low Low Very High Low None Anti-structure (hard) Med Low Low High Med None Anti-electronics Low None None Low Low Very High Anti-ship High Low Med Low Med Low Stand-off (km) 0–5 0 0–0.5 0–1 0 1–10 Collateral risk High Low Low High Low Low Fuze complexity Low Med Med High None Very High Cost (relative) Low Med Med Med Low Very High IM compliance Easy Hard Med Med N/A N/A

The selection matrix shows no single warhead type dominates all attributes. In practice, most missiles carry a compromise design: a fragmentation case (steel or tungsten alloy) surrounding a shaped charge liner and HE fill, providing HEAT performance against armour and fragmentation against personnel—the dual-purpose HEAT-FRAG warhead type used in Hellfire, TOW, and similar systems.

docs.title: 22.13 Summary and Design Trade Space
docs.text:
Warhead selection is driven by the target set, delivery platform, accuracy, and collateral damage constraints. The dominant modern trend is toward precision effects: smaller warheads delivering lethal energy to specific aim points, enabled by CEP \(<\)3 m guidance accuracy. This allows a 250 lb class warhead to achieve effects previously requiring 2000 lb area weapons, with dramatically reduced collateral damage.

The second dominant trend is insensitive munitions (IM): replacing high-performance but sensitive explosives (RDX, HMX) with safer formulations (PBXN-109, TATB) that do not detonate on accidental stimulus. IM compliance is now mandatory for all new US DoD acquisitions under USD(AT&L) policy.

Multi-effect warheads (simultaneously delivering blast, fragmentation, HEAT, and incendiary effects) in a compact package remain the gold standard for general-purpose strike weapons, exemplified by the BLU-111/B JDAM fill, which uses a shaped steel case for fragmentation, PBXH-135 insensitive explosive, and an OPT (optional proximity and impact time) fuze providing both air-burst and point-detonating fuzing modes.

Key equations summary: CJ pressure ((22.1)); \(P_k\) lethal area ((22.2)); Friedlander waveform ((22.6)); scaled distance ((22.8)); Mott distribution ((22.11)); Gurney velocity ((22.13)); Birkhoff jet velocity ((22.17)); penetration ((22.18)); EFP velocity ((22.22)); FAE cloud radius ((22.25)); Tate KE penetration ((22.30)); FCG current ((22.34)); SFW kill probability ((22.37)); DT fusion ((22.39)); \(P_k\) chain ((22.42)); salvo theory ((22.44)); fragment deceleration ((22.46)); lethal radius ((22.47)).

docs.title: 23.1 Fuze Fundamentals
docs.text: A fuze is the electromechanical, electronic, or purely mechanical device responsible for initiating the explosive train of a warhead at precisely the correct time, place, and physical condition. The fuze must discriminate between the operational firing environment and all other situations — including transportation, storage, accidental shock, and electromagnetic interference — and must initiate only when the target engagement criteria are satisfied. This dual demand — extreme reliability of function combined with extreme resistance to inadvertent initiation — makes fuze engineering one of the most tightly regulated disciplines in the defence industry.

docs.title: 23.1.1 Safety and Reliability Requirements
docs.text:
The governing standard in the United States and many allied nations is MIL-STD-1316, which specifies the safety philosophy for fuze design. The primary quantitative safety requirement is:

\[P_{\text{inadvertent}} \leq 1 \times 10^{-6}\tag{23.1}\]

That is, the probability of inadvertent initiation under any out-of-design environment shall not exceed one in one million. This is achieved through the use of multiple, independent safety devices arranged in series so that all must be defeated simultaneously before the fuze can arm. If each device has an individual failure probability \(p_i\), the combined probability satisfies:

\[P_{\text{combined}} = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p_i\tag{23.2}\]

For \(N = 3\) devices each with \(p_i = 10^{-2}\), the product yields \(10^{-6}\), meeting the requirement. In practice, high-reliability components drive individual \(p_i\) far below \(10^{-2}\).

The complementary requirement is reliability of function: once the fuze is armed and target-engagement criteria are met, initiation must occur with a probability of no less than \(0.999\) (three nines). These two requirements — safety and reliability — form opposing design drivers that must be balanced through careful engineering.

docs.title: 23.1.2 The Arming Sequence
docs.text:
Every fuze passes through a defined sequence of states:

  1. Safe: The detonator is mechanically or electronically isolated from the warhead explosive train. The weapon may be handled, transported, and loaded.

  2. Armed: All safety devices have been released by the detection of authorised environmental stimuli. The detonator is in line with the explosive train. The fuze actively monitors for firing criteria.

  3. Fired: The initiator has been triggered and energy has propagated through the fuze train to detonate the warhead.

Transition from Safe to Armed requires the simultaneous satisfaction of all independent arming conditions. Transition from Armed to Fired requires the detection of target-engagement criteria (impact, proximity, time-on-target, or command).

docs.title: 23.1.3 Fuze Classification
docs.text:
Fuzes are classified according to their method of initiating detonation:

  • Point Detonating (PD): Initiates on physical contact with the target surface. Sub-types: superquick (\(<0.1\) ms), delay (10–100 ms), and graze (functions at shallow angle of impact).

  • Proximity (VT): Initiates when the projectile or missile passes within a preset standoff distance of the target, without physical contact. Sub-types: radio frequency (RF), laser, optical shadow, acoustic.

  • Time: Initiates after a preset elapsed time from launch. Mechanical clockwork or electronic timing.

  • Command: Initiates upon receipt of a coded signal from an external platform (aircraft, ground station, or datalink).

  • Delay: Allows the projectile to penetrate before detonation. Used against hardened bunkers and reinforced concrete.

  • Combination: Implements two or more modes in a single body (e.g., PD + delay selectable, or proximity + PD back-up).

docs.title: 23.1.4 The Fuze Train
docs.text:
The explosive energy path from the fuze initiator to the warhead main charge is called the fuze train:

\[\text{Initiator} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Booster (secondary explosive)} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Lead / Relay charge} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Main detonator charge} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Warhead main fill}\]

Each component in the train amplifies the detonation energy while reducing sensitivity to accidental initiation. The initiator (stab, electric, or piezoelectric) is the most sensitive; the warhead main fill (RDX, HMX, PBXN) is the least sensitive. The booster (typically PETN or RDX-based composition) bridges the gap.

The critical parameter is the gap sensitivity: the maximum air gap over which the detonation wave can propagate reliably. For military boosters this is typically 2–6 mm. The out-of-line initiator concept exploits this: by misaligning the initiator by more than the gap sensitivity distance, inadvertent initiation cannot propagate to the warhead even if the initiator fires.

Table 23.1. Fuze train explosive components and their properties Component Typical Explosive Density (g/cm\(^3\)) VOD (m/s) Sensitivity Primary initiator Lead azide / DDNP 3.0 / 1.6 4,600 / 6,900 High Booster PETN / RDX 1.65 / 1.77 8,300 / 8,750 Medium Lead charge RDX / HMX 1.77 / 1.89 8,750 / 9,100 Low Main fill Comp B / PBXN-109 1.65 / 1.78 7,900 / 8,500 Very Low

VOD = velocity of detonation; DDNP = diazodinitrophenol; PETN = pentaerythritol tetranitrate; PBXN = plastic-bonded explosive (Navy formulation).

docs.title: 23.2 Safe and Arm Devices
docs.text: Safe and Arm (S&A) devices are the hardware implementations of the safety philosophy. They physically prevent the detonation train from being complete until all arming conditions are met.

docs.title: 23.2.1 Electromechanical Rotor S&A
docs.text:
The electromechanical rotor is the most widely used S&A design. A cylindrical rotor contains the initiator charge in a bore perpendicular to its rotation axis. In the safe position, the initiator bore is misaligned with the booster column by \(90°\) (or other angle), ensuring an air gap greater than the detonation gap sensitivity. An electric motor (or clockwork spring in older designs) rotates the rotor to the armed position when all sensor inputs are satisfied.

The rotation is controlled by a logic circuit monitoring environmental sensors. A mechanical detent latches the rotor in both the safe and the armed positions, preventing intermediate states. The rotor also carries an environmental sensor that must detect the prescribed launch stimuli — setback acceleration, spin rate, time delay, or altitude — before the motor is energised.

Arming distance (minimum travel before arming):

\[D_{\text{arm}} = V_0 \cdot t_{\text{arm}}\tag{23.3}\]

where \(V_0\) is the muzzle or launch velocity and \(t_{\text{arm}}\) is the minimum arming time (typically 20–60 m for artillery fuzes, 1–5 m for guided missiles depending on the platform).

docs.title: 23.2.2 MEMS Safe and Arm Devices
docs.text:
Micro-Electromechanical Systems (MEMS) S&A devices are silicon micro-machined equivalents of the rotor S&A. Fabricated using standard semiconductor photolithography, they achieve very small size (2–10 mm die) with inherently reliable performance due to lack of wear-prone mechanical assemblies.

A typical MEMS S&A consists of:

  • A MEMS accelerometer sensing setback \(g\) (the launch-phase inertial load).

  • A micro-rotor or slide mechanism driven by comb-drive electrostatic actuator.

  • A micro-initiator (semiconductor bridge or thin-film resistor) in the detonation channel, which becomes in-line only after the mechanism reaches the armed position.

The silicon micro-machined slide typically requires a sustained acceleration above a threshold \(a_{\text{arm}}\) for a minimum time \(t_{\min}\) to overcome a restoring spring force:

\[\int_0^{t_{\min}} a(t)\, dt \geq v_{\text{threshold}}\tag{23.4}\]

This impulse criterion prevents single-shock events (drops, handling shocks) from arming the device, since their duration is too short to accumulate sufficient velocity.

docs.title: 23.2.3 Environmental Sensing and Arming Conditions
docs.text:
Multiple independent environmental conditions are sensed to confirm the munition is in a legitimate launch profile:

  1. Setback acceleration: For gun-launched projectiles, setback \(g\) values of \(1{,}000\)–\(20{,}000\,g\) for 1–10 ms are characteristic and extremely difficult to replicate by accident. For rocket-launched missiles, setback may be \(5\)–\(50\,g\).

  2. Spin rate (centrifugal arming): For spin-stabilised projectiles, a centrifugal arming pin is displaced outward by spin rate above a threshold \(\omega_{\text{arm}}\):

    \[F_{\text{centrifugal}} = m_{\text{pin}} \cdot \omega^2 \cdot r \geq F_{\text{spring}}\tag{23.5}\]

    Typically \(\omega_{\text{arm}} \sim 50\)–\(200\,\text{rev/s}\) for spin-stabilised rounds.

  3. Time delay: An electronic or mechanical timer prevents arming before a minimum elapsed time, ensuring safe separation from the launch platform.

  4. Altitude or pressure: For air-dropped munitions, a barometric switch confirms that the munition has descended (or ascended to target altitude), preventing premature arming at the aircraft.

  5. Velocity: Pitot-static measurement confirms the munition is in supersonic or high-subsonic flight.

docs.title: 23.2.4 Thermal Battery Arming
docs.text:
Missile fuzes and electronic warhead systems require electrical power. The preferred power source is a thermal battery: a lithium/iron disulphide (Li/FeS\(_2\)) or lithium/calcium chromate (Li/CaCrO\(_4\)) primary cell that is activated by a pyrotechnic heat pellet. In the unactivated state, the electrolyte is solid and non-conductive; no power is available to the fuze. On launch, the squib (small pyrotechnic charge) ignites the heat pellet, melting the electrolyte, and the battery delivers full voltage within 0.5–2 s:

\[V_{\text{batt}}(t) = V_{\text{OC}} \left(1 - e^{-t / \tau_{\text{batt}}}\right)\tag{23.6}\]

where \(V_{\text{OC}}\) is the open-circuit voltage (28 V typical) and \(\tau_{\text{batt}}\) is the electrochemical activation time constant. The thermal battery itself constitutes an arming event: without it, no electrical energy reaches the electronic fuze, rendering it inert.

docs.title: 23.3.1 Superquick (Instantaneous) PD Fuzes
docs.text:
The superquick PD fuze initiates within \(0.1\) ms of impact. At an impact velocity of \(400\) m/s, this corresponds to a penetration depth of only \(40\) mm before detonation — effectively surface burst. This is desired for anti-personnel and soft-target fragmentation effects.

The functional sequence is:

\[\text{Nose impact (crush element)} \rightarrow \text{Stab initiator fires} \rightarrow \text{Booster} \rightarrow \text{Detonation}\]

The crush element (also called the nose piece or ogive) deforms on impact, driving a firing pin into the stab initiator. The force required to initiate the stab initiator is typically \(5\)–\(15\,\text{N}\) at impact velocities exceeding \(30\,\text{m/s}\).

docs.title: 23.3.2 Delay Fuzes
docs.text:
For penetration of hardened targets (reinforced concrete, armour, hardened bunkers), a delay fuze allows the projectile to penetrate before detonation. The delay element is a pyrotechnic column (e.g., barium chromate/boron mixture) or an electronic RC-timer circuit.

Pyrotechnic delay column burn time:

\[t_d = \frac{L_{\text{col}}}{\dot{r}_{\text{burn}}}\tag{23.7}\]

where \(L_{\text{col}}\) is the column length and \(\dot{r}_{\text{burn}}\) is the linear burn rate (typically 20–100 mm/s). Electronic delay timers achieve accuracy of \(\pm 1\,\mu\text{s}\), far superior to pyrotechnic elements (\(\pm 5\%\) of nominal).

Penetration depth before detonation (simplified):

\[d_{\text{pen}} = V_{\text{impact}} \cdot t_d - \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{decel}} \cdot t_d^2\tag{23.8}\]

where \(a_{\text{decel}}\) is the mean deceleration during penetration, estimated from cavity expansion theory (Forrestal–Warren model).

docs.title: 23.3.3 Graze Fuzes
docs.text: A graze fuze initiates when the projectile impacts at a very shallow angle of attack (graze angle \(\gamma < 5°\)). Standard nose-impact fuzes fail to function at graze because the axial crush force is insufficient. Graze fuzes use a side-acting or base-acting initiator that responds to the lateral deceleration pulse during oblique impact.

docs.title: 23.3.4 Piezoelectric Initiators
docs.text:
Piezoelectric crystals (PZT, quartz, or tourmaline) generate a high-voltage pulse on mechanical impact without requiring any electrical power supply. The open-circuit voltage on impact is:

\[V_{\text{piezo}} = \frac{g_{33} \cdot \sigma \cdot L}{t_{\text{crystal}}}\tag{23.9}\]

where \(g_{33}\) is the piezoelectric voltage constant (\(\approx 24 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{V·m/N}\) for PZT-5A), \(\sigma\) is the applied stress, \(L\) is the crystal length, and \(t_{\text{crystal}}\) is the crystal thickness. Voltages of 500–5,000 V are achievable, far exceeding the 50–100 V required to fire an electric detonator. The self-powered nature of piezoelectric fuzes makes them attractive for simple PD applications where no battery is available.

Table 23.2. Point detonating fuze characteristics Type Initiation Delay Penetration Target Example Superquick PD \(< 0.1\) ms Negligible (\(< 0.05\) m) Soft / area M557 Short delay PD 10–25 ms 0.2–1.0 m Masonry, earth M739A1 Long delay PD 25–100 ms 1.0–5.0 m Hardened bunker FMU-143 Graze \(< 0.5\) ms Negligible Flat trajectories M582 Piezoelectric \(< 0.05\) ms Negligible Shaped-charge ATGM base fuze

docs.title: 23.4 Proximity Fuzes
docs.text: Proximity fuzes detonate the warhead at a standoff distance from the target, maximising the damage radius of the fragmentation or blast effect without requiring a direct hit. This is particularly important for air-defence missiles engaging high-speed manoeuvring aircraft, where a direct hit is geometrically improbable.

docs.title: 23.4.1 Radio Frequency Proximity Fuzes
docs.text:
The RF proximity fuze transmits a continuous-wave (CW) or pulsed RF signal and detects the Doppler shift or time-of-flight of the return signal reflected from the target. The classic Doppler proximity fuze (first employed in the VT fuze of World War II) detects the beat frequency between the transmitted and received signals:

\[f_D = \frac{2 V_r}{\lambda}\tag{23.10}\]

where \(V_r\) is the radial closure velocity between the fuze and target and \(\lambda\) is the RF wavelength. For a missile approaching a target at \(V_r = 500\,\text{m/s}\) with \(\lambda = 0.15\,\text{m}\) (2 GHz), \(f_D \approx 6.7\,\text{kHz}\) — well within the audio range and easily detected by simple electronics.

The fuze fires when the Doppler signal exceeds a threshold amplitude, corresponding to a miss distance of 3–10 m depending on the antenna pattern and signal processing. Modern RF fuzes use pulsed or FMCW waveforms to measure range directly:

\[R_{\text{target}} = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2}\tag{23.11}\]

where \(\Delta t\) is the round-trip propagation time. The fuze fires when \(R_{\text{target}}\) falls below \(R_{\text{opt}}\) (optimal burst radius).

docs.title: 23.4.2 Active Millimetre-Wave Proximity Fuzes
docs.text:
Operating at 35–94 GHz, millimetre-wave (mmW) fuzes achieve narrow beamwidths (\(\theta \sim 5°\)–\(10°\)) that reduce ground-clutter interference. They are used on modern surface-to-air missiles (e.g., Patriot PAC-3) where the missile must discriminate between the target aircraft and ground returns at low elevation angles.

The radar cross-section of the target at mmW frequencies:

\[\sigma_{\text{target}}(\text{dBsm}) = \sigma_0 + 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{R_{\text{ref}}}{R}\right)\tag{23.12}\]

The received power at range \(R\) follows the radar range equation:

\[P_r = \frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2 \sigma}{(4\pi)^3 R^4 L_s}\tag{23.13}\]

where \(P_t\) is transmit power, \(G_t\) and \(G_r\) are transmit and receive antenna gains, \(\sigma\) is target radar cross-section, and \(L_s\) is system losses.

docs.title: 23.4.3 Laser Proximity Fuzes
docs.text:
Laser fuzes transmit a pulsed or modulated infrared beam and measure time-of-flight to the target. The narrow beam (\(<2°\) full angle) rejects off-axis clutter and is inherently immune to RF jamming. Detection range:

\[R_{\text{max}} = \left( \frac{P_t \cdot A_r \cdot \rho_t \cdot \tau_a^2 \cdot \eta_{\text{sys}}}{4 \pi \cdot E_{\text{min}}} \right)^{1/2}\tag{23.14}\]

where \(P_t\) is peak pulse power, \(A_r\) is receiver aperture area, \(\rho_t\) is target reflectance, \(\tau_a\) is one-way atmospheric transmissivity, \(\eta_{\text{sys}}\) is optical efficiency, and \(E_{\text{min}}\) is minimum detectable energy.

Multiple laser beams arranged around the missile body allow \(360°\) azimuthal coverage. The fuze fires when any beam returns within the arming gate time window.

docs.title: 23.4.4 Acoustic Proximity Fuzes
docs.text: Used primarily in underwater torpedoes, acoustic proximity fuzes detect the broadband noise signature of a ship’s propellers or machinery, or the pressure perturbation in the ship’s wake. Wake-homing fuzes detect the reduced dissolved oxygen content or the micro-bubble density of the wake. Target detection range in acoustic fuzes is typically 2–8 m depending on target noise level and ambient sea noise.

docs.title: 23.4.5 Optical Shadow Fuze
docs.text:
The optical shadow fuze uses a photodiode array or phototransistor to detect the reduction in solar irradiance when an aircraft passes between the fuze and the sun. It is passive and therefore undetectable by electronic warfare. The irradiance change:

\[\Delta E = E_{\text{solar}} \cdot \frac{A_{\text{shadow}}}{4\pi R^2}\tag{23.15}\]

where \(A_{\text{shadow}}\) is the projected shadow area of the target aircraft at range \(R\).

docs.title: 23.4.6 Optimal Burst Height
docs.text:
The optimal burst height (OBH) maximises the fragment density (fragments per unit area) incident on the target. For a cylindrical warhead with fragment spray half-angle \(\alpha\) and total fragment number \(N_f\), the fragment surface density at range \(R\) from detonation:

\[\rho_f(R) = \frac{N_f}{2\pi R^2 (1 - \cos\alpha)}\tag{23.16}\]

The optimum standoff \(R_{\text{opt}}\) balances fragment density against lateral dispersion over the target projected area \(A_t\):

\[R_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{\frac{N_f \cdot A_t}{2\pi \cdot n_{\text{kill}} \cdot (1-\cos\alpha)}}\tag{23.17}\]

where \(n_{\text{kill}}\) is the required number of fragments on target for a kill. For typical SAM fuzes engaging aircraft, OBH is in the range of 3–15 m depending on warhead size and target type.

docs.title: 23.5.1 Programmable Height-of-Burst Fuzes
docs.text:
Modern artillery and air-delivered weapons employ programmable fuzes that receive their settings via a fuze setter (inductive or contact coupling) immediately before firing. The fuze stores the selected mode — superquick, delay, time-to-burst, or height-of-burst — in a non-volatile register. The electronic timer counts elapsed time from launch:

\[t_{\text{HOB}} = t_{\text{flight}} - \Delta t_{\text{margin}}\tag{23.18}\]

where \(\Delta t_{\text{margin}}\) provides a safety margin before ground impact. For height-of-burst fuzing, the fuze incorporates a radar altimeter that measures altitude above ground and triggers at a commanded AGL height.

docs.title: 23.5.2 Smart Fuzes with Target Recognition
docs.text:
Smart fuzes incorporate a microprocessor and sensor suite (accelerometer, deceleration profile measurement) that infers the target type from the penetration signature. The deceleration pulse during target penetration is diagnostic:

  • Soil/earth: gradual deceleration, \(50\)–\(200\,g\), duration \(>5\) ms.

  • Masonry: sharp deceleration spike, \(200\)–\(500\,g\), then residual.

  • Reinforced concrete: \(500\)–\(2{,}000\,g\) with distinct rebar signature pulses.

  • Steel armour: Very sharp spike, \(2{,}000\)–\(10{,}000\,g\), short duration.

Based on the signature, the fuze selects the appropriate delay (or switches to a different detonation mode). Pattern recognition is implemented via a trained threshold classifier or simple peak-detection with duration gating in firmware.

docs.title: 23.5.3 GPS-Aided Fuzes
docs.text:
Precision-guided munitions carry a GPS receiver in the fuze body. The fuze tracks GPS position throughout flight and calculates predicted impact time from the current state vector. Burst point can be commanded as a GPS coordinate:

\[\mathbf{r}_{\text{burst}} = \mathbf{r}_{\text{target}} + \Delta h \cdot \hat{z}\tag{23.19}\]

where \(\Delta h\) is the commanded burst height. Combined with an inertial measurement unit (IMU), the GPS-aided fuze can achieve burst-point accuracy with CEP \(< 5\) m even after GPS is denied in terminal phase (GPS coasting with IMU).

docs.title: 23.5.4 Multi-Option Fuze for Artillery (MOFA)
docs.text:
The MOFA (adopted by the US Army as M782) provides four functions in a single fuze body: (1) superquick PD, (2) delay PD, (3) proximity airburst, and (4) time-of-flight airburst. The operator selects the mode via a portable fuze setter (PFS) which communicates with the fuze via a 1553B or RS-422 serial interface. The fuze stores up to four different burst settings simultaneously.

Table 23.3. Multi-option fuze operational modes Mode Initiation Trigger Timing Accuracy Application Superquick PD Impact (\(< 0.1\) ms) N/A Anti-personnel, vehicles Delay PD Impact + timer (10–100 ms) \(\pm 1\,\mu\)s Bunkers, masonry Proximity airburst Radar/laser HOB 4–10 m \(\pm 0.5\) m Anti-personnel in defilade Time airburst Elapsed time from firing \(\pm 5\) ms Suppression, illumination

docs.title: 23.5.5 Wind Correction in the Fuze Computer
docs.text:
For precision air-burst fuzing, ballistic drift must be accounted for. A nose-mounted anemometer or inertially-derived wind estimate feeds a fuze-resident ballistic computer. The lateral displacement due to cross-wind over time of flight \(T\):

\[y_{\text{drift}} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{W_{\text{cross}}}{V_0}\right) g T^2\tag{23.20}\]

where \(W_{\text{cross}}\) is the cross-wind component and \(V_0\) is initial velocity. The fuze computer applies a correction to the burst time or proximity threshold to account for this drift, maintaining target engagement geometry.

docs.title: 23.6 Fuze Testing and Qualification
docs.text: Fuze qualification follows a structured program combining environmental, functional, and safety testing.

docs.title: 23.6.1 Acceleration and Setback Testing
docs.text:
An acceleration sled or air gun reproduces launch setback loads without propellant, allowing instrumented fuze function testing at controlled \(g\) levels. Typical test parameters:

  • Peak acceleration: 100 g to 20,000 g (depending on platform).

  • Pulse duration: 1–50 ms (half-sine or trapezoidal profile).

  • Required result: fuze does NOT arm below minimum stimulus; DOES arm above.

The probability of arming as a function of stimulus level follows a logistic (sigmoid) function:

\[P_{\text{arm}}(a) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-k(a - a_{50})}}\tag{23.21}\]

where \(a_{50}\) is the 50% arming acceleration and \(k\) is the slope parameter. The fuze must have a sharp transition (large \(k\)) to maximise the discrimination between safe and armed stimuli.

docs.title: 23.6.2 Spin Table Testing
docs.text: For spin-arming fuzes, a centrifuge or spin table applies controlled angular velocity. The fuze is mounted with its spin axis aligned with the table axis. Spin arming must occur above \(\omega_{\text{arm}}\) and must NOT occur below \(\omega_{\text{safe}}\), providing a defined no-arm band below the arming threshold.

docs.title: 23.6.3 MIL-STD-810 Environmental Tests
docs.text:
All fuzes must survive the following environmental conditions without malfunction or degradation of safety:

  • Temperature: \(-54°C\) to \(+71°C\) operational; \(-62°C\) to \(+85°C\) storage (MIL-STD-810 Method 501/502).

  • Humidity: 95% RH at \(40°C\) for 240 hours (Method 507).

  • Vibration: Frequency sweep 5–2,000 Hz; power spectral density per platform specification (Method 514).

  • Shock: Half-sine 40 g, 11 ms (transport shock); sawtooth 100 g, 6 ms (handling drop) (Method 516).

  • Salt fog: 5% NaCl solution at \(35°C\) for 48 hours (Method 509).

docs.title: 23.6.4 Insensitive Munition (IM) Fuze Tests
docs.text:
Under MIL-STD-2105, munitions (including fuzes) must not undergo mass detonation (Reaction Level 1) when subjected to the following Insensitive Munition stimuli:

  • Slow cook-off (SCO): 3.3°C/hour ramp from ambient to function.

  • Fast cook-off (FCO): Pool fire at \(800°C\) for minimum 10 minutes.

  • Bullet impact (BI): 12.7 mm projectile at 850 m/s.

  • Fragment impact (FI): 16.6 g FSP at 2,530 ft/s.

  • Shaped charge jet (SCJ): 84 mm HEAT warhead.

  • Sympathetic detonation (SYD): Adjacent donor detonation.

Fuze designs must minimise the probability of inducing mass detonation in these events, using insensitive explosive compositions and protective structural features.

docs.title: 23.6.5 Statistical Proof Testing and Lot Acceptance
docs.text:
Lot acceptance testing uses statistical sampling to demonstrate compliance with the reliability specification. For a required reliability \(R = 0.999\) (one failure per thousand) with confidence level \(C = 0.95\), the required sample size \(n\) for zero-failure acceptance is derived from the binomial distribution:

\[n = \frac{\ln(1 - C)}{\ln(R)} = \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.999)} \approx 2{,}995\tag{23.22}\]

This means that if \(n = 2{,}995\) fuzes are tested with zero failures, we can be 95% confident that the true reliability is at least 0.999. In practice, round-to-fire testing is supplemented by component-level testing and analysis to reduce the total number of complete system firings.

The binomial confidence interval on observed reliability \(\hat{R} = 1 - k/n\) (where \(k\) is the number of failures):

\[P\left(R \geq 1 - \frac{\chi^2_{1-\alpha,\,2(k+1)}}{2n}\right) = 1 - \alpha\tag{23.23}\] Table 23.4. Fuze qualification test matrix summary Test Category Standard Key Parameter Pass Criterion Function (arming) MIL-STD-1316 Arming probability vs \(g\) \(P_{\text{arm}} \geq 0.999\) at rated \(g\) Function (initiation) MIL-STD-1316 Fuze train propagation 100% propagation Safety (no-arm) MIL-STD-1316 Sub-threshold stimulus 0 initiations in \(10^6\) tests Environmental (thermal) MIL-STD-810 501 \(-54\)°C / \(+71\)°C No degradation Environmental (vibe) MIL-STD-810 514 Mission profile PSD Function retained IM (bullet impact) MIL-STD-2105 12.7 mm AP at 850 m/s Reaction \(\leq\) Type V IM (fast cook-off) MIL-STD-2105 Pool fire 10 min No mass detonation Lot acceptance DEF-STAN / AMSAA \(n\) rounds, \(k=0\) failures 95% CL on \(R \geq 0.999\)

docs.title: 23.6.6 Electromagnetic Compatibility and RF Hazard
docs.text:
Fuzes containing electric initiators must demonstrate immunity to RF-induced firing (HERO — Hazards of Electromagnetic Radiation to Ordnance). The test methodology per MIL-STD-1310 includes:

  • CW field exposure at frequencies 14 kHz to 40 GHz.

  • EMP simulation (MIL-STD-461 RS105): 50,000 V/m field rise \(\leq 2.5\) ns.

  • Lightning indirect effects (DO-160 Section 22).

  • The firing current threshold for the initiator must not be reached under any plausible ambient EM environment.

The no-fire current for a standard M55 electric initiator is \(0.45\) A (all-fire at \(1.0\) A). The induced current in the firing circuit under an external field \(E\) (V/m) through a loop of area \(A\) and circuit resistance \(Z\):

\[I_{\text{induced}} = \frac{E \cdot \sqrt{A}}{\lambda \cdot Z}\tag{23.24}\]

Fuze circuit designs incorporate spark gaps, ferrite beads, bypass capacitors, and twisted-pair wiring to limit \(I_{\text{induced}}\) to no more than \(20\%\) of the no-fire current.

docs.title: 23.6.7 Fuze Development Programme Timeline
docs.text:
A typical fuze development programme from concept to qualification spans 5–8 years:

  1. Technology Maturation: 12–18 months (component breadboards, lethality modelling).

  2. Engineering Development Model (EDM): 18–24 months (first hardware, DT&E).

  3. System Development and Demonstration (SDD): 24–36 months (qualification testing).

  4. Production Qualification Testing (PQT): 6–12 months (first lot acceptance).

Cost drivers include the large number of explosive function tests required, the specialised range and sled facilities needed, and the strict configuration management of explosive compositions and component tolerances.

docs.title: 23.6.8 Summary of Fuze Design Equations
docs.text:
The following table collects the primary design equations referenced in this chapter:

Table 23.5. Summary of key fuze design equations Equation Description Reference \(P_{\text{combined}} = \prod p_i\) Combined safety probability Eq. (23.2) \(D_{\text{arm}} = V_0 \cdot t_{\text{arm}}\) Arming distance Eq. (23.3) \(f_D = 2V_r/\lambda\) Doppler fuze frequency Eq. (23.10) \(R = c\Delta t / 2\) Pulsed radar range Eq. (23.11) \(\rho_f = N_f / [2\pi R^2(1-\cos\alpha)]\) Fragment surface density Eq. (23.16) \(n = \ln(1-C)/\ln(R)\) Lot acceptance sample size Eq. (23.22) \(P_{\text{arm}} = 1/(1+e^{-k(a-a_{50})})\) Arming probability sigmoid Eq. (23.21)

docs.title: 24.1 Structural Design Requirements
docs.text: The missile airframe is a precision structure whose primary function is to provide a rigid, lightweight shell that carries all internal subsystems, transmits aerodynamic and propulsive loads, and survives the thermal and mechanical environment of its complete flight profile. Unlike aircraft structures designed for many thousands of flight hours, the missile airframe is optimised for a single use — though its storage life must span 10–25 years.

docs.title: 24.1.1 Load Cases
docs.text:
Structural analysis identifies the critical load cases that size each airframe section:

  • Launch axial load: Motor thrust minus aerodynamic drag minus inertial resistance of the missile mass. At ignition the net axial force on the airframe is:

    \[F_{\text{ax}} = T_{\text{motor}} - D_{\text{aero}} - m \ddot{x}\tag{24.1}\]

    Peak axial load typically occurs at peak thrust (end of the boost phase for a regressive-burning motor) when drag has not yet reached its maximum because the missile is still accelerating.

  • Manoeuvre lateral loads: During a pulling manoeuvre at load factor \(n\), the net lateral force is:

    \[F_{\text{lat}} = n \cdot W = n \cdot m g\tag{24.2}\]

    Applied at the centre of pressure (CP), reacted at the centre of mass (CM), this produces a bending moment along the body that is maximum at the CM station. Design load factors for tactical missiles range from \(n = 20\,g\) (SAMs and AAMs) to \(n = 40\,g\) for highly agile short-range interceptors.

  • Aerodynamic pressure: Dynamic pressure \(q = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2\) acts on all external surfaces. For a missile at Mach 3 at sea level:

    \[q = \frac{1}{2} \times 1.225 \times (3 \times 340)^2 \approx 635{,}000\,\text{Pa}\tag{24.3}\]

    This drives fin bending loads and radome pressure differential.

  • Thermal loads: Aerodynamic heating produces temperature gradients that introduce thermal stresses, particularly at material interfaces with different coefficients of thermal expansion.

docs.title: 24.1.2 Safety Factors and Design Margins
docs.text:
Structural design safety factors per MIL-HDBK-310 and AIAA S-110:

  • Limit load: Maximum load expected in service.

  • Design limit load factor: 1.0 (structure must not yield at limit load).

  • Ultimate load factor: 1.5 × limit load (structure must not fracture).

  • Fatigue/damage tolerance: 1.4 additional factor on repeated-load components.

The margin of safety (MS) is defined as:

\[MS = \frac{F_{\text{allow}}}{F_{\text{applied}} \times FS} - 1 \geq 0\tag{24.4}\]

where \(F_{\text{allow}}\) is material allowable (yield or ultimate), \(F_{\text{applied}}\) is the applied load, and \(FS\) is the factor of safety (1.0 for yield check, 1.5 for ultimate). A positive MS indicates adequate structural margin; design targets MS \(= +0.10\) to \(+0.20\) to allow for manufacturing variability.

docs.title: 24.1.3 Mass Fraction and Structural Efficiency
docs.text:
The structural mass fraction defines the fraction of total launch mass devoted to the airframe (excluding motor case, which is counted separately in propulsion):

\[f_{\text{struct}} = \frac{m_{\text{airframe}}}{m_{\text{launch}}} \approx 0.05 \text{ to } 0.15\tag{24.5}\]

Advanced CFRP airframes achieve \(f_{\text{struct}} \approx 0.05\)–\(0.08\), while all-metal designs are typically \(0.10\)–\(0.15\). The structural efficiency of a thin-walled cylinder under axial compression is characterised by the knockdown factor \(\gamma_{\text{KD}}\), which accounts for geometric imperfections reducing buckling load below the classical Euler–Donnell prediction:

\[F_{\text{crit}} = \gamma_{\text{KD}} \cdot \frac{2\pi E t^2}{\sqrt{3(1-\nu^2)}} \cdot \frac{t}{R}\tag{24.6}\]

where \(E\) is Young’s modulus, \(t\) is skin thickness, \(R\) is body radius, \(\nu\) is Poisson’s ratio, and \(\gamma_{\text{KD}} \approx 0.3\)–\(0.7\) depending on \(R/t\) and manufacturing quality.

docs.title: 24.2 Airframe Sections and Interfaces
docs.text: A tactical missile body is divided into longitudinal sections assembled at mechanical interfaces. Each section encapsulates one or more subsystems:

docs.title: 24.2.1 Nose Section and Radome
docs.text:
The nose section houses the seeker or sensor head. The outer shell (radome) must be transparent to the seeker’s operating wavelength (RF, laser, optical, or infrared) while sustaining high aerodynamic loads. The nose section typically carries:

  • The radome (RF or IR transparent material).

  • Seeker gimbal assembly.

  • Nose boom (if pitot-static port is required).

  • Forward antenna for command guidance datalink.

Mechanical interface to the guidance section is typically a threaded ring or bayonet coupling with a positive lock. Electrical connections route through a multi-way connector at the interface plane.

docs.title: 24.2.2 Guidance Section
docs.text:
The guidance section contains the avionics — navigation computer, signal processors, RF receivers, inertial measurement unit — packaged on printed circuit boards (PCBs) mounted on a chassis inside the pressure shell. Key design features:

  • Shock isolation: The chassis is mounted on silicone elastomer mounts to attenuate high-frequency vibration and shock from propulsion and flight.

  • Thermal control: Potted electronics, thermal interface materials, and metallic heat spreaders conduct waste heat to the airframe skin.

  • EMC shielding: Aluminium or copper-plated electronics chassis forms a Faraday cage; filtered feedthroughs for all external signals.

docs.title: 24.2.3 Warhead Section
docs.text:
The warhead section houses the explosive fill and fuze. Structural requirements include:

  • Mechanical isolation from guidance electronics (blast partition).

  • Fuze pocket with electrical connector and sealing.

  • Sufficient structural rigidity to prevent deformation that would compromise fuze alignment.

  • Bore-sight accuracy of fuze initiator axis relative to body axis: \(< 0.5°\).

docs.title: 24.2.4 Motor Section
docs.text:
The motor section is the structural backbone. It is a pressure vessel (the motor case) that also serves as the primary load-carrying member in axial compression during boost. The motor section must:

  • Withstand maximum expected operating pressure (MEOP) with safety factor 1.25 (burst pressure test at 1.5 × MEOP).

  • Accept propellant loading access (inhibitor panels or spin-cast closure).

  • Provide flange interfaces fore and aft for attachment to adjacent sections.

  • Carry TVC nozzle loads at the aft closure.

docs.title: 24.2.5 Fin and Tail Section
docs.text:
The tail section carries the fin assembly and the TVC nozzle. Critical requirements:

  • Fin attachment must withstand maximum fin root bending moment without yielding.

  • Fin-fold mechanisms (for tube-launched weapons) must deploy reliably in \(< 0.2\) s.

  • Tail can provide the interface for the launch rail ejector shoe.

  • Nozzle-to-tail interface must be airtight to prevent hot gas leakage.

docs.title: 24.3 Structural Materials
docs.text: Material selection for missile airframes involves trade-offs among specific strength, specific stiffness, high-temperature capability, density, machinability, and cost.

docs.title: 24.3.1 Aluminium Alloys
docs.text:
7075-T73 aluminium is the workhorse material for missile airframe sections not subject to elevated temperature. Its properties:

  • Density: \(\rho = 2.81\,\text{g/cm}^3\).

  • Yield strength: \(\sigma_y = 435\,\text{MPa}\).

  • Ultimate tensile strength: \(\sigma_u = 505\,\text{MPa}\).

  • Young’s modulus: \(E = 71\,\text{GPa}\).

  • Maximum service temperature: \(\approx 120°C\) (beyond which stress-corrosion properties degrade).

The T73 temper provides superior stress-corrosion cracking (SCC) resistance compared to the stronger T6 temper — critical for long-term storage. Body rings, interface flanges, and guidance section housings are typically CNC-machined from 7075-T73 billet or forgings.

docs.title: 24.3.2 High-Strength Steels
docs.text:
300M (AMS 6257) and D6AC steels are used where very high strength is required in a smaller cross-section: bolt flanges, pin-loaded lugs, motor aft closures:

  • 300M: \(\sigma_y = 1,655\,\text{MPa}\); \(\sigma_u = 2,000\,\text{MPa}\); KIC = 60–90 MPa\(\sqrt{\text{m}}\).

  • D6AC: \(\sigma_y = 1,480\,\text{MPa}\); used in motor cases; excellent fracture toughness.

  • Density: \(7.83\,\text{g/cm}^3\) — approximately \(2.8\times\) heavier than aluminium per unit volume, but used in small highly-loaded sections where section geometry is constrained.

docs.title: 24.3.3 Titanium Ti-6Al-4V
docs.text:
Titanium Ti-6Al-4V (Grade 5) offers the best strength-to-weight ratio of metallic alloys at temperatures up to \(315°C\), and it is non-magnetic — important for proximity fuze function:

  • Density: \(4.43\,\text{g/cm}^3\).

  • Yield strength: \(\sigma_y = 880\,\text{MPa}\) (annealed).

  • Ultimate strength: \(\sigma_u = 950\,\text{MPa}\).

  • Young’s modulus: \(E = 114\,\text{GPa}\).

  • Fatigue strength (10\(^7\) cycles): \(\approx 500\,\text{MPa}\) (R = 0.1).

Typical applications: seeker support structure, TVC actuator brackets, high-temperature fin attachment fittings, and nose tip structure for Mach 3–4 flight.

docs.title: 24.3.4 Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP)
docs.text:
Filament-wound or prepreg CFRP provides the best specific strength of any airframe material:

  • Unidirectional IM7/8552 laminate: \(\sigma_{\text{tensile}} = 2,724\,\text{MPa}\); \(E_1 = 164\,\text{GPa}\); \(\rho = 1.57\,\text{g/cm}^3\).

  • Quasi-isotropic layup (\([0/\pm45/90]_s\)): \(\sigma_u \approx 600\,\text{MPa}\); \(E \approx 55\,\text{GPa}\).

  • Specific strength advantage over 7075-T6 Al: approximately \(3.5\times\) in tension.

CFRP body tubes are fabricated by filament winding over a mandrel. The winding angle is optimised to balance hoop and axial strength:

\[\frac{N_\theta}{N_x} = \tan^2\theta_{\text{wind}}\tag{24.7}\]

where \(N_\theta\) is hoop load per unit length, \(N_x\) is axial load per unit length, and \(\theta_{\text{wind}}\) is the helix angle of the filament.

docs.title: 24.3.5 Graphite-Phenolic and Ablative Composites
docs.text:
Carbon/phenolic and silica/phenolic composites are used for high-temperature components exposed to motor exhaust plumes: nozzle exit cones, TVC vanes, and ablative nose tips. Their primary property is controlled ablation — the resin pyrolyses and chars, absorbing heat and protecting the underlying structure.

Ablation rate (simplified):

\[\dot{s} = \frac{\dot{q}”_{\text{aero}} - \dot{q}”_{\text{re-rad}}}{\rho_c \cdot \left(H_{\text{pyro}} + c_p \Delta T\right)}\tag{24.8}\]

where \(\dot{q}”_{\text{aero}}\) is the incident heat flux, \(\dot{q}”_{\text{re-rad}}\) is the re-radiated flux (\(\epsilon \sigma T^4\)), \(\rho_c\) is composite density, \(H_{\text{pyro}}\) is the pyrolysis enthalpy, \(c_p\) is specific heat, and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature rise.

docs.title: 24.3.6 Maraging Steel 350
docs.text: Maraging 350 steel (\(\sigma_u = 2{,}400\,\text{MPa}\)) is used for motor case closures and high-pressure fittings in boost motors where extreme burst pressure resistance is required. The material achieves its strength through martensite aging rather than carbon hardening, resulting in very high fracture toughness despite extreme strength.

docs.title: 24.3.7 Beryllium (Strategic Applications)
docs.text:
Beryllium’s unique combination of low density (\(1.85\,\text{g/cm}^3\)), high Young’s modulus (\(287\,\text{GPa}\)), and good thermal stability makes it attractive for inertial instrument flexures, mirror substrates, and precision structure in seeker assemblies. However, beryllium dust is highly toxic (berylliosis), requiring specialised machining and handling facilities. Strategic use is limited to components where no alternative meets the performance requirement.

Table 24.1. Missile airframe structural materials comparison Material \(\rho\) \(\sigma_y\) \(\sigma_u\) \(E\) \(T_{\max}\) Application (g/cm\(^3\)) (MPa) (MPa) (GPa) (°C) 7075-T73 Al 2.81 435 505 71 120 Body rings, housings D6AC steel 7.83 1480 1690 207 400 Motor cases, flanges 300M steel 7.83 1655 2000 207 300 Pin lugs, closures Ti-6Al-4V 4.43 880 950 114 315 Seeker structure, fins Maraging 350 8.00 2415 2500 190 450 Motor case closures CFRP (UD IM7) 1.57 — 2724 164 150 Body tubes, fins CFRP (QI layup) 1.57 — 600 55 150 Structural shells Beryllium 1.85 270 380 287 400 Precision instruments

docs.title: 24.4 Aerodynamic Heating and Thermal Protection
docs.text: Aerodynamic heating is a critical design driver for missiles operating above Mach 2.5, and the dominant challenge for hypersonic vehicles above Mach 5.

docs.title: 24.4.1 Stagnation Point Heat Rate
docs.text:
The Sutton–Graves correlation estimates the stagnation point convective heat flux:

\[\dot{q}_s = C \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\rho_\infty}{R_n}} \cdot V_\infty^3\tag{24.9}\]

where \(C = 1.741 \times 10^{-4}\) (SI units, \(\dot{q}_s\) in W/m\(^2\)), \(\rho_\infty\) is free-stream density (kg/m\(^3\)), \(R_n\) is nose radius (m), and \(V_\infty\) is free-stream velocity (m/s). For a missile with \(R_n = 0.01\) m at Mach 5 at sea level (\(V_\infty = 1{,}700\,\text{m/s}\), \(\rho_\infty = 1.225\,\text{kg/m}^3\)):

\[\dot{q}_s \approx 1.741\times10^{-4} \times \sqrt{1.225/0.01} \times (1700)^3 \approx 10\,\text{MW/m}^2\]

This underscores the severe requirement for thermal protection at hypersonic speeds.

docs.title: 24.4.2 Flat Surface Heating
docs.text:
Along the body surface away from the stagnation point, the turbulent flat-plate reference enthalpy method provides heating rate distribution:

\[\dot{q}_x = 0.0296 \cdot \rho_e^{0.8} \mu_e^{0.2} V_e \cdot c_{pe} \cdot (T_{\text{aw}} - T_w) \cdot x^{-0.2}\tag{24.10}\]

where \(\rho_e\), \(\mu_e\), \(V_e\), \(c_{pe}\) are edge-condition properties, \(T_{\text{aw}}\) is adiabatic wall temperature, \(T_w\) is wall temperature, and \(x\) is distance from leading edge.

docs.title: 24.4.3 Adiabatic Wall Temperature
docs.text:
The adiabatic wall temperature (recovery temperature) is:

\[T_{\text{aw}} = T_\infty \left(1 + r \cdot \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M_\infty^2\right)\tag{24.11}\]

where \(r\) is the recovery factor (\(r = \sqrt{Pr}\) for laminar; \(r = Pr^{1/3}\) for turbulent), \(\gamma = 1.4\) for air, and \(M_\infty\) is free-stream Mach number. At Mach 4, \(T_{\text{aw}} \approx 3.7 \times 288 = 1{,}065\,\text{K}\) — far exceeding the melting point of aluminium.

docs.title: 24.4.4 Ablative Nose Tips
docs.text:
Carbon-phenolic (C/Ph) and PICA (Phenolic Impregnated Carbon Ablator) are the primary ablative materials for missile nose tips:

  • PICA: Density 0.26 g/cm\(^3\); \(H_{\text{pyro}} \approx 8\,\text{MJ/kg}\); operating up to 3,000 K surface temperature.

  • Carbon-phenolic: Density 1.45 g/cm\(^3\); high ablation resistance; used in ICBM re-entry vehicles.

  • Silica-phenolic: Lower performance but cheaper; used for moderate heat flux (\(< 1\,\text{MW/m}^2\)) applications.

Shape change during ablation must be predicted (coupled aero-thermal-ablation model) to ensure the nose maintains acceptable radar signature and aerodynamic drag characteristics.

docs.title: 24.4.5 Seeker Dome Thermal Limits
docs.text:
The seeker dome material must maintain electromagnetic transparency while surviving the thermal environment:

  • Sapphire (Al\(_2\)O\(_3\)): IR transparent 0.2–5.5 \(\mu\)m; service temperature to 1,900°C; excellent rain erosion resistance; expensive.

  • ZnS (Zinc sulphide): IR transparent to 12 \(\mu\)m; limited to \(300°C\); used on FLIR-seeker missiles with modest speed.

  • Zinc selenide (ZnSe): Transparent 0.5–22 \(\mu\)m; similar temp limit to ZnS.

  • Spinel (MgAl\(_2\)O\(_4\)): 0.2–5.5 \(\mu\)m; 1,600°C; better mechanical toughness than sapphire.

docs.title: 24.4.6 Radome Electromagnetic and Thermal Properties
docs.text: Table 24.2. Radome material properties for RF-guided missiles Material Dielectric Loss Max Temp Rain Erosion Constant \(\varepsilon_r\) Tangent \(\tan\delta\) (°C) Rating Silicon nitride (Si\(_3\)N\(_4\)) 7.8 0.002 1,200 Excellent Pyroceram (Corning) 5.6 0.002 900 Good Fused silica (SiO\(_2\)) 3.8 0.0002 1,100 Poor (soft) PTFE/fibre glass (RT-duroid) 2.2 0.0009 260 Poor Raydel (PEEK-based) 3.3 0.003 250 Moderate Alumina (99% Al\(_2\)O\(_3\)) 9.9 0.0003 1,600 Excellent

docs.title: 24.5.1 Axial Load Distribution
docs.text:
The axial load at any cross-section \(x\) along the body (measured from nose) is the net of thrust, drag, and inertia of the missile mass aft of station \(x\):

\[F_{\text{ax}}(x) = T(t) \cdot \delta(x - x_{\text{nozzle}}) - D \cdot \frac{x}{L} - m_{\text{aft}}(x) \cdot \ddot{x}\tag{24.12}\]

Peak compressive axial load typically occurs at the motor-to-guidance interface during maximum thrust, where the full motor thrust minus only the forward-body drag must be reacted.

docs.title: 24.5.2 Body Bending Moment
docs.text:
Treating the missile as a free-free beam under distributed aerodynamic load \(w(x)\) (N/m) and with lateral acceleration \(\ddot{y}\) applied at every mass element, the shear force \(V(x)\) and bending moment \(M(x)\) are obtained by integration:

\[\frac{dV}{dx} = m'(x) \ddot{y} - w(x)\tag{24.13}\] \[\frac{dM}{dx} = V(x)\tag{24.14}\]

where \(m'(x)\) is mass per unit length. For a first-order estimate, treating the missile as a uniform beam of length \(L\) with point lateral force \(F_{\text{lat}} = nW\) at \(x = x_{\text{CP}}\):

\[M_{\max} = F_{\text{lat}} \cdot (x_{\text{CP}} - x_{\text{CM}}) \cdot \frac{x_{\text{CM}}}{L}\tag{24.15}\]

The resulting bending stress at the outer fibre (radius \(R\), second moment of area \(I\)):

\[\sigma_{\text{bend}} = \frac{M_{\max} \cdot R}{I}\tag{24.16}\]

For a thin-walled tube: \(I = \pi R^3 t\) where \(t\) is wall thickness.

docs.title: 24.5.3 Fin Root Bending Moment
docs.text:
Each fin generates lift \(L_{\text{fin}}\) and experiences a bending moment at its root:

\[M_{\text{fin\,root}} = q \cdot C_{N_\alpha}^{\text{fin}} \cdot \alpha \cdot S_{\text{fin}} \cdot \bar{c}_{\text{fin}}\tag{24.17}\]

where \(q\) is dynamic pressure, \(C_{N_\alpha}^{\text{fin}}\) is fin normal force slope (per radian), \(\alpha\) is angle of attack, \(S_{\text{fin}}\) is fin planform area, and \(\bar{c}_{\text{fin}}\) is the span-wise moment arm from root to aerodynamic centre.

docs.title: 24.5.4 Vibration and Acoustic Loads
docs.text:
The launch vibration environment is specified as a power spectral density (PSD) in units of g\(^2\)/Hz. The root-mean-square (RMS) acceleration response of the structure at frequency \(f_n\):

\[a_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2} f_n Q \cdot W(f_n)}\tag{24.18}\]

where \(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\) is the quality factor and \(W(f_n)\) is the input PSD at the natural frequency. This is Miles’ equation, widely used for single-degree-of-freedom response to broadband random vibration.

docs.title: 24.6.1 Fixed Fin Configuration
docs.text:
Fixed fins are bonded and bolted into slots machined in the tail section. Bonding uses structural film adhesive (Redux 312 or equivalent); bolting provides positive mechanical retention and redundant load path. Fin planform shapes used in practice:

  • Delta: Simple manufacturing; high aspect ratio at transonic; common on SAMs.

  • Clipped delta: Removes inefficient tip region; favoured for Mach 2+.

  • Double-tapered (diamond section): Minimises wave drag at supersonic speed.

  • Rectangular: Simplest; acceptable for subsonic and low supersonic.

docs.title: 24.6.2 Fin Flutter Analysis
docs.text:
Fin flutter occurs when the aerodynamic forces excite the bending and torsional modes in phase. The simplified two-degree-of-freedom flutter speed (Garrick–Bisplinghoff approach for thin wings):

\[V_F = \pi \omega_\theta b \sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{\rho_\infty C_{L_\alpha}}} \cdot \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{\omega_h}{\omega_\theta}\right)^2}\tag{24.19}\]

where \(\omega_\theta\) is the first torsional frequency (rad/s), \(\omega_h\) is the first bending frequency (rad/s), \(b\) is semi-chord (m), \(\mu = m/(\rho_\infty \pi b^2 s)\) is the mass ratio (\(m\) is fin mass, \(s\) is fin span), and \(C_{L_\alpha}\) is the lift curve slope (per radian). The design requirement is \(V_F > 1.15 \times V_{\max}\) (structural speed limit).

docs.title: 24.6.3 Roll Stabilisation by Canted Fins
docs.text:
Canted fins at angle \(\delta_{\text{cant}}\) to the body meridional plane produce a rolling moment:

\[\dot{p} = \frac{M_{\text{roll}}}{I_x} = \frac{4 \cdot q \cdot S_{\text{fin}} \cdot r_{\text{fin}} \cdot C_{L_\alpha} \cdot \delta_{\text{cant}}}{I_x}\tag{24.20}\]

where \(r_{\text{fin}}\) is the radial distance of the fin aerodynamic centre from the missile centreline and \(I_x\) is the roll moment of inertia. Equilibrium spin rate is achieved when roll damping equals roll driving moment.

docs.title: 24.6.4 Folding Fin Mechanisms
docs.text:
Tube-launched weapons (from man-portable launchers, aircraft pods, ship VLS cells) require fins to fold into the tube cross-section. Typical fold mechanisms:

  • Spring-loaded pivot: Torsion spring drives fin to deployed position; spring is pre-loaded at assembly; positive detent locks fin when deployed.

  • Wrap-around fins (WAF): Fins curve around the body during storage; spring or aerodynamic force deploys them.

  • Gas-driven actuator: Gas generator drives a piston that pivots fin to deployed position; faster than spring but adds complexity.

Deployment time must be \(< 0.2\) s (typically \(50\)–\(100\) ms) to ensure roll stabilisation before the missile exits the launch tube or clears the aircraft pylon.

docs.title: 24.7.1 Electrical Design Fundamentals
docs.text:
For a monolithic radome wall with dielectric constant \(\varepsilon_r\) and thickness \(d\), the transmission coefficient for normal incidence is:

\[T = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{4}\left(\sqrt{\varepsilon_r} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}\right)^2 \sin^2\left(\frac{2\pi d}{\lambda_d}\right)}\tag{24.21}\]

where \(\lambda_d = \lambda_0 / \sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\) is the wavelength in the dielectric. Perfect transmission (\(T = 1\)) occurs when \(d = n\lambda_d/2\) (half-wave or full-wave wall). The design equation for half-wave wall thickness:

\[d_{\text{HW}} = \frac{\lambda_0}{2\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}\tag{24.22}\]

For Si\(_3\)N\(_4\) (\(\varepsilon_r = 7.8\)) at \(10\) GHz (\(\lambda_0 = 30\) mm): \(d_{\text{HW}} = 30/(2\sqrt{7.8}) = 5.37\) mm — a practical structural thickness.

docs.title: 24.7.2 Boresight Error
docs.text:
The boresight error (BSE) is the angular difference between the true target direction and the apparent direction due to radome refraction. For an ogive radome, BSE is a function of seeker gimbal angle \(\theta_g\):

\[\text{BSE}(\theta_g) \approx K_{\text{BSE}} \cdot \theta_g\tag{24.23}\]

where \(K_{\text{BSE}}\) is the BSE slope (mrad/deg). Requirement: \(|K_{\text{BSE}}| < 0.1\) mrad/deg (i.e., \(< 0.3\) mrad at \(\theta_g = 3°\)). Boresight error rate (BSER) — the derivative \(d(\text{BSE})/d\theta_g\) — couples with the guidance loop and can cause limit cycles if excessive.

docs.title: 24.7.3 Rain Erosion
docs.text:
At supersonic speeds, impact with rain drops generates a water-hammer pressure pulse at the radome leading edge:

\[p_{\text{WH}} = \rho_w \cdot c_w \cdot V_{\text{impact}}\tag{24.24}\]

where \(\rho_w = 1{,}000\,\text{kg/m}^3\), \(c_w = 1{,}500\,\text{m/s}\), and \(V_{\text{impact}}\) is the relative velocity. At Mach 3 (\(V = 1{,}020\,\text{m/s}\)): \(p_{\text{WH}} \approx 1.5\,\text{GPa}\) — exceeding the compressive strength of most ceramics. Erosion mitigation:

  • Hard coatings: PVD alumina or titanium nitride coating 50–200 \(\mu\)m thick; dissipates energy before bulk material damage.

  • Nose shape optimisation: Sharper ogive (Von Kármán profile) reduces drop impact rate.

  • Material selection: Si\(_3\)N\(_4\) best resistance; PTFE/fibreglass worst.

docs.title: 24.8.1 Body Tube Fabrication
docs.text:
• Spun aluminium: Hot-spinning of aluminium billet on mandrel; forms seamless tube with good mechanical properties; suitable for up to 300 mm diameter.

  • Roll-formed steel: Sheet material roll-formed into cylinder and seam-welded; lower cost for large-diameter motor cases.

  • Filament winding (CFRP): Continuous carbon fibre tow impregnated with epoxy, wound at controlled angle over mandrel, cured at 120–180°C in autoclave. Void content \(< 1\%\) required for structural credibility.

Filament-wound motor cases are proof-pressure tested after manufacture at 1.1 × MEOP using an inert hydraulic fluid (water/glycol mixture). This verifies structural integrity without risk of propellant ignition.

docs.title: 24.8.2 CNC Machining
docs.text:
Interface rings and flanges are CNC-turned from 7075-T73 or D6AC billet. Key tolerances:

  • Bore diameter: \(\pm 0.025\) mm (running fit for O-ring sealing).

  • Flange flatness: \(< 0.05\) mm over diameter (ensures even bolt load distribution).

  • Thread form: ISO metric fine; lubricated with Molykote.

docs.title: 24.8.3 Interface Control and Cleanliness
docs.text:
The Interface Control Document (ICD) defines mechanical, electrical, and environmental requirements at every section joint. Cleanliness control is essential:

  • Particle contamination \(> 500\,\mu\)m must not be present near the fuze detonation train.

  • Seeker optics: Class 100 cleanroom for assembly (ISO 5).

  • Electronics: ESD-protected environment; relative humidity 40–60%.

docs.title: 24.9.1 Isolator Design
docs.text:
Silicone elastomer shock mounts isolate the guidance electronics from the missile airframe. The isolator is characterised by its static stiffness \(k_s\) and damping ratio \(\zeta\). The natural frequency of the isolated system:

\[f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k_s}{m_{\text{payload}}}}\tag{24.25}\]

Typical design targets: \(f_n = 15\)–\(30\) Hz so that launch environment energy (concentrated above 50 Hz) is attenuated by the isolation system. Transmissibility above \(f_n\):

\[T_R(f) = \sqrt{\frac{1 + (2\zeta f/f_n)^2}{(1 - (f/f_n)^2)^2 + (2\zeta f/f_n)^2}}\tag{24.26}\]

At \(f \gg f_n\), \(T_R \rightarrow (f_n/f)^2 / (2\zeta)\), showing attenuation proportional to \((f_n/f)^2\).

docs.title: 24.9.2 Shock Response Spectrum
docs.text:
Pyroshock events (separation charges, fin deployment squibs) generate extremely high amplitude, short-duration shocks. The shock environment is characterised by the Shock Response Spectrum (SRS), which represents the peak response of a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator of natural frequency \(f_n\) to the measured shock:

\[\text{SRS}(f_n) = \max_t \left| \omega_n \int_0^t \ddot{x}(\tau) e^{-\zeta \omega_n (t-\tau)} \sin[\omega_n(t-\tau)]\, d\tau \right|\tag{24.27}\]

Equipment is designed to survive the SRS plus 3 dB margin. Fragility levels for typical electronics: 30–100 g depending on construction (through-hole vs SMD, potted vs un-potted).

docs.title: 24.10.1 Body Bending Mode Coupling with Guidance
docs.text:
If the missile body bending natural frequency \(\omega_b\) is insufficiently separated from the guidance loop bandwidth \(\omega_g\), the rate gyros sense structural bending motion as flight path rate, feeding spurious signals into the autopilot. This coupling can cause instability.

Design requirement:

\[\omega_b > 3 \omega_g\tag{24.28}\]

For a guidance bandwidth \(\omega_g = 10\) rad/s, the first body bending mode must exceed \(30\) rad/s (4.8 Hz). This requirement drives minimum wall thickness and material selection for slender missile bodies (\(L/D > 15\)).

The effective natural frequency of a uniform beam (first mode):

\[\omega_{b1} = \frac{(1.875)^2}{L^2} \sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho_L}}\tag{24.29}\]

where \(EI\) is bending stiffness, \(L\) is missile length, and \(\rho_L\) is linear mass density.

docs.title: 24.10.2 Structural Damping
docs.text:
Structural damping in CFRP airframes is characterised by the loss factor \(\eta = 2\zeta\):

  • CFRP: \(\zeta = 0.01\)–\(0.03\) (loss factor 0.02–0.06).

  • Aluminium: \(\zeta = 0.001\)–\(0.005\).

  • Steel: \(\zeta = 0.001\)–\(0.003\).

The higher intrinsic damping of CFRP relative to metals is beneficial for reducing structural resonance amplification (\(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\)) and for aeroacoustic fatigue.

docs.title: 24.10.3 Fin Flutter Speed Requirement
docs.text:
Flutter speed must exceed the maximum structural speed with adequate margin:

\[V_F \geq 1.20 \times V_{\text{max,struct}}\tag{24.30}\]

\(V_{\text{max,struct}}\) is the maximum dive speed including a 15% overspeed allowance above the maximum operating airspeed. If \(V_F\) is insufficient, design options include:

  • Increase torsional stiffness (thicker skin, carbon orientation change).

  • Reduce fin span (reduces aerodynamic forces but also reduces stability).

  • Add mass balance weight near leading edge (shifts frequency ratio \(\omega_h/\omega_\theta\)).

Table 24.3. Aeroelastic and vibration design requirements summary Requirement Parameter Design Value Body bending–guidance separation \(\omega_b / \omega_g\) \(> 3\) Flutter margin \(V_F / V_{\max}\) \(> 1.20\) CFRP structural damping \(\zeta\) \(0.01\)–\(0.03\) Isolation system natural freq. \(f_n\) 15–30 Hz Transmissibility at 200 Hz \(T_R\) \(< 0.05\) (with \(\zeta = 0.15\) isolator) Fragility level (electronics) Peak \(g\) 30–100 g Table 24.4. Summary of key airframe structural equations Equation Physical meaning Reference \(F_{\text{ax}} = T - D - m\ddot{x}\) Axial load balance Eq. (24.1) \(MS = F_{\text{allow}}/(F \cdot FS) - 1\) Structural margin of safety Eq. (24.4) \(\sigma_{\text{bend}} = MR/I\) Bending stress (outer fibre) Eq. (24.16) \(\dot{s} = \dot{q}”_{\text{aero}}/(\rho_c H_{\text{py}})\) Ablation rate (simplified) Eq. (32.39) \(T_{\text{aw}} = T_\infty(1 + r(\gamma-1)M^2/2)\) Adiabatic wall temperature Eq. (24.11) \(d_{\text{HW}} = \lambda_0/(2\sqrt{\varepsilon_r})\) Half-wave radome thickness Eq. (24.22) \(V_F \geq 1.20 V_{\max}\) Flutter margin requirement Eq. (24.30) \(\omega_b > 3\omega_g\) Bending–guidance decoupling Eq. (24.28) \(a_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\pi f_n Q W(f_n)/2}\) Miles’ random vibration response Eq. (24.18) \(\text{SRS}(f_n) = \max|\omega_n \int ...|\) Shock response spectrum Eq. (24.27)

docs.title: 25.1 Introduction to Missile Flight Control Systems
docs.text:
A missile flight control system (FCS) is the integrated set of hardware and algorithms that translates guidance acceleration commands into controlled, stable airframe motion throughout every phase of flight—boost, midcourse, and terminal. The FCS sits between the guidance processor (which computes the required lateral acceleration to intercept a target or follow a trajectory) and the physical world of aerodynamics and propulsion. Without a properly designed FCS, even the most sophisticated seeker and optimal guidance law will produce a vehicle that oscillates, diverges, or fails to execute the commanded manoeuvre.

The engineering challenge is severe: aerodynamic derivatives shift by an order of magnitude across the flight envelope as the missile accelerates through the transonic region and climbs or dives through pressure altitudes from sea level to 30 km. Control effectors must be sized for the worst-case combination of dynamic pressure and angle-of-attack, yet must not destabilise the vehicle in the much softer conditions at boost ignition. Actuators must respond within milliseconds while consuming minimal energy from the missile’s limited power budget. The entire assembly must survive the shock and vibration of launch, the thermal environment of aerodynamic heating, and the electromagnetic environment of modern battlefields.
