Accelerated aging at \(+70\,^\circ\text{C}\) for 1000 h is used to verify 20-year storage life at \(+20\,^\circ\text{C}\). Electronic components with solid-state construction have inherently longer storage life; electrolytic capacitors and batteries are the dominant life-limiters.

Table 26.3. Representative Missile Electronics Component MTBF Budget Subsystem MTBF (hours) Quality Level Key Life Limiter Guidance processor (FPGA+CPU) \(>50{,}000\) Class S / RHBD Single-event latch-up Inertial measurement unit \(>10{,}000\) Mil grade FOG source (LED/SLD) ageing Power conditioning module \(>15{,}000\) MIL-PRF-38534 Electrolytic capacitor ESR Seeker electronics \(>20{,}000\) Mil grade Detector array dark current Thermal battery 20-yr shelf N/A (inert) Heat pellet damp penetration Actuation electronics \(>30{,}000\) Mil grade MOSFET gate oxide Datalink RF module \(>15{,}000\) Mil grade PA GaN HEMT reliability

docs.title: 26.10.5 Summary
docs.text: Missile electronics engineering is a discipline defined by extremes: extreme packaging density, extreme environmental conditions, extreme reliability demands for a one-shot system, and extreme performance requirements from guidance computers that must execute advanced tracking algorithms in microseconds. The convergence of COTS-heritage FPGA/SoC technology with radiation-hardened, mil-qualified packaging is the dominant trend, enabling unprecedented guidance precision while containing the non-recurring engineering cost. The data bus ecosystem centred on MIL-STD-1553B has proven remarkably durable and will coexist with SpaceWire and fibre Ethernet as bandwidth demands escalate with AESA seekers and synthetic aperture modes. Power system design remains dominated by the thermal battery for tactical systems, with turbogenerators reserving their role for sustained-cruise applications. Reliability assurance through HALT, HASS, and Arrhenius-validated storage life remains the cornerstone of programmatic risk reduction for missile electronics programmes.

docs.title: 27.1 Introduction to Launch Systems
docs.text:
The launch system is the complete assembly of mechanical, pyrotechnic, electrical, and fire-control equipment that takes a stored, inert missile from its magazine, canister, or suspension and transforms it into an airborne weapon pursuing its target. A launch system failure—whether mechanical separation anomaly, electrical interface fault, fuze arming failure, or simple improper ignition sequencing—will at best destroy a mission and at worst endanger the launch platform and its crew.

Launch system engineering encompasses a remarkable breadth of disciplines: structural dynamics (separation trajectories), thermodynamics (exhaust management), electromagnetic compatibility (EMI protection of ordnance), software (fire control and weapon management), reliability engineering (safe-and-arm sequences), and logistics (long-term canister storage). This chapter provides a comprehensive reference treatment of each element.

The chapter proceeds from an overview of launch platform types and requirements through detailed treatments of vertical launch systems, air launch, ground mobile launch, submarine launch, canister design, missile handling logistics, fire control systems, safe-and-arm devices, and integration testing.

docs.title: 27.2.1 Platform Categories
docs.text:
Launch platforms divide into four primary domains, each imposing distinct requirements on the launch system:

Ground-fixed.

Fixed installations (missile defence batteries, coastal defence sites, base air defence) offer essentially unlimited power, crew size, and magazine volume. The launch system can be heavy and complex. Environmental requirements emphasise corrosion resistance for coastal sites and thermal management for arctic deployment, but are less stringent than naval requirements.

Ground-mobile.

Transporter-erector-launchers (TELs) and truck-mounted systems must be road- or off-road-deployable, erect and fire within strict reaction-time budgets (typically \(<\)10 min), and immediately relocate (shoot-and-scoot). Weight, stow height, and road clearance drive the design.

Naval (surface).

Ship-borne launch systems must operate in the salt-spray environment of the marine boundary layer, withstand shock loads from ship manoeuvring and gunfire (MIL-S-901D shock test), function through the ship’s roll and pitch (\(\pm\)45\(^\circ\) roll, \(\pm\)15\(^\circ\) pitch under some definitions), and be integrated with the ship’s combat management system (CMS).

Airborne.

Air launch imposes the most stringent weight and volume constraints, adds the complication of safe weapon-aircraft separation at varying airspeeds (100– 500 m/s) and altitudes, and requires compliance with an elaborate suite of electrical interface and carriage environment standards.

Submarine.

Submarine launch must function at periscope depth or below, require no surface exposure until after ejection, and produce no acoustic signature that would compromise the submarine’s position.

docs.title: 27.2.2 Common Launch Requirements
docs.text:
Regardless of platform, every launch system must satisfy these functional requirements:

  1. Safe separation: the missile clears the launch platform without contact; structural damage margins \(>\)1.5 on all contact loads during the separation trajectory.

  2. Ignition sequence: motor ignition occurs only after the missile has safely separated; ignition timing is enforced by both the fire control system and by the missile’s own safe-and-arm device.

  3. Arming delay: the warhead cannot reach its armed state until after a defined time-of-flight or environmental sensing sequence has been satisfied, preventing detonation near the launch platform.

  4. Initial guidance: the missile autopilot is operational within \(<\)500 ms of launch; target data is loaded to the missile’s computer before or during launch.

  5. No fratricide: the launch event does not damage the platform, crew, or adjacent weapons.

docs.title: 27.2.3 Environmental Requirements
docs.text:
Launch systems must operate across the environmental extremes defined in MIL-STD-810 Method 500 (altitude), Method 501 (high temperature), Method 502 (low temperature), Method 506 (rain), Method 507 (humidity), and Method 509 (salt fog). Table 27.1 summarises key environmental limits.

Table 27.1. Standard environmental limits for launch systems (MIL-STD-810H) Parameter Storage / Transport Operational Temperature \(-54^\circ\)C to \(+71^\circ\)C \(-40^\circ\)C to \(+55^\circ\)C Humidity 95% RH non-condensing 95% RH condensing Salt fog 5% NaCl, 96 h 5% NaCl, 48 h Altitude (ground) Sea level to 4600 m Sea level to 3050 m Vibration (transport) MIL-STD-810 Cat. I road MIL-STD-810 Fig. 514.6-1 Shock (naval) MIL-S-901D Grade A MIL-S-901D Grade A EMI MIL-STD-461G MIL-STD-461G

docs.title: 27.2.4 Fire Control System Role
docs.text:
The fire control system (FCS1) orchestrates the engagement sequence:

  1. Receives target track data from sensors (radar, IR, acoustic)

  2. Computes engagement geometry: time to intercept, required seeker look angle, fuze setting

  3. Assigns weapons to targets: threat prioritisation algorithm

  4. Obtains launch authorisation from operator or autonomous algorithm

  5. Issues pre-launch data load to missile (waypoints, target state, fuze data)

  6. Issues fire command; monitors launch confirmation

  7. Tracks the missile and target; issues in-flight updates if datalink is available

docs.title: 27.3.1 Mk 41 Vertical Launch System
docs.text:
The Mk 41 VLS (developed by Lockheed Martin) is the most widely deployed naval vertical launch system, fielded on US Navy Ticonderoga-class cruisers (122 cells), Arleigh Burke-class destroyers (90 or 96 cells), and the naval forces of 12 allied nations. Key physical parameters:

  • Cell dimensions: 0.635 m \(\times\) 0.635 m cross-section; standard strike-length cell depth 7.7 m; tactical-length 5.3 m.

  • Maximum missile mass: 1,400 kg per cell (tactical length), 2,450 kg per cell (strike length).

  • Module configuration: 8-cell modules; each module has a dedicated launcher control unit (LCU) and plenum for exhaust gas.

  • Missiles certified: SM-2 Block IV, SM-3 Block IIA, SM-6, Evolved Sea Sparrow Missile (ESSM, 4-packed per cell), Tomahawk TLAM, ASROC VL.

The Mk 41 uses a hot-launch configuration in which the motor ignites within the cell. Exhaust gases are channelled through a water-cooled flame duct running below the deck, venting through two uptakes at the forward and aft ends of the module. Water deluge flow rates of \(\sim\)400 L/s are required for thermal management during a full-module salvo.

docs.title: 27.3.2 Cold Launch vs Hot Launch
docs.text:
The choice between cold and hot launch fundamentally drives the mechanical architecture of the VLS:

Hot launch.

Motor ignites inside the cell. Requires robust flame duct and exhaust management. Advantages: simpler ejection mechanism; no separate gas generator required; shorter ignition delay. Disadvantages: thermal loading on adjacent cells limits salvo rate; exhaust gas recirculation risks motor re-ingestion in unfavourable wind conditions; failed-to-ignite missile remains in burning cell (fire hazard).

Cold launch.

A gas generator (pyrotechnic piston or steam generator) ejects the missile vertically from the cell. The motor ignites after the missile is safely above the deck (\(\sim\)10–30 m altitude). The ejection velocity required:

\[V_{eject} = \sqrt{2\,g\,h_{clearance} + 2\,g\,h_{cell}}\tag{27.1}\]

In practice \(V_{eject} \approx 20\)–\(40\) m/s. The ejection impulse from the gas generator:

\[J_{ej} = m_{missile}\,V_{eject} + \int_0^{t_{ej}} F_{drag}(V)\,dt\tag{27.2}\]

Cold launch advantages: no flame duct required; failed-to-ignite missile can be jettisoned safely; adjacent cells are undamaged. Russian S-300/S-400 systems use cold launch; French Sylver VLS uses cold launch; US Mk 41 uses hot launch.

docs.title: 27.3.3 Sylver A50 and A70
docs.text:
The Sylver (Système de Lancement Vertical) VLS designed by DCNS/Naval Group for MBDA Aster missiles uses a cold-launch architecture with an 8-cell module configuration. Two variants:

  • Sylver A50: 5.0 m cell depth; Aster 15 (45 km range); used on French FREMM frigates and Type 45 destroyer (with Aster 30).

  • Sylver A70: 7.0 m cell depth; Aster 30 and Aster 30 Block 1NT (extended range); to accommodate longer missile body.

The Sylver modules use a gas generator of pyrotechnic type producing \(\sim\)250 kPa over-pressure in the cell to achieve the required ejection velocity in 0.3–0.5 s.

docs.title: 27.3.4 UKMS / Containerised VLS
docs.text: Universal Vertical Launch Systems (known commercially as UKMS or Mk 70 Payload Delivery System in the US) are self-contained modules that can be installed on any surface with a flat deck: destroyer, frigate, Fast Attack Craft, ground vehicle, or fixed platform. The containerised concept reuses standard ISO shipping containers with a reinforced deck frame. Eight to twelve missile cells per container can be placed in minutes by crane; fire control integration uses a standardised datalink. This concept dramatically reduces the cost of equipping smaller navies and provides dispersed ground basing options.

docs.title: 27.3.5 Salvo Rate and Interlock
docs.text:
Sequential missile launches are constrained by interlock timers that prevent two cells from igniting simultaneously. The thermal and structural constraints set a minimum inter-launch interval \(\Delta t_{interlock}\):

\[\Delta t_{interlock} \geq \max\!\left(\frac{Q_{exhaust}}{P_{duct,cool}},\; \frac{\Delta M_{gas}}{|\dot M_{supply}|}\right)\tag{27.3}\]

For the Mk 41, the declared salvo rate is one missile per second from the same magazine under the thermal limitation of the flame duct water cooling system. Electrical interlocks prevent two launcher control units from sending fire commands within 0.5 s of each other.

docs.title: 27.4.1 Pylon and Ejector Rack Interfaces
docs.text:
Air-launched missiles are carried on aircraft on pylon-mounted ejector racks or on conformal pylon adapters. The primary US standards are:

  • BRU-33: dual-store ejector rack; 762 mm and 356 mm hook spacing variants; 2,270 kg maximum store load per hook.

  • BRU-46: advanced multipurpose rack; AMRAAM, JDAM; lower profile for F-22 internal bays.

  • LAU-61 / LAU-68: rocket pods (70 mm FFAR); not used for guided missiles but illustrate variety of carriage hardware.

The mechanical interface between missile and rack is defined by MIL-STD-8591: lug dimensions (\(14.7\,mm\) diameter lug pin), hook face geometry, release force (\(22\)–\(27\) N release load on hooks), and ejector foot placement. Two hook-lug pairs per missile (forward and aft) provide the attachment. The ejector cartridges fire propellant gas into pistons below the missile feet, pushing the missile down and away from the pylon with a defined velocity.

docs.title: 27.4.2 Ejection Force and Separation Velocity
docs.text:
The ejection force from a piston ejector:

\[F_{ej}(t) = P_{gas}(t) \cdot A_{piston}\tag{27.4}\]

where \(P_{gas}(t)\) is the gas pressure (decaying exponentially after cartridge initiation) and \(A_{piston}\) is the piston area. The resulting separation velocity at the end of piston stroke \(s_{stroke}\):

\[V_{sep} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{m_{store}}\int_0^{s_{stroke}} F_{ej}(x)\,dx}\tag{27.5}\]

For a typical 200 kg missile, \(V_{sep} \approx 2\)–\(5\) m/s downward. The ejector must also overcome the aerodynamic lift on the missile at carriage conditions (which acts upward, opposing separation) and the missile weight component along the piston axis. The minimum ejection force margin:

\[F_{ej,min} = m_{store}\,g + L_{store}(q,\alpha) + F_{friction}\tag{27.6}\]

docs.title: 27.4.3 Store Separation Analysis
docs.text:
Store separation is the most complex aerodynamic problem in aircraft/weapon integration. The missile experiences the non-uniform flow field of the pylon and aircraft fuselage during the critical first 1–2 m of descent. Analysis methods in order of fidelity:

  1. Empirical: DATCOM-based interference factors; fast but inaccurate for unusual configurations.

  2. Wind tunnel captive trajectory system (CTS): store mounted on a 6-DOF sting that moves in real time based on measured forces and moments; gold standard for separation testing.

  3. CFD: RANS or URANS simulation; requires careful grid generation around the pylon and store; validated against CTS data.

Separation trajectory is simulated for the aircraft speed, altitude, and angle of attack envelope. A cleared separation envelope defines the conditions under which the store can be released without contacting the aircraft. MIL-HDBK-244A defines the methodology and documentation requirements.

docs.title: 27.4.4 Captive Carriage Environment
docs.text:
During captive carriage (from aircraft take-off to weapon release), the missile is exposed to a severe combined environment:

  • Vibration: broadband random vibration from airframe structure, engines, and turbulent boundary layer; power spectral density peaks at pylon attachment resonances (50–200 Hz). MIL-STD-810 Method 514, Category 20 (aircraft pylons) defines the spectrum.

  • Temperature: from \(-54^\circ\)C (high altitude cold soak) to \(+71^\circ\)C (ground static on hot day with solar loading on dark-painted skin).

  • Acoustic: high-intensity noise from jet engines and aerodynamic turbulence; OASPL 155 dB at proximity of after-burner aircraft.

  • EMI: aircraft radar and electronic warfare emitters at close range; HERO susceptibility of fuze and initiation circuits.

docs.title: 27.4.5 Internal Weapons Bay
docs.text:
Stealth aircraft (F-22A, F-35A/C, B-21) carry weapons in internal bays to preserve a low radar cross-section. Internal carriage adds complexity:

  • Bay doors must open within \(<\)0.5 s to minimise radar exposure during weapon release; doors are driven by high-rate hydraulic actuators.

  • Weapons on an ejector rail are propelled downward at 2–5 m/s into the airstream before motor ignition.

  • Bay acoustics (Helmholtz resonance of the open bay) can produce tones at 50–300 Hz and SPL 170 dB at weapon location; acoustic suppression devices (leading edge spoilers) are required.

  • The weapon must not re-enter the bay after ejection; trajectory must clear the door edge and aircraft belly by \(>\)0.15 m at all release conditions.

docs.title: 27.4.6 MIL-STD-1760 Electrical Interface
docs.text:
MIL-STD-1760 (Aircraft/Store Electrical Interconnection System) defines the electrical interface between the aircraft mission computer and the weapon. It provides:

  • Power: 28 V DC (primary) and 115 V 400 Hz AC (for older seekers and gyros); isolated from aircraft bus by weapon isolation relay.

  • Data bus: MIL-STD-1553B dual-redundant serial bus at 1 Mbps; aircraft sends target state, fuze settings, built-in test commands; weapon returns BIT status, seeker track status.

  • Fuze arming: separate dedicated wire for arm/safe signal; hardware-interlock prevents arming while hooks are closed.

  • Launch consent: single-wire discrete signal from ejector rack to weapon initiation circuit.

The MIL-STD-1553 data loading sequence:

\[t_{load} = N_{words} / f_{bus} = N_{words} / 1 \times 10^6 \;\text{bps}\tag{27.7}\]

For a 256-word pre-launch message, \(t_{load} = 256 \times 20\,\mu\text{s} = 5.12\,\text{ms}\). The pre-launch sequence completes in \(<\)1 s including BIT and seeker cool-down confirmation.

docs.title: 27.4.7 Safe Escape and Motor Ignition Timing
docs.text:
After ejection, the missile must travel a minimum safe-escape distance \(d_{esc}\) before the motor ignites to prevent rocket exhaust from damaging the aircraft. The ignition delay timer \(\tau_{ign}\):

\[\tau_{ign} \geq \frac{d_{esc}}{V_{sep} + V_{aircraft} \cdot \cos\alpha_{ej}}\tag{27.8}\]

Typical values: \(d_{esc} = 10\)–\(30\) m; \(\tau_{ign} = 0.1\)–\(0.5\) s. The ignition signal is issued by the missile’s own timer circuit (started at hook-open) and cannot be overridden except by FTS command.

docs.title: 27.4.8 Helicopter Launch Considerations
docs.text:
Helicopter-launched missiles (Hellfire, Brimstone, Spike ER) introduce unique constraints:

  • Rotor downwash: 5–15 m/s downward velocity beneath the rotor disk; rocket exhaust plume deflects toward fuselage and tail rotor if ignition occurs inside the rotor disk area.

  • Back-blast: rocket motor exhaust must not impinge on the helicopter airframe; minimum stand-off distances are defined by back-blast hazard analyses.

  • Crosswind effect: main rotor torque produces aircraft yaw; weapon must be mounted on a rail that allows limited azimuth traverse to compensate.

  • Sling suspension: Hellfire uses a rail launcher (M299/LAU-61) bolted to hard points; the rail provides positive retention until motor ignition.

docs.title: 27.5.1 TEL Design and Operations
docs.text:
The transporter-erector-launcher (TEL) is the fundamental ground mobile launch platform for ballistic and cruise missiles. It integrates in a single vehicle:

  • Transport chassis (wheeled: 8\(\times\)8, 12\(\times\)12; or tracked)

  • Missile canister(s) on an erector arm

  • Electrical power generator (diesel APU)

  • Fire control computer and communications suite

  • Navigation system (GPS + INS) for launch site survey

  • Environmental control unit for missile conditioning

The erection sequence: from travel to erect (vertical) takes 3–8 minutes depending on design. The erector arm is typically driven by hydraulic cylinders powered by the APU. Alignment is verified by inertial reference comparison between the TEL IMU and the missile IMU (loaded before departure from the garrison).

docs.title: 27.5.2 Reaction Time and Survivability
docs.text:
TEL survivability in a contested environment depends critically on minimising the time from move-in to shoot and from shoot to move-out (shoot-and-scoot manoeuvre). Requirements:

\[\begin{align*} t_{react} &= t_{move-in} + t_{erect} + t_{align} + t_{FC} < 10\,\text{min} \\ t_{scoot} &= t_{lower} + t_{move-out} < 3\,\text{min} \end{align*}\]

The Iskander-M (Russia) achieves approximately 4 minutes reaction time from halt; the ATACMS/M270 system requires approximately 8 minutes. HIMARS (a wheeled single-pod MLRS) achieves faster reaction by eliminating the erection step—it launches at a fixed elevation.

docs.title: 27.5.3 ATACMS on M270/HIMARS
docs.text: The Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) is launched from the M270 MLRS or M142 HIMARS using the M57 launch pod. Two ATACMS missiles fill the standard MLRS 12-rocket pod space. The launcher elevates to the required firing angle (\(\sim\)55\(^\circ\)) and the missile is rail-launched (hot launch). The M57 pod provides a hermetically sealed environment maintaining missile storage temperature.

docs.title: 27.5.4 Iskander-M TEL
docs.text:
The 9K720 Iskander-M uses the MZKT-7930 Astrolog 8\(\times\)8 chassis carrying two 9M723 ballistic missiles on a fold-out cradle-launcher. Specifications:

  • Rail launch angle: \(\sim\)78\(^\circ\) from horizontal at launch

  • Reaction time: \(\leq\)4 minutes from travel

  • Scoot time: \(\leq\)1 minute after launch

  • Missile mass at launch: \(\sim\)3,800 kg

  • Maximum range: 500 km (treaty-limited); post-INF variants \(>\)500 km

docs.title: 27.5.5 Containerised Ground Launch
docs.text: The US Navy Mk 70 Payload Delivery System places Mk 41 VLS cells inside an ISO 20-foot container. Eight cells per container can be transported by standard logistics trucks, CH-47 helicopter (limited), or cargo aircraft. Power is provided by a containerised diesel generator. Fire control integrates with the NIFC-CA (Naval Integrated Fire Control—Counter Air) architecture via tactical data link. The containerised VLS provides dispersal options that make targeting more complex for adversary planners.

docs.title: 27.6.1 Torpedo Tube Launch
docs.text:
The 533 mm torpedo tube is the universal submarine weapon interface. A torpedo-tube-launched cruise missile (TLAM, UUM-44 SUBROC) is packaged in a capsule that is water-ejected by a piston pump or swim-out and then surfaces before motor ignition. The ejection sequence:

  1. Torpedo tube flooded and equalised to sea pressure

  2. Muzzle door opened

  3. Gas piston fires: missile capsule ejected at 15–25 m/s relative to submarine

  4. Capsule ascends through water column (3–15 s for 10–50 m depth)

  5. Surface: capsule splits open or dissolves; missile motor ignites

Ejection velocity must provide positive buoyancy margin throughout the water-transit phase to ensure the capsule reaches the surface even at maximum firing depth.

docs.title: 27.6.2 Submarine VLS (Ohio-Class Trident)
docs.text:
The Ohio-class SSBN carries 24 Trident II D5 SLBMs in 2.11 m diameter VLS tubes running 13 m through the pressure hull. Cold launch uses a compressed- gas (steam from water-gas reaction) piston:

\[F_{piston} = P_{steam} \cdot A_{tube} = P_{steam} \cdot \pi r_{tube}^2\tag{27.11}\]

For a tube radius \(r_{tube} = 1.055\) m and steam pressure \(P_{steam} = 800\) kPa, \(F_{piston} \approx 2.8\) MN—sufficient to eject the 59,000 kg D5 at approximately \(V_{eject} = 40\) m/s. The missile ascends through \(\sim\)50 m of water, surfaces, and fires all three stages sequentially.

The D5 first-stage motor ignition is triggered by an altitude sensor (barometric or radio altimeter) within 1 s of surface emergence. No command from the submarine is required after the ejection sequence is initiated.

docs.title: 27.6.3 Communication and Launch Order
docs.text:
Communicating a launch order to a submerged SSBN requires transmission through seawater, which attenuates radio frequency signals exponentially with depth. The ELF (Extremely Low Frequency, 76 Hz) system used by the US Navy (Seafarer replacement) penetrates seawater to depths of \(\sim\)100 m at power levels of megawatts, transmitted from land-based antenna arrays. The ELF message contains only a brief code authorising the submarine to come to periscope depth and receive the full launch order via VLF (Very Low Frequency, 3–30 kHz) or satellite.

The relationship between skin depth and frequency:

\[\delta_{skin} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega\,\mu\,\sigma}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega\,\mu}}\tag{27.12}\]

For seawater (\(\sigma \approx 4\) S/m, \(\mu \approx \mu_0\)) at 76 Hz: \(\delta_{skin} \approx 29\) m. Penetration to 100 m requires field strength of \(e^{100/29} \approx 31\) times the 1/\(e\) surface level, explaining the need for megawatt transmitters and multi-km antenna arrays.

docs.title: 27.6.4 Position Accuracy Before Launch
docs.text:
The SLBM guidance system requires an accurate initial position and velocity to achieve the required CEP on the target. The submarine must obtain a GPS fix at periscope depth and update its Ship’s Inertial Navigation System (SINS) before launch. After GPS fix, SINS maintains position with drift:

\[\sigma_{pos}(t) = \sigma_{GPS} + \dot\sigma_{INS} \cdot (t - t_{GPS})\tag{27.13}\]

where \(\sigma_{GPS} \approx 5\) m (CEP), \(\dot\sigma_{INS} \approx 0.5\) nm/h (nautical miles per hour) for a modern ring-laser gyro SINS. Maximum time from GPS fix to last missile launch must be controlled to keep \(\sigma_{pos}\) within the system accuracy budget.

docs.title: 27.7.1 Hermetically Sealed Canister Design
docs.text:
The hermetically sealed launch canister provides the missile with a controlled environment throughout its service life. The canister is the primary barrier between the missile and environmental hazards: moisture, corrosive gases, salt spray, fungal growth, and physical damage. Key design elements:

  • Pressure vessel: aluminium alloy 6061-T6 or 7075-T6 tube; wall thickness determined by internal positive-pressure maintenance (typically 0.5–2 psig dry nitrogen) and external crush load from transport.

  • Humidity control: silica gel desiccant packs sized for 10–25 year absorption; relative humidity inside \(<\)5% RH.

  • Front burst disc: metallic (stainless steel, 0.2–0.5 mm) diaphragm that ruptures at 2–5 bar differential to allow missile egress on launch. Burst pressure:

    \[P_{burst} = \frac{2\,\sigma_u\,t_{disc}}{D_{tube}}\tag{27.14}\]

    where \(\sigma_u\) is ultimate tensile stress, \(t_{disc}\) is disc thickness, \(D_{tube}\) is tube diameter.

  • Rear vent disc: ruptures on motor ignition (cold launch) or is pre-vented (hot launch) to allow exhaust gas exit.

docs.title: 27.7.2 Shelf Life and Accelerated Aging
docs.text:
The NATO standard for missile shelf life in a sealed canister is 10 years without maintenance intervention; extended-life designs achieve 20–25 years. Accelerated aging tests (per MIL-HDBK-698) expose canisters to elevated temperature and humidity to simulate long-term storage, then verify missile function. The Arrhenius relationship is used to relate test temperature \(T_{test}\) to service temperature \(T_{serv}\):

\[t_{test} = t_{serv} \cdot \exp\!\left[-\frac{E_a}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{test}} - \frac{1}{T_{serv}}\right)\right]\tag{27.15}\]

where \(E_a\) is the activation energy for the dominant aging mechanism (typically \(E_a/k \approx 9000\) K for propellant oxidiser migration) and \(k\) is Boltzmann’s constant. At \(T_{test} = 343\) K (70\(^\circ\)C) vs \(T_{serv} = 298\) K (25\(^\circ\)C), the acceleration factor is \(\approx 8.8\), so 1 year of testing represents \(\approx\)8.8 years of storage.

docs.title: 27.7.3 Modular Canister Concept
docs.text: The common canister concept, pursued by MBDA (CAMM family) and others, designs the canister-missile assembly to be platform-agnostic: the same sealed canister can be installed on a VLS cell, a TEL launch rail, or a ship deck-mount, by adapting only the canister interface collar. This reduces logistics complexity (single supply chain for multiple platform types) and allows missiles purchased for one platform to be diverted to another during conflict.

docs.title: 27.8.1 Weight Handling and Fixtures
docs.text:
Missile assembly and installation require dedicated handling equipment certified to the missile mass plus safety factor. Crane and hoist ratings per ASME B30.2:

\[W_{rated} \geq SF_{lift} \cdot m_{missile} \cdot g\tag{27.16}\]

where \(SF_{lift} \geq 5\) for personnel overhead lifts. Spreader bars distribute the load between multiple attachment points on the missile, keeping loads within the structural limit at each lug. Bending moment at the centre of the missile during two-point lift:

\[M_{bend,lift} = \frac{m\,g}{2} \cdot \left(\frac{L}{2} - d_{lug}\right)\tag{27.17}\]

where \(L\) is missile length and \(d_{lug}\) is the lug position from the nose. This moment must be less than the missile structural limit under combined gravity and \(4g\) dynamic factor for ship-motion handling.

docs.title: 27.8.2 HERO, HERP, HERF
docs.text:
Electromagnetic radiation poses a significant hazard to electro-explosive devices (EEDs) and electronic fuzes:

  • HERO (Hazard of Electromagnetic Radiation to Ordnance): induced current in EED bridgewire from stray RF field. MIL-STD-464C and MIL-STD-1512 define RF immunity requirements for EEDs. The HERO susceptibility power density limit for a standard bridgewire:

    \[S_{HERO} = \frac{P_{nofire}}{4\,R_{bridgewire} \cdot A_{antenna,eff}}\tag{27.18}\]

  • HERP (Hazard of Electromagnetic Radiation to Personnel): RF power density limits for personnel (\(<\)10 W/m\(^2\) for continuous exposure at most frequencies per IEEE C95.1).

  • HERF (Hazard of Electromagnetic Radiation to Fuel): electrostatic ignition of fuel vapour; relevant during fueling operations near high-power transmitters.

HERO safe-separation distances are maintained during weapon loading and fueling operations aboard ships and aircraft. Transmitters are powered off or reduced during specified maintenance windows.

docs.title: 27.8.3 Insensitive High Explosive (IHE)
docs.text:
MIL-DTL-23659 and STANAG 4439 mandate IHE for all new missile warhead programs. IHE must survive all hazard stimuli without detonation (partial reaction or burning is acceptable):

  1. Bullet impact test: 12.7 mm AP bullet at 850 m/s; no detonation.

  2. Fragment impact test: 1.6 g steel fragment at \(>\)2,530 m/s.

  3. Fast cook-off: heated in fire at \(800^\circ\)C per minute; no detonation.

  4. Slow cook-off: heated at \(3.3^\circ\)C/hour to auto-ignition; no detonation.

  5. Sympathetic detonation: adjacent warhead detonates; no propagation.

PBXN-109 (with RDX/HTPB), PBXN-110, and PBXIH-135 are common IHE formulations meeting these criteria. PBXIH-135 achieves \(>\)90% RDX density while remaining IHE-compliant.

docs.title: 27.8.4 Transportation Standards
docs.text:
Missiles with live warheads are classified UN 0181 (article, explosive) and require:

  • Road: UN-approved packaging; ADR regulations; hazmat placards; driver training; route approval; escort for nuclear or Category I conventional.

  • Rail: no detonators on same car; buffer cars each end; speed limit 64 km/h for Category I munitions.

  • Sea: IMDG Code classification; segregation from oxidisers and flammables; quantity limits per ship type.

  • Air: IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations Class 1 Explosives; military exemptions via AFJMAN 24-204 equivalent; cargo aircraft only.

The MIL-STD-648 vibration and shock profiles for road transport characterise the worst-case truck bed environment. The spectrum is reproduced on a vibration test table during development to verify that the canister and missile survive the transportation environment.

docs.title: 27.9 Fire Control and Weapon Management Systems
27.9.1 Weapon Management System (WMS)
docs.text:
The weapon management system (WMS) maintains real-time situational awareness of the weapons complement on the platform:

  • Inventory: serial number, type, status, cell/pylon location

  • Readiness: BIT passed/failed; seeker status; battery voltage; fuze continuity

  • Assignment: which weapon is assigned to which track number

  • Expenditure log: fired time, target position, estimated impact time

The WMS interfaces with the combat management system (CMS) via a MIL-STD-1553 bus on aircraft or an ETHERNET/NTDS-E serial bus on ships.

docs.title: 27.9.2 Target Track Data and Engagement Geometry
docs.text:
The fire control computer receives target tracks from the sensor suite (air search radar, fire control radar, ESM, IR search and track) and computes:

\[\begin{align*} t_{TI} &= \frac{R_T}{V_{closure}} \\ \theta_{seeker} &= \arctan\!\left(\frac{\Delta y_T}{\Delta x_T}\right) \\ n_{required} &= V_m^2 / (R_{min} \cdot g) \end{align*}\]

where \(t_{TI}\) is the time to intercept, \(R_T\) is range to target, \(V_{closure}\) is closing velocity, \(\theta_{seeker}\) is the initial seeker look angle (must be within the seeker’s acquisition angle), and \(n_{required}\) is the required lateral acceleration to fly the intercept trajectory.

docs.title: 27.9.3 Pre-Launch Data Transfer
docs.text:
Pre-launch data loaded to the missile includes:

  • Target state vector: position \((x_T, y_T, z_T)\), velocity \((\dot x_T, \dot y_T, \dot z_T)\) in local navigation frame; time tag.

  • Waypoints: for terrain-hugging cruise missiles; up to 128 waypoints with altitude, time-on-target.

  • Fuze settings: proximity burst height; impact delay; self-destruct timer.

  • Mode of engagement: radar active, datalink, pre-programmed.

  • Platform state: own-ship position, velocity, attitude (for fire- control-to-missile coordinate transformation).

The total pre-launch data package is typically 256–512 bytes; transfer via MIL-STD-1553 completes in \(<\)50 ms.

docs.title: 27.9.4 Shoot-Look-Shoot Doctrine
docs.text:
Shoot-look-shoot (SLS) is the engagement doctrine in which a first weapon is fired at the target, and a second is fired only after the engagement result of the first is assessed (via mid-course datalink, active radar tracking, or EO/IR sensor). The SLS time budget:

\[t_{SLS} = t_{TI,1} + t_{BDA} + t_{assign,2} + t_{launch,2}\tag{27.22}\]

SLS requires that the second missile can still intercept the target after the additional delay:

\[R_T(t_{SLS}) = R_T(0) - V_{closure} \cdot t_{SLS} > R_{min}\tag{27.23}\]

where \(R_{min}\) is the missile’s minimum intercept range. If \(R_T(t_{SLS}) < R_{min}\), salvo fire (both missiles simultaneously) is required.

docs.title: 27.9.5 Battle Damage Assessment
docs.text:
Battle damage assessment (BDA) after a strike is conducted by:

  • Missile terminal seeker imagery (transmitted via datalink in last seconds of flight)

  • Overhead ISR (satellite, high-altitude UAV)

  • Signals intelligence (cessation of emissions from target)

  • Acoustic or seismic sensors (for underground targets)

The re-engagement decision compares the estimated target damage state against the mission requirement. If BDA indicates a partial kill, a follow-on strike is planned using updated target coordinates from the BDA sensor data.

docs.title: 27.10.1 Functions and Principles
docs.text:
The safe-and-arm (S&A) device is the critical safety barrier between the initiating stimulus (fuze output) and the explosive train leading to warhead detonation. Its function:

  • Safe: in all pre-launch and launch handling conditions, the S&A blocks the explosive train even if the fuze fires (due to malfunction or inadvertent stimulus).

  • Arm: after a defined set of environmental conditions have been sensed and satisfied, the S&A aligns the explosive train to allow detonation on fuze command.

The arm sequence requires satisfaction of at least two independent environmental sensing conditions (MIL-DTL-23659 requires \(\geq\)2 for Category 1 rockets):

\[\text{ARM} = \text{Condition}_1 \;\text{AND}\; \text{Condition}_2\tag{27.24}\]

docs.title: 27.10.2 Environmental Sensing Conditions
docs.text:
Typical sensing conditions:

  • Set-back: linear deceleration (acceleration rearward on launch) sensed by a weighted rotor that cocks on launch. Threshold: typically 100–500 \(g\) for 50 ms.

  • Spin: centrifugal force on a flyweight that moves a pin out of the rotor; requires \(>\)10 Hz spin rate for \(>\)500 ms.

  • All-fire time delay: mechanical clock or pyrotechnic delay element; prevents arming within the minimum arming range.

  • Altitude: barometric sensor; prevents arming below a defined altitude (ensures weapon has left the ship/aircraft).

  • Electronic arming: coded electrical signal from the fire control system; ESD-protected.

docs.title: 27.10.3 Electromechanical Safe/Arm Device
docs.text:
The rotor-type ESAD (Electro-mechanical Safe/Arm Device) is the traditional implementation. An explosive pellet (transfer charge) is embedded in a cylindrical rotor. In the safe position, the rotor is rotated 90\(^\circ\) from alignment so the pellet is out of line with the explosive train. On arming:

  1. Environmental conditions satisfied simultaneously

  2. Solenoid releases rotor restraint

  3. Rotor rotates to aligned position (spring-driven or set-back driven)

  4. All-fire channel is open: fuze output fires through pellet to booster

The rotor alignment precision: \(<\)0.5\(^\circ\) tolerance on alignment position to ensure complete explosive coupling. Failure mode: rotor jams in transit \(\rightarrow\) fail-safe (incomplete alignment, does not fire).

docs.title: 27.10.4 MEMS Safe/Arm Devices
docs.text:
Micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) S&A devices use photolithographically fabricated silicon structures to achieve the blocking function in a package \(<\)1 cm\(^3\). A MEMS S&A may use:

  • Silicon chip with a micro-fabricated explosive bridge (semiconductor bridge, SCB) that fires only when a specific voltage pulse is applied

  • Multiple silicon interlock sliders each requiring a different stimulus to translate to the aligned position

  • Electrical AND logic replacing mechanical rotor: ARM = AND\((V_1, V_2, V_3)\) where each \(V_i\) is output of an independent environmental sensor

MEMS S&A offers programmable arm sequences, digital diagnostics, and integration with the missile’s built-in test system.

docs.title: 27.10.5 Unexploded Ordnance (UXO) Mitigation
docs.text:
Self-destruct and self-neutralisation functions reduce the UXO hazard:

  • Self-destruct timer: after maximum time of flight + margin, a pyrotechnic timer fires the fuze initiation circuit, detonating the warhead at altitude above ground (air burst, smaller ground hazard radius than dud on ground).

  • Impact self-destruct: if the fuze fails to fire on impact (stony ground, very shallow angle), a delayed initiator fires 50 ms after impact deceleration.

  • Self-neutralisation: if detonation is not feasible (e.g., chemical munitions), an initiator destroys the fuze/explosive train without main-charge detonation, rendering the weapon chemically safe.

The UXO rate requirement per NATO STANAG 4526: \(<\)1% of delivered weapons remain as UXO hazards.

docs.title: 27.11.1 Captive Carry Electrical Integration Test
docs.text:
Before any flight test, the complete missile-aircraft interface is validated on the ground. The missile (or a mass simulator with full electronics) is installed on the aircraft pylon; all MIL-STD-1760 lines are exercised:

  • Power application and regulation check; bus voltage \(28.5 \pm 0.5\) V DC

  • MIL-STD-1553 data transfer: all defined messages sent and acknowledged

  • Fuze arming status (safe confirmed in all ground conditions)

  • Built-in test execution: missile BIT complete in \(<\)60 s; pass/fail status to WMS

  • Seeker BIT: gimbal articulation; detector cool-down time; acquisition of built-in test target

Data is recorded on the aircraft maintenance data recorder and downloaded for analysis against the weapons integration specification.

docs.title: 27.11.2 Sled Track Separation Test
docs.text:
Store separation on a sled track replaces expensive flight tests for initial separation clearance validation. The missile (or mass simulator) is mounted on a rocket-powered sled at the correct pylon height and angle. At the desired test speed, the ejection system fires, and high-speed cameras and strain gauges measure the separation trajectory and loads. The trajectory data is compared with the CFD/wind-tunnel prediction:

\[\Delta r_{sep}(t) = r_{measured}(t) - r_{predicted}(t)\tag{27.25}\]

Acceptance: \(|\Delta r_{sep}| < 0.10\) m at all times from release to motor ignition.

docs.title: 27.11.3 First Article and Live Firing Test
docs.text:
The first article firing (FAF) is the first complete end-to-end missile firing including motor ignition, autopilot operation, and fuze function. Test objectives:

  1. Verify ignition sequence and safe escape (no aircraft contact or hot-gas impingement)

  2. Verify autopilot stabilisation within the first 3 s of flight

  3. Verify seeker acquisition of test target (drone or towed banner)

  4. Verify fuze function (proximity or impact) against instrumented target

  5. Record telemetry: all FCS signals at 500 Hz; GPS position; timing

docs.title: 27.11.4 Electromagnetic Compatibility Testing
docs.text:
The complete aircraft-weapon system combination is tested for mutual EMI in an electromagnetically controlled test facility (OATS or anechoic chamber):

  • Aircraft radiated emissions measured with weapon installed; compared against MIL-STD-461G RE102/RE101 limits

  • Weapon susceptibility: aircraft systems energised at maximum power; weapon monitors for interference on MIL-STD-1553 bus

  • HERO tests: aircraft transmitters at maximum power with weapon in launch-ready state; EED bridgewire current measured; must be \(<\)1 mA (no-fire current)

  • High-intensity radiated fields (HIRF): weapon in simulated launch environment; exposed to FAR Part 25 or MIL-STD-461 field levels

docs.title: 27.11.5 Weapon System Qualification
docs.text:
Full weapon system qualification follows the Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP), which defines:

  • Developmental Test (DT): contractor-led; verifies specification compliance; controlled conditions; typically 15–30 rounds.

  • Operational Test (OT): government/user-led; realistic operational conditions; operators with minimum training; typically 10–20 rounds.

  • Live Fire Test (LFT): required by US law (10 USC 2366) for major defence acquisitions; full-up system test against realistic targets; assesses survivability (for manned systems) and lethality.

Table 27.2 summarises the qualification test matrix for a representative air-launched missile program.

Table 27.2. Representative qualification test matrix for an air-launched missile Test Phase Quantity Conditions Platform Goal Ground integration 4 Lab/pylon F/A-18E Interface verification Captive carry 6 Flight \(\leq\)M1.2 F/A-18E Carriage environment Separation (sled) 3 120–250 m/s Sled track Separation clearance DT flights (inert) 12 Full envelope F/A-18E/F-35 Autopilot; seeker DT live fire 18 Controlled Range Fuze; guidance; lethality OT live fire 12 Operational User pilots SLS; salvo; hostile EMI

docs.title: 27.11.6 TEMP and DT/OT Phase Requirements
docs.text:
The Test and Evaluation Master Plan is the governing document for the qualification program. It defines:

\[\begin{align*} P_{SSKP,required} &\geq 0.85 \quad \text{(single-shot kill probability)} \\ N_{DT} &\geq \frac{\ln(1 - C_{conf})}{\ln(1 - P_{SSKP})} \end{align*}\]

For \(P_{SSKP} = 0.85\) and confidence level \(C_{conf} = 0.90\):

\[N_{DT} \geq \frac{\ln(0.10)}{\ln(0.15)} \approx 12\;\text{rounds}\tag{27.28}\]

This is the minimum number of successes required; accounting for expected failures and statistical margin, programs typically plan 20–30 DT rounds.

docs.title: 27.12 Launch Platform Integration Summary
docs.text:
Table 27.3 provides a consolidated comparison of the key parameters across launch platform types.

Table 27.3. Launch platform type comparison: key integration parameters Parameter Ground Fixed TEL Naval VLS Air Submarine Reaction time \(>\)10 min 4–10 min \(<\)10 s (ready) \(<\)5 s 15 min (submerged) Salvo rate 1/2 s 1/30 s 1/s (Mk 41) 1/2 s 1/30 s (SLBM) Max missile mass Unlimited \(\sim\)5 t \(\sim\)2.5 t \(\sim\)1 t \(\sim\)60 t (SLBM) Reload time Hours Not field Hours (tender) Hours (ground) Not field Survivability Low (fixed) High (mobile) Moderate Very high Very high Crew HERO risk Low Moderate High (deck) Low (remote) Low (submerged)

Launch system design is ultimately a systems engineering trade between responsiveness, survivability, magazine depth, and cost. The trend in modern programs is toward modular, canisterised systems that allow the same missile to be deployed from multiple platform types with minimal re- engineering, reducing per-unit cost and simplifying the joint logistics chain. Fire control integration complexity—the software challenge of interfacing a new weapon to an existing ship or aircraft combat system—often exceeds the missile hardware development cost and schedule and must be treated as a first-order program risk from contract award.

  1. In this chapter, FCS denotes fire control system; the missile autopilot is referred to as the autopilot or flight control system to avoid ambiguity. ↩

docs.title: 28.1 Missile Manufacturing Overview
docs.text: Missile manufacturing occupies a unique niche in the broader aerospace and defence manufacturing landscape. Unlike commercial aircraft production, which is governed primarily by structural airworthiness and schedule-driven economics, missile production integrates energetic materials, classified electronic payloads, and precision guidance assemblies under a unified, tightly regulated quality regime. The convergence of explosive components with advanced composites, microelectronics, and precision machining creates a manufacturing environment found nowhere else in industry.

docs.title: 28.1.1 Fundamental Differences from Aircraft Manufacturing
docs.text:
Several characteristics sharply distinguish missile manufacturing from conventional aerospace production.

Energetic materials. Solid-propellant rocket motors and warheads contain high explosives (HE) and deflagrating propellants that are present throughout much of the assembly sequence. This imposes continuous electrostatic-discharge (ESD) control, no-lone-zone procedures, and personnel limits in process cells. Aircraft fuelling and armament loading are transient events; in a missile factory they are central, long-duration processes.

HERO and HERF hazards. Hazards of Electromagnetic Radiation to Ordnance (HERO) and Hazards of Electromagnetic Radiation to Fuel (HERF) require that radio-frequency emitters—including portable radios, radar, and cellular devices—be excluded from explosive areas. MIL-STD-464C establishes susceptibility limits; missile factories implement controlled electromagnetic environments (CEME) with building shielding, door interlocks, and RF-absorbing panels.

Classified processes. Guidance-system assembly, propellant formulations, and seeker algorithms are classified at various levels (CUI, SECRET, or above). Facilities must hold the appropriate facility security clearances (FSC) and implement SCIF-level protections for the most sensitive operations.

Build sequence dependency. The order of assembly is dictated as much by explosive-safety logic as by mechanical assembly logic. Propellant is loaded before the warhead is integrated; the fuze is armed only in the final stage. This means production cannot be freely re-sequenced to optimise flow as is common in lean aircraft manufacturing.

docs.title: 28.1.2 Facility Requirements
docs.text:
Facilities that manufacture or handle explosives in the United States must be licensed by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and comply with the DoD Explosives Safety Board (DDESB) standard DoD 6055.09-STD. Key physical requirements include:

  • Blast-resistant construction: Explosive-process buildings use reinforced-concrete walls (typically 200–400 mm) or earth-bermed structures with frangible roofs designed to vent overpressure upward.

  • Grounding and bonding: All surfaces, personnel, and tooling in explosive areas must be bonded to a common ground. Floor resistivity is maintained at \(10^{4}\)–\(10^{8}\,\Omega\) per MIL-STD-1495.

  • Quantity-distance (QD) siting: Buildings are sited so that the maximum credible event (MCE) yield does not damage inhabited structures. The inhibited weight of explosives (IWE) drives minimum inter-magazine distances per DDESB Table 6-3.

  • Environmental controls: Temperature and relative humidity must be controlled during propellant mixing, casting, and curing (\(\pm 2\,^\circ\)C, \(\pm 5\%\) RH) to ensure reproducible mechanical properties in the cured grain.

  • Ventilation: Explosive vapour concentrations must remain below 25% of the lower explosive limit (LEL) measured continuously by catalytic-bead or photoionisation detectors.

docs.title: 28.1.3 Quality Management and Regulatory Compliance
docs.text:
AS9100 Rev D is the aerospace quality management standard applied to missile manufacturing. It extends ISO 9001 with requirements for configuration management, risk management, and first-article inspection (FAI) per AS9102. Military contracts typically invoke MIL-Q-9858A (superseded but still referenced in legacy contracts) or AQAP-2110 for NATO programs.

ITAR compliance. The International Traffic in Arms Regulations (22 CFR Parts 120–130) control the export of defence articles listed on the US Munitions List (USML). Missile systems, components, technical data, and manufacturing equipment are typically USML Category IV. Foreign nationals may not access ITAR data without a Department of State licence or applicable exemption (e.g., 22 CFR §126.18 for bona fide employees). Violations carry criminal penalties up to $1 million per violation and 20 years imprisonment.

Government-owned, contractor-operated (GOCO) facilities. Because the capital investment for explosive-loading and large-motor-test facilities is enormous and the demand is episodic, the US government owns many propellant-production and warhead-filling facilities while contractors operate them under management and operating (M&O) contracts. Examples include the Holston Army Ammunition Plant (RDX and HMX production), the Radford Army Ammunition Plant (nitrocellulose and double- base propellant), and the McAlester Army Ammunition Plant (warhead assembly).

docs.title: 28.1.4 Build Sequence
docs.text:
A representative build sequence for a tactical air-to-ground missile is:

  1. Motor case fabrication (composite winding or metal forging)

  2. Liner application and propellant casting

  3. Propellant cure and motor inspection

  4. Nozzle assembly and attachment

  5. Aft section assembly (fins, control actuators)

  6. Warhead loading (explosive fill, fuze pocket machining)

  7. Guidance section assembly (IMU, electronics, seeker)

  8. Mid-body integration (warhead to guidance section)

  9. Forward section mating (seeker dome, radome, or window)

  10. Final assembly (motor + warhead + guidance)

  11. Acceptance testing (electrical, BIT, mass properties)

  12. Packaging, proof of acceptance, transfer to storage or fleet

docs.title: 28.2.1 Metal Airframe Fabrication
docs.text:
Aluminium alloys (7075-T6, 2024-T3), titanium alloys (Ti-6Al-4V), and high-strength steels (4340, 17-4PH) are the primary metallic airframe materials. Material selection is driven by the thermal environment, structural loads, and compatibility with propellants and explosives.

Spin-forming of nose cones. Ogival and conical nose cones are produced by power spinning (shear spinning) aluminium or titanium blanks over a mandrel. Wall thickness tolerance is \(\pm 0.15\,\text{mm}\); the forming operation work-hardens the alloy approximately 15–20% beyond the base temper. Post-forming heat treatment restores the design temper. CNC-controlled spinning machines apply forces up to 200 kN at feed rates of 0.1–0.5 mm/rev.

Machined rings and bulkheads. Structural ring frames that join body sections are turned from forged billets. Key dimensions:

\[\sigma_\text{hoop} = \frac{p \cdot r}{t}\tag{28.1}\]

where \(p\) is internal pressure (motor burnout), \(r\) is mean radius, and \(t\) is wall thickness. For a 150 mm diameter motor case at 10 MPa with \(t = 3\) mm:

\[\sigma_\text{hoop} = \frac{10 \times 10^6 \times 0.075}{0.003} = 250\,\text{MPa}\tag{28.2}\]

which is within the yield strength of 7075-T6 (\(\sigma_y = 503\,\text{MPa}\)) with a factor of safety of 2.0.

Tolerances. Critical dimensional tolerances for missile airframe components are much tighter than those for aircraft structures due to the need for aerodynamic consistency and inter-lot interchangeability:

Table 28.1. Representative airframe dimensional tolerances Feature Tolerance Method Airframe OD \(\pm 0.10\,\text{mm}\) CMM / air gauge Fin attachment slot \(\pm 0.05\,\text{mm}\) CMM Nozzle bore \(\pm 0.025\,\text{mm}\) Air plug gauge Nose cone concentricity \(0.05\,\text{mm TIR}\) CMM Section joint face flatness \(0.025\,\text{mm}\) Surface plate

docs.title: 28.2.2 Composite Airframe Fabrication
docs.text:
Composite missile bodies offer significant weight savings (15–30% versus aluminium) and can be tailored for aeroelastic stiffness. Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CFRP) and glass-CFRP hybrids are typical.

Filament winding. A CNC winding machine deposits resin-impregnated (wet winding) or pre-impregnated (dry towpreg) fibres over a mandrel at prescribed angles. The winding angle \(\alpha\) controls the axial-to-hoop stiffness ratio. For a closed-end pressure vessel the netting-analysis optimum winding angle is:

\[\tan^2\alpha = \frac{N_\phi}{N_\theta}\tag{28.3}\]

where \(N_\phi\) is the meridional stress resultant and \(N_\theta\) is the hoop stress resultant. For a cylindrical section under axial and pressure loads, \(\alpha = 54.7°\) (the “magic angle”).

Prepreg layup. Flat and complex-curved panels are built from unidirectional or woven prepreg plies placed in matched-metal or composite tooling. Ply sequence is typically \([0/\pm 45/90]_s\) to achieve quasi-isotropic stiffness. Autoclave cure at \(121°\)C/585 kPa (180°C/700 kPa for bismaleimide systems) achieves void contents below 1%.

Surface finish and coating. Post-cure surfaces are lightly sanded to \(R_a = 0.8\)–\(1.6\,\mu\text{m}\) and primed with a MIL-PRF-23377 epoxy primer before application of a MIL-PRF-85285 polyurethane topcoat. The topcoat provides UV resistance, chemical resistance, and a controlled emissivity for thermal management.

docs.title: 28.2.3 Joining Processes
docs.text:
Electron beam welding (EBW). Thin-wall titanium sections (1–3 mm) are joined by EBW in vacuum (\(10^{-4}\) Pa). The narrow heat-affected zone (HAZ) (\(\le 1\,\text{mm}\)) preserves the base metal temper. Weld penetration depth \(d\) scales with beam power \(P\) and travel speed \(v\):

\[d \propto \frac{P}{v \cdot \sqrt{k \rho c_p}}\tag{28.4}\]

where \(k\) is thermal conductivity, \(\rho\) is density, and \(c_p\) is specific heat. Welds are 100% inspected by X-ray and dye-penetrant (PT) per AWS D17.1.

TIG welding. Gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW/TIG) is used for thicker steel sections. Trailing gas shields protect titanium welds from oxidation. Preheat (150–200°C) is required for 4340 steel to prevent hydrogen embrittlement.

docs.title: 28.3.1 Propellant Formulation and Ingredients
docs.text:
Modern composite solid propellants are physically and chemically complex systems. The primary ingredients of a typical HTPB (hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene) propellant are:

Table 28.2. Representative HTPB propellant formulation Ingredient Function Mass fraction (%) HTPB (R-45M) Binder / fuel 10–14 Isocyanate (IPDI) Cross-linking agent 1–3 Ammonium perchlorate (AP) Oxidiser (coarse + fine) 65–72 Aluminium powder (30–400 extmum) Metal fuel 16–20 Bonding agent (MAPO/HX-880) AP–binder adhesion 0.1–0.5 Stabiliser (MNA) Thermal stability 0.1–0.3 Plasticiser (DOA) Flexibility at low-T 0–3 Burn-rate catalyst (Fe2O3) Rate modifier 0–0.5

The specific impulse \(I_{sp}\) of an HTPB/AP/Al propellant at optimum mixture ratio is approximately 260–275 s (sea level) and 280–295 s (vacuum). Theoretical specific impulse is computed from:

\[I_{sp} = \frac{1}{g_0} \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1} \cdot \frac{R_u T_c}{M_w} \left[1 - \left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\right]}\tag{28.5}\]

where \(\gamma\) is the product-gas ratio of specific heats (\(\approx 1.2\)), \(R_u\) is the universal gas constant, \(T_c\) is combustion temperature (typically 3,100–3,600 K), \(M_w\) is the mean molecular weight of combustion products, and \(p_e/p_c\) is the nozzle expansion ratio.

docs.title: 28.3.2 Mixing Operations
docs.text:
Propellant mixing is conducted in vertical-sigma-blade (VSB) or planetary mixers with vacuum capability. Typical production mixer sizes range from 11 litres (development) to 2,300 litres (production). Key process parameters:

  • Mixing sequence: Binder components (HTPB, plasticiser, bonding agent) are premixed; then coarse AP is added; then fine AP; aluminium is added last to minimise ignition risk.

  • Temperature: Maintained at 25–35°C; elevated temperature reduces viscosity but shortens pot life.

  • Vacuum: Vacuum (\(\le 10\,\text{kPa}\)) applied during mixing to remove entrapped air and residual moisture.

  • Pot life: The time from addition of isocyanate (cross-linker) to the point at which viscosity exceeds the castable limit is 4–8 hours. Pot life \(t_{pot}\) follows Arrhenius kinetics:

\[t_{pot} = A \cdot \exp\!\left(\frac{E_a}{R_u T}\right)\tag{28.6}\]

where \(E_a\) is the activation energy for gel formation (\(\approx 60\)–80 kJ/mol) and \(A\) is a pre-exponential factor. Reducing temperature from 35°C to 25°C approximately doubles pot life.

docs.title: 28.3.3 Casting and Cure
docs.text:
Propellant is transferred from the mixer to a casting vessel and cast into the motor case (which has been pre-lined and pre-heated to 40°C) via gravity or vacuum-assisted casting. A central mandrel displaces material to form the internal grain geometry (star, finocyl, etc.).

The degree of cure \(\alpha_c\) is related to the isocyanate/hydroxyl (NCO/OH) ratio \(r\):

\[\alpha_c = 1 - \exp(-k \cdot r \cdot t)\tag{28.7}\]

Cure takes place in a temperature-controlled oven at 50–60°C for 3–7 days. The cross-linking reaction increases storage modulus \(E'\) from approximately 0.2 MPa (uncured) to 1–5 MPa (cured). Final Shore A hardness target is 30–60, depending on the grain design.

The stress relaxation modulus is characterised by:

\[E_r(t) = \frac{\sigma(t)}{\varepsilon_0}\tag{28.8}\]

where \(\sigma(t)\) is the decaying stress at a fixed imposed strain \(\varepsilon_0\), measured in a relaxation test. This function determines the structural response of the grain to thermal cycling and pressure loading throughout storage life.

docs.title: 28.3.4 Quality Control of Propellant
docs.text:
X-ray radiography. 100% of production motors are X-rayed using linear accelerators or industrial X-ray sources to detect voids, cracks, and AP agglomerates. Minimum detectable void size is approximately 1.5 mm diameter. Acceptance criteria per drawing callout typically limit voids to \(\le 1.5\,\text{mm}\) in any dimension with no more than five per 300 mm length.

Ultrasonic inspection. Pulse-echo or through-transmission ultrasonics detects liner/propellant bond-line disbonds. A disbond larger than 6 mm in any direction is a cause for rejection.

Mechanical property coupons. Each mix is sampled; uniaxial tensile coupons (dogbone, per JANNAF test protocol) are cured alongside the production grain and tested at \(-40°C\), \(+25°C\), and \(+65°C\). Minimum required elongation is typically \(>25\%\) and tensile strength \(>0.8\,\text{MPa}\).

Burn rate is measured on strand burner samples. The empirical Vieille burn-rate law:

\[\dot{r} = a \cdot p^n\tag{28.9}\]

gives burn rate \(\dot{r}\) (mm/s) as a function of chamber pressure \(p\) (MPa) and empirical constants \(a\) and \(n\) (pressure exponent, typically 0.3–0.4 for HTPB/AP).

docs.title: 28.3.5 Minimum Signature Propellants
docs.text: Minimum-signature (reduced-smoke) propellants substitute RDX or HMX for part of the AP oxidiser and eliminate or reduce the aluminium fuel content. This produces a nearly transparent plume at the cost of lower \(I_{sp}\) (240–260 s). Double-base propellants (nitrocellulose + nitroglycerine) produce essentially no smoke but have lower \(I_{sp}\) and poorer mechanical properties. For infrared countermeasure reduction the plume temperature is also reduced.

docs.title: 28.3.6 Explosive Safety in Propellant Manufacturing
docs.text:
All propellant-manufacturing facilities are sited per DDESB 6055.09 quantity-distance (QD) requirements. The inhabited building distance (IBD) for exposed personnel is:

\[D_{IBD} = K_D \cdot W^{1/3}\tag{28.10}\]

where \(W\) is the net explosive weight (NEW) in kg, and \(K_D\) is the QD constant (18 for TNT-equivalent for the IBD in the US customary form, or 44.4 m/kg\(^{1/3}\) for high-explosive process buildings). Lightning protection is mandatory; a grounding grid with \(\le 10\,\Omega\) impedance must be demonstrated by earth-resistance testing.

docs.title: 28.4.1 Explosive Loading Processes
docs.text:
Three primary processes are used to load explosive fills into warhead cases.

Melt-pour loading. TNT and TNT-based compositions (Composition B, Octol) are melted at 82–95°C in steam-jacketed kettles and poured into the pre-warmed warhead case. Vibration during solidification (frequency 50–120 Hz) drives out trapped gas. Slow cooling (1–2°C/hr) prevents differential thermal cracking. Void acceptance criteria are defined per drawing; typical rejection limit is any void \(>3\,\text{mm}\) diameter revealed by X-ray.

Press loading. Insensitive high explosives (IHE) such as TATB (triaminotrinitrobenzene) and PBXN formulations cannot be melt-poured; they are pressed isostatically at 50–200 MPa in rubber tooling (cold isostatic pressing, CIP). Pressed density \(\rho_p\) relative to theoretical maximum density (TMD) is a key quality parameter:

\[\rho_\% = \frac{\rho_p}{\rho_{TMD}} \times 100\%\tag{28.11}\]

Acceptance requires \(\rho_\% \ge 98\%\) TMD. Any cracks detected by X-ray or dye-penetrant constitute automatic rejection.

Slurry casting. Water-slurry casting (used for PBXW formulations) disperses the explosive in an aqueous binder solution that is cast into the case and dried. This process allows very dense explosive charges at reduced ignition sensitivity.

docs.title: 28.4.2 Shaped Charge Liner Manufacture
docs.text:
The liner of a shaped charge controls the jet formation. Liner materials include electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper, OFHC copper, tantalum, and steel. The liner profile (conical, bi-conical, hemispherical, trumpet) is machined to very tight tolerances:

  • Wall thickness uniformity: \(\pm 0.05\,\text{mm}\) (electroformed copper)

  • Surface roughness: \(R_a \le 0.4\,\mu\text{m}\) (turned); \(R_a \le 0.8\,\mu\text{m}\) (electroformed)

  • Apex eccentricity: \(\le 0.1\,\text{mm}\) TIR

The penetration capability \(P\) of a shaped-charge jet into rolled homogeneous armour (RHA) is approximated by the Birkhoff formula:

\[P = L_j \sqrt{\frac{\rho_j}{\rho_t}}\tag{28.12}\]

where \(L_j\) is effective jet length (\(\approx 5\)–8 calibre for optimised designs), \(\rho_j\) is jet material density, and \(\rho_t\) is target density (\(7,850\,\text{kg/m}^3\) for RHA). For a copper jet (\(\rho_j = 8,960\,\text{kg/m}^3\)) penetrating steel, \(\sqrt{\rho_j/\rho_t} \approx 1.07\).

docs.title: 28.4.3 Non-destructive Evaluation of Warheads
docs.text: Table 28.3. NDT methods applied to warhead assemblies Method Defects Detected Notes Industrial X-ray Voids, cracks, liner contact 100% of production units Gamma-ray densitometry Explosive density variation Collimated source; \(\pm 0.5\%\) density resolution Ultrasonic C-scan Liner disbond, case cracks Immersion or contact; 3 MHz typical Flash X-ray Dynamic event imaging R&D / firing tests only Dye penetrant (PT) Surface cracks on metal case Per ASTM E165

docs.title: 28.4.4 Sensitivity Testing of Explosives
docs.text:
Before and after loading, explosive materials are characterised by standard sensitiveness tests:

  • Drop-weight impact: Height at which 50% of samples initiate (DH50) per STANAG 4489. For TATB, DH50 \(> 320\,\text{cm}\) (32 J), versus \(< 20\,\text{cm}\) for primary explosives.

  • Friction test: Sliding friction apparatus; \(P_{50}\) is the load at which 50% of trials initiate.

  • Electrostatic spark: Energy at which 50% of trials ignite (ES50 in mJ).

  • Thermal stability (DSC/DTA): Onset temperature of exotherm; minimum required decomposition onset \(> 180\)°C for IHE.

Fuze and warhead integration is performed only at the final assembly stage; safe-arm devices are verified functional (mechanically and electrically safe) before warhead attachment.

docs.title: 28.5.1 Inertial Measurement Unit Assembly
docs.text:
The IMU is the most precision-sensitive subassembly in the missile. Assembly takes place in ISO Class 7 (FED-STD-209E Class 10,000) or better cleanrooms to prevent particulate contamination of gyroscopes and accelerometers.

Key alignment requirements:

  • Input axis misalignment: \(\le 0.01°\) (\(\le 175\,\mu\text{rad}\))

  • Scale factor error: \(\le 50\,\text{ppm}\)

  • Bias (accelerometer): \(\le 100\,\mu g\) (1 \(\sigma\))

  • Bias (gyroscope): \(\le 0.01°/\text{hr}\) (tactical), \(\le 0.001°/\text{hr}\) (strategic)

The navigation error arising from gyro bias \(\omega_b\) in position grows as:

\[\delta x \approx \frac{1}{2} g \cdot \omega_b \cdot t^2\tag{28.13}\]

For a 60-second flight with \(\omega_b = 1°/\text{hr} = 4.85 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{rad/s}\): \(\delta x \approx \frac{1}{2} \times 9.81 \times 4.85 \times 10^{-6} \times 3600 = 0.085\,\text{m}\).

docs.title: 28.5.2 Electronic Assembly
docs.text:
Printed circuit boards. Missile electronics boards are manufactured to IPC-6012 Class 3 (most reliable) using polyimide (PI) substrates, which retain dielectric properties to 300°C. High-density interconnect (HDI) boards use laser-drilled microvias (\(< 150\,\mu\text{m}\)). Solder alloy is SAC305 or indium-based for extreme thermal cycling.

Military-grade components. All active ICs are specified to Military or Industrial temperature ranges (\(-55°\)C to \(+125°\)C). Strategic systems use radiation-hardened (rad-hard) ASICs and FPGAs (total ionising dose \(> 100\) krad). Components are sourced to MIL-PRF-38535 (integrated circuits) or commercial equivalents with DLA-approved qualification.

Conformal coating. After assembly and test, boards are coated with acrylic, silicone, or polyurethane conformal coat (IPC-CC-830) to 25–75 extmum depth to resist moisture, salt, and vibration-induced fretting corrosion.

docs.title: 28.5.3 Seeker Assembly and Calibration
docs.text:
Seeker subassemblies (imaging infrared, semi-active laser, active radar) are assembled in specialised environments:

  • Focal plane arrays (FPA) are bonded and wire-bonded under nitrogen purge at \(< 50\) ppm moisture.

  • Optical alignment: boresight is aligned to the missile axis to \(\le 0.1\,\text{mrad}\).

  • Gimbal balance: static unbalance \(\le 1\,\text{g-mm}\) to prevent vibration-induced bias.

  • Radiometric calibration: blackbody source at multiple temperatures; non-uniformity correction (NUC) coefficients stored in EEPROM.

docs.title: 28.5.4 Cable Harness and Connector Practice
docs.text: Cable harnesses comply with MIL-DTL-22759 (wire) and MIL-DTL-38999 (circular connectors). All signal harnesses use shielded twisted pairs to achieve \(\ge 60\,\text{dB}\) common-mode rejection. Connector torque is specified per manufacturer data and verified by a calibrated torque wrench. Every harness undergoes 100% continuity, insulation resistance (\(> 100\,\text{M}\Omega\) at 500 V DC), and hipot testing (1,500 V AC for 60 s).

docs.title: 28.5.5 Environmental Stress Screening
docs.text:
ESS is applied to 100% of production units to precipitate latent defects (infant mortality). A HALT-derived ESS profile for missile electronics typically consists of:

  1. Thermal cycling: \(-40°\)C to \(+85°\)C; 5 cycles; ramp rate 5–10°C/min

  2. Random vibration: \(0.04\,\text{g}^2/\text{Hz}\) PSD; 20–2,000 Hz; 30 min per axis

  3. Combined temperature/vibration simultaneously

  4. Burn-in at elevated temperature (if required by contract)

The ESS screening effectiveness \(SE\) is related to the screening strength \(SS\):

\[SE = 1 - \exp(-SS)\tag{28.14}\]

A \(SS = 2.0\) achieves \(SE = 0.865\) (86.5% of latent defects precipitated).

docs.title: 28.5.6 Acceptance Sampling
docs.text:
After ESS, lot acceptance sampling per MIL-STD-105 (now ANSI/ASQ Z1.4) is applied to non-100%-inspectable characteristics. At Acceptable Quality Level (AQL) 1.0, a lot of 90 units uses a sample size of 13; the accept number is 0, reject number is 1. The producer’s risk (Type I error) \(\alpha\) and consumer’s risk (Type II error) \(\beta\) are:

\[P_{accept}(p) = \sum_{k=0}^{c} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}\tag{28.15}\]

where \(c\) is the acceptance number, \(n\) is sample size, and \(p\) is the true fraction defective.

docs.title: 28.6.1 Mandrel Preparation and Liner
docs.text:
The motor case mandrel may be a steel or aluminium wash-out mandrel, a segmented steel mandrel, or a sacrificial mandrel (plaster, salt) for complex shapes. Before winding:

  1. Mandrel surfaces are grit-blasted and release agent applied (carnauba wax or silicone).

  2. An elastomeric liner (EPDM, HTPB-based, or filled EPDM) 1–5 mm thick is applied to the interior by casting or calendering. The liner bonds to both the case and the propellant, acting as a thermal insulator and barrier.

  3. The liner is cured partially (B-stage) so that final propellant casting completes the bond.

docs.title: 28.6.2 Filament Winding Process
docs.text:
CNC filament winding machines with up to 6 axes control the fibre placement angle, bandwidth, tension, and speed. Key parameters:

\[t_{case} = \frac{p \cdot r}{2 \sigma_{f} \cdot V_f \cdot \cos^2\!\alpha}\tag{28.16}\]

where \(\sigma_f\) is fibre tensile strength, \(V_f\) is fibre volume fraction (\(\approx 0.6\)), and \(\alpha\) is winding angle. Fibre tension during winding is controlled to \(\pm 5\%\) to ensure uniform compaction. Typical composite motor cases use T700 or T1000 carbon fibre in an epoxy matrix.

For geodesic (isotensoid) dome winding, the winding angle at radius \(r\) from the axis is governed by:

\[r \cdot \sin\alpha = r_0 \cdot \sin\alpha_0 = \text{constant}\tag{28.17}\]

where \(r_0\) is the polar boss radius and \(\alpha_0\) is the winding angle at the equator. This ensures equal fibre tension throughout the dome, preventing fibre slippage.

docs.title: 28.6.3 Autoclave Cure and Post-Processing
docs.text:
Wound cases are cured in an autoclave or oven:

  • Temperature: 120–180°C depending on resin system

  • Pressure: 3–7 bar

  • Hold time: 2–4 hours

  • Cool rate: \(\le 1\)°C/min to minimise residual thermal stress

Post-cure, the mandrel is extracted; the case is trimmed to length; and boss fittings are machined. A hydrostatic proof pressure test is conducted at 1.1 times the maximum expected operating pressure (MEOP):

\[p_{proof} = 1.1 \times p_{MEOP}\tag{28.18}\]

Burst pressure must exceed \(1.5 \times p_{MEOP}\) (safety factor). X-ray computed tomography (CT) scanning is used for critical applications to detect delaminations and dry spots.

The fibre-dominated burst pressure of the cylinder is:

\[p_{burst} = \frac{2 \sigma_f V_f t}{D/2}\tag{28.19}\]

docs.title: 28.7.1 Throat Insert
docs.text:
The throat insert experiences the most severe thermochemical environment in a rocket motor: stagnation temperatures of 3,000–3,600 K and hot-gas velocities approaching Mach 1. Graphite (ATJ grade, isostatically pressed) is the workhorse material. CNC turning achieves the nozzle contour to \(\pm 0.025\,\text{mm}\); surface finish \(R_a \le 0.4\,\mu\text{m}\) minimises roughness-induced boundary layer transition and ablation asymmetry.

The throat area \(A_t\) and its relationship to motor thrust \(F\) and chamber pressure \(p_c\):

\[F = C_F \cdot p_c \cdot A_t\tag{28.20}\]

where the thrust coefficient \(C_F\) is:

\[C_F = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma^2}{\gamma-1}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)} \left[1-\left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\right]} + \frac{p_e - p_a}{p_c} \cdot \frac{A_e}{A_t}\tag{28.21}\]

The erosion rate of the graphite throat \(\dot{\varepsilon}\) is empirically:

\[\dot{\varepsilon} \approx \frac{\dot{r}_s \cdot A_s}{A_t}\tag{28.22}\]

where \(\dot{r}_s\) is the surface regression rate (typically 0.1–0.5 mm/s for filled propellants on graphite).

docs.title: 28.7.2 Exit Cone
docs.text:
Carbon-carbon (C/C) composites are used for exit cones in high-performance motors due to their exceptional strength retention at temperatures above 2,000°C. The manufacturing process:

  1. Preform fabrication: 3D woven, needle-punched, or filament-wound carbon fibre preform shaped to the exit cone geometry.

  2. CVI densification: Chemical vapour infiltration deposits pyrolytic carbon from a hydrocarbon gas (methane or propane) at 900–1,100°C and 1–10 kPa. Each cycle fills pores; multiple cycles (100+ hours total) build up density from 0.3 to 1.8–1.95 g/cm\(^3\).

  3. Oxidation protection: Silicon carbide (SiC) coating by CVD or pack cementation protects against oxidation in air up to 1,700°C.

  4. Final machining: Diamond tooling; tight tolerance on exit diameter (determines area ratio \(\varepsilon = A_e/A_t\) and hence \(I_{sp}\)).

docs.title: 28.7.3 Flex Bearing (TVC)
docs.text:
The flex bearing (flexible bearing) enables thrust vector control by tilting the nozzle up to \(\pm 8°\). It consists of alternating layers of high-strength steel shims (1–2 mm) and elastomer (natural rubber or silicone; 2–5 mm layers), bonded by heat and pressure. Manufacturing requirements:

  • Shim flatness: \(\le 0.025\,\text{mm}\) per shim

  • Elastomer bond strength: \(> 14\,\text{MPa}\) (lap shear)

  • Proof test: hydrostatic to 1.25 × MEOP; deflection through full range

  • Lateral stiffness: characterised; must remain \(< K_{max}\) to not limit actuator

The restoring moment \(M\) of the flex bearing at deflection angle \(\theta\):

\[M = k_\theta \cdot \theta\tag{28.23}\]

where the rotational stiffness \(k_\theta\) (N-m/rad) is calculated from the geometry and elastomer shear modulus \(G\) via laminated-bearing theory.

docs.title: 28.8.1 Assembly Sequence and Integration
docs.text:
Final assembly of a surface-to-air missile (SAM) follows a sequence that enforces the explosive-safety logic while also managing the alignment and electrical verification steps:

  1. Aft section build-up: fins attached and torqued; actuators installed; aft connector checked.

  2. Motor mated to aft section: O-ring seals; torqued bolts to specified preload.

  3. Mid-section attached to motor: explosive interface (warhead forward bulkhead to motor aft bulkhead) completed under explosive-safe conditions.

  4. Guidance section pre-checked: self-test passed; alignment verified by laser tracker before mating.

  5. Fuze installed (armed only in final step before delivery).

  6. Seeker dome or radome mated; seeker bore-sight re-verified.

  7. Full missile electrical continuity: all harnesses connected; pin-for-pin verified with wiring diagram.

docs.title: 28.8.2 Mass Properties Measurement
docs.text:
Mass properties are measured on a dedicated mass properties instrument (Space Electronics, Raptor series, or equivalent):

Table 28.4. Mass properties measurement methods and tolerances Property Method Accuracy Typical Value Total mass Load cell \(\pm 0.1\,\text{kg}\) 150–2,000 kg CG (axial) Roll fixture balance \(\pm 1\,\text{mm}\) Design-specific CG (lateral) Balance table \(\pm 0.5\,\text{mm}\) \(< 2\,\text{mm}\) offset spec \(I_{yy}\), \(I_{zz}\) Swing pendulum \(\pm 0.5\%\) Design-specific \(I_{xx}\) (roll) Torsion pendulum \(\pm 1\%\) Design-specific Imbalance Dynamic balance \(\pm 10\,\text{g-cm}\) \(< 50\,\text{g-cm}\) typical

The natural period of the swing pendulum gives the moment of inertia:

\[I = \frac{m g L}{(2\pi/T)^2} - m L^2\tag{28.24}\]

where \(L\) is the distance from pivot to CG, \(T\) is the oscillation period, and \(m\) is total mass.

docs.title: 28.8.3 Built-in Test and Acceptance
docs.text:
Built-in test (BIT) initiates at power-on and verifies:

  • IMU bias and scale factor within limits (self-calibration)

  • Seeker: acquisition and tracking of internal reference target

  • Flight control: actuator step response; bandwidth \(> 30\,\text{Hz}\)

  • Fuze: arming circuit continuity; safe-arm state verified

  • Power: bus voltages within \(\pm 5\%\); thermal management operational

A captive-carry test with the delivery platform verifies all umbilical and MIL-STD-1760 digital interfaces before the first free-flight test.

docs.title: 28.9.1 Acceptance Test Procedures
docs.text:
The Acceptance Test Procedure (ATP) is a contractually mandated document specifying the sequence, equipment, and pass/fail criteria for every parameter to be verified on each production unit. ATP content includes:

  • Reference drawings and specifications (with revision letters)

  • Test equipment calibration requirements (MIL-STD-45662)

  • Environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, vibration during test)

  • Pass/fail limits for each parameter (numerically stated)

  • Required signatures and data recording format

docs.title: 28.9.2 Reliability Prediction and Allocation
docs.text:
System reliability is predicted using MIL-HDBK-217F (electronics failure rates) and NPRD-2016 (non-electronic part reliability data). The system failure rate:

\[\lambda_{system} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i\tag{28.25}\]

Mean time between failures (MTBF):

\[MTBF = \frac{1}{\lambda_{system}}\tag{28.26}\]

For a missile guidance section with \(N = 1{,}200\) components, \(\lambda_{system}\) may be \(1.2 \times 10^{-4}\) failures/hour, giving \(MTBF = 8{,}333\) hours. However, for a single-shot missile the relevant metric is the probability of success \(P_s\) over the engagement duration \(t_m\) (typically 20–300 seconds):

\[P_s = \exp(-\lambda_{system} \cdot t_m)\tag{28.27}\]

For \(t_m = 60\,\text{s}\) and \(\lambda = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{hr}^{-1}\): \(P_s = \exp(-1.2\times10^{-4}/3600 \times 60) = \exp(-2\times10^{-6}) \approx 0.999998\).

docs.title: 28.9.3 Reliability Growth
docs.text:
During development testing, the AMSAA (Army Materiel Systems Analysis Activity) reliability growth model tracks cumulative failures \(N(t)\) versus cumulative test time \(T\):

\[N(T) = \lambda_0 \cdot T^\beta\tag{28.28}\]

The growth parameter \(\beta < 1\) indicates improving reliability. The current (instantaneous) failure rate is:

\[\lambda(T) = \lambda_0 \cdot \beta \cdot T^{\beta-1}\tag{28.29}\]

A Duane plot (\(\log\) cumulative failure rate vs. \(\log\) cumulative time) reveals whether the program is on track to achieve the reliability requirement by the start of production.

docs.title: 28.9.4 FRACAS
docs.text:
Failure Reporting, Analysis, and Corrective Action System (FRACAS) is a closed-loop failure management process mandatory on all US DoD missile development programs (per MIL-HDBK-2155). Every anomaly is:

  1. Identified and classified (hardware, software, test-induced, operator error)

  2. Analysed for root cause (fault tree, 5-Why, Ishikawa diagram)

  3. Corrected (design change, process change, specification revision)

  4. Verified by retest

  5. Closed with documented evidence

docs.title: 28.9.5 Shelf Life Determination
docs.text:
