docs.text: The Laser Weapon System (LAWS) aboard USS Ponce was the first US Navy laser weapon deployed operationally in 2014. The solid-state, 30 kW system demonstrated the ability to engage small boats, UAVs, and mortar rounds in the Persian Gulf region. It used a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) beam director and was integrated with the ship’s combat management system. Engagement of a small UAV at ranges up to 1 km was demonstrated, with burn-through times of 1–3 s.

docs.title: 32.3.2 HELIOS — High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance
docs.text:
HELIOS, developed by Lockheed Martin, represents the first production HEL system for the US Navy’s Arleigh Burke–class destroyers (DDG-51 Flight III). Key specifications:

  • Laser power: 60 kW (upgradeable to 150 kW)

  • Wavelength: 1070 nm (Yb fibre)

  • Mission: C-UAS, C-USV (counter unmanned surface vessel), ISR (surveillance/dazzle mode)

  • Beam director: 0.3 m aperture; inertially stabilised gimbal

  • IOC: DDG-72 USS Dewey, 2022

  • Integration: Ship’s Aegis combat system; direct cueing from SPY-1D(V) radar

docs.title: 32.3.3 HEL TVD — High Energy Laser Tactical Vehicle Demonstrator
docs.text: Mounted on a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV), the HEL TVD programme (50 kW, Raytheon/Kord Technologies) targets short-range air defence: UAVs, RPGs, and RAM (Rockets, Artillery, Mortars). The system demonstrated engagement of a 60 mm mortar round in 2023 trials, representing the hardest C-RAM intercept class for HEL due to the small RCS and short exposure time.

docs.title: 32.3.4 Iron Beam (Israel)
docs.text: Iron Beam, developed by Rafael and Elbit Systems, reached operational status in 2025 as the first HEL C-RAM system deployed in combat conditions. At 100 kW, it can engage rockets at 7–10 km range and drones at 4–7 km. During the 2023 Gaza conflict, Iron Dome intercepted  \(90\%\) of incoming rockets; Iron Beam is designed to handle the lower-cost saturation attacks that challenge kinetic interceptors. Cost per engagement is approximately $5 (electricity), versus $50,000–$100,000 per Iron Dome Tamir interceptor.

docs.title: 32.3.5 DragonFire (United Kingdom)
docs.text: DragonFire is a consortium programme involving Leonardo UK, MBDA, and QinetiQ, funded by the UK MOD. After successful trials at BUTEC (British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre) range in 2023, the 50 kW system demonstrated engagement of aerial targets at ranges up to 3 km. The programme targets ship and ground vehicle integration, with service entry planned for 2027–2030.

docs.title: 32.4.1 HPM Principles
docs.text:
High Power Microwave weapons deliver nanosecond-to-microsecond pulses of radiofrequency energy at peak powers of 10 MW–10 GW into a target’s electronic subsystems. Damage is through:

  • Front-door coupling: Energy enters via the target’s own receive antenna; amplified by antenna gain; can destroy receiver front-ends with relatively modest field strengths.

  • Back-door coupling: Energy couples through structural apertures — seams, cable penetrations, vents — and propagates as a conducted or radiated disturbance onto circuit boards.

The susceptibility threshold for semiconductor junctions is expressed in terms of electric field \(E_{\text{thresh}}\) or power density \(S_{\text{thresh}}\):

\[P_{\text{damage}} = \frac{E_{\text{thresh}}^2}{Z_0} \cdot A_{\text{eff}}\tag{32.23}\]

where \(Z_0 = 377\;\Omega\) is the impedance of free space and \(A_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective receiving aperture of the coupling path.

docs.title: Magnetron
docs.text: The magnetron is a crossed-field device (perpendicular electric and magnetic fields) that produces high-power microwave pulses. Widely used in radar and industrial applications; wall-plug efficiency 50–70%; pulsed peak power 1 kW–5 MW; frequency 1–18 GHz. Magnetrons are coherent only within a single pulse — they lack phase memory pulse-to-pulse.

docs.title: Klystron
docs.text: The klystron is a linear-beam amplifier driven by an RF input signal; it produces very high-power, coherent output at fixed frequencies. Used in large radar transmitters and particle accelerators; peak power up to 100 MW; efficiency 40–60%.

docs.title: Vircator (Virtual Cathode Oscillator)
docs.text:
The vircator is a compact, single-pulse HPM source requiring no external magnetic field. A high-current electron beam is injected into a resonant cavity; when the space-charge limit is exceeded, a virtual cathode forms and oscillates, radiating at a frequency:

\[f_{\text{vircator}} \approx \frac{\omega_p}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{n_e e^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}}\tag{32.24}\]

where \(n_e\) is electron density, \(e\) electron charge, and \(m_e\) electron mass. Peak powers of 1–10 GW are achievable in a package of \(<\)50 kg, making the vircator attractive for missile-deliverable HPM payloads. Efficiency is typically 1–5%.

docs.title: CHAMP (Counter-electronics High-powered Microwave Advanced Missile Project)
docs.text:
CHAMP, developed by Boeing for AFRL, is a cruise-missile-based HPM weapon. The weapon carries a repetitively-pulsed HPM source powered by a turbine generator from the JP-10 fuel supply. In a 2012 demonstration at the Utah Test and Training Range, CHAMP made ten passes over seven targets, successfully neutralising the electronics at each. The weapon then self-destructed. CHAMP demonstrated:

  • Multiple target engagement in a single sortie

  • Non-kinetic defeat of hardened facilities

  • Standoff engagement at cruise missile range (500–1000 km)

  • No collateral structural damage

docs.title: Active Denial System (ADS)
docs.text:
The ADS operates at 95 GHz, where the millimetre-wave radiation is absorbed in the outermost 0.4 mm of human skin (the epidermis), producing an intense heating sensation without penetrating to underlying tissue. Parameters:

  • Frequency: 95 GHz (3.16 mm wavelength)

  • Power: 100 kW (system); 10–50 kW at aperture

  • Beam divergence: \(\sim\)0.5° (Gaussian)

  • Effective range: 500–1000 m

  • Skin penetration: \(\delta = \sqrt{2/(\omega\mu\sigma)} \approx 0.4\;\text{mm}\) at 95 GHz

  • Pain onset: \(T_{\text{skin}} > 44^{\circ}\text{C}\) after \(\sim\)3 s exposure

The ADS is classified as a non-lethal weapon for crowd control. It was deployed to Afghanistan in 2010 but not operationally used; the perception of the weapon as a pain ray made it politically sensitive.

Table 32.3. HPM System Comparison System Freq. Peak Power Effect Platform Status CHAMP 1–3 GHz \(>\)1 GW (pulse) Electronics burnout Cruise missile Demo 2012 ADS 95 GHz 100 kW Non-lethal pain Vehicle Limited fielding THOR 3 GHz \(>\)100 MW C-UAS electronics Ground Demo 2020 EMP bomb 1–10 GHz \(>\)10 GW Area EMP Gravity bomb Classified Vircator warhead 1–5 GHz 1–10 GW Facility electronics Warhead R&D

docs.title: 32.4.4 THOR — Tactical High-power Operational Responder
docs.text: THOR, developed by AFRL, is a containerised ground-based HPM system designed specifically for counter-UAS applications. A single HPM pulse is sufficient to cause electronic upset or burnout in a small drone’s flight controller. THOR can engage multiple drones simultaneously within its beam footprint — a key advantage over single-track HEL systems. THOR underwent desert environment testing in 2020 and was loaned to the US Air Force for base perimeter defence evaluation.

docs.title: 32.4.5 Coupling Analysis
docs.text:
For a target at range \(R\) in the main beam of an HPM antenna with gain \(G_t\):

\[S_{\text{target}} = \frac{P_t G_t}{4\pi R^2}\tag{32.25}\]

Power coupled into a target aperture of effective area \(A_{\text{coup}}\):

\[P_{\text{coup}} = S_{\text{target}} \cdot A_{\text{coup}} = \frac{P_t G_t A_{\text{coup}}}{4\pi R^2}\tag{32.26}\]

For \(P_t = 1\;\text{GW}\), \(G_t = 30\;\text{dB} = 1000\), \(R = 1\;\text{km}\), \(A_{\text{coup}} = 0.01\;\text{m}^2\):

\[P_{\text{coup}} = \frac{10^9 \times 10^3 \times 0.01}{4\pi \times 10^6} = 796\;\text{W}\tag{32.27}\]

This is far above the semiconductor burnout threshold of milliwatts to watts, indicating that HPM readily defeats unshielded electronics at tactical ranges.

docs.title: 32.5.1 Principles
docs.text:
Particle beam weapons accelerate charged particles — electrons, protons, or heavier ions — through a particle accelerator to relativistic velocities. At the target, the beam deposits energy through:

  • Coulomb interactions: elastic and inelastic scattering; produces ionisation, excitation, and radiation damage in semiconductors and biological tissue;

  • Nuclear interactions: for protons and ions, nuclear spallation at high enough energies can disrupt nuclear material;

  • Bremsstrahlung radiation: electrons produce X-ray secondary radiation in dense targets.

The range of a proton in air (the Bragg curve) at kinetic energy \(E_k\) (MeV) follows approximately:

\[R_{\text{proton}} \approx 0.0022 \cdot E_k^{1.77}\;\text{m (in air at STP)}\tag{32.28}\]

A 100 MeV proton has a range of \(\sim\)8 m in air — far too short for weaponisable beam weapons in atmosphere.

docs.title: 32.5.2 Neutral Particle Beam (NPB)
docs.text: In space, where there is no atmosphere, a charged particle beam can propagate freely, though space-charge repulsion eventually spreads the beam. The NPB concept involves accelerating ions to high energy, then stripping an electron to produce a neutral atom beam that is unaffected by magnetic fields but propagates in a straight line. The SDI (Strategic Defense Initiative) programme in the 1980s developed NPB concepts for boost-phase intercept of ICBMs in mid-course. The Alpha Project demonstrated a 1 MeV hydrogen neutral beam. No operational space-based NPB system has been deployed.

docs.title: 32.5.3 Current Status
docs.text:
Particle beam weapons remain at TRL 2–4. The fundamental challenges are:

  1. Accelerator mass: linear accelerators producing 100 MeV beams weigh tens of tonnes;

  2. Atmospheric propagation: utterly impractical below 80 km altitude;

  3. Power: continuous high-energy beams require hundreds of megawatts;

  4. Beam pointing: relativistic beam deflection requires large superconducting magnets.

docs.title: 32.6.1 Slant Range for Ship-Based Engagement
docs.text:
For a ship-based HEL system at height \(H\) above the waterline engaging a target at elevation angle \(\varepsilon\):

\[R_{\text{slant}} = \frac{H}{\sin\varepsilon}\tag{32.29}\]

For a sea-skimming missile at 5 m altitude, hull height 15 m, and minimum detection range 10 km: \(\varepsilon = \arcsin(15/10{,}000) \approx 0.086°\) — very shallow, requiring a highly stabilised low-elevation beam director.

docs.title: 32.6.2 Effective Spot Size with Jitter
docs.text:
Beam wander due to platform vibration and atmospheric tip-tilt introduces an additional pointing error \(\sigma_j\) (rad). The effective irradiance-equivalent spot radius is:

\[r_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{r_{\text{diff}}^2 + (\sigma_j R)^2}\tag{32.30}\]

where \(r_{\text{diff}} = M^2 \lambda R / (\pi w_0)\) is the diffraction-limited radius. Jitter reduces peak irradiance:

\[I_{\text{jitter}} = I_{\text{ideal}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\sigma_j^2 R^2}{r_{\text{diff}}^2}\right) \quad \text{(for } \sigma_j R \ll r_{\text{diff}}\text{)}\tag{32.31}\]

For \(\sigma_j = 1\;\mu\text{rad}\) (achievable with inertially stabilised beam director), \(R = 5\;\text{km}\), \(r_{\text{diff}} = 10\;\text{cm}\): \(\sigma_j R = 5\;\text{mm}\), which is small compared to \(r_{\text{diff}}\), so jitter is manageable. At longer ranges or with higher jitter (ship in sea-state 4), \(\sigma_j\) may rise to 5–10 \(\mu\)rad, significantly degrading irradiance.

docs.title: 32.6.3 Tracking Slew Rate Requirement
docs.text:
The fire-control system must track the target throughout the dwell time. The required angular slew rate:

\[\dot{\theta}_{\text{track}} = \frac{V_T}{R}\tag{32.32}\]

For a drone at \(V_T = 50\;\text{m/s}\), \(R = 2\;\text{km}\): \(\dot{\theta} = 25\;\text{mrad/s}\), easily achieved by modern gimbals (\(>\)3 rad/s). For a fast jet at \(V_T = 300\;\text{m/s}\), \(R = 1\;\text{km}\): \(\dot{\theta} = 300\;\text{mrad/s} = 17°/\text{s}\), requiring a fast-slewing gimbal and high control bandwidth.

docs.title: 32.6.4 Power Scaling Laws
docs.text:
From Equation (32.8), irradiance at range \(R\) scales as:

\[I \propto \frac{P}{R^2}\tag{32.33}\]

Halving the dwell time requires doubling \(I\), which requires doubling \(P\) (at fixed range). Halving the range at constant power quadruples \(I\), quartering the dwell time. These scaling laws drive the operational tactic of closing range before engaging with HEL.

docs.title: 32.7 Power Systems for Directed Energy Weapons
32.7.1 Wall-Plug Efficiency and Waste Heat
docs.text:
For a laser of wall-plug efficiency \(\eta_{\text{wall}}\), the thermal waste heat per unit of laser output power:

\[P_{\text{waste}} = P_{\text{laser}}\left(\frac{1}{\eta_{\text{wall}}} - 1\right)\tag{32.34}\]

For Yb fibre at \(\eta_{\text{wall}} = 0.40\) and \(P_{\text{laser}} = 100\;\text{kW}\):

\[P_{\text{waste}} = 10^5 \times (2.5 - 1) = 150\;\text{kW}\tag{32.35}\]

This 150 kW of waste heat must be managed by a thermal management system (TMS). At sea, seawater provides a convenient heat sink. For ground vehicles, the TMS is a major mass and volume driver.

docs.title: 32.7.2 Pulsed Power Systems
docs.text:
HPM weapons require very high instantaneous power (gigawatts) for very short durations (nanoseconds–microseconds). This is achieved through pulsed power systems:

  • Capacitor bank: stores energy \(U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2\); typical parameters: \(C = 10\;\text{mF}\), \(V = 100\;\text{kV}\), \(U = 50\;\text{kJ}\); switched by spark gaps or solid-state switches;

  • Marx generator: charges \(N\) capacitors in parallel, discharges in series; output voltage \(NV_0\); achieves \(>\)1 MV at \(>\)100 kJ in compact geometry;

  • Flux compression generator (FCG): single-use explosive-driven device; compresses magnetic flux to produce \(>\)100 MJ pulse; used in EMP bombs.

Pulse compression and forming: a pulse-forming network (PFN) shapes the discharge into a rectangular pulse of impedance-matched duration. For a transmission-line PFN of impedance \(Z_0\), pulse duration \(\tau = 2l/v_p\), where \(l\) is the electrical length and \(v_p\) is the propagation speed.

docs.title: 32.7.3 Continuous Power — Ship and Vehicle
docs.text:
For shipboard HEL, the vessel’s gas turbine or combined diesel-and-gas (CODAG) plant typically produces 30–100 MW. A 100 kW laser drawing 250 kW at the wall adds \(<\)1% to total ship load — entirely manageable. For ground vehicles, a JLTV-class platform produces \(\sim\)40 kW; a 50 kW HEL requires a dedicated generator trailer or next-generation vehicle with enhanced power generation. The US Army’s XM1299 Extended-Range Cannon Artillery (ERCA) programme considered a dedicated prime-mover for HEL power.

Table 32.4. DEW Power System Requirements Summary Platform DEW Power Wall-plug draw Waste heat Power source DDG destroyer 60 kW HEL 150 kW 90 kW Ship turbine DDG destroyer 100 kW HEL 250 kW 150 kW Ship turbine JLTV vehicle 50 kW HEL 125 kW 75 kW Generator trailer Cruise missile 1 GW HPM (pulse) N/A (pulsed) N/A Capacitor/Marx Ground base 100 kW HEL 250 kW 150 kW Grid/diesel gen B-747 (ABL) 1 MW COIL N/A (chemical) 3 MW (pumping) Chemical reaction

docs.title: 32.8.1 Reflective Coatings
docs.text: High-reflectivity coatings reduce the fraction of incident laser energy absorbed. Gold (\(\rho_r \approx 0.98\) at 1  extmum) and silver (\(\rho_r \approx 0.96\) at 1  extmum) are effective. However, at a sustained irradiance of 100 W/cm\(^2\), even 2% absorption equates to 2 W/cm\(^2\) deposited — sufficient for thermal damage over time. Furthermore, ablation of the coating itself eventually exposes the substrate.

docs.title: 32.8.2 Spinning and Tumbling
docs.text:
Inducing spin or tumble in the target distributes the laser energy around the circumference rather than concentrating it at one spot. For a cylinder of radius \(r\) and surface thermal conductivity \(k\), the reduction in peak temperature rise is approximately:

\[\frac{\Delta T_{\text{spin}}}{\Delta T_{\text{static}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{\text{th}}}{r^2 \omega_{\text{spin}}}}\tag{32.36}\]

At high spin rate the target effectively sees a time-averaged irradiance, reducing the peak temperature rise. This is particularly relevant for spin-stabilised rockets.

docs.title: 32.8.3 Obscurants and Smoke
docs.text:
Aerosol clouds of graphite, aluminium flakes, or metallic foil chaff scatter and absorb laser energy. Attenuation in a dense smoke cloud can exceed 10 dB (90% energy loss) per 100 m. The extinction coefficient of a cloud of spherical particles of radius \(a\), number density \(n\), and extinction efficiency \(Q_{\text{ext}}\) is:

\[\mu_{\text{ext}} = n \cdot Q_{\text{ext}} \cdot \pi a^2\tag{32.37}\]

Modern obscurant grenades (e.g., L8 on UK Challenger 2 MBT) deploy within 0.5 s and create a cloud effective against 1–12 \(\mu\)m wavelengths. However, obscurants also blind the target’s own sensors.

docs.title: 32.8.4 Speed as a Counter-DEW Measure
docs.text:
For a fast-moving target at velocity \(V_T\) at range \(R\), the beam slew rate required is \(\dot\theta = V_T/R\). At extreme approach velocities, dwell time is limited by the finite length of the engagement window. For a Mach 3 (1020 m/s) target crossing the laser’s lethal range from \(R_{\text{outer}} = 5\;\text{km}\) to \(R_{\text{inner}} = 1\;\text{km}\):

\[t_{\text{window}} = \frac{R_{\text{outer}} - R_{\text{inner}}}{V_T} = \frac{4000}{1020} \approx 3.9\;\text{s}\tag{32.38}\]

If the target requires 5 s of continuous dwell at the beam irradiance achievable at those ranges, the laser cannot complete the engagement — speed is an effective countermeasure.

docs.title: 32.8.5 Ablative Shielding
docs.text:
Ablative materials absorb laser energy through pyrolysis (chemical decomposition) rather than conduction. The ablation rate limits temperature rise:

\[\dot{m}_{\text{abl}} = \frac{I \cdot A_{\text{spot}}}{L_{\text{abl}}}\tag{32.39}\]

where \(L_{\text{abl}}\) (J/kg) is the ablation enthalpy (latent heat plus decomposition energy). Carbon–phenolic ablators have \(L_{\text{abl}} \approx 10^7\;\text{J/kg}\), providing effective protection at moderate fluences, at the cost of added mass.

docs.title: 32.9 Future Directions in Directed Energy Weapons
32.9.1 Multi-Kilowatt to Megawatt Scaling
docs.text:
The path to megawatt-class solid-state HEL involves:

  1. Coherent Beam Combination (CBC): Phase-locking hundreds of fibre amplifiers; each fibre limited to \(\sim\)3–5 kW before nonlinear effects (stimulated Brillouin scattering) degrade beam quality;

  2. Spectral Beam Combination (SBC): Combining beams at different wavelengths with a diffraction grating; no phase-locking required; multi-wavelength output;

  3. Next-generation gain media: Tm-fibre (2 \(\mu\)m), Ho-YAG (2.1 \(\mu\)m) for atmospheric window matching.

docs.title: 32.9.2 Tactical High Energy Laser (THEL) and IRON BEAM Succession
docs.text: Post-2025, the Israel MOD plans integration of Iron Beam into a multi-tier air defence architecture alongside Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Arrow. The key technology push is to extend HEL range to 10–15 km while maintaining kill probability \(>\)95% against salvo attacks of 10+ simultaneous targets.

docs.title: 32.9.3 DEW for Anti-Satellite (ASAT) Applications
docs.text: Ground-based DEW has been used for satellite dazzling (temporary blinding of imaging sensors) since the 1970s. Permanent damage to satellite solar panels or sensors requires fluences of \(>\)0.1 kJ/cm\(^2\) through the full atmospheric column (\(\sim\)80 km effective zenith path). Adaptive optics on large-aperture telescopes (1–4 m) can deliver this level under good seeing conditions.

docs.title: 32.9.4 Integration with AI Fire Control
docs.text:
Modern DEW fire-control systems incorporate AI-based algorithms for:

  • Real-time atmospheric propagation estimation (using guide-star or point-ahead angle data);

  • Predictive aimpoint selection (targeting the most vulnerable sub-system);

  • Multi-target prioritisation in swarm engagements;

  • Engagement authority management (human-machine interface for Rules of Engagement compliance).

docs.title: 32.10 Summary
docs.text:
Directed energy weapons represent a transformative technology in the aerospace and defence sector. High Energy Laser systems have crossed the threshold from laboratory demonstrations to operational deployment, with HEL weapons now defending naval vessels and fixed sites in multiple countries. High Power Microwave weapons have demonstrated the ability to non-kinetically neutralise electronics over wide areas. Both technologies address a critical cost asymmetry: a $5 laser shot versus a $100,000 missile interceptor fundamentally changes the economics of air defence against mass drone and rocket attacks.

Critical remaining challenges are: improving atmospheric propagation in adverse weather; reducing SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power) of the power conditioning and thermal management systems; and achieving multi-target, multi-layer DEW architectures that can handle saturation attacks by large drone swarms. The next decade will likely see 300 kW–1 MW HEL systems deployed on major surface combatants, providing a qualitative step change in air defence capability.

docs.title: 33.1 Introduction: The Counter-UAS Challenge
docs.text:
The proliferation of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) across commercial, recreational, and military domains has created an asymmetric threat of unprecedented scale. A decade ago, air defence doctrine focused almost exclusively on crewed aircraft and ballistic missiles. Today, operational commanders must simultaneously defend against a threat spectrum ranging from sub-250 g toy quadrotors carrying improvised explosives to military-grade group 4/5 unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) with precision strike capability, and — most challenging of all — coordinated swarms of hundreds to thousands of autonomous vehicles executing distributed attack profiles.

Counter-UAS (C-UAS) is the collective term for all measures, systems, and operational concepts designed to detect, identify, track, and defeat hostile unmanned systems. The discipline is characterised by extreme cost asymmetry, multi-domain complexity (kinetic, electronic, cyber, legal), and the need to operate in densely populated civil environments where collateral damage constraints are severe.

docs.title: 33.1.1 Threat Taxonomy
docs.text:
The UAS threat spans five DoD Group classifications:

Table 33.1. DoD UAS Group Classification and Counter-UAS Implications Group Max GW (kg) Alt (ft AGL) Speed (kt) RCS (m\(^2\)) C-UAS Challenge 1 \(<\) 9 \(<\) 1200 \(<\) 100 0.001–0.01 Micro-Doppler; clutter; no ADS-B 2 9.5–25 \(<\) 3500 \(<\) 250 0.01–0.1 Low RCS; speed; small target 3 25–600 \(<\) FL180 \(<\) 250 0.1–1.0 Manoeuvre; standoff payload 4 \(<\) 600 \(>\) FL180 Any 0.5–5.0 Similar to crewed aircraft 5 \(>\) 600 \(>\) FL180 Any 5–50 UCAV; stealth possible

Groups 1–3 represent the most challenging C-UAS problem: their small size yields radar cross-sections of \(0.001\)–\(1.0\) m\(^2\), compared to \(1\)–\(10\) m\(^2\) for fighter aircraft. Combined with flight at low altitude in terrain and urban clutter, and with no cooperative identification, they are exceptionally difficult to detect and engage.

docs.title: 33.1.2 Attack Vectors
docs.text:
Hostile UAS exploit multiple attack vectors:

  1. Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR): Persistent overhead observation of positions, routes, and activities; enables accurate mortar/artillery fire correction.

  2. Precision payload delivery: Dropping grenades, IEDs, or chemical/biological agents from altitude; highly effective when defender’s perimeter sensor coverage is incomplete.

  3. Kamikaze (loitering munition) impact: Commercial FPV drone modified with explosive payload; direct-impact attack on vehicles, personnel, and light infrastructure. Widely used in Ukraine (2022–present): FPV drones with RPG warheads disabled dozens of armoured vehicles at a material cost of $500–$2000 per drone.

  4. Swarm saturation: Coordinated multi-vehicle attack; overwhelms point-defence engagement rates; forces defender to exhaust expensive interceptors against cheap threats.

  5. EW/SIGINT drone: Drone equipped with SDR to map defender’s RF emissions; locate radio communications; jam C2 nets.

docs.title: 33.1.3 The Asymmetric Cost Problem
docs.text:
The fundamental economic problem in C-UAS is the exchange ratio. A Raytheon Coyote interceptor costs approximately $25,000. The Stinger missile costs $38,000. A Patriot interceptor costs $3–4 M. Against a $500 commercial quadrotor loaded with a grenade, the defender faces:

\[\text{Cost Exchange Ratio} = \frac{C_{interceptor}}{C_{threat}} = \frac{\$38{,}000}{\$500} = 76:1\tag{33.1}\]

At swarm scale (100 drones), the attacker spends $50,000 while forcing the defender to expend $3.8 M in missiles — and the defender may simply run out of interceptors. This asymmetry drives the C-UAS community toward directed energy (speed-of-light; essentially zero marginal cost per shot) and electronic attack (reversible; low cost) solutions rather than kinetic intercept missiles.

docs.title: 33.1.4 Historical Incidents
docs.text:
Key operational incidents that shaped C-UAS requirements:

  • Hmeimim Airbase, Syria (January 2018): Russian forces at Hmeimim AB repelled a coordinated attack by 13 fixed-wing UAS carrying GPS-guided sub-munitions. Pantsir-S1 systems engaged several; electronic spoofing diverted others. First documented large-scale swarm attack against a defended military base.

  • Abqaiq-Khurais, Saudi Arabia (September 2019): Saudi Aramco oil processing facilities attacked by a combination of cruise missiles and UAS; 17 drone strikes caused fires that temporarily halved Saudi oil production. Attributed to Iranian-backed forces. Demonstrated UAS effectiveness against critical infrastructure.

  • Nagorno-Karabakh (2020): Azerbaijan’s TB2 Bayraktar and Israeli Harop loitering munitions systematically destroyed Armenian air defence radar and artillery. Demonstrated Group 4/5 UAS lethality against integrated air defence systems.

  • Ukraine conflict (2022–present): Ubiquitous FPV drone use by both sides; Russian Shahed-136 kamikaze drones targeting Ukrainian infrastructure; Ukrainian commercial DJI Mavics for fire correction; Lancet loitering munitions destroying armoured vehicles. Forced rapid fielding of improvised and formal C-UAS systems.

docs.title: 33.2 Detection Systems
docs.text: Detection is the first and most critical layer of any C-UAS system. A target that cannot be detected cannot be defeated. Detection must provide sufficient track quality (position, velocity, heading) to cue identification, and ultimately engagement systems, with false alarm rates low enough to avoid saturation of human operators.

docs.title: 33.2.1 Radar Detection
docs.text: Radar is the primary all-weather, 24/7 sensor for C-UAS at ranges beyond visual. Conventional air traffic control and air defence radars are poorly suited to small UAS detection for several reasons: their clutter filters (MTI, Doppler notch) often notch out slow-moving drones along with terrain clutter; their volume search dwell times are too long to track agile mini-UAS; and their angular resolution is insufficient to resolve small targets from nearby clutter.

docs.title: Dedicated C-UAS Radar Design Requirements
docs.text:
For reliable detection of a Group 1 UAS with \(\sigma = 0.01\) m\(^2\):

\[R_{det} = \left(\frac{P_t G_t G_r \lambda^2 \sigma}{(4\pi)^3 k T_0 F B_n S_{min}}\right)^{1/4}\tag{33.2}\]

where \(S_{min} = S/N_{min} \cdot kT_0 F B_n\) is the minimum detectable signal. Setting \(P_t = 2\) kW, \(G_t = G_r = 25\) dBi, \(\lambda = 0.03\) m (X-band), \(\sigma = 0.01\) m\(^2\), NF \(= 5\) dB, \(B_n = 5\) MHz, \(S/N_{min} = 13\) dB:

\[R_{det} = \left(\frac{2000 \times 316 \times 316 \times 9\times10^{-4} \times 0.01} {(4\pi)^3 \times 4\times10^{-21} \times 3.16 \times 5\times10^6 \times 20}\right)^{1/4} \approx 4.7\,\text{km}\tag{33.3}\]

This represents a modest detection range for a Group 1 target; real systems compensate with longer coherent integration, which increases effective \(S/N\) by \(\sqrt{N_{pulses}}\):

\[S/N_{CPI} = S/N_{single} \cdot N_{pulses}\tag{33.4}\]

for coherent integration of \(N_{pulses}\) pulses in a coherent processing interval (CPI).

docs.title: Micro-Doppler Signature
docs.text:
The rotating blades of a multi-rotor UAS produce a characteristic micro-Doppler signature that is uniquely identifiable and separable from bird returns. A rotor blade of length \(L\) rotating at angular velocity \(\Omega\) (rad/s) produces a Doppler frequency modulation:

\[f_{micro}(t) = \frac{2\Omega L \cos(\theta)}{\lambda} \cos(\Omega t + \phi_0)\tag{33.5}\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the rotor disk normal and the radar LOS, and \(\phi_0\) is the initial blade phase. The peak-to-peak micro-Doppler extent is:

\[\Delta f_{D,max} = \frac{4\Omega L \cos\theta}{\lambda}\tag{33.6}\]

For a DJI Phantom 4 (quad-rotor; blade span \(L = 0.23\) m; \(\Omega = 2\pi \times 100\) rad/s) at \(\theta = 30°\), at X-band (\(\lambda = 0.03\) m):

\[\Delta f_{D} = \frac{4 \times 2\pi \times 100 \times 0.23 \times \cos(30°)}{0.03} \approx 16{,}700\,\text{Hz} = 16.7\,\text{kHz}\tag{33.7}\]

This micro-Doppler spread (\(\pm\)8.3 kHz around the body Doppler) is clearly distinguishable in a range-Doppler map. Machine learning classifiers trained on micro-Doppler spectrograms (Short-Time Fourier Transform, STFT) achieve classification accuracy exceeding 95% between bird, quadrotor, fixed-wing UAS, and helicopter in benign environments (SNR \(>\) 10 dB).

Dedicated C-UAS radar systems include the Fortem Technologies SkyDome (X-band FMCW; 2.5 km detection range for Group 1), Robin Radar Systems IRIS (S/X dual-band; 3 km for micro-drones), and the Dedrone DroneTracker Radar (FMCW; 1.5 km; integrated sensor fusion platform).

docs.title: 33.2.2 Electro-Optical and Infrared Detection
docs.text:
EO/IR sensors provide passive detection and high-resolution classification capability but are limited by range, field of regard (scanning requirement), and adverse weather.

Detection range of an EO sensor for a drone of cross-sectional area \(A_{target}\) against a sky background of radiance \(L_{sky}\):

\[R_{EO} = \frac{D_{aperture}}{2.44\lambda} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{A_{target}}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{\text{MRC}}{\Delta L}\tag{33.8}\]

where \(\text{MRC}\) is the minimum resolvable contrast of the sensor, \(D_{aperture}\) is aperture diameter, and \(\Delta L\) is the target-background radiance contrast. In practice, AI-based object detection algorithms operating on HD video achieve drone detection at 2–5 km against clear sky backgrounds and 0.5–1 km in cluttered urban scenes.

Thermal IR offers superior contrast for drones with warm motors and electronics against cool sky backgrounds, particularly at dawn and dusk. MWIR (3–5 \(\mu\)m) cameras achieve 1.5\(\times\)–3\(\times\) greater detection range than comparable SWIR sensors against Group 1 UAS.

docs.title: 33.2.3 RF Detection and Direction Finding
docs.text: The vast majority of commercial and small military UAS operate control links in the ISM bands at 2.4 GHz or 5.8 GHz. RF detection identifies these transmissions, computes direction of arrival, and correlates with known drone protocols to identify model and operator location.

docs.title: Direction Finding
docs.text:
An interferometric direction finding array with \(N\) elements and inter-element spacing \(d_{ij}\) measures angle of arrival \(\psi\) by comparing signal phase:

\[\psi = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{\lambda \Delta\phi_{ij}}{2\pi d_{ij}}\right)\tag{33.9}\]

Multiple baselines resolve the ambiguity (same as Section 31.4) and improve angular accuracy. With a 4-element array of 1 m baseline at 2.4 GHz (\(\lambda = 0.125\) m):

\[\sigma_\psi = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi d \sqrt{2\,\text{SNR}}} = \frac{0.125}{2\pi \times 1 \times \sqrt{2\times100}} \approx 1.4°\tag{33.10}\]

at SNR = 20 dB. Combining two DF stations with known separation enables TDOA-based geolocation of both the drone and its ground control station (GCS).

docs.title: DroneID and Protocol Identification
docs.text:
DJI’s OcuSync/O3 link broadcasts a proprietary telemetry frame including drone serial number, GPS position, and operator position in the 2.4/5.8 GHz ISM bands. Purpose-built RF sensors (Dedrone DroneTracker, Aaronia AARTOS, DJI AeroScope) passively monitor these transmissions and decode the embedded identification data at ranges up to 5 km. The decoded serial number cross-references DJI’s drone registration database (where available), potentially identifying the operator.

The FAA’s Remote ID regulation (14 CFR Part 89), effective September 2023, mandates that all drones \(>\)250 g manufactured or operated in the US broadcast:

  • UAV serial number or session ID (privacy-preserving for recreational operators).

  • Drone GPS position, altitude, and velocity.

  • Operator GPS position (or take-off point).

  • Broadcast via Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) or Bluetooth 5 at 1-second intervals.

docs.title: 33.2.4 Acoustic Detection
docs.text:
Acoustic sensor arrays detect the characteristic propeller noise of multi-rotor UAS. The fundamental propeller tone frequency is:

\[f_{prop} = \frac{n \cdot N_{blades}}{60} \quad [\text{Hz}]\tag{33.11}\]

where \(n\) is rotational speed in RPM and \(N_{blades}\) is the number of blades per rotor. A DJI Phantom 4 at 7000 RPM with 2-blade propellers: \(f_{prop} = 7000 \times 2 / 60 = 233\) Hz. Harmonics extend to 5 kHz; the characteristic signature occupies 100 Hz–10 kHz.

The signal-to-noise ratio for an acoustic sensor at range \(R\) from a UAS with source level \(SL\) (dB re 20 \(\mu\)Pa at 1 m):

\[\text{SNR}_{acoustic} = SL - 20\log_{10}(R) - \alpha R - L_{ambient}\tag{33.12}\]

where \(\alpha\) is the atmospheric absorption coefficient (0.001–0.01 dB/m at 1–10 kHz) and \(L_{ambient}\) is the ambient noise level (dB). In urban environments, \(L_{ambient}\) = 65–80 dB, limiting reliable acoustic detection to ranges of \(< 200\) m. Acoustic is therefore useful only as a short-range cueing sensor or for perimeter close-in detection.

Beamforming with a microphone array of \(M\) elements and aperture \(D_{mic}\) achieves directional gain:

\[G_{BF} = 10\log_{10}(M) \quad [\text{dB}]\tag{33.13}\]

and angular resolution:

\[\Delta\theta_{BF} = \frac{\lambda_{acoustic}}{D_{mic}} = \frac{c_{sound}}{f \cdot D_{mic}}\tag{33.14}\]

docs.title: 33.2.5 Multi-Sensor Fusion
docs.text:
No single sensor is adequate for reliable C-UAS in all environments. A robust system fuses radar, EO/IR, RF, and (optionally) acoustic detections using a probabilistic track-before-detect framework. The fused probability of detection is:

\[P_{D,fused} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{N_{sensors}} (1 - P_{D,i})\tag{33.15}\]

and the fused false alarm rate (assuming independent sensors):

\[P_{FA,fused} = \prod_{i=1}^{N_{sensors}} P_{FA,i}\tag{33.16}\]

For four sensors each with \(P_{D,i} = 0.7\) and \(P_{FA,i} = 0.01\): \(P_{D,fused} = 1 - 0.3^4 = 0.992\) and \(P_{FA,fused} = 10^{-8}\) — dramatically better than any single sensor. The penalty is system complexity and the requirement for precise time and space registration across sensor modalities.

docs.title: 33.3 Identification and Classification
docs.text: Detection produces a track; identification assigns a class (drone type, friendly/hostile/unknown) and ideally a specific identity (serial number, registration). Classification drives rules of engagement and appropriate countermeasure selection.

docs.title: 33.3.1 Classification Hierarchy
docs.text:
1. Object vs. non-object: Reject birds, paper, weather targets.

  2. UAS vs. crewed aircraft: Flight profile, speed, altitude, manoeuvre signatures.

  3. UAS group classification: Groups 1–5 by size/performance.

  4. Type classification: Fixed-wing, multi-rotor, hybrid VTOL, loitering munition.

  5. Model identification: Match RF signature, visual signature, performance to database entry (e.g., DJI Phantom 4, Shahed-136, TB2 Bayraktar).

  6. Intent classification: Surveillance, payload carrier, kamikaze; requires behavioural analysis and context (altitude, heading, proximity to assets).

docs.title: 33.3.2 AI-Based Classification
docs.text:
Deep learning classifiers operating on radar micro-Doppler spectrograms, EO images, and RF signals achieve high-accuracy classification with sub-second latency:

  • Micro-Doppler CNN: Short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of radar I/Q produces a time-frequency image; ResNet-50 or similar CNN achieves \(>\)93% accuracy on 5-class (bird/quadrotor/fixed-wing/heli/other) at SNR \(\geq\) 5 dB.

  • RF fingerprinting: Neural network trained on I/Q samples of known drone link signals; identifies manufacturer and model from hardware-specific emission characteristics (frequency offset, phase noise, turn-on transient) even without packet decoding.

  • Multi-modal fusion CNN: Joint processing of radar, EO, and RF features through a shared embedding space; improves robustness when any single modality is degraded.

docs.title: 33.4 Kinetic Defeat Systems
docs.text: Kinetic defeat physically destroys or captures the target UAS. Kinetic solutions are reliable and effective but face constraints of cost, collateral damage, engagement rate, and ammunition supply.

docs.title: 33.4.1 Dedicated Gun Systems
docs.text:
Short-range gun systems offer high engagement rates against Group 1–3 UAS at low cost per round:

  • General Dynamics Phalanx CIWS (adapted): 20 mm M61 Vulcan; 4500 rd/min; effective range \(\sim\)1.5 km against UAS; radar guidance; adapted for land C-UAS.

  • Rheinmetall Skyranger 30: 30 mm Ahead programmable ammunition; detonates a time-fused sub-projectile cloud in front of the target; effective against Group 1–3 without direct hit requirement; 1200 rd/min.

  • Leonardo Dragonfire (HEL) / MANTIS (30 mm): German Oerlikon MANTIS counter-rocket system; 6\(\times\)35 mm guns; radar-cued; demonstrated vs small UAS.

The hit probability for a gun system against a maneuvering UAS depends on target maneuver rate \(\dot{\theta}\) and fire control latency \(\tau_{FC}\):

\[P_{hit} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\dot{\theta}\,\tau_{FC})^2}{2\sigma_{aimpoint}^2}\right)\tag{33.17}\]

where \(\sigma_{aimpoint}\) is the gun aiming standard deviation. With \(\dot{\theta} = 10°/\text{s}\), \(\tau_{FC} = 0.5\) s, and \(\sigma_{aimpoint} = 5°\): \(P_{hit} = \exp(-1) = 0.37\) per burst — poor for a single round, but high with a burst of \(N_r\) rounds:

\[P_{hit,burst} = 1 - (1-P_{hit})^{N_r}\tag{33.18}\]

docs.title: 33.4.2 Interceptor Missiles
docs.text:
Dedicated mini-missiles for C-UAS applications:

  • Raytheon Coyote Block 2: Modified quad-rotor interceptor; launched from canister; active radar + EO seeker; manoeuvrable; 1 km+ intercept range. Cost: \(\sim\)$25,000.

  • IAI Drone Dome missile interceptor: 1 kg interceptor; semi-active laser guidance; 2 km range; designed for large commercial drone defeat.

  • Moog MRIC (Multi-Role Interceptor): Modular; swappable seeker; targets Groups 1–3; fielded on SHORAD vehicles.

  • MBDA Mistral VSHORAD: IR-guided; adapted proximity fuze for UAS; \(>\)90% \(P_k\) against Group 3+; cost: \(\sim\)$300,000 per round.

The minimum intercept range for a missile engaging a UAS with closing speed \(v_c\) and missile time-of-flight \(t_{TOF}\) is:

\[R_{min} = v_c \cdot (t_{TOF} + t_{reaction})\tag{33.19}\]

where \(t_{reaction}\) includes detection-to-launch decision time. For \(v_c = 100\) m/s, \(t_{TOF} = 5\) s, \(t_{reaction} = 3\) s: \(R_{min} = 800\) m — large compared to the physical perimeter most C-UAS systems must protect.

docs.title: 33.4.3 Net Capture Systems
docs.text:
Net guns and net-carrying interceptors capture drones intact (forensic value):

  • Net gun: CO\(_2\) or pyrotechnic-propelled net cartridge; range \(< 30\) m; operator-aimed or robot-mounted; reliable for slow-moving drones.

  • Net-carrying drone interceptor: "Drone-to-drone" intercept; net deployed beneath or above target; entangles rotors; forces controlled descent. OpenWorks Engineering SkyWall 100 (shoulder-launch); SkyWall 300 (tripod-mounted).

  • Drone-deployed net: Larger UAV deploys a wide net on a trajectory that intercepts the target; effective against fast-moving FPV drones when net deployment timing is accurate.

Table 33.2 provides a consolidated comparison of kinetic C-UAS defeat options.

docs.title: 33.5 Directed Energy Defeat Systems
docs.text: Directed energy weapons (DEW) are uniquely suited to C-UAS for three reasons: the effective cost per shot is negligible (electrical power only); the engagement rate is limited by thermal management rather than magazine depth; and a single DEW system can defeat swarms that would exhaust kinetic interceptors.

docs.title: 33.5.1 High Energy Laser (HEL)
docs.text: A HEL weapon defeats a UAS by sustained irradiance of a vulnerable point (motor, battery, control surface) until structural failure or thermal runaway occurs.

docs.title: Required Fluence and Engagement Time
docs.text:
The fluence required to fail a given material is:

\[F_{req} = \frac{E_{threshold}}{A_{spot}} \quad [\text{J/cm}^2]\tag{33.20}\]

where \(E_{threshold}\) is the energy density needed to reach material failure temperature and \(A_{spot}\) is the laser spot area on target. For the engagement time at laser power \(P_L\):

\[t_{engage} = \frac{F_{req} \cdot A_{spot}}{P_L \cdot \eta_{beam} \cdot T_{atm}(R)}\tag{33.21}\]

where \(\eta_{beam}\) accounts for beam quality (M\(^2\) factor) and \(T_{atm}\) is atmospheric transmission. For a 20 kW laser with \(M^2 = 1.5\), targeting a CFRP airframe (\(F_{req} = 500\) J/cm\(^2\)) at 1 km with \(T_{atm} = 0.8\) and spot diameter 10 cm (\(A_{spot} = 78.5\) cm\(^2\)):

\[t_{engage} = \frac{500 \times 78.5}{20{,}000 \times (1/1.5) \times 0.8} \approx 3.7\,\text{s}\tag{33.22}\]

docs.title: Atmospheric Effects on Laser Propagation
docs.text:
Atmospheric turbulence degrades laser beam quality through random refractive index fluctuations. The Fried coherence length \(r_0\) characterises the turbulence strength:

\[r_0 = 0.185\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{\int_0^L C_n^2(z)\,dz}\right)^{3/5}\tag{33.23}\]

where \(C_n^2(z)\) is the atmospheric refractive index structure parameter profile. When the laser beam diameter exceeds \(r_0\), wavefront distortion limits the achievable on-target irradiance. Adaptive optics systems measure the wavefront error and compensate via deformable mirror, recovering near-diffraction-limited performance.

The diffraction-limited spot size at range \(R\) for an aperture \(D_L\) is:

\[d_{spot} = \frac{2.44\,\lambda R}{D_L}\tag{33.24}\]

and the on-target irradiance (neglecting atmospheric effects):

\[I_{target} = \frac{4 P_L}{\pi d_{spot}^2} = \frac{P_L D_L^2}{\pi (1.22\lambda R)^2}\tag{33.25}\]

docs.title: Operational HEL C-UAS Systems
docs.text:
• Raytheon HELWS-MRZR: 15 kW fibre laser; vehicle-mounted; precision-track; demonstrated kills on Group 1–3 UAS at \(>\)1 km; deployed in Middle East.

  • Rheinmetall HEL (20 kW): Integrated with Skyranger platform; radar-cued; high track bandwidth for fast-manoeuvring targets.

  • Boeing Compact Laser Weapon System (CLWS): 2 kW; man-portable; primarily Group 1 defeat at \(<\)500 m; battery powered; recoiless.

  • Rafael Iron Beam: 100 kW class; intended to complement Iron Dome against rockets, drones, and mortar rounds; demonstrated operational use (2024).

  • HELIOS (Lockheed Martin): Ship-mounted; 60 kW; USN DDG-class integration; UAS and small boat defeat.

docs.title: 33.5.2 High Power Microwave (HPM)
docs.text: HPM systems generate intense microwave pulses that couple energy into drone electronics through apertures (sensor windows, ventilation holes, circuit board traces, cables), causing logic upset, data corruption, or permanent component damage.

docs.title: HPM Energy Coupling
docs.text:
The energy coupled into a target electronic system scales with peak power and pulse duration:

\[E_{coupled} = P_{peak} \cdot \tau_{pulse} \cdot C_{coupling}\tag{33.26}\]

where \(C_{coupling}\) is the coupling efficiency, which depends on target aperture size relative to wavelength, incidence angle, and shielding:

\[C_{coupling} = \frac{A_{eff,aperture} \cdot (1 - \Gamma^2)}{A_{beam}}\tag{33.27}\]

where \(A_{eff,aperture}\) is the effective aperture area of the target entry point and \(\Gamma\) is the reflective loss. The threshold for electronic component damage is typically:

\[E_{threshold} = \frac{V_{damage}^2}{R_{imp}} \cdot \tau_{pulse} \approx 0.1 \text{--} 1\,\mu\text{J}\tag{33.28}\]

for typical CMOS logic (\(V_{damage} \approx 2 \times V_{supply}\), \(R_{imp} \approx 50\,\Omega\)).

docs.title: HPM System Architecture
docs.text:
An HPM C-UAS system consists of:

  1. Prime power: Diesel generator or capacitor bank; peak power 1–100 MW for microsecond pulses.

  2. Pulse-forming network (PFN): Stores energy; discharges through high-power switch (spark gap, thyratron, or solid-state) to generate the HPM pulse.

  3. Microwave source: Magnetron (narrow band; \(<\)1 GHz), gyrotron (mm-wave; high power), or solid-state GaN array (low peak power but wideband).

  4. Phased array antenna: Steers beam electronically; avoids mechanical pointing; illuminates multiple targets in rapid succession.

docs.title: JNLWD Leonidas
docs.text:
The Joint Non-Lethal Weapons Directorate Leonidas pod (Epirus Inc.) is an airborne or vehicle-mounted HPM system operating across a broad microwave band. Key characteristics:

  • Phased array antenna; electronic beam steering over \(\pm\)60° cone.

  • Effective range: \(\sim\)1 km; demonstrated simultaneous defeat of 100+ drones in testing.

  • Pulse repetition rate: hundreds of pulses per second; effective engagement rate limited only by beam steering speed.

  • Friendly force risk: HPM must be deconflicted with friendly UAS and ground electronics.

  • Podded configuration: fits on MQ-9, F-16, C-130 aircraft; vehicle-mounted variant on HMMWV.

docs.title: 33.6 Electronic Attack for C-UAS
docs.text: Electronic attack is arguably the most cost-effective C-UAS defeat mechanism for Groups 1–3, as it operates at zero marginal cost per engagement, does not produce kinetic hazard from falling debris, and can be reversible (jam only, no destruction).

docs.title: 33.6.1 RC Link Jamming
docs.text:
The RC command link and video downlink operating in the 2.4/5.8 GHz ISM bands can be jammed to force the drone into a fail-safe state (land or return-to-home). The jamming power required to suppress the RC link at drone range \(R_d\) from the jammer:

\[P_j \geq \frac{P_{link} \cdot (J/S)_{req} \cdot G_{link} \cdot R_j^2}{G_j \cdot R_d^2 \cdot G_{rx,j}}\tag{33.29}\]

where \(P_{link}\) is the RC transmitter power, \(G_{link}\) is the GCS antenna gain, \(R_j\) is jammer-to-drone range, and \((J/S)_{req}\) is the minimum J/S to suppress the receiver (typically 6–20 dB for FHSS systems). A 10 W omnidirectional jammer can suppress a 100 mW DJI RC link at:

\[R_{j,eff} = R_{link,max} \sqrt{\frac{P_j G_j}{P_{link} G_{link} \cdot (J/S)_{req}}} = 5000 \sqrt{\frac{10 \times 1}{0.1 \times 1 \times 10}} = 5000\,\text{m}\tag{33.30}\]

However, frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) links used by DJI OcuSync and many military UAS hop pseudorandomly across 2.4 GHz sub-channels. Barrage jamming the entire band is required, incurring the power penalty of Equation (31.20). For a 83 MHz band (2.4 GHz ISM) jammer against a 1 MHz hop channel: penalty = \(10\log(83) = 19\) dB.

docs.title: 33.6.2 GPS Jamming and Spoofing for C-UAS
docs.text:
GPS jamming denies the drone’s navigation. Most commercial autopilots enter a fail-safe mode (hover and land, or return-to-home) when GPS is lost. However, GPS-denied drones operating on inertial navigation continue flying and may home on pre-programmed waypoints. GPS spoofing is more effective: by providing false position data, the drone is steered away from the defended area or made to land in a controlled location.

The spoofing signal must exceed the authentic GPS signal by 3–6 dB to capture the tracking loop:

\[P_{spoof} \geq P_{GPS,receiver} + (J/S)_{capture} = -130 + 5 = -125\,\text{dBm}\tag{33.31}\]

at the drone antenna, requiring only \(\sim\)1 mW of transmitted power from a nearby ground station.

docs.title: 33.6.3 Protocol-Level and Cyber Attacks
docs.text:
• MAVLink injection: Many open-source autopilots (ArduPilot, PX4) use the MAVLink protocol over the datalink. An attacker who can inject forge packets can send a SET_MODE command (disarm, RTL) or SET_POSITION_TARGET redirect. MAVLink v2 supports AES-128 message signing, which prevents injection against signed links.

  • Wi-Fi deauthentication: Wi-Fi-linked drones (DJI Spark; early DJI Phantom) can be disconnected by transmitting IEEE 802.11 deauthentication frames spoofed from the GCS MAC address; management frame protection (IEEE 802.11w) mitigates this.

  • Protocol reverse-engineering and takeover: DJI’s OcuSync protocol has been partially reverse-engineered by researchers; demonstration of unauthenticated control injection has been published. DJI has addressed some vulnerabilities via firmware updates, but legacy hardware remains vulnerable.

docs.title: 33.6.4 Effective Jamming Range vs Friendly Force Risk
docs.text:
Electronic jamming is non-discriminating: it affects all drones in the jammers’ coverage area, including friendly ISR drones, civil aviation GPS, and emergency communications. Frequency deconfliction planning is mandatory before deploying C-UAS jammers, and directional antennas are preferred over omnidirectional to minimise the fratricide zone.

The effective jamming radius in a given direction \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) from a directional jammer:

\[R_{eff}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) = \sqrt{\frac{P_j G_j(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) \lambda^2 G_{rx}} {(4\pi)^2 \cdot (J/S)_{req} \cdot P_{link}}}\tag{33.32}\]

A 10-dBi directional antenna reduces the jamming footprint in the side-lobe directions by 10 dB (factor 3.16 in range), significantly reducing friendly force risk.

docs.title: 33.7 C-UAS System Integration and Kill Chain
33.7.1 The C-UAS Kill Chain
docs.text:
The C-UAS kill chain encompasses six sequential functions, each with its own latency budget:

  1. Detect: Sensor network acquires UAS track with \(P_D \geq 0.90\), \(P_{FA} \leq 10^{-4}\). Latency: 0.1–2 s (radar first detection).

  2. Identify: Classifier assigns group, type, intent. Latency: 0.5–3 s.

  3. Track: Multi-sensor fusion maintains continuous kinematics estimate; fire control quality track with position uncertainty \(<\) 5 m at 1 km. Latency: ongoing.

  4. Decide: Automated or human decision to engage; rules of engagement assessment; weapon assignment. Latency: 0.5–10 s (human-in-the-loop adds greatest uncertainty).

  5. Engage: Weapon system fires or activates. Latency: \(<\) 1 s kinetic; \(<\) 0.1 s DEW.

  6. Assess: Battle damage assessment; re-engagement decision. Latency: 1–5 s.

Total kill chain latency goal: \(<\) 10 s for Group 1–2 threats; \(<\) 30 s for Group 3+. Against a 30 m/s kamikaze drone at 500 m range, the available engagement time is only 17 s — requiring highly automated, low-latency processing throughout.

docs.title: 33.7.2 Layered Defence Architecture
docs.text:
A mature fixed-site C-UAS architecture employs concentric defence layers:

Table 33.4. Layered C-UAS Defence Architecture Layer Range (km) Primary Sensor Primary Effector Target Groups Outer 5–20 Long-range AESA radar EA + MALD-J; EW decoys Groups 3–5 Middle 1–5 Radar + EO/IR + RF HEL (100 kW); interceptor missile Groups 1–4 Inner 0.1–1 EO/IR + radar + acoustic HEL (15 kW); HPM; gun Groups 1–3 Point \(<\) 0.1 EO/IR + acoustic Net gun; HPM; short-range DEW Groups 1–2

docs.title: 33.7.3 Command and Control Automation
docs.text:
Rules of Engagement (ROE) for C-UAS must balance timely engagement against risk of fratricide and civilian harm. Modern C-UAS C2 systems implement three engagement modes:

  • Autonomous: Pre-authorised automatic engagement when classification confidence \(> P_{thresh}\) and predicted impact point is within defence perimeter. Used at inner layer for fast kamikaze threats.

  • Automated with human confirmation: System presents threat assessment and recommended action; human approves within a time window (\(<\) 5 s); used for middle layer.

  • Manual: Human initiates all engagements; system provides cueing only; used for outer layer against ambiguous or politically sensitive targets.

The automation level must comply with IHL (International Humanitarian Law) requirements for meaningful human control, DoD Directive 3000.09 (Autonomous Weapons Systems), and applicable national policy. Lethal kinetic effects against any target with potential civilian status must have human authorisation.

docs.title: 33.7.4 Mobile C-UAS Systems
docs.text:
Mobile C-UAS protects convoys, forward operating bases (FOBs), and manoeuvre units:

  • MSHORAD (Manportable/Short-Range Air Defence): Vehicle-mounted Stinger/SHORAD with C-UAS adaptation; radar-cued; man-in-loop.

  • LMAMS (Leonidas pod on vehicle): HPM; drives alongside convoy; activates automatically when drone approach is detected.

  • Drone Defender / Dronebuster: Handheld directional jammer; 2.4/5.8/1.2 GHz; operator points at drone; 400 m effective range; 2 kg.

  • Skyranger 30 (Rheinmetall): Wheeled vehicle; 30 mm AHEAD; fully automatic; 360° coverage; network-enabled sensor integration.

docs.title: 33.7.5 Naval C-UAS Integration
docs.text:
Naval vessels present unique C-UAS challenges: sea-surface clutter complicates low-altitude drone detection; ship motion introduces tracking errors; international maritime law governs engagement authority.

  • Phalanx Block 1B: Upgraded CIWS with surface search mode; EO/IR sensor; effective against Group 1–2 UAS at \(<\)1 km.

  • SeaRAM: Rolling Airframe Missile; 11-round launcher; infrared-guided; adapted for UAS engagement.

  • HELIOS (Lockheed): 60 kW HEL; DDG-class integration; approved for FY2024 deployment; unlimited engagements per sortie.

  • DroneTracker Naval (Dedrone): RF + radar sensor fusion; covers 360°; interfaces with ship C2.

docs.title: 33.8.1 The Swarm Saturation Problem
docs.text:
A coordinated drone swarm presents the most severe C-UAS challenge. If \(N_{swarm}\) drones attack simultaneously and the defender’s engagement rate is \(\dot{N}_{kill}\) drones per second, the number of drones that penetrate the defence is:

\[N_{penetrate} = N_{swarm} - \dot{N}_{kill} \cdot T_{engagement}\tag{33.33}\]

where \(T_{engagement}\) is the available engagement window. For kinetic interceptors with \(\dot{N}_{kill} = 1\) drone/s and 30-second engagement window against a 100-drone swarm: \(N_{penetrate} = 70\) drones — most penetrate. Only DEW systems can achieve the engagement rates required:

\[\dot{N}_{kill,DEW} = \frac{1}{t_{engage} + t_{slew}}\tag{33.34}\]

where \(t_{slew}\) is beam-pointing transition time. A HEL system with \(t_{engage} = 3\) s and \(t_{slew} = 0.5\) s achieves \(\dot{N}_{kill} \approx 0.29\) drone/s — still insufficient for large swarms. HPM systems that illuminate a wide cone simultaneously achieve:

\[\dot{N}_{kill,HPM} = \frac{N_{in\,beam}}{t_{HPM\,pulse}} \gg \dot{N}_{kill,HEL}\tag{33.35}\]

since \(t_{HPM\,pulse} < 1\,\mu\)s and \(N_{in\,beam}\) can be tens to hundreds.

docs.title: 33.8.2 Counter-Swarm UAS
docs.text:
An emerging concept employs a "counter-swarm": a friendly drone swarm that intercepts and defeats the hostile swarm through coordinated kinetic or EW engagement:

  • DARPA OFFSET programme: 250-node friendly swarm autonomy framework.

  • Raytheon/AFRL Perdix swarm: 3-inch expendable drones launched from F-16 flare dispensers; 103-drone coordination demonstrated; payload includes RF jamming, visual obstruction, or kinetic mini-charge.

  • Counter-swarm tactics: Interception at maximum range before swarm achieves coordinated attack formation; decentralised swarm C2 makes decapitation attack (destroying C2 node) ineffective against fully autonomous swarms.

docs.title: 33.8.3 Swarm C2 Network Targeting
docs.text:
Semi-autonomous swarms that require a centralised C2 radio link can be defeated by targeting the C2 network:

\[P_{swarm\,defeat} = P(C2\,link\,jammed) \cdot (1 - P_{autonomous\,fallback})\tag{33.36}\]

Modern swarm designs incorporate decentralised coordination algorithms (e.g., consensus-based formation control, MANET mesh networking) that continue to function after loss of the C2 link, reducing the effectiveness of C2-targeting strategies. Future swarms using optical (laser) inter-drone links will be immune to RF jamming of the coordination network.

docs.title: 33.9.1 FAA Remote ID (14 CFR Part 89)
docs.text:
The FAA Remote ID rule, effective September 2023, mandates that all UAS \(> 250\) g operating in the US National Airspace System must:

  • Broadcast the drone’s identifier, position, altitude, velocity, and operator location.

  • Comply with the Standard Remote ID specification or fly within an FAA-recognised Identification Area (FRIA).

  • Enable law enforcement and C-UAS systems to access drone identity data in real time.

Remote ID provides the cooperative detection layer that makes RF-based C-UAS more effective for compliant operators, but does not address non-cooperative (adversarial) drones.

docs.title: 33.9.2 NATO STANAG 4703 and C-UAS Standards
docs.text:
STANAG 4703 defines NATO standard UAS classifications and provides the framework for interoperability of C-UAS systems across alliance members. Key provisions relevant to C-UAS:

  • UAS classification by mass, altitude, and range (aligns with DoD Groups).

  • Standardised data format for UAS track reporting across C2 systems (Link 16/JREAP).

  • ROE framework for joint operations including C-UAS engagement authority.

  • Interoperability requirements for sensor-to-shooter datalinks.

The NATO Counter-UAS Working Group (through AC/322) is developing additional STANAGs for DEW integration (power levels, safety zones) and swarm defeat doctrine.

docs.title: 33.9.3 Airport Protection Standards
docs.text:
UAS incursions into controlled airspace around airports represent a major safety and security risk. ICAO Annex 14 and EASA NPA 2021-14 require:

  • Detection and identification capability covering the airport’s airspace protection zone (typically 5 nm radius; \(<\) 500 ft AGL for small drones).

  • Coordination with ATC to avoid confusion between drone tracks and crewed aircraft.

  • Proportional response protocols (detection-first; defeat only if safety threat confirmed).

  • Integration with the wider Air Traffic Management (ATM) system via UTM (UAS Traffic Management).

Major incidents include London Gatwick (December 2018: 140,000 passengers stranded; Gatwick closed 36 hours due to repeated drone sightings) and Newark Liberty (multiple closures 2019–2023), which accelerated ICAO and regulatory action.

docs.title: 33.9.4 C-UAS Legal Framework
docs.text:
The legal authority to take action against a UAS varies significantly by jurisdiction:

  • USA: Federal law (18 U.S.C. § 32) criminalises destruction of aircraft; a UAS is an “aircraft” under FAA definition. Shooting down a private drone — even a hostile one over private property — is therefore potentially a federal crime. DoD authority to engage is limited to designated zones under specific statutes. The FAA Reauthorization Act (2018) granted DHS, DoJ, and DoD authority to track, jam, and take control of drones deemed a national security threat.

  • Military ROE: Under LOAC (Law of Armed Conflict), a UAS used as a weapon system or intelligence platform against a military force is a lawful military objective. Proportionality assessment is still required.

  • IHL: Autonomous C-UAS engagement of potential civilian drones must comply with distinction, proportionality, and precaution principles.

docs.title: 33.9.5 Geofencing and Technical Countermeasures
docs.text:
Many commercial UAS manufacturers implement geofencing — on-board flight restrictions that prevent drone operation in prohibited areas (airports, government facilities, prisons):

  • DJI FlySafe geofencing: 300+ m radius around airports encoded in drone firmware; can be unlocked by verified operators; updated via internet.

  • FAA UAS Facility Maps (UASFM): Define altitude limits near airports; integrated into DJI, Parrot, Skydio autopilots.

  • Limitation: Geofencing can be defeated by modified firmware (“jailbroken” drones); provides no protection against purpose-built hostile UAS.

  • Combined approach: Remote ID + geofencing + C-UAS detection provides a layered policy and technical framework, but requires coordinated regulatory enforcement.

docs.title: 33.10 C-UAS Performance Metrics and System Evaluation
33.10.1 Key Performance Parameters
docs.text:
C-UAS system performance is characterised by the following key performance parameters (KPPs):

Table 33.5. C-UAS Key Performance Parameters and Representative Values Parameter Symbol Target Value Notes Detection range (Group 1) \(R_{det}\) \(>\) 2 km Radar; \(P_D \geq 0.9\); \(P_{FA} \leq 10^{-4}\)/scan Detection range (Group 3) \(R_{det,3}\) \(>\) 10 km Radar; similar \(P_D/P_{FA}\) Track accuracy (pos) \(\sigma_{pos}\) \(<\) 5 m at 1 km Fire control quality Classification accuracy \(P_c\) \(>\) 90% At \(P_D\) range; SNR \(>\) 10 dB Kill chain latency \(t_{KC}\) \(<\) 10 s Detect to engage; Group 1 Probability of kill (HEL) \(P_k\) \(>\) 90% Group 1 at design range False alarm rate \(P_{FA}\) \(<\) 1/hr System-level; human-curated Simultaneous track capacity \(N_{track}\) \(>\) 50 Fire control tracks

docs.title: 33.10.2 Test and Evaluation
docs.text:
C-UAS system T&E requires a carefully constructed test matrix spanning the full threat space:

  • Benign environment: Open range, low clutter, good visibility; establishes maximum performance bounds.

  • Urban environment: Building clutter; RF noise floor; \(\sim\)50% reduction in detection range expected.

  • Adverse weather: Rain, fog, temperature inversion; EO/IR degradation; potential acoustic masking.

  • Electronic attack: Threat drone employing RF-silent autonomy (no command link); GPS-spoofing of C-UAS sensors; HPM hardened drones.

  • Swarm stress test: 5/10/50/100 drone simultaneous engagement; saturates kill chain; reveals engagement rate bottlenecks.

The US DoD Joint C-UAS Office (JCO) conducts formal Capability Assessment events at Yuma Proving Ground (Arizona) and other ranges using a standardised threat library of representative commercial and military-grade drones.

docs.title: 33.10.3 Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
docs.text:
The cost-effectiveness metric for a C-UAS system weighs the defence cost against the threat value denied. Defining the defence cost ratio:

\[\text{DCR} = \frac{C_{system} + N_{engagements} \cdot C_{shot}}{N_{kills} \cdot V_{threat}}\tag{33.37}\]

where \(C_{system}\) is the system procurement and operating cost, \(C_{shot}\) is the per-engagement cost, \(N_{kills}\) is the number of successful kills, and \(V_{threat}\) is the average value of the threats defeated (replacement cost or damage prevented). For a DEW system with \(C_{system} = \$10\)M, \(C_{shot} \approx \$50\) (electricity per engagement), \(N_{kills} = 10{,}000\) over system life, and \(V_{threat} = \$1{,}000\) per drone: DCR \(= (10^7 + 10{,}000 \times 50) / (10{,}000 \times 1{,}000) = 1.05\) — barely cost-effective. Against threats carrying $50,000 payloads or causing $1M damage, DCR \(\ll 1\) and the DEW investment is clearly justified.

docs.title: 33.11.1 AI-Enhanced Autonomous C-UAS
docs.text:
The trend toward fully autonomous C-UAS kill chains is driven by the impossibility of human-in-the-loop response to millisecond-scale threats. Key developments include:

  • Edge AI inference: On-sensor neural network inference (ResNet, YOLO) for real-time drone classification without communications latency.

  • Multi-agent task allocation: Multiple C-UAS nodes negotiate engagement assignments to avoid duplication and maximise coverage against swarms.

  • Predictive track: Kalman + ML hybrid tracker predicts drone intent (attack trajectory extrapolation); pre-cues engagement before drone reaches dangerous range.

  • Continuous learning: C-UAS AI retrained on-the-fly from new threat encounters; requires rapid OTA update mechanism and adversarial ML robustness.

docs.title: 33.11.2 Counter-Counter-UAS (C2UAS) — The Adversary Response
docs.text:
As C-UAS matures, adversaries are adapting drone designs to defeat detection and defeat systems:

  • RF-silent drones: Pre-programmed waypoint navigation with optical inter-drone communication; no RF link for jamming or DF detection.

  • Low-RCS airframes: Carbon fibre construction; radar-absorbing material coatings; \(\sigma < 0.001\) m\(^2\); defeats many dedicated C-UAS radars.

  • HPM-hardened electronics: Metal-enclosed drone body; filtered apertures; faraday cage around flight controller; increases HPM defeat threshold by 20–40 dB.

  • GPS-independent navigation: Terrain matching; visual odometry; star tracker; SLAM — denies GPS jamming/spoofing as a C-UAS tool.

  • Decoy + payload split: Swarm includes decoy drones (cheap, high RCS) to saturate C-UAS engagement capacity while payload drones approach low and slow.

The C-UAS vs UAS technology competition will continue to escalate, demanding continuous engineering investment and operational adaptation from C-UAS system developers and military users.

docs.title: 33.11.3 Integrated Air Defence System (IADS) Integration
docs.text:
Future C-UAS will integrate seamlessly into the broader IADS architecture via:

  • JADC2 (Joint All-Domain Command and Control): Automated data sharing between C-UAS nodes, air defence radars, and theatre C2; enables cross-domain engagement (e.g., a fighter intercepts a Group 5 UCAV detected by a ground C-UAS radar).

  • Multi-domain operations: C-UAS and offensive cyber/EW coordinated at operational level; simultaneous drone swarm defeat and suppression of the operator command node.

  • Space integration: LEO ISR satellites detecting launch signatures of large drone swarms; cueing ground C-UAS systems at maximum range.

  • Common tactical picture: Standardised data formats (STANAG 4703, Link 16, ASTERIX) enabling civilian and military C-UAS sensors to contribute to a unified air picture available to all defending forces.

docs.title: 33.12 Summary
docs.text:
Counter-UAS is one of the most rapidly evolving disciplines in contemporary defence engineering, driven by the explosive proliferation of drone technology and its operational exploitation by both state and non-state actors. The core engineering challenges are:

  1. Detection: Small RCS, low altitude, cluttered environments demand dedicated waveforms (FMCW, micro-Doppler), multi-sensor fusion, and AI-based classification.

  2. Engagement rate: Kinetic systems are cost-limited and magazine-limited against swarms; only DEW (HEL, HPM) provides the required engagement throughput.

  3. Cost asymmetry: The defender must achieve sub-unity DCR against cheap threats; forces adoption of low marginal-cost effectors (DEW, jamming).

  4. Autonomy and ROE: Kill chain latency demands automation; legal and ethical constraints demand human oversight; balancing these is the central C2 challenge.

  5. Adaptation: Adversary drone designs continuously evolve to defeat current C-UAS; open system architectures and AI-enabled adaptation are essential.

The most capable near-term C-UAS architectures will combine persistent multi-sensor detection (radar + EO/IR + RF), AI-based classification, directed energy engagement (HEL for precision, HPM for swarm), and tightly integrated C2 with human oversight for lethal-force decisions. The longer-term trajectory points toward fully networked, AI-driven, multi-domain C-UAS systems capable of defending against hundreds of simultaneous threats in contested electromagnetic and informational environments.

docs.title: Chapter 34: Autonomous Lethal Systems and Ethics
34.1 Introduction to Autonomous Weapons Systems
docs.text: The application of artificial intelligence and robotics to lethal force represents one of the most consequential technological developments of the twenty-first century. As sensors, computing power, and machine-learning capabilities advance, military systems increasingly operate with reduced human oversight over the decision to use force. Understanding the technical, legal, and ethical dimensions of this development requires precise terminology, a clear picture of the current operational landscape, and engagement with the stakeholders shaping the governance debate.

docs.title: 34.1.1 Definitional Framework
docs.text:
Three principal terms delineate the spectrum of human involvement in weapon system operation:

  • Automated weapon system: Operates according to pre-programmed rules within a constrained, well-defined environment. The human operator makes the decision to deploy the system; thereafter the system executes without further human input. Decision logic is deterministic and fully specified at design time. Example: Phalanx Close-In Weapon System (CIWS), which executes autonomous fire-control once activated by a human operator.

  • Semi-autonomous weapon system: Capable of independent action against a pre-specified target set, but requires positive human authorisation for each individual engagement or for a bounded engagement package. The human remains in a supervisory role with meaningful ability to halt, redirect, or cancel the attack. Examples include many current loitering munitions operated in man-in-loop mode.

  • Autonomous weapon system (AWS): Selects and engages targets through its own sensing and decision-making processes, without human intervention during the engagement cycle. The system exercises discretion over whom to attack, when to attack, and with what level of force. When such systems are designed to apply lethal force, they are termed Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems (LAWS).

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) refined the core concept in its 2021 position paper, defining LAWS as systems that can independently identify, track, select, and attack targets. The critical distinguishing feature is not the level of automation in flight control, navigation, or even target detection—it is autonomy over the critical functions of target selection and the decision to apply lethal force.

docs.title: Human Control Topologies
docs.text:
Four canonical human-machine control configurations are recognised in the literature:

Table 34.1. Human Control Topologies in Autonomous Weapon Systems Configuration Human Role System Role Example Human-in-the-loop Authorises every individual engagement; can abort at any point Provides targeting data, flight control; awaits human command Predator/Reaper with GCS Human-on-the-loop Monitors engagement; can interrupt but system acts autonomously Selects and engages autonomously within authorised parameters Phalanx CIWS (auto mode) Human-out-of-the-loop Not present during engagement; sets mission parameters before launch Fully autonomous sensing, decision, and engagement Harpy anti-radiation munition (terminal phase) Human-over-the-loop Commander authorises an engagement envelope; may not see individual targets Selects targets within envelope; no per-target authorisation Proposed future swarm configurations

docs.title: 34.1.2 Why Autonomy in Weapons: Operational Drivers
docs.text:
Several converging military requirements create demand for increased weapon autonomy:

Speed of Combat.

Hypersonic threats (Mach 5+) transit a ship’s radar horizon to impact in seconds. The OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) for a human operator may require 3–8 seconds; a Mach 8 missile travels approximately 2.7 km per second, giving a reaction window of perhaps 10–20 km under ideal sensor conditions. Automated engagement is therefore operationally necessary for hard-kill counter-hypersonic defence. This imperative does not, however, automatically justify autonomy in offensive operations or against human targets.

GPS-Denied Environments.

Adversary electronic warfare capabilities increasingly deny GPS navigation to munitions and aircraft. In such environments, a munition relying on satellite guidance requires an autonomous fallback—whether inertial navigation with scene matching, terrain contour matching (TERCOM), or AI-based visual odometry.

Contested Command and Control (C2).

Electronic jamming and cyber attacks may sever communication links between unmanned systems and their operators. A system that cannot communicate with its ground station must either abort its mission or continue autonomously. The choice made at design time determines the system’s level of autonomy under degraded communications.

Swarm Scale.

Operating a 100-drone swarm with individual human operators for each platform is logistically infeasible. Swarm concepts require autonomous coordination, task allocation, and in some concepts, autonomous engagement decisions at scale. The multiplication of decision points far exceeds human cognitive bandwidth.

Cognitive Load and Operator Fatigue.

Even where human oversight is notionally retained, the practical ability of a single operator to meaningfully review and authorise hundreds of AI-generated target engagements per hour is questionable. Speed and scale degrade the quality of human decision-making.

docs.title: 34.1.3 The Current Operational Spectrum
docs.text:
A taxonomy of currently-deployed and near-term systems illustrates the spectrum:

  • Phalanx CIWS (Raytheon, USA): 20 mm rotary cannon; autonomous track-and-engage once activated; hard-coded rules; purely reactive; human-on-loop activation.

  • Iron Dome (Rafael, Israel): Air defence; autonomous intercept selection and engagement; human sets engagement parameters; demonstrated in operational use.

  • Samsung SGR-A1 (South Korea): Ground sentry robot on DMZ; equipped with autonomous detection and engagement; claimed human-on-loop override; raises questions about reliability in practice.

  • Harpy / Harop (IAI, Israel): Anti-radiation loitering munition; loiters until radar emissions detected, then autonomous terminal dive; human launches but does not authorise individual engagements.

  • STM Kargu-2 (Turkey): Multi-rotor loitering munition; autonomous engagement mode; reported use in Libya 2020; subject of UN Panel of Experts scrutiny.

  • AeroVironment Switchblade: Human-in-loop; operator designates target via video feed; operator must confirm engagement; current generation retains meaningful human control.

  • Future LAWS (notional): Fully autonomous target selection and engagement against human combatants; no per-engagement human authorisation; object of the current governance debate.

docs.title: 34.1.4 Key Stakeholders
docs.text:
The debate over LAWS involves a diverse and sometimes adversarial coalition of actors:

States.

Permanent members of the UN Security Council hold diametrically opposed positions. The United States maintains that meaningful human control is required but resists a binding treaty, preferring operational policies. Russia opposes binding restrictions. China has called for a ban on use of LAWS but not development, a position critics interpret as preserving domestic research freedom. The United Kingdom supports existing IHL as sufficient without new treaty law. Austria, Belgium, and numerous smaller states advocate a binding prohibition.

Non-Governmental Organisations.

The Campaign to Stop Killer Robots (CSKR), founded 2012, is a coalition of over 170 NGOs in 68 countries. It advocates a preemptive prohibition on LAWS. The ICRC maintains an authoritative technical and legal voice, calling for both prohibitions on specific categories of LAWS and positive rules on human control.

Academic Community.

Researchers across computer science, law, philosophy, and security studies contribute technical assessments, legal analyses, and ethical frameworks. The Future of Life Institute and the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER, Cambridge) publish extensively on long-term risks.

Technology Companies.

The Google Project Maven controversy (2018) revealed deep tensions within the technology sector. When Google employees learned the company held a contract to apply machine learning to drone surveillance footage for the US Department of Defense, over 4,000 employees signed a petition and 12 resigned. Google subsequently declined to renew the contract and published AI principles excluding weapons applications. This episode established that technology workers consider themselves ethical stakeholders in the deployment of their tools.

docs.title: 34.2 International Humanitarian Law
docs.text: International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also known as the Law of Armed Conflict (LOAC) or the Laws of War, comprises the body of international law regulating the conduct of armed conflict. Its primary sources are the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, the two Additional Protocols of 1977 (AP I and AP II), customary international law, and the Hague Regulations. LAWS must comply fully with IHL; the question is whether compliance is technically achievable and, if not, whether any level of human control is required as a legal prerequisite.

docs.title: 34.2.1 The Four Core Principles of IHL
docs.text: Four peremptory principles constrain all attacks under IHL:

docs.title: Principle of Distinction
docs.text:
Article 48 of AP I requires that parties to a conflict distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives. Only military objectives may be attacked. A combatant is a member of the armed forces of a party to a conflict (with exceptions for medical and religious personnel). A civilian is anyone who is not a combatant; civilians lose protection against direct attack only while and for such time as they directly participate in hostilities.

Formally, define the target space \(\mathcal{T}\) partitioned into lawful military targets \(\mathcal{M}\) and protected civilian objects \(\mathcal{C}\):

\[\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{M} \cup \mathcal{C}, \quad \mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{C} = \emptyset\tag{34.1}\]

An IHL-compliant engagement function \(f: \mathcal{S} \to \{0,1\}\) (where \(\mathcal{S}\) is the sensor observation space) must satisfy:

\[\Pr[f(s) = 1 \mid s \in \phi(\mathcal{C})] \leq \epsilon_c\tag{34.2}\]

where \(\phi: \mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{S}\) is the sensing function and \(\epsilon_c\) is the maximum permissible false-positive rate for civilian targets. IHL provides no explicit numerical value for \(\epsilon_c\); it is determined by the proportionality assessment (Section 34.6). The practical challenge is that \(\phi\) is noisy, \(\mathcal{C}\) is dynamic and context-dependent, and the boundary between \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) shifts continuously during urban combat.

docs.title: Principle of Proportionality
docs.text: Article 51(5)(b) AP I prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian casualties or damage to civilian objects that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle requires a comparison of incommensurable values—human life against military gain—a comparison that some philosophers argue cannot be reduced to an algorithmic computation (see Section 34.6).

docs.title: Principle of Precaution
docs.text:
