Article 57 AP I requires attackers to take all feasible precautions to minimise civilian harm. Precautionary obligations include:

  • Verify that the target is a military objective.

  • Choose means and methods of attack expected to minimise civilian casualties.

  • Give effective advance warning to civilians when circumstances permit.

  • Cancel or suspend an attack if it becomes apparent that the target is civilian or that incidental casualties would be excessive.

The duty to cancel or suspend an attack in real time is particularly challenging for autonomous systems. Once a terminal-phase autonomous weapon has committed to an engagement, whether it possesses sufficient sensor resolution and processing capability to detect and respond to a civilian appearing in the engagement zone is an engineering—and legal—question.

docs.title: Principle of Military Necessity
docs.text: Military necessity permits only such force as is actually necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective. It prohibits destruction and injury beyond what is required for military success. This principle interacts with proportionality: even a small military advantage does not justify large civilian casualties, but a proportionate attack against a legitimate target is permissible even if it results in collateral civilian harm.

docs.title: 34.2.2 Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols
docs.text:
The four Geneva Conventions (GC I–IV, 1949) primarily protect the wounded, sick, shipwrecked, prisoners of war, and civilians in occupied territory. Additional Protocol I (1977) extends protections and codifies the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution for international armed conflicts. Additional Protocol II (1977) extends protections in non-international armed conflicts. 174 states are parties to the Additional Protocols; notable non-signatories to AP I include the United States and Israel.

Article 36 of AP I imposes a weapons review obligation: states must determine whether new weapons, means, or methods of warfare are prohibited by IHL. This review obligation applies to all new weapons, including software-defined or AI-enabled systems, and is the primary legal mechanism through which LAWS should be assessed.

docs.title: 34.2.3 Command Responsibility and the Accountability Gap
docs.text:
IHL establishes both individual criminal responsibility (the Nuremberg principle) and command responsibility (Article 86–87 AP I; Yamashita standard). Command responsibility holds a superior responsible for crimes committed by subordinates if:

  1. The superior knew or had reason to know the subordinate was about to commit or had committed an offence.

  2. The superior failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish.

When a LAWS commits what would constitute a war crime—attacking a civilian, disproportionate harm—the accountability gap arises: the machine cannot be prosecuted, the operator may be geographically and temporally remote, the programmer wrote code at a prior time, and the commander authorised a class of engagements without knowledge of each individual act.

Table 34.2. Accountability Gap Analysis for LAWS War Crimes Actor Potential Liability Basis Defence / Gap Mitigation Operator Command responsibility; direct participation May not have seen individual engagement; link severed by autonomy Require per-engagement authorisation Commander Superior responsibility; mission authorisation Authorised engagement envelope, not specific target Restrict engagement envelope Programmer Negligence; product liability (civil) Wrote code years before; could not foresee specific incident Rigorous safety cases; documentation State State responsibility under international law Cannot be criminally prosecuted; sanctions possible Treaty obligations; domestic law Machine None in current legal framework No legal personhood; cannot be deterred N/A

Legal scholars including Sassòli (2014) and Roff (2016) conclude that in many plausible scenarios involving fully autonomous lethal decisions, no individual can be held legally responsible in a meaningful sense. This structural accountability gap is itself argued to violate the spirit of IHL, which depends on individual responsibility to deter violations.

docs.title: 34.2.4 ICRC Position and State Practice
docs.text:
The ICRC, in its 2021 position paper, called for:

  1. A prohibition on autonomous weapon systems that are designed or used to apply force against persons.

  2. A prohibition on autonomous weapon systems that cannot be used in accordance with IHL (e.g., because they cannot distinguish or assess proportionality).

  3. Positive requirements of human control over all other autonomous weapons, including the ability to deactivate.

State positions diverge significantly. Austria submitted a draft treaty calling for a prohibition, supported by approximately 50 states. The United States issued DoD Directive 3000.09 (updated 2023), which requires meaningful human judgment over the selection and engagement of targets and mandates senior DoD official approval for any waiver. Russia opposes binding regulation. China’s position— prohibit use, not development—is viewed by many as strategically inconsistent.

docs.title: 34.3.1 The CCW Framework
docs.text: The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), opened for signature 1980, prohibits or restricts the use of specific weapons deemed to cause unnecessary suffering or to strike indiscriminately. It operates through Protocols (mines, incendiary weapons, laser blinding weapons, explosive remnants of war) and through a process of diplomatic deliberation. The CCW meets in Geneva under UN auspices and requires consensus among High Contracting Parties for binding decisions.

docs.title: 34.3.2 Group of Governmental Experts
docs.text:
In 2014, the CCW established an informal Meeting of Experts on LAWS, elevated to a formal Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) in 2016. The GGE meets annually in Geneva and has produced three key documents:

  1. 2018 Possible Guiding Principles: Ten non-binding principles on LAWS, including that IHL applies fully; that human responsibility cannot be transferred to machines; and that a core element of human judgement must be retained.

  2. 2019 Guiding Principles: Eleven principles endorsed by the GGE, including that human accountability for decisions on LAWS must be retained; that new weapons must be reviewed under Article 36; and that a precautionary approach should be taken.

  3. 2021–2023 Working Papers: Detailed technical and legal analyses without consensus on binding measures.

docs.title: 34.3.3 The Deadlock Problem
docs.text:
The CCW operates by consensus. Any single High Contracting Party can block adoption of a new Protocol. The permanent members of the UN Security Council—particularly Russia, China, and to a lesser extent the United States and United Kingdom—have consistently blocked progress toward binding regulation. Russia has explicitly stated that a ban on LAWS would be premature and that existing IHL is sufficient.

This procedural constraint has led advocacy groups to propose alternative forums:

  • UN General Assembly: Can adopt resolutions (non-binding) and convene treaty conferences outside the CCW. The Ottawa Process on anti-personnel mines succeeded outside the CCW framework.

  • Standalone Treaty: Modelled on the Mine Ban Treaty (1997) or the Convention on Cluster Munitions (2008); negotiated among a coalition of willing states; does not require unanimity; major military powers likely would not join.

  • UNGA First Committee: Has passed resolutions on LAWS (A/RES/78/241, 2023) calling for the Secretary-General to seek state views; non-binding but signals emerging norm.

docs.title: 34.3.4 Draft Treaty Proposals
docs.text:
The Campaign to Stop Killer Robots has circulated draft treaty language calling for:

  • A prohibition on the development, production, and use of fully autonomous weapons.

  • A prohibition on any weapon that selects and attacks targets without meaningful human control.

  • Positive obligation to retain human control over the critical functions of selecting and attacking human targets.

Austria submitted formal draft elements to the CCW GGE in 2019 and 2022. As of 2025, no binding instrument has been agreed under the CCW framework.

docs.title: 34.4.1 Conceptual Dimensions
docs.text:
Meaningful Human Control (MHC) is the dominant concept in the current governance debate, yet it lacks a universally accepted definition. Proposed dimensions of MHC include:

  1. Target selection: A human must identify and designate the specific target.

  2. Engagement authorisation: A human must positively authorise the use of force against the designated target.

  3. Temporal control: The human must be able to halt the engagement up to and including the terminal phase.

  4. Spatial control: The engagement must occur within a geographically bounded area that the human has verified is appropriate.

  5. Force level: The human must set and verify the level of force employed.

  6. Contextual understanding: The human must have sufficient situational awareness to make an informed decision consistent with IHL.

Define a control adequacy function \(\Psi\):

\[\Psi = \sum_{i=1}^{6} w_i \cdot c_i\tag{34.3}\]

where \(w_i\) is the weight (importance) of control dimension \(i\) and \(c_i \in [0,1]\) is the degree of control exercised. MHC is satisfied when \(\Psi \geq \Psi_{\min}\), where \(\Psi_{\min}\) is the minimum legally and ethically required control threshold. No current international agreement specifies \(\Psi_{\min}\) or the weights \(w_i\).

docs.title: 34.4.2 Human-Machine Teaming and Cognitive Constraints
docs.text:
A central challenge is that the notional preservation of human oversight may not constitute meaningful control when the system operates at machine speed and scale. Consider an AI-enabled system that generates 100 targeting recommendations per minute. Even with a human operator nominally “in the loop”, each target receives on average 0.6 seconds of human attention—insufficient for meaningful judgement, IHL assessment, or informed decision-making.

The information-processing constraint can be formalised. Let \(\lambda\) be the target presentation rate (targets/second), \(T_h\) be the minimum human deliberation time per target (seconds), and \(N_o\) be the number of operators:

\[\lambda \cdot T_h \leq N_o\tag{34.4}\]

For \(\lambda = 2\) targets/s, \(T_h = 5\) s, and \(N_o = 1\): \(2 \times 5 = 10 \gg 1\). The system violates the cognitive constraint; human control is nominal, not meaningful.

Research in cognitive science (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010; Cummings, 2012) consistently finds that automation bias—the tendency to accept automated recommendations without critical evaluation—degrades decision quality precisely when operators are overloaded. A human rubber-stamping AI recommendations is not exercising meaningful control.

docs.title: 34.4.3 Technical Approaches to MHC by Design
docs.text:
Engineering approaches to preserving MHC include:

  1. Engagement Authorisation Interface: A positive physical action (e.g., two-key turn, biometric confirm) required before each engagement; prevents autonomous fire.

  2. Abort Capability: Hardware and software interrupt that the operator can trigger at any point; must operate on a communication link verified to be unjammable or with a fail-safe default (abort on comms loss).

  3. Engagement Envelope Constraints: Hard-coded geographic, temporal, and target-class constraints within which autonomous action is permitted; any target outside the envelope requires human override.

  4. Confidence Threshold Gates: The system only autonomously engages if its target classification confidence exceeds a high threshold \(\tau_c\) (e.g., \(\tau_c = 0.99\)); lower-confidence detections are queued for human review.

  5. Explainability Interface: The system presents to the operator not only its target recommendation but the evidence and reasoning supporting it, enabling informed review.

docs.title: 34.4.4 Article 36 Weapons Review
docs.text:
Article 36 of AP I imposes a legal obligation on all states party to review new weapons in their development, acquisition, or adoption. The review must determine whether the weapon is prohibited under IHL in all circumstances or in some circumstances. The United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and a small number of other states have established formal weapons review processes. The vast majority of states have not.

The Article 36 review of an AI-enabled weapon system raises novel challenges:

  • How do you certify the behaviour of a system whose behaviour emerges from trained parameters rather than explicit rules?

  • How do you test a system that may exhibit emergent behaviour not seen in training?

  • How do you review a system whose behaviour may adapt after deployment?

These questions highlight the need for new technical standards and legal frameworks tailored to AI-enabled weapons.

docs.title: 34.5.1 Computer Vision for Target Identification
docs.text:
Modern military target identification increasingly relies on deep neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures, applied to electro-optical (EO), infrared (IR), synthetic aperture radar (SAR), and hyperspectral imagery. The fundamental object of discrimination is to correctly classify each object in the sensor field as belonging to \(\mathcal{M}\) or \(\mathcal{C}\) (Equation (34.1)).

The performance of a binary classifier is characterised by the confusion matrix. Let:

  • \(\text{TP}\): True Positives — military targets correctly identified

  • \(\text{FP}\): False Positives — civilians misclassified as military targets (illegal engagement)

  • \(\text{TN}\): True Negatives — civilians correctly spared

  • \(\text{FN}\): False Negatives — military targets missed (operational failure)

Key performance metrics:

\[\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}}\tag{34.5}\] \[\text{Recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\tag{34.6}\] \[\text{False Positive Rate (FPR)} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}\tag{34.7}\]

From a legal and ethical perspective, minimising FPR—attacks on civilians—is paramount. There is an inherent precision-recall trade-off: as the confidence threshold \(\tau_c\) increases, FPR decreases but FN rate increases. For an autonomous weapon system, the legally required FPR is effectively zero; any systematic misclassification of civilians as military targets constitutes a fundamental IHL violation.

docs.title: 34.5.2 Training Data Bias
docs.text:
Deep learning models learn from training datasets. In military applications, training datasets typically comprise imagery of Western military equipment—US/NATO vehicles, uniforms, and equipment types—collected in controlled testing environments. Deployment in geographically and culturally different contexts introduces systematic bias:

  • A model trained on NATO military vehicles may fail to correctly classify Russian, Chinese, or non-state actor equipment.

  • A model trained on desert environments may perform poorly in dense urban jungle settings.

  • A model that never encountered a particular ambiguous scenario during training cannot generalise reliably to it.

  • Biased training data produces a model whose \(\text{FPR}\) is not uniformly distributed across target classes and environments.

Quantitatively, if the model’s decision boundary was trained on a distribution \(p_{\text{train}}\) and deployed on \(p_{\text{deploy}}\), the expected FPR on deployment:

\[\text{FPR}_{\text{deploy}} = \text{FPR}_{\text{train}} + \int_{\mathcal{X}} |p_{\text{deploy}}(x) - p_{\text{train}}(x)| \, \Delta \text{FPR}(x) \, dx\tag{34.8}\]

where \(\Delta \text{FPR}(x)\) is the local FPR change due to distribution shift. This integral will generally be non-zero for any realistic deployment outside the training domain.

docs.title: 34.5.3 Adversarial Examples and Deception
docs.text:
A profound vulnerability of deep neural network classifiers is their susceptibility to adversarial examples: inputs crafted with small, often imperceptible perturbations that cause the model to misclassify. Goodfellow et al. (2014) demonstrated that adding a small perturbation \(\delta\) to an image \(x\) can cause a high-confidence misclassification:

\[\arg\max_k f_k(x + \delta) \neq \arg\max_k f_k(x), \quad \|\delta\|_\infty \leq \epsilon\tag{34.9}\]

In the military context, this means:

  • An adversary can apply carefully designed paint patterns to vehicles, personnel, or structures to cause an autonomous weapon to misclassify them.

  • Printed patterns on clothing, termed adversarial camouflage, can cause a person to be classified as an inanimate object.

  • Adversarial stickers placed on an object can cause misclassification across a wide range of viewing angles and lighting conditions.

This creates both an attack vector (adversary deceives the autonomous weapon) and a defensive vulnerability (the autonomous weapon attacks deceived-to targets). The existence of adversarial examples fundamentally undermines reliance on neural network classifiers for legally consequential decisions in adversarial environments.

docs.title: 34.5.4 The “Direct Participation in Hostilities” Problem
docs.text:
IHL protects civilians except for such time as they take direct part in hostilities (DPH). The ICRC Interpretive Guidance on DPH (Melzer, 2009) specifies that DPH requires:

  1. A threshold of harm likely to result.

  2. Direct causal link between the act and the harm.

  3. Belligerent nexus—the act must be specifically designed to directly cause the harm.

An algorithm cannot assess belligerent nexus. DPH assessment requires understanding intent, context, role, and the specific act being performed—judgements that depend on situational awareness, cultural understanding, and contextual reasoning beyond current AI capabilities. A person carrying a weapon may be a soldier, a farmer, or a child in some regions; context determines the legal status. An AI system trained to associate weapon-carrying with combatant status will systematically misclassify civilians in such contexts.

docs.title: 34.6.1 Military Advantage and Collateral Damage
docs.text:
The proportionality rule (Section 34.2.1) requires balancing the anticipated military advantage against expected incidental civilian harm. Define:

\[P = \text{MA} - \lambda_c \cdot \text{CDE}\tag{34.10}\]

where \(\text{MA}\) is military advantage (measured in relevant military terms), \(\text{CDE}\) is the collateral damage estimate (number of civilians expected to be harmed), and \(\lambda_c\) is a weighting coefficient. An attack is proportionate if \(P \geq 0\), but IHL does not provide values for \(\lambda_c\) or units for \(\text{MA}\). The comparison is deliberated by a “reasonable military commander” applying military experience and moral judgment.

docs.title: 34.6.2 US Joint Targeting Methodology
docs.text:
The United States employs a six-step Collateral Damage Estimation (CDE) methodology defined in JP 3-60 (Joint Targeting) and implemented via the Bugsplat software system:

  1. Target characterisation: Identify target type, dimensions, construction.

  2. Weaponeering: Select munition type, fusing, delivery parameters to achieve required effects on target.

  3. Collateral damage radius calculation: Compute the distance from the aim point at which specific injury/damage probabilities fall below thresholds.

  4. Collateral object analysis: Identify civilian objects within the collateral damage radius.

  5. Collateral casualty estimate: Estimate civilians at risk based on time of day, population patterns, and shelter.

  6. Commander’s proportionality assessment: Commander weighs CDE against MA.

Steps 1–5 can, in principle, be automated with appropriate sensor data and databases. Step 6 is the human moral judgement that IHL arguably requires to be exercised by a human commander. Whether an algorithm can substitute for this judgement—given that MA and civilian life are incommensurable—is a fundamental ethical question examined in Section 34.9.

docs.title: 34.6.3 Automated Proportionality: Limitations
docs.text:
Several authors (Schmitt, 2013; Sassòli, 2014) argue that while an algorithm can compute a numerical proxy for proportionality, it cannot perform the genuine moral weighing IHL requires. Key limitations:

  • Incommensurability: Military advantage and human life are not on the same scale; no conversion factor is universally agreed.

  • Context dependence: The same military objective may have vastly different strategic value at different points in a conflict.

  • Uncertainty: Both MA and CDE are estimates with large uncertainties; a proportionality decision under deep uncertainty requires human judgment.

  • Dynamic change: A target may move; civilians may enter or leave the target area; the system may not be able to update its assessment in real time.

docs.title: 34.7 Cyber and Safety Risks of Autonomous Weapons
34.7.1 Attack Surfaces
docs.text:
An autonomous weapon system presents an expanded cyber attack surface compared to a crewed platform. Key vectors:

  1. Sensor spoofing: GPS spoofing, radar jamming, laser dazzling, or acoustic interference alters the system’s perception of its environment, causing misnavigation or misidentification.

  2. Data link compromise: If the system can receive target updates or software updates over a data link, an adversary who compromises the link can alter targeting parameters or inject malicious commands.

  3. Supply chain attack: Compromised hardware or firmware introduced at manufacture can create exploitable backdoors.

  4. Model poisoning: If the AI model was trained on adversary-influenced data, backdoor triggers can cause predictable misclassification.

  5. Physical interface exploitation: Maintenance access ports, JTAG, or recovery mode can be exploited during field maintenance.

docs.title: 34.7.2 Fail-Safe Design
docs.text:
For conventional safety-critical systems, failure mode analysis (FMEA) and fault tree analysis (FTA) guide the design of fail-safe behaviour. For an autonomous weapon, the fail-safe default must be non-lethal: a system that defaults to attacking on sensor failure is a fail-deadly design and is ethically and legally impermissible.

Define the system state \(S_k\) at time \(k\). The fail-safe condition is:

\[\forall S_k \in \mathcal{F}: \quad a(S_k) = a_{\text{safe}}\tag{34.11}\]

where \(\mathcal{F}\) is the set of fault states and \(a_{\text{safe}}\) is a safe action (abort mission, self-destruct in a pre-cleared area, return to base). This is straightforward to specify but difficult to guarantee: fault states include scenarios not anticipated at design time, software bugs, and adversarially-induced states.

docs.title: 34.7.3 Certification and Verification
docs.text:
Aviation software certification standard DO-178C (Software Considerations in Airborne Systems) defines rigorous processes for software verification and validation, including structural coverage requirements at four Design Assurance Levels (DAL A–D). DO-178C was designed for deterministic, rule-based software. Its applicability to learned neural network systems is fundamentally limited:

  • Structural coverage (MC/DC) is not defined for neural network weights.

  • The number of inputs to a neural network is effectively infinite; exhaustive testing is impossible.

  • A neural network’s decision boundary can change after retraining; re-certification would be required.

  • Emergent behaviours—capabilities not explicitly programmed—may arise from training but are not discoverable by conventional test methods.

EASA (European Union Aviation Safety Agency) has published AI Roadmap 2.0 (2023) and the USAF has proposed ML qualification guidelines, but as of 2025 no military-specific certification standard for AI-enabled weapons exists. The DARPA Assured Autonomy programme is developing formal verification approaches for safety-critical autonomous systems using Lyapunov-based neural network verification and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers.

Table 34.3. Comparison of Safety Certification Approaches for Autonomous Weapons Approach Applicability to AI Limitations Status DO-178C Partial — process requirements applicable No neural network coverage criteria; deterministic assumption Adapted for UAV avionics; not AI targeting IEEE P7009 (Fail-safe AI) Directly applicable Standard still in development Draft under revision DARPA Assured Autonomy High — designed for ML Limited to reachability properties; scalability issues Active research programme ISO/IEC 42001 (AI Management) Process/governance only Does not address technical weapon behaviour Published 2023; adoption beginning Formal verification (SMT/model checking) Applicable to small networks Does not scale to large CNNs; state space explosion Research stage

docs.title: 34.7.4 Emergent Behaviour and Testing Limitations
docs.text:
AI systems, particularly those trained with reinforcement learning, can exhibit emergent behaviours— strategies and capabilities that were not explicitly designed and may not have appeared in testing. In the context of weapons, emergent behaviour is a safety risk of the first order. OpenAI’s work on hide-and-seek agents (Baker et al., 2020) demonstrated that RL agents develop unexpected strategies that exploit environment physics. A weapon trained to maximise target destruction with minimum exposure may develop strategies that violate rules of engagement in unexpected ways.

The coverage problem is fundamental: a neural network with \(n\) parameters has a decision boundary of dimension \(n - 1\) embedded in \(n\)-dimensional space. Even \(10^9\) test cases do not provide meaningful coverage of a space with \(n = 10^6\) parameters. The formal notion of neural network verification—proving that no input within a perturbation ball \(\|x - x_0\|_\infty \leq \epsilon\) causes a misclassification—is NP-hard in general (Katz et al., 2017).

docs.title: 34.8.1 Project Maven: Machine Learning for Drone Surveillance
docs.text:
Project Maven (officially the Algorithmic Warfare Cross-Functional Team) was established by the US Department of Defense in April 2017 to accelerate the fielding of AI capabilities. Its initial application was object recognition in drone video footage: automatically detecting and labelling vehicles, people, and buildings in full-motion video (FMV) from MQ-1/MQ-9 platforms.

In 2017, Google won a contract to provide TensorFlow-based object recognition capabilities for Project Maven. In March 2018, The Intercept published details of the contract; within weeks, over 4,000 Google employees signed an internal petition objecting to participation in “warfare technology.” Twelve employees resigned. In June 2018, Google declined to renew the contract upon its expiry and published its AI Principles, which excluded weapons applications.

Lessons: (1) Technology workers consider themselves ethical stakeholders in downstream uses of their work. (2) Corporate decisions on AI and weapons applications occur in a public arena and have reputational consequences. (3) The boundary between civilian AI research and military AI application is functionally non-existent in dual-use technologies.

docs.title: 34.8.2 STM Kargu-2: Autonomous Engagement in Libya
docs.text:
The Kargu-2 is a Turkish-manufactured rotary-wing loitering munition produced by STM (Savunma Teknolojileri Mühendislik). It is equipped with computer vision for autonomous target identification and, according to the manufacturer, can operate in an autonomous engagement mode. A March 2021 UN Panel of Experts report on Libya (S/2021/229) stated:

“The logistics convoy and the Haftar Affiliated Forces (HAF) were subsequently hunted down and remotely engaged by the lethal autonomous weapons systems such as the lethal autonomous weapons systems Kargu-2 and other loitering munitions.”

This is the first documented probable use of a LAWS with autonomous engagement capability against human targets in an armed conflict. Subsequent analysis disputed whether the autonomous mode was actually used; the manufacturer disputed the Panel’s characterisation. The episode illustrates the governance gap: an autonomous lethal engagement may occur before any international rules are in place to prohibit or regulate it.

docs.title: 34.8.3 Samsung SGR-A1: Autonomous Sentry in the DMZ
docs.text:
The SGR-A1 is a stationary sentry robot deployed by the Republic of Korea Army in the demilitarized zone (DMZ) with North Korea. It is equipped with a day/night camera, pattern recognition for intruder detection, a loudspeaker for voice challenges, and a 5.56 mm rifle and 40 mm grenade launcher. It reportedly has an autonomous engagement mode in which it can detect and fire on targets without human authorisation; the South Korean Ministry of Defence has stated that human authorisation is required for lethal engagement.

The SGR-A1 illustrates the human-on-loop configuration: the system autonomously tracks and aims; a human operator can observe and must (in principle) authorise fire. The practical reliability of this human override, under conditions of battlefield stress, communication latency, and alert fatigue, is not publicly documented.

docs.title: 34.8.4 IAI Harpy: Autonomous Anti-Radiation Munition
docs.text:
The Harpy, produced by Israel Aerospace Industries, is a loitering munition specifically designed to detect and destroy radar emitters. Launched from a ground vehicle or aircraft, it autonomously patrols a designated area, detects radar emissions, homes on the emitter, and dives to destroy it—all without any per-engagement human authorisation after launch. The Harpy has been operational since the 1990s and exported to multiple states.

The Harpy represents a narrow but clearly autonomous engagement capability: the target class (radar emitter) and discriminating characteristic (specific emissions) are well-defined and technically assessable, making false-positive engagement of a civilian radar plausible if civilian and military radar emissions overlap in frequency and waveform.

docs.title: 34.8.5 US DoD Directive 3000.09
docs.text:
DoD Directive 3000.09, “Autonomy in Weapon Systems” (originally 2012, updated 2023), is the primary US policy instrument governing autonomous weapons. Key provisions:

  • Requires that autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems shall be designed to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgement over the use of force.

  • Requires that such systems shall only engage targets in accordance with mission parameters, ROE, LOAC, and commander’s intent.

  • Requires USD(P) approval for any program of record that intends to use full autonomy in the lethal selection and engagement of targets.

  • Establishes a Senior Designated Official review process.

The Directive does not define “meaningful human control” numerically or specify technical requirements. Critics note that the approval process provides an exception mechanism while nominally maintaining the policy.

docs.title: 34.9.1 Just War Theory
docs.text:
The Just War Tradition, deriving from Augustine and Aquinas and developed in modern form by Michael Walzer (Just and Unjust Wars, 1977), provides the moral framework underlying IHL. It comprises two components:

  • Jus ad bellum: The justice of going to war—requires just cause, right intention, legitimate authority, last resort, probability of success, and proportionality.

  • Jus in bello: Justice in the conduct of war—requires discrimination and proportionality in all attacks, regardless of the justice of the war itself.

LAWS do not alter jus ad bellum directly, but critics argue they lower the threshold for resort to force by reducing the human cost to the attacking side. A state that can conduct warfare without risking the lives of its own soldiers may be more willing to initiate conflict, undermining the deterrent effect of mutual vulnerability. This is the “risk transfer” objection.

docs.title: 34.9.2 Consequentialist Analysis
docs.text:
Consequentialist ethics judges actions by their outcomes. The consequentialist case for LAWS:

  • If LAWS are more precise than human combatants, they may cause fewer civilian casualties.

  • If LAWS do not experience fear, anger, revenge, or peer pressure, they may make more consistent decisions than stressed human soldiers.

  • If LAWS reduce friendly casualties, states may be willing to engage in fewer wars of attrition.

Counter-arguments:

  • Precision claims are unproven in real adversarial environments (see Section 34.5).

  • Reducing the cost of war for one side may increase its frequency.

  • Consequentialist calculations do not capture the moral significance of the act of killing.

docs.title: 34.9.3 Deontological Analysis
docs.text:
Kantian deontological ethics holds that some acts are intrinsically right or wrong, regardless of their consequences. The deontological case against LAWS rests on:

  • Human dignity: The decision to take a human life must be made by a moral agent capable of recognising the victim’s humanity. A machine cannot recognise or respect human dignity.

  • Categorical Imperative: “Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” Universal deployment of LAWS would create a world in which machines routinely kill humans without moral agency—universalisably impermissible.

  • Treating persons as ends: Kant requires we treat persons as ends in themselves, never merely as means. A machine that kills a person treats that person purely as a means—a military obstacle—without any recognition of their humanity.

docs.title: 34.9.4 Virtue Ethics
docs.text:
Virtue ethics, following Aristotle, evaluates actions by the character traits (virtues) they express. Warfare, even in the just war tradition, requires the exercise of virtues: courage (facing personal risk to achieve a just objective), practical wisdom (phronesis—discerning the right action in complex circumstances), and justice (treating enemies with appropriate respect for their humanity, including permitting surrender).

A machine cannot possess virtues; it can only simulate behavioural outputs associated with virtuous action. The soldier who spares an enemy combatant who throws down his weapon acts virtuously; a machine programmed to spare surrendering combatants only simulates the outcome, not the virtue. Shannon Vallor (2016) argues that technologies that replace virtue with automation degrade moral agency at the civilisational level.

docs.title: 34.9.5 Engineering Ethics
docs.text:
The IEEE Code of Ethics requires engineers to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. The NSPE Code of Ethics states that engineers shall hold public safety, health, and welfare paramount and shall notify appropriate authorities if their professional judgment is overruled in a matter involving public safety.

The dual-use dilemma is acute in autonomous weapons engineering: the same computer vision, reinforcement learning, and robotics capabilities developed for civilian autonomous vehicles, medical imaging, and industrial automation are directly applicable to autonomous weapons. An engineer who develops object recognition software cannot fully control its downstream military application.

Table 34.4. Summary of Ethical Framework Positions on LAWS Framework Key Criterion Position on LAWS Key Objection Consequentialism Outcomes: minimise harm Potentially permissible if more precise Precision unproven; lowers threshold for war Deontology Intrinsic rightness; human dignity Impermissible — machine cannot respect human dignity Overly absolute; ignores empirical outcomes Just War Theory Discrimination, proportionality Permissible only if IHL compliance demonstrated IHL compliance technically unachievable Virtue Ethics Character; moral agency Impermissible — machine cannot possess virtues Not all killing requires virtue Engineering Ethics Public safety paramount Duty to refuse participation in LAWS without safety proof Collective action problem

docs.title: 34.10.1 Tiered Regulatory Approach
docs.text:
Given the deadlock in the CCW and the diversity of state positions, a tiered approach—regulating different categories of LAWS differently—may achieve broader agreement:

  • Tier 1 — Absolute prohibition: Autonomous weapon systems designed or used to apply lethal force against human beings without positive human authorisation for each engagement.

  • Tier 2 — Restricted use: Autonomous countermeasures against inanimate military objects (radar, vehicles), permitted within defined engagement envelopes and subject to Article 36 review.

  • Tier 3 — Regulated autonomy: Autonomous flight, navigation, and sensor processing permitted without restriction; lethal force decisions require human authorisation.

  • Tier 4 — Defensive systems: Automated defensive systems (CIWS against incoming missiles) not requiring per-engagement authorisation, given the speed constraints of defensive response.

docs.title: 34.10.2 Article 36 Implementation
docs.text:
States should implement Article 36 weapons review processes specifically adapted to AI-enabled systems. A minimum review process for an AI weapon should include:

  1. Documented training data provenance and bias assessment.

  2. Statistical characterisation of FPR across all anticipated deployment contexts.

  3. Adversarial robustness testing under realistic conditions.

  4. Fail-safe behaviour verification.

  5. Red-team assessment of emergent behaviour.

  6. Legal review of proportionality computation methods.

  7. Commander’s operational judgment on adequacy of MHC.

docs.title: 34.10.3 Technical Standards
docs.text:
Several technical standards initiatives are directly relevant:

  • IEEE P7009: Standard for Fail-Safe Design of Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems; requires that autonomous systems default to a safe state on failure.

  • ISO/IEC 42001: AI Management System standard; provides a governance framework for responsible AI development.

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Identifies and mitigates AI risks including harmful outcomes; adaptable to military context.

  • STANAG 4671: NATO airworthiness certification for unmanned aircraft systems; basis for extending to autonomy.

docs.title: 34.10.4 International Treaty Pathways
docs.text:
The Ottawa Process on anti-personnel landmines (1996–1997) succeeded in creating a binding prohibition treaty outside the CCW framework in 14 months, driven by a coalition of middle powers and civil society. A similar process for LAWS could:

  1. Draft treaty text with clear, technically precise definitions.

  2. Circulate among states committed to a prohibition or strong regulation.

  3. Convene a diplomatic conference outside the CCW.

  4. Open the treaty for signature with a practical entry-into-force threshold.

The treaty would not bind the United States, Russia, or China in the short term, but would establish a norm and create reputational costs for non-compliance, as the Mine Ban Treaty has done.

docs.title: 34.10.5 Confidence Building Measures
docs.text:
Short of a binding treaty, confidence building measures (CBMs) can reduce risks:

  • Transparency reports: Annual publication of states’ LAWS policy, weapons under development, and Article 36 review processes.

  • Notification mechanisms: Pre-notification of autonomous weapon deployment zones and engagement envelopes, similar to military exercise notifications.

  • Incident reporting: Agreed mechanism for reporting autonomous weapon malfunctions or unintended engagements.

  • Shared testing standards: Agreement on technical benchmarks for IHL compliance testing of AI targeting systems.

docs.title: 34.10.6 Research Priorities
docs.text:
The governance debate depends on resolving technical questions that are open research problems:

  1. Explainable AI for targeting: Systems that can articulate their target classification reasoning in human-understandable terms, enabling meaningful operator review.

  2. Formal verification of neural networks: Scalable methods for proving safety properties of large neural networks.

  3. Out-of-distribution detection: Reliable detection when an input is outside the training distribution, triggering a default to human control.

  4. Robust adversarial defences: Certifiably robust classifiers with proven resistance to adversarial perturbations.

  5. Human-AI teaming optimisation: Cognitive engineering of interfaces that enable genuine—not nominal—human oversight at operationally relevant timescales.

Define the out-of-distribution (OOD) detection problem formally. Given training distribution \(p_{\text{train}}\) and input \(x\), an OOD detector \(D\) should satisfy:

\[D(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } p_{\text{train}}(x) < \delta_{\text{ood}} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\tag{34.12}\]

where \(\delta_{\text{ood}}\) is the OOD threshold. On detection (\(D(x)=1\)), the system should route the decision to a human operator rather than act autonomously. Current OOD detection methods (energy-based, Mahalanobis distance, deep ensembles) have false negative rates that are operationally unacceptable for high-stakes decisions.

docs.title: 34.11 Summary and Conclusions
docs.text:
The development of lethal autonomous weapon systems poses challenges that span engineering, law, ethics, and governance in ways that existing frameworks are not fully equipped to address. The following conclusions emerge from the analysis in this chapter:

  1. Technical compliance with IHL is not currently demonstrated. No known AI system has been validated to perform target discrimination, proportionality assessment, and precautionary verification at the level IHL requires, in an adversarial environment with distribution shift, adversarial examples, and dynamic civilian presence.

  2. The accountability gap is real and unresolved. The existing framework of individual criminal responsibility and command responsibility does not map cleanly onto the diffuse, distributed responsibility structure of autonomous weapon systems.

  3. Meaningful human control is technically achievable in principle but requires deliberate design. Systems can be designed with per-engagement authorisation requirements, abort capabilities, and engagement envelope constraints that preserve genuine human oversight. Whether operational requirements permit this depends on the specific context.

  4. The CCW process is deadlocked. Progress toward binding international regulation requires either a breakthrough in the CCW or an Ottawa-process alternative. Civil society, middle-power states, and the ICRC are the most likely drivers of treaty progress.

  5. Technical standards are needed urgently. Article 36 review processes must be updated for AI-enabled weapons; international technical standards for AI weapon safety certification are a prerequisite for both governance and responsible development.

  6. The ethical objections to LAWS are not merely sentimental. Deontological, virtue-ethical, and dignity-based arguments identify structural problems—the accountability gap, the impossibility of machine moral agency—that cannot be dismissed as technological conservatism.

The engineer working on drone or missile systems in the twenty-first century is, whether consciously or not, a participant in these debates. The professional obligation to hold public safety paramount requires active engagement with these questions, not mere deference to policy and procurement decisions.

Table 34.5. Key Formal Definitions and Equations in Autonomous Weapons Ethics Concept Equation Description Target partition \(\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{M} \cup \mathcal{C}\), \(\mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{C} = \emptyset\) Lawful vs. protected targets Distinction constraint \(\Pr[f(s)=1 \mid s \in \phi(\mathcal{C})] \leq \epsilon_c\) Max false positive rate on civilians MHC adequacy \(\Psi = \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i c_i \geq \Psi_{\min}\) Meaningful human control threshold Cognitive constraint \(\lambda \cdot T_h \leq N_o\) Operator bandwidth for LAWS oversight Proportionality \(P = \text{MA} - \lambda_c \cdot \text{CDE} \geq 0\) Attack permissible if proportionate Fail-safe condition \(\forall S_k \in \mathcal{F}: a(S_k) = a_{\text{safe}}\) Safe action in all fault states OOD detection \(D(x) = \mathbf{1}[p_{\text{train}}(x) < \delta_{\text{ood}}]\) Route OOD inputs to human

docs.title: 35.1 Advanced Propulsion Technologies
docs.text: Propulsion is the single greatest constraint on the performance, range, and endurance of unmanned and autonomous weapon systems. Current state-of-the-art propulsion technologies are mature and approaching fundamental thermodynamic and electrochemical limits. The technologies described in this section—some near-term, some speculative—represent the trajectories most likely to reshape the performance envelope of future drone and missile systems in the 2025–2045 horizon.

docs.title: Solid-State Batteries
docs.text:
Conventional lithium-ion batteries use a liquid electrolyte, which imposes thermal management requirements, limits voltage windows, and presents flammability risks. Solid-state batteries (SSBs) replace the liquid electrolyte with a solid ionic conductor. The two principal solid electrolyte chemistries for aerospace applications are:

  • LLZO (Li\(_7\)La\(_3\)Zr\(_2\)O\(_{12}\), Garnet-type): ionic conductivity \(\sigma_{\text{Li}} \approx 10^{-3}\) S/cm at 25° C; electrochemically stable against lithium metal; wide voltage window (0–6 V vs. Li/Li\(^+\)).

  • LiPON (Lithium Phosphorus Oxynitride): thin-film electrolyte; \(\sigma_{\text{Li}} \approx 10^{-6}\) S/cm; used in thin-film microbatteries; suitable for MEMS-scale systems.

The energy density of a solid-state cell at the pack level is projected to reach 400–500 Wh/kg by 2027–2030, compared to approximately 250–280 Wh/kg for current Li-ion packs. The fundamental electrochemical constraint on cathode-limited cells is:

\[E_{\text{pack}} = \frac{n F \Delta V \cdot m_{\text{active}}}{M_{\text{cathode}} \cdot (1 + r_{\text{overhead}})}\tag{35.1}\]

where \(n\) is the charge transfer per formula unit, \(F\) is the Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol), \(\Delta V\) is the cell voltage, \(m_{\text{active}}\) is the active cathode mass, \(M_{\text{cathode}}\) is the molar mass, and \(r_{\text{overhead}}\) is the mass ratio of packaging and non-active components. SSBs reduce \(r_{\text{overhead}}\) by eliminating liquid management and thermal management systems.

Military applications: MALE/HALE UAV endurance extension; loitering munition extended loiter time; electric propulsion for micro-UAV swarms. The challenge for military adoption is manufacturing scalability, cycle life at wide temperature extremes (\(-40\)° C to \(+70\)° C operational), and mechanical integrity under vibration and shock loads.

docs.title: Lithium-Sulphur Batteries
docs.text:
Lithium-sulphur (Li-S) chemistry offers a theoretical specific energy of 2600 Wh/kg (vs. 387 Wh/kg theoretical for Li-ion). The practical pack-level projection is 500+ Wh/kg by 2028–2032. The theoretical cell voltage is:

\[E_{\text{cell}} = \frac{\Delta G_{\text{rxn}}}{n F} = \frac{-418 \text{ kJ/mol}}{2 \times 96485} \approx 2.15 \text{ V}\tag{35.2}\]

The fundamental challenge is the polysulphide shuttle: lithium polysulphides (Li\(_2\)S\(_x\), \(4 \leq x \leq 8\)) formed during discharge dissolve in the electrolyte, migrate to the lithium anode, and react destructively, causing capacity fade:

\[\text{Li}_2\text{S}_8 \xrightarrow{\text{reduction}} \text{Li}_2\text{S}_4 \xrightarrow{} \text{Li}_2\text{S}_2 \xrightarrow{} \text{Li}_2\text{S}\tag{35.3}\]

Commercial developers include Lyten (San Jose, USA), which uses 3D graphene cathode scaffolding to confine polysulphides; and the now-acquired Oxis Energy (UK), which demonstrated 470 Wh/kg at the cell level before its 2021 insolvency. Military-oriented development is active in the US AFRL and UK DSTL.

docs.title: Hydrogen Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells
docs.text:
Hydrogen PEM fuel cells have a theoretical specific energy exceeding 33,000 Wh/kg for pure hydrogen (lower heating value). At the system level, including compressed or cryogenic hydrogen storage, a complete PEMFC propulsion system can achieve 1,000–2,000 Wh/kg—roughly 4\(\times\) current Li-ion. The reversible cell voltage for the hydrogen-oxygen reaction is:

\[E_{\text{rev}} = \frac{\Delta G_f^{\circ}(\text{H}_2\text{O})}{n F} = \frac{237.1 \text{ kJ/mol}}{2 \times 96485} = 1.229 \text{ V}\tag{35.4}\]

Actual cell voltage under load:

\[V_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{rev}} - \eta_{\text{act}} - \eta_{\text{ohm}} - \eta_{\text{conc}}\tag{35.5}\]

where \(\eta_{\text{act}}\) is activation overpotential (kinetic losses), \(\eta_{\text{ohm}}\) is ohmic losses (membrane resistance), and \(\eta_{\text{conc}}\) is concentration losses at high current densities. Practical cell voltages of 0.6–0.7 V at rated power give stack efficiencies of 50–60%.

Military logistics challenges include hydrogen storage (700 bar compressed or cryogenic), ground infrastructure, and refuelling under field conditions. Boeing’s Phantom Eye HALE demonstrator used liquid hydrogen; the UK Rapid Capabilities Office has demonstrated PEMFC-powered micro-UAVs under Project Herius.

docs.title: 35.1.2 Rotating Detonation Engine
docs.text:
The rotating detonation engine (RDE) operates on a fundamentally different thermodynamic cycle from the constant-pressure Brayton cycle used in gas turbines. In an RDE, a continuous detonation wave rotates azimuthally around an annular combustion chamber, detonating fuel-oxidiser mixture continuously. The Fickett-Jacobs (detonation) cycle has a thermodynamic efficiency:

\[\eta_{\text{FJ}} = 1 - \frac{T_1}{T_{\text{CJ}}} \cdot \frac{\gamma R}{\Delta h_f^0 / M}\tag{35.6}\]

where \(T_{\text{CJ}}\) is the Chapman-Jouguet detonation temperature, \(T_1\) is the initial temperature, \(\gamma\) is the ratio of specific heats, and \(\Delta h_f^0 / M\) is the fuel’s mass heat of detonation. The detonation cycle achieves a pressure gain of 15–25 atm across the combustion zone versus effectively zero pressure gain in deflagrative combustion, yielding a projected thermodynamic efficiency advantage of 10–15% over equivalent gas turbine cycles.

The US Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and Rotating Detonation Engine Turbine Integration Project (RDET) have demonstrated RDE operation integrated with turbines. Key engineering challenges include: managing back-pressure to prevent detonation wave propagation upstream into fuel manifolds; multi-wave instability; and combustor material survivability under the intense thermal cycling of continuous detonation.

docs.title: 35.1.3 Nuclear Thermal Propulsion
docs.text:
Nuclear thermal propulsion (NTP) heats a propellant (typically liquid hydrogen) by passing it through or around a nuclear reactor core, then expands it through a nozzle. No combustion occurs; the energy source is fission. The specific impulse:

\[I_{sp}^{\text{NTP}} = \frac{1}{g_0} \sqrt{\frac{2 \gamma R_u T_c}{(\gamma - 1) M_p}}\tag{35.7}\]

where \(T_c\) is the reactor core temperature, \(M_p\) is the propellant molecular mass, \(R_u\) is the universal gas constant, and \(\gamma\) is the specific heat ratio. For hydrogen (\(M_p = 2\) g/mol) at \(T_c = 2700\) K, \(I_{sp} \approx 800\)–1,000 s—approximately twice that of the best chemical propellants. DARPA’s Demonstration Rocket for Agile Cislunar Operations (DRACO) programme (2021–present) is developing an NTP demonstrator. Treaty constraints (the Outer Space Treaty and CTBT interpretation) complicate atmospheric NTP use for offensive missiles; Russia’s SSC-X-9 Skyfall (9M730 Burevestnik) nuclear-powered cruise missile is the most prominent claimed operational NTP weapon.

docs.title: 35.1.4 Laser Propulsion
docs.text:
Ablative laser propulsion imparts momentum to a vehicle by focusing a high-power laser beam on a target material, ablating surface mass and generating thrust via the reaction force. The thrust-to-power ratio (specific impulse and momentum coupling coefficient) satisfies:

\[C_m = \frac{F}{P_{\text{laser}}} = \frac{I_{sp} g_0}{v_e}\tag{35.8}\]

where \(C_m\) is the momentum coupling coefficient (N/W), \(F\) is thrust, \(P_{\text{laser}}\) is laser power, and \(v_e\) is the effective exhaust velocity. Typical \(C_m \approx 10\)–100 \(\mu\)N/W, far below chemical propulsion efficiency. Ground-based laser propulsion is being investigated for low-cost microsatellite launch (ICAN laser project, Regensburg); military interest focuses on directed-energy launch of reconnaissance payloads from denied areas. Practical constraints include atmospheric turbulence, pointing accuracy, and laser power availability.

docs.title: 35.1.5 Distributed Electric Propulsion for HALE
docs.text:
Distributed electric propulsion (DEP) replaces a small number of large engines with many smaller electric motors driving propellers or fans distributed across the airframe. For a HALE UAV with wingspan \(b\) and \(N\) motors:

\[C_{L,\text{DEP}} = C_{L,\text{clean}} + \Delta C_L(q_{\text{slipstream}}, N, x_{\text{motor}})\tag{35.9}\]

where \(\Delta C_L\) is the lift increment from propeller slipstream energising the wing boundary layer. NASA’s X-57 Maxwell demonstrated a 5\(\times\) reduction in wing area for the same takeoff performance with DEP. For HALE platforms such as the Airbus Zephyr (solar-electric), DEP enables aeroelastic load management: individual motors can be throttled to reshape the lift distribution and reduce bending moments on the ultra-light flexible wing, extending structural fatigue life.

docs.title: 35.2.1 Ultra-High Temperature Ceramics
docs.text:
Ultra-high temperature ceramics (UHTCs) are a class of materials with melting points above 3000° C, essential for hypersonic vehicle leading edges and nosecones that experience aerothermal heating rates of \(10^3\)–\(10^5\) W/cm\(^2\). Key UHTCs include:

  • HfB\(_2\) (hafnium diboride): \(T_m = 3380\)° C; thermal conductivity \(k = 104\) W/mK; oxidation resistance enhanced by SiC addition.

  • ZrB\(_2\) (zirconium diboride): \(T_m = 3245\)° C; \(k = 60\) W/mK; less expensive than hafnium; used in ZrB\(_2\)-SiC composites.

  • HfC (hafnium carbide): \(T_m = 3900\)° C (highest of any known binary compound); low thermal conductivity; used as coating on C/C composites.

The critical thermal-mechanical design constraint for a UHTC leading edge of radius \(R\) and length \(L\) subject to stagnation heating \(\dot{q}_s\) is:

\[\dot{q}_s = \frac{k (T_s - T_c)}{R} + \epsilon \sigma T_s^4\tag{35.10}\]

where \(T_s\) is the surface temperature, \(T_c\) is the core temperature, \(\epsilon\) is emissivity, and \(\sigma\) is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The first term represents conductive heat rejection; the second, radiative cooling. At Mach 10, \(\dot{q}_s\) at a 1 mm leading edge radius can exceed \(5000\) W/cm\(^2\), requiring \(T_s > 2500\)° C and relying on high emissivity (\(\epsilon > 0.8\)) for radiative cooling. Current UHTC leading edges have demonstrated 1800–2500° C survival in arc-jet testing.

docs.title: 35.2.2 Carbon Nanotube Composites
docs.text:
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are cylindrical allotropes of carbon with sp\(^2\) bonding, diameters of 0.4–2 nm (single-wall, SWCNT) or 2–100 nm (multi-wall, MWCNT), and extraordinary mechanical properties. Young’s modulus \(E = 1\) TPa, tensile strength \(\sigma_{\text{UTS}} = 100+\) GPa (theoretical), and thermal conductivity \(k_{\text{axial}} > 3000\) W/mK along the tube axis.

Incorporation into carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) matrices can improve:

  • Interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) by 30–50% through improved matrix toughness.

  • Electrical conductivity for lightning strike protection (replacing copper mesh).

  • Electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding (surface density \(< 200\) g/m\(^2\)).

The key fabrication challenge is achieving aligned, well-dispersed CNT networks within the matrix without agglomeration. CNT forest growth by chemical vapour deposition (CVD), combined with transfer printing onto prepreg layers, achieves partial alignment but at industrial scales remains expensive. The specific strength advantage of CNT composite versus baseline CFRP:

\[\frac{\sigma_{\text{UTS}}}{\rho} \bigg|_{\text{CNT/CFRP}} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{UTS}}}{\rho} \bigg|_{\text{CFRP}} \cdot \left(1 + f_{\text{CNT}} \cdot \eta_l \cdot \eta_o \cdot \frac{E_{\text{CNT}}}{E_{\text{CFRP}}}\right)\tag{35.11}\]

where \(f_{\text{CNT}}\) is the CNT volume fraction, \(\eta_l\) is the length efficiency factor, and \(\eta_o\) is the orientation efficiency factor.

docs.title: 35.2.3 Graphene
docs.text:
Graphene is a single-atom-thick layer of sp\(^2\)-bonded carbon arranged in a hexagonal lattice. Its intrinsic properties: \(E \approx 1\) TPa; breaking strength \(\sigma \approx 130\) GPa; thermal conductivity \(\kappa \approx 5000\) W/mK; electrical conductivity \(\sigma_e \approx 10^8\) S/m; optical transmittance \(T = 97.7\%\); impermeability to all gases. Key aerospace and weapons applications:

  • EMI shielding: Few-layer graphene coatings at 1–10 nm thickness achieve EMI shielding efficiency of 20–30 dB; graphene foam achieves 90+ dB at 2 g/cm\(^3\).

  • Thermal interface materials: Graphene sheets between power electronics and heat sinks reduce junction temperature by 20–30° C.

  • Strain sensors: Graphene piezoresistive gauges; gauge factor \(GF > 1000\) vs. \(GF \approx 2\) for metallic strain gauges; structural health monitoring.

  • Transparent antenna substrates: Graphene transparent conducting electrode replacing ITO in conformal antenna arrays.

docs.title: 35.2.4 Shape Memory Alloys and Morphing Structures
docs.text:
Nickel-titanium (NiTi, Nitinol) shape memory alloys exhibit the shape memory effect (SME) and superelastic (pseudoelastic) behaviour. The transformation between the high-temperature austenite phase (B2 cubic) and the low-temperature martensite phase (B19’ monoclinic) is thermoelastic and reversible. The recoverable transformation strain:

\[\epsilon_{\text{recovery}} = \frac{\epsilon_{\text{martensite}} - \epsilon_{\text{austenite}}}{\epsilon_{\text{austenite}}} \leq 8\%\tag{35.12}\]

Morphing wing applications use NiTi wires or torque tubes as solid-state actuators that change shape when heated (electrically or by aerodynamic heat), replacing conventional hinged control surfaces. Benefits: no gaps (stealth), smooth surface (drag reduction), reduced radar cross-section (RCS). The University of Bristol MORPHLET programme demonstrated NiTi-actuated adaptive winglets on a UAV; DARPA’s MAS programme funded morphing wing SMA actuators for tactical missiles.

docs.title: 35.2.5 Electromagnetic Metamaterials
docs.text:
Metamaterials are engineered structures with periodically arranged sub-wavelength unit cells that produce effective electromagnetic (EM) permittivity \(\varepsilon_{\text{eff}}\) and permeability \(\mu_{\text{eff}}\) not found in natural materials, including negative values. The dispersion relation for a metamaterial:

\[k = \frac{\omega}{c} \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\text{eff}}(\omega) \cdot \mu_{\text{eff}}(\omega)}\tag{35.13}\]

When both \(\varepsilon_{\text{eff}} < 0\) and \(\mu_{\text{eff}} < 0\) simultaneously (double-negative medium), \(k\) is real but the phase velocity is anti-parallel to the group velocity—a “left-handed” medium. Applications in drones and missiles:

  • Perfect absorbers: Unit cells tuned to absorb specific radar frequencies; supplement or replace RAM coatings on stealth platforms.

  • Frequency selective surfaces (FSS): Bandpass or bandstop filter for EM waves; protects internal electronics from specific jamming frequencies.

  • Metasurface antennas: 2D metamaterial apertures; beam steering without mechanical gimbal; flat phased array with electronic reconfiguration.

docs.title: 35.2.6 Self-Healing Polymers
docs.text:
Self-healing polymer composites can autonomously repair damage—impact cracking, delamination, oxidation damage—without human intervention. Two principal mechanisms:

  1. Microencapsulation: Healing agent (e.g., dicyclopentadiene) encapsulated in micro-spheres (5–200 \(\mu\)m diameter) dispersed in the matrix. Crack propagation ruptures capsules; healing agent flows into crack and polymerises when it contacts the embedded catalyst (Grubbs’ catalyst). Achieves 75–90% fracture toughness recovery. Single-use per capsule location.

  2. Vascular network: Hollow microchannels (diameter 50–500 \(\mu\)m) embedded in the composite carry healing agent; resupplied from a reservoir. Multiple healing cycles possible.

For an aircraft structure subject to \(N\) fatigue cycles with crack density \(\rho_c\), the self-healing life extension factor \(\xi\) satisfies:

\[N_{\text{healed}} = N_{\text{baseline}} \cdot \xi(\rho_c, \eta_{\text{repair}})\tag{35.14}\]

where \(\eta_{\text{repair}} \in [0,1]\) is the healing efficiency. For UAV structures subject to operational damage from birds, debris, or fragments, self-healing composites could significantly extend service life without depot maintenance.

docs.title: 35.3.1 Quantum Inertial Navigation
docs.text:
Cold-atom interferometry uses laser-cooled atoms (typically \(^{87}\)Rb or \(^{133}\)Cs at temperatures of 1–100 nK) in an atom interferometer to measure acceleration and rotation with extraordinary precision. The phase shift in an atom interferometer:

\[\Delta \phi = \mathbf{k}_{\text{eff}} \cdot \mathbf{a} \cdot T^2\tag{35.15}\]

where \(\mathbf{k}_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective wavevector of the Raman laser pulses, \(\mathbf{a}\) is the acceleration to be measured, and \(T\) is the interrogation time between laser pulses. Accelerometer sensitivity scales as \(T^2\); for \(T = 1\) s, sensitivities approaching \(10^{-12}\) g are theoretically achievable—six orders of magnitude better than MEMS accelerometers.

Quantum INS would achieve navigation drift rates below 0.001 nautical miles per hour, providing GPS-level accuracy in GPS-denied environments. DARPA’s QUANTUM programme and UK DSTL’s cold-atom inertial sensor programme are developing miniaturised quantum sensors for platform integration. The primary engineering challenge is reducing the size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C) of the vacuum systems, laser systems, and magnetic shielding required.

docs.title: 35.3.2 Deep Reinforcement Learning for Guidance
docs.text:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) formulates guidance as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The state \(s_t\) includes the relative position and velocity of the interceptor and target; the action \(a_t\) is the commanded lateral acceleration; the reward \(r_t\) penalises miss distance and control effort:

\[r_t = -\left(\|\mathbf{r}_{\text{rel}}(T_f)\|^2 + \lambda_u \int_0^{T_f} \|a_t\|^2 \, dt\right)\tag{35.16}\]

The DRL agent maximises the expected return \(J = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T_f} \gamma^t r_t\right]\) using algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) or Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). DRL guidance laws have been demonstrated to outperform classical proportional navigation in non-linear evasive manoeuvre scenarios, generalising across target dynamics not seen during training. Key challenges: formal verification of safety properties; distribution shift in adversarial environments; training compute requirements.

docs.title: 35.3.3 Cognitive Electronic Warfare
docs.text:
Cognitive electronic warfare (CEW) systems sense the electromagnetic environment, learn the characteristics of specific emitters, and adaptively optimise jamming waveforms in real time. The CEW signal-processing chain:

\[\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{jam}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \; J(\mathbf{w}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \leq P_{\max}\tag{35.17}\]

where \(\mathbf{w}\) is the jamming waveform vector and \(J(\mathbf{w})\) is the jamming effectiveness metric (e.g., degradation of radar cross-correlation function, disruption of communications link). CEW systems can respond to adaptive radar waveforms and frequency-hopping communications in milliseconds—faster than human EWSO can act. US programmes include DARPA Behavioral Learning for Adaptive Electronic Warfare (BLADE) and the Navy COLDS programme.

docs.title: 35.3.4 Swarm Autonomy
docs.text:
Autonomous swarming extends drone-formation flight to emergent, decentralised coordination. Each agent \(i\) maintains local state \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and applies a control law derived from interactions with neighbours \(\mathcal{N}_i\). The canonical consensus-based flocking law (Reynolds, 1987; Olfati-Saber, 2006):

\[\mathbf{u}_i = -\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \nabla_{\mathbf{x}_i} V_{ij}(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|) + \mathbf{u}_{\text{mission},i}\tag{35.18}\]

where \(V_{ij}\) is the inter-agent potential function (repulsive at short range, attractive at medium range) and \(\mathbf{u}_{\text{mission},i}\) is the mission-directed component. Advanced swarm behaviours include:

  • Dynamic task reallocation on attrition: When agent \(j\) is lost, its assigned target is auctioned among surviving agents via a distributed contract net protocol.

  • Deceptive manoeuvre: Sub-swarms execute feint attacks to saturate point defences while the primary strike element approaches from a different vector.

  • Emergent coalition formation: Agents with complementary capabilities (ISR, EW, strike) self-organise into mission-optimised coalitions without central assignment.

docs.title: 35.4.1 Boost-Glide Vehicles
docs.text:
Hypersonic glide vehicles (HGVs) are released from a ballistic missile booster at altitudes of 40–100 km, then glide at Mach 5–20 in the upper atmosphere (20–60 km), manoeuvring to evade missile defence systems. The glide phase trajectory is governed by:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = \mathbf{g} + \frac{1}{\rho_{\text{veh}}} \left(\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{D}\right)\tag{35.19}\]

where \(\mathbf{L}\) and \(\mathbf{D}\) are the aerodynamic lift and drag per unit mass and \(\rho_{\text{veh}}\) is the vehicle density. The lift-to-drag ratio of current HGV designs is \(L/D \approx 2\)–4; range extension compared to a purely ballistic trajectory is a factor of 3–6. Deployed systems include China’s DF-17 (IRBM + HGV), Russia’s Avangard (ICBM-launched), and the US Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS, Navy) and Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (LRHW, Army).

docs.title: 35.4.2 Air-Breathing Hypersonic Cruise Missiles
docs.text:
Hypersonic cruise missiles (HCMs) maintain sustained air-breathing propulsion throughout cruise at Mach 5–8. The US HAWC (Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept), HASTE (Hypersonic Air-breathing Scramjet Testbed Engine), and the Russian 3M22 Tsirkon (claimed Mach 6–9) are examples.

The scramjet combustion efficiency at Mach 8 cruise altitude (30 km) is constrained by the residence time \(\tau_{\text{res}}\) in the combustor:

\[\tau_{\text{res}} = \frac{L_c}{v_{\text{flow}}} = \frac{L_c}{M \cdot a_\infty}\tag{35.20}\]

where \(L_c\) is combustor length, \(M\) is Mach number, and \(a_\infty\) is the freestream speed of sound. For \(M = 8\), \(a_\infty = 295\) m/s, and \(L_c = 1\) m: \(\tau_{\text{res}} \approx 0.4\) ms. Combustion of hydrocarbon fuel must be initiated and completed in this time—the fundamental challenge of scramjet combustion engineering.

docs.title: 35.4.3 Hypersonic Interception
docs.text:
Intercepting HGVs requires extended acquisition range, track continuity through manoeuvre, and an interceptor with divert capability for the glide phase. The SM-3 Block IIA (Aegis BMD) has demonstrated kill vehicle velocities sufficient for high-endoatmospheric intercept. The miss distance for a proportional navigation interceptor against a manoeuvring target:

\[\sigma_{\text{miss}} = \frac{a_T T_{go}^2}{2 N' (N'-1)}\tag{35.21}\]

where \(a_T\) is the target lateral acceleration, \(T_{go}\) is the time to go, and \(N'\) is the effective navigation ratio. For an HGV pulling \(5g\) lateral acceleration at \(T_{go} = 5\) s with \(N' = 4\): \(\sigma_{\text{miss}} \approx 39\) m—beyond the lethal radius of a hit-to-kill interceptor. Larger blast-fragmentation warheads or nuclear warheads are being studied for HGV interception; conventional hit-to-kill may require guidance accuracy of \(<\) 5 m.

docs.title: 35.5.1 High-Power Laser Weapon Systems
docs.text:
The US Navy’s HELIOS (High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance) system fields a 150+ kW class fibre laser weapon integrated with the Arleigh Burke DDG platform. The lethality of a HEL against an airborne target is characterised by the fluence \(H\) deposited:

\[H = \frac{P_{\text{laser}} \cdot t_{\text{dwell}}}{\pi \left(\frac{\lambda f}{D_{\text{tx}}}\right)^2} \cdot \eta_{\text{atm}}\tag{35.22}\]

where \(P_{\text{laser}}\) is the laser power, \(t_{\text{dwell}}\) is the dwell time on target, \(\lambda\) is wavelength, \(f\) is range, \(D_{\text{tx}}\) is the transmitter aperture, and \(\eta_{\text{atm}}\) is the atmospheric transmission. Thermal blooming—thermally-induced phase distortion of the beam by the heated air column—degrades \(\eta_{\text{atm}}\) at high power and long range. Adaptive optics (deformable mirror + wavefront sensor) corrects atmospheric distortion:

\[\phi_{\text{corrected}} = \phi_{\text{incident}} - \hat{\phi}_{\text{aberration}}\tag{35.23}\]

where \(\hat{\phi}_{\text{aberration}}\) is the estimated wavefront distortion from a Hartmann-Shack wavefront sensor. A 300 kW-class laser on a surface combatant, with a 60 cm aperture and effective adaptive optics, can achieve lethal fluence against low-flying cruise missiles and drone swarms at ranges of 4–8 km in good atmospheric conditions.

docs.title: 35.5.2 Gyrotron Microwave Weapons
docs.text:
The Active Denial System (ADS) uses a 95 GHz gyrotron microwave source to deposit energy in the skin to a depth of 0.4 mm, producing an intense burning sensation without permanent harm—a non-lethal area denial weapon. Gyrotrons generate millimetre-wave radiation through the electron-cyclotron maser instability in a magnetic field:

\[f_{\text{ECM}} = \frac{e B}{2 \pi m_e \gamma}\tag{35.24}\]

where \(B\) is the magnetic field strength, \(m_e\) is the electron mass, and \(\gamma\) is the relativistic Lorentz factor. Output powers of 100 kW to 1 MW CW at 95 GHz are achievable. High-power (HPM) variants at 2–4 GHz can couple energy into electronic systems, degrading or destroying electronic components at ranges of hundreds of metres—an anti-electronics, not anti-personnel, weapon.

docs.title: 35.5.3 Free Electron Laser
docs.text:
The free electron laser (FEL) uses a relativistic electron beam passing through an alternating magnetic field (undulator) to generate stimulated emission at a wavelength:

\[\lambda_{\text{FEL}} = \frac{\lambda_u}{2 \gamma^2} \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{2}\right)\tag{35.25}\]

where \(\lambda_u\) is the undulator period, \(\gamma\) is the beam Lorentz factor, and \(K = e B_0 \lambda_u / (2 \pi m_e c)\) is the undulator parameter. The FEL is uniquely tunable: by adjusting \(\gamma\) (beam energy) or \(\lambda_u\) (undulator gap), the output wavelength can be swept across a wide range. This enables optimising output wavelength to minimise atmospheric absorption (selecting an atmospheric transmission window) or to match the absorption spectrum of target materials. The US Navy ONR FEL programme demonstrated 14 kW average power; scaling to 100+ kW requires kilowatt-class electron beam sources and high-efficiency energy recovery.

docs.title: 35.6.1 Multi-Domain Autonomous Teams
docs.text:
Future operations will involve teams of unmanned systems across all physical domains: UAS (air), UGV (ground), UUV (undersea), USV (surface), and potentially on-orbit platforms. The coordination framework is Multi-Domain Operations (MDO), in which effects in one domain create exploitable opportunities in another. A heterogeneous UxS team tasked with maritime strike might operate:

  1. USV provides close-in ISR and designates targets.

  2. UUV positions covertly and deploys decoy torpedoes.

  3. UAS swarm saturates point defences.

  4. Loitering munitions prosecute designated targets.

Coordination requires a common operational picture (COP), shared data architecture (JADC2/CJADC2), and inter-domain communication. The US Department of Defense’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) initiative provides the architectural framework; individual service programmes (Project Convergence, Project Overmatch) are developing the enabling capabilities.

docs.title: 35.6.2 Loyal Wingman Concept
docs.text:
The loyal wingman is an uncrewed combat aircraft that operates in coordination with a crewed 6th-generation fighter, executing tasks allocated by the crewed aircraft to extend the crewed pilot’s reach and protect the crewed aircraft from risk. Current programmes:

  • MQ-28 Ghost Bat (Boeing Australia): Operational since 2023; AI-enabled mission management; modular payload bay; range 3700+ km.

  • XQ-58A Valkyrie (Kratos, USA): Low-cost attritable; 56-foot wingspan; Mach 0.85+; tested with F-22 and F-35 as crewed leader.

  • LANCA (BAE Systems, UK): Lightweight Affordable Novel Combat Aircraft; part of Tempest 6th-gen programme.

The human-machine interface for loyal wingman teaming must enable the crewed pilot to allocate tasks, monitor wingman status, and retask the wingman in seconds under high cognitive load. Cognitive engineering studies (Cummings, 2017; Boy, 2020) show that simple natural language or intent-based tasking interfaces outperform explicit menu-based allocation.

docs.title: 35.6.3 Urban Warfare Micro-Drones
docs.text:
Sub-100g quadrotor micro-drones capable of autonomous indoor navigation and engagement represent a qualitatively new challenge for security and armed conflict. These systems use:

  • Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) for GPS-denied indoor navigation.

  • Onboard neural processing (Nvidia Jetson Orin, Qualcomm Flight RB5) for real-time obstacle detection and tracking.

  • Shaped charge or Claymore-type fragmentation payloads of 1–5 g for personnel effects.

The “Slaughterbots” concept video (Future of Life Institute, 2017) dramatised the risk; the technology required is largely available commercially. Countermeasures include RF jamming (but VIO systems may not require RF), faraday cage buildings, and anti-drone shotguns or lasers.

docs.title: 35.7.1 Quantum Radar
docs.text:
Quantum radar exploits entangled photon pairs to illuminate targets with a noise-immune probe. The quantum illumination (QI) protocol (Lloyd, 2008; Tan et al., 2008) transmits one photon of an entangled pair (the signal) and retains the other (the idler) for joint measurement:

\[|\Psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_s}} \sum_{n=0}^{N_s-1} |n\rangle_s |n\rangle_i\tag{35.26}\]

The advantage over classical radar of the same transmitted power and bandwidth is:

\[\text{SNR}_{\text{QI}} = \frac{4 \kappa N_s N_B}{1} \gg \text{SNR}_{\text{classical}} = \frac{\kappa N_s}{N_B}\tag{35.27}\]

where \(\kappa\) is the reflectivity, \(N_s\) is the mean signal photon number, and \(N_B\) is the mean thermal noise photon number. Shapiro (MIT) showed a 6 dB SNR advantage in the highly noisy regime \(N_B \gg 1\)—the regime relevant to microwave radar. However, this advantage requires coherent joint measurement of signal and idler, which is technically extremely difficult at microwave frequencies. Current experimental demonstrations are at optical frequencies where quantum-optical tools exist; the microwave regime remains a research challenge.

docs.title: 35.7.2 Quantum Key Distribution
docs.text:
Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) uses quantum mechanical properties to establish an information-theoretically secure cryptographic key between two parties. The BB84 protocol (Bennett and Brassard, 1984) encodes key bits in the polarisation states of individual photons:

\[|\psi\rangle \in \{|H\rangle, |V\rangle, |+\rangle, |-\rangle\}\tag{35.28}\]

Any eavesdropper (Eve) must measure the quantum state to extract information, but the no-cloning theorem ensures that any measurement disturbs the state, introducing detectable errors. The security proof bounds the information Eve can gain:

\[I(A:E) \leq H(Q)\tag{35.29}\]

where \(I(A:E)\) is the mutual information between Alice’s key and Eve’s knowledge, \(H(Q)\) is the binary entropy of the observed error rate \(Q\), and security is guaranteed when \(Q < 11\%\) for BB84. Military applications include satellite QKD (China’s Micius satellite demonstrated QKD at 1200 km range in 2017), tactical fibre QKD for command posts, and drone-based QKD relay nodes.

docs.title: 35.7.3 Quantum Sensing for Submarine and Tunnel Detection
docs.text:
Quantum gravimeters based on atom interferometry measure the gravitational acceleration \(g\) with a sensitivity approaching \(\Delta g / g \approx 10^{-11}\) (state of the art: Bodart et al., 2010). Gravity gradiometry—measuring \(\partial^2 g / \partial x^2\)—can detect density anomalies corresponding to submarine hulls, underground tunnels, or buried ordnance from airborne or surface platforms. The resolution limit of a gravity gradiometer is:

\[\Delta \Gamma_{\min} = \frac{\hbar k_{\text{eff}} g}{m \sigma_v^2 T^2 \sqrt{N_{\text{atoms}}}}\tag{35.30}\]

where \(\sigma_v\) is the atomic velocity spread, \(T\) is the interrogation time, and \(N_{\text{atoms}}\) is the number of atoms per shot. A 100 kg airborne gravity gradiometer with 1000-atom ensembles and 1 s interrogation time could theoretically resolve a submarine at 100 m depth beneath the surface.
